To: "Kevin Walker (kwalker@PENNQUARTERPARTNERS.COM)" <kwalker@pennquarterpartners.com>




Derek Naten Sr. Director, Govt Affairs & Advocacy
202-459-4143 (office)

Begin forwarded message:


From: "Sciarra, Rhonda" <Rhonda.Sciarra@mallinckrodt.com>
Date: June 10, 2015 at 11:55:52 AM EDT
To: 'Stephanie Koze' <stephanie@greenroompr.com>, "Webb, Kevin J" <Kevin.Webb@mallinckrodt.com>
Cc: "Tyndall, Mark" <Mark.Tyndall@mallinckrodt.com>, "Long, Erika" <Erika.Long@mallinckrodt.com>, "Naten, Derek" <Derek.Naten@mallinckrodt.com>, "Gouveia, Staci" <Staci.Gouveia@mallinckrodt.com>, "Stauder, Nancy R" <Nancy.Stauder@mallinckrodt.com>
Subject: Mary Bono, CADCA CEO author Op-Ed in USA Today / When painkillers kill



Please see below for awareness.

 

http://www.usatoday.com/story/opinion/2015/06/10/painkillers-opioids-abuse-prevention-column/28466747/

 

When painkillers kill: Column

Mary Bono, Arthur T. Dean and Jeffrey Levi 9:36 a.m. EDT June 10, 2015

With opioid abuse and fatalities on the rise, it's time for a truly collaborative effort.

{635690197948435724-AX219-294A-9}

Students at Chad's Hope, a Christian drug addiction treatment center in Kentucky, pray before eating dinner. Kentucky sued Purdue Pharma, the makers of OxyContin, a few years ago for misrepresenting the addictiveness of its painkiller. 2015.(Photo: Luke Sharrett, Freelance)

 

The faces that represent today's opioid abuse epidemic are startling. So often, they are people with familiar stories of jobs, of families, of college or even of high school and the unbridled optimism of a life ahead. As this epidemic has spread throughout America, it's disturbing to note that {http://www.cdc.gov/drugoverdose/data/overdose.html} more Americans died in 2013 from a drug overdose than from any other form of injury. Half of these overdose deaths involved prescription drugs, just over two-thirds of which were opioids.

 

Thankfully, this situation is beginning to change.

 

The American public, media, and policymakers are learning about the true nature of this crisis. Earlier this spring, for example, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services launched a multi-faceted {http://www.hhs.gov/news/press/2015pres/03/20150326a.html} initiative to reduce deaths from prescription opioids and related substances. With a {http://www.cdc.gov/drugoverdose/data/index.html} quadrupling of fatalities related to this abuse between 1999 and 2013, these actions could not come soon enough.

 

A Complex Problem

Preventing abuse of prescription painkillers is a particularly challenging problem because the medicines that are {http://www.drugabuse.gov/drugs-abuse/prescription-drugs-cold-medicines} most widely abused are those that also help relieve pain and suffering for so many patients. They must remain accessible, for patients who need them and have been prescribed by a health care professional. Efforts to curb prescription drug abuse contrast sharply with campaigns to combat the misuse of other substances where any use is illegal and where zero tolerance is justifiable.

 

According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), nearly {http://www.cdc.gov/media/releases/2014/p0701-opioid-painkiller.html} 260 million prescriptions for opioids were written in 2012. This represents a significant {http://www.drugabuse.gov/about-nida/legislative-activities/testimony-to-congress/2014/americas-addiction-to-opioids-heroin-prescription-drug-abuse} increase over the previous two decades. Some of this trend has questionable clinical benefit. Inappropriate prescribing of opioids — intentional or unintentional — must be addressed through a combination of patient and provider education and enforcement actions against rogue actors.

 

This challenge also is partly about advancements in medicine that have resulted in {http://www.agencymeddirectors.wa.gov/Files/GuidelineMaster041615ForPubComment.pdf} more effective therapies to help people manage pain, the causes of which can stem from chronic illness, injuries, or other {http://www.researchgate.net/profile/Javad_Parvizi2/publication/51203945_Multimodal_pain_management_after_total_joint_arthroplasty/links/0deec53567418a0f06000000.pdf} medical procedures. In some cases, newer therapies help patients not only manage their pain, but allow for the restoration of function that can also allow them to live more fulfilling and active lives.Our response must encourage innovation in how we treat people with pain therapies, while not limiting legitimate access to those who need it.



An effective response to the prescription drug abuse epidemic requires stakeholders from all perspectives to rally around a comprehensive plan. We at the {http://cepoponline.org/}Collaborative for Effective Prescription Opioid Policies (CEPOP) call on patients, healthcare providers, pharmacists, law enforcement, public health, treatment centers, health plans, distributors and manufacturers to join us in this collaborative effort. Our approach supports strategies like greater access to medication monitoring that aids in preventing abuse, education for providers about the many dimensions of the problem, access to evidence-based treatment and recovery services, increased development of abuse-deterrent pain therapies and community-based prevention and education efforts. Together, we must seize this opportunity to promote the most effective government and private sector solutions. Far too many lives hang in the balance.

 

Mary Bono was a member of the U.S. House of Representatives from California for 15 years and is now a principal at {http://www.faegrebdc.com/}FaegreBD Consulting. Retired Major General Arthur T. Dean is CEO of {http://www.cadca.org/}Community Anti-Drug Coalitions of America (CADCA). Jeffrey Levi is executive director of the {http://healthyamericans.org/pages/?id=29} Trust for America's Health.

 

In addition to its own editorials, USA TODAY publishes diverse opinions from outside writers, including our {http://www.usatoday.com/reporters/boc.html} Board of Contributors. To read more columns like this, go to the {http://www.usatoday.com/opinion/} Opinion front page.

Kevin

      _____________________________________________
      From: Meisner, Randy J
      Sent: Tuesday, October 04, 2011 9:56 AM
      To: Vorderstrasse, Kevin
      Subject: RE: New G2N Rates


      Kevin,

      That table provides the Chargeback and Wholesaler Differential % that when applied to Modified Gross Sales (contract price) will equal Gross Sales (invoice price or list price).  For instance. If Hydrocodone Mod Gross Sales is $1 and the Chgb/WD % is 79.30%, then Gross Sales equals $1.793 ($1 + $1 x 79.30%).  For Morphine, this would be $3.939 ($1 + $1 x 293.9%).  The smaller the percentage, the closer the invoice price is to the contract price (e.g. Addiction Treatment).

      The Marketing Team always provides me Modified Gross Sales ASP for the forecast, so the Chgb/WD % is never an issue.

      Randy Meisner

            _____________________________________________
            From: Vorderstrasse, Kevin
            Sent: Tuesday, October 04, 2011 9:45 AM
            To: Meisner, Randy J
            Subject: RE: New G2N Rates


            Randy,

            I'm having some trouble interpreting the "chargebacks" tab.  What are we looking at in that table?

            Thanks,
            Kevin

                  _____________________________________________
                  From: Meisner, Randy J
                  Sent: Tuesday, October 04, 2011 9:27 AM
                  To: Cardetti, Lisa M (Lundergan); Bullerdick, Jennifer M; Kayich, Natalie (Tretter); Vorderstrasse, Kevin; Collier, Ginger L
                  Cc: Lasker, Karen L; Thomas, Angie F; Erdal, Dean L
                  Subject: New G2N Rates


                  ALL,

                  Finance has completed our quarterly review of G2N rates.  Our review was based on:
                        (1) pricing and customer mix data in the Gained Accounts file,
                        (2) distributor VIP rebates and contract fees
                        (3) Medicaid and Product Return data and trends.

                  The first tab in the attached file provides a comparison of the rates for F10 Actual, F11 Budget, F11 YTD Actual, Prior Forecast and the new F12 Forecast (last column).   The rates are detailed by Product Family and G2N Type.  Most rates did increase, but the overall impact for F12 is close to zero (based on the SEPLE), due to the reduction in Oxycodone rates offsetting larger increases in OxyAPAP, Morphine and Fentanyl Patch.  Another key reason for the near zero impact was the reduction in the Allowances% for all Product Families.  Finance had used this as a means of covering any inaccuracies in our estimate of G2N rates.  However, by using Gained Accounts in our process, our accuracy should improve.  Consequently, the "cushion" in our G2N forecast is now gone.

DEA Announces  Groundbreaking  Guidance that is Inconsistent with the Settlement they are Announcing   Time at Last for Rulemaking?

Posted: 20 Jul 2017 06:58 PM PDT

By John A. Gilbert, Jr.  

On July 11, 2017, the Department of Justice and the Drug Enforcement Administration ( DEA ) announced that Mallinckrodt LLC, a pharmaceutical manufacturer, agreed to pay $35 million to settle allegations related to the adequacy of its efforts to detect and inform DEA of suspicious orders of controlled substances.  Although DEA has reached similar settlements with distributors and pharmacy chains (see, e.g., here), this is the first settlement of its kind with an opioid manufacturer.  DOJ s press release states that the settlement reflects manufacturers  obligation to monitor orders not only from their own customers, but also between distributors and pharmacies and clinics downstream in the distribution chain.  However, this statement appears  inconsistent with the language in the settlement document, marks a stark shift in the prevailing understanding of manufacturers  suspicious order monitoring obligations and raises serious questions about the legal basis and workability of such a requirement.

For years, DEA has been criticized for failure to provide guidance on the suspicious order monitoring regulation, 21 C.F.R.   1301.74(b).  The language in that section has remained unchanged since its enactment in 1971 and while DEA issued informal guidance letters to certain industry groups in 2006, 2007 and 2012,  DEA s interpretation of that regulation has evolved significantly beyond that guidance.  More important, a fundamental deficiency in the regulation is that it fails to recognize the differences between manufacturers and distributors, including the level of data available to each concerning sales between distributors and pharmacies.  Thus, the lack of a clear regulation has continued to hinder industry s ability to meet DEA s expectations.

Unfortunately for industry, in the last several years, DEA has set forth its evolving view of the regulation primarily in presentations at conferences, through Memoranda of Agreement ( MOAs ) related to enforcement actions and in the Southwood and, more recently, the Masters decisions. (see, e.g., here and here).  While this approach has allowed DEA to avoid the notice and comment rulemaking requirement under the Administrative Procedure Act ( APA ), it has also left industry with little clarity about their obligations around the reporting of suspicious orders. A critical element of notice and comment rulemaking is for an agency to solicit important industry input on the impact of potential rulemaking, with the ultimate goal being effective and clear regulations.  Such clarity would result in a more secure supply chain for controlled substances, which would better serve the public interest as the U.S. continues to struggle with the issue of opioid diversion and abuse.

The press release concerning the Mallinckrodt settlement, which purported to set out  groundbreaking  new rules, is another example of DEA establishing a new standard while avoiding notice and comment rulemaking. 

The problem revolves around DEA s discussion of chargebacks (which are a common pharmaceutical pricing feature), for the first time, and a critical discrepancy between the language set forth in the government s press release and the obligation outlined in the MOA with Mallinckrodt.  (In general, a chargeback is a payment made by a manufacturer to a distributor to make the distributor whole when it sells the manufacturer s product at a price below a specified rate. After a distributor sells a manufacturer s product to the pharmacy, for example, it requests a chargeback from the manufacturer and to support that request for payment, the distributor identifies the product, volume and the pharmacy to which it sold the product.) In its press release, the government stated that,  [t]he groundbreaking nature of the settlement involves requiring a manufacturer to utilize chargeback and similar data to monitor and report to DEA suspicious sales of its oxycodone at the next level in the supply chain, typically sales from distributors to independent and small chain pharmacy and pain clinic customers.  (emphasis added). This appears to set forth DEA s position that manufacturers must review chargebacks and report the underlying sales from the distributor to downstream pharmacies as suspicious orders.

However, we have reviewed Mallinckrodt s MOA and it does not require reporting downstream transactions as suspicious orders.  Rather, the MOA provides that Mallinckrodt review chargeback data and alert DEA of pharmacies (not orders) that may be concerning.   The clear focus of the language is a reporting of pharmacies as a condition of the MOA, not the reporting of chargebacks as suspicious orders under 21 CFR 1301.74(b). Note, as of this writing, the MOA has not been posted to the government s websites.

As an initial matter, it is not clear that DEA can create such a new requirement by announcing it in a press release. First, nothing in the language of 21 C.F.R.   1301.74(b) suggests that a manufacturer must review orders between two downstream third parties and report them as suspicious. Second, we could find no prior public statement from DEA that a manufacturer must report such third party transactions as suspicious under 21 C.F.R.   1301.74(b). Finally, if this really is  groundbreaking    to use the government s own word   surely such a change should warrant notice and comment rulemaking.

Moreover, there is no indication manufacturers  attempts to monitor downstream transactions would be productive. It appears instead that manufacturers will be expected to second guess distributors  decisions to fill orders from pharmacies (well after those sales have been completed), even though the manufacturers have far less information than the distributors have about those pharmacies. Distributors often have longstanding relationships with their pharmacy customers and sophisticated monitoring programs to evaluate pharmacy orders.  In contrast, a manufacturer can only see   after the fact   the manufacturer s products a distributor sells to a pharmacy and for which the distributor submits a chargeback request. With such limited visibility, a simple and perfectly legitimate switch by a pharmacy from one manufacturer s product to another s, for example, could look like a suspicious  increase  in the distributor s sales to that pharmacy. 

DEA s position raises many additional practical questions. If the manufacturer and distributor disagree about which orders are suspicious, will DEA hold manufacturers  reports of suspicious orders against the distributor, even if the distributor is better positioned to assess those orders?  How many orders that appear  suspicious  to a manufacturer can be filled by a distributor before the manufacturer must stop selling to that distributor?  And how should a manufacturer structure a program designed to monitor distributor sales to tens of thousands of pharmacies with which the manufacturer has no contact?

Manufacturers will likely be struggling with these issues for years to come. That ongoing confusion and its negative impact on the security of the supply chain emphasizes, once again, the need for DEA to make clear the obligations of manufacturers through notice and comment rulemaking on this critical issue, especially as the country continues to struggle with the problem of opioid diversion and abuse.



 
FDA Finalizes List of Class II Devices for 510(k) Exemption

Posted: 20 Jul 2017 10:26 AM PDT

By Rachael E. Hunt*  

On July 11, 2017, in the Federal Register, FDA published the finalized list of Class II devices that are now exempt from the 510(k) requirements. This list is identical in substance to the proposed list published on March 14, 2017 (see our prior post here). The only change noted is that FDA grouped those products that contain a limitation on the exemption, and those that do not. Companies with products in the former category are well advised to carefully read the limitations that apply to their product to make sure that they do not fall within a limitation. If they do, a premarket notification will be required. The limitations vary, including, for example, a partial limitation for enzyme immunoassays for amphetamine. For those immunoassays, the exemption applies only where the test system is intended for employment or insurance testing. The same test system used for other purposes, for example Federal drug testing programs, would not be subject to the exemption.

Notably, all products are subject to the .9 limitations, which require a manufacturer to obtain 510(k) clearance for an exempt device type, if either: (i) the device is intended for a use different from the intended use of a legally marketed device in that generic type of device; (ii) the device operates using a different fundamental scientific technology than a legally marketed device in that generic type of device; or (iii) if it falls within an enumerated list of IVDs, such as those used in the screening or diagnosis of familial or acquired genetic disorders.

Lastly, FDA notes in the Federal Register that companies with pending 510(k) submissions for devices now exempt from premarket notification, when taking into consideration any applicable limitations on those exemptions, should withdraw their submissions.

*Not admitted in the District of Columbia.

From: James Ottinger [mailto:James.Ottinger@premier-research.com]
Sent: Friday, November 06, 2009 11:07 AM
To: PharmD, PhD Gene Wright
Cc: Kim, Stuart K. ; rod.hughes@synchronymedical.com; Susan Franks; cfinn@rrdintl.com; fhurley@rrdintl.com; Neuman, Herbert R; Mannebach, Mark ; Mike Nelson; mkrane@rrdintl.com
Subject: RE: Exalgo REMS package complete



Dear Gene,

 

As you advised, the JDC had approved submission of the REMS on Monday, November 2, and the documents were sent to the agency and are now under active review.  We have reviewed the additional changes forwarded by Stu Kim and have the following observations:

 

·         In general, the changes are inconsistent with labeling, the REMS Supporting Document, and FDA advice on the REMS.

·         The goals of the REMS were dictated by the FDA in their advice letter, and are the same as Embeda, and we note that these have changed.

·         The changes to the REMS do not match the REMS supporting document.

·         The FDA’s advice was to remove promotional language in the HCP letters such as “pleased to announce” and this has been re-inserted into the text.

·         The FDA’s advice was to include the full indication in the HCP letters, and this has been truncated in the revised versions.

·         The revised letters contain a black box, which does not match the warnings in the black box, and would not be accepted by FDA.  Additionally, FDA specifically advised that text boxes not be used to highlight specific information as it minimizes the importance of other information in the letter, and minimizes the REMS risks associated with EXALGO.

·         The HCP letters contain language which is inconsistent with the label.

·         The track changes files do not match the versions submitted in the NDA, thus, we cannot use these files as presented.

·         The “clean” versions of the files contain substantial formatting changes relative to the track changes version, and are not entirely accurate, e.g., the toll free phone number on REMS disappears in the clean version so these are not direct ‘accept changes’ versions.

·         There are a large number of editorial changes which would require a new FDA review of the entire REMS.

 

We recommend to the JDC that we maintain the current REMS text as submitted on Monday (11/2/09).

 

Regards,

Jim

 

James G. Ottinger, RPh

Premier Research Group

Horsham, PA 19044, USA

215.907.1330 ext 1008

{HDMA Weekly Digest: A Newsletter for HDMA Members}

 
{A Newsletter for HDMA Members}

 September 30, 2014

 


 

 


 
   
In This Issue

   
 

 Dakota Drug's Ted Scherr Named HDMA Chairman

 


 Registration Now Open for HDMA's 2015 Distribution Management Conference and Expo

 


 FDA Announces "Know Your Source" Campaign to Educate Prescribers on Rogue Distributors

 

  

 Register for "Contracts and Chargebacks Seminar: Perspectives on Process Improvement" — October 15–16

 


 Registration Continues for the Center's November 12–13 Specialty Seminar

 



  


 

 

   

 
   
{Turn SOM on its Head for Enhanced Compliance | BuzzeoPDMA}

 
   
 {corner}

  
{divider}

Dakota Drug's Ted Scherr Named HDMA Chairman

Ted Scherr, President/CEO of Dakota Drug, Inc., was elected as Chairman of HDMA's Board of Directors at the fifth Annual Board & Membership Meeting in Laguna Beach, Calif. Scherr assumes the chairmanship from David Neu, President, AmerisourceBergen Drug Corporation, who was elected to the position in October 2012 and remains a member of the HDMA Board and Executive Committee.

Two additional Board members also were announced at the meeting. Jon Giacomin, President, U.S. Pharmaceutical Distribution, Cardinal Health, Inc., will replace Michael Kaufmann, Chief Executive Officer, Pharmaceutical Segment, Cardinal Health, Inc., on the Board and Executive Committee. Mr. Kaufmann served on the Board and Executive Committee since 2008. Timothy Booth, President/COO, Metro Medical Supply, Inc., was named to the Board in June.

"It was truly an honor to work closely with Dave as Chairman, and Mike as a member of the Executive Committee, during their tenures," said HDMA President and CEO John M. Gray, in a statement. "Ted, Jon and Tim all bring fresh perspectives to our organization, and I look forward to working with them and the entire Board of Directors to ensure that HDMA continues to deliver value to our members and the industry."

A complete listing of the HDMA Board is available here. For more information, contact Anne Johnson.

{top of page}

Registration Now Open for HDMA's 2015 Distribution Management Conference and Expo

Registration for the 2015 Distribution Management Conference and Expo is now open, with early bird rates available through December 15. Early registration ensures saving up to $800 on conference registration fees for this annual event.

Slated to take place March 8–11 at the JW Marriott Orlando Grande Lakes, the event will provide attendees with a forum to engage in discussions on topics ranging from reverse logistics and disposal to traceability and licensure. With nearly 500 attendees present each year, the Conference and Expo is HDMA's largest supply chain education event.

Sessions for the 2015 conference include:

"Big Data: a Revolution That Will Change How We Live, Work and Think," a presentation by Viktor Mayer-Schönberger, bestselling Author of Delete and Big Data and expert on the networked economy;
"Achieving the Impossible," words from Ben Saunders, the world record-breaking polar explorer and endurance athlete;
"What's In, What's Out, What's Ahead: 2015 Healthcare Marketplace Trends," a presentation by Doug Long of IMS Health, Inc.; and,
"Washington From a Different Angle," with Katty Kay, Author and Lead Anchor of BBC World News America.

For early bird registration information, visit the conference website. Contact HDMA's Meetings & Conferences Department at (703) 885-0278 for registration questions. For program questions, contact Jo-Anne Torres.

{top of page}

FDA Announces "Know Your Source" Campaign to Educate Prescribers on Rogue Distributors

FDA announced a new campaign called "Know Your Source" aimed at advising healthcare professionals and practice administrators to purchase prescription drugs only from wholesale drug distributors licensed in their states to protect patients from unsafe or ineffective drugs. The campaign website includes tips to identify rogue distributors, flyers and a map of state licensing authorities for prescribers to verify that wholesale drug distributors are licensed in their states.

For more information, contact Allison Tuszynski.

{top of page}

Register for "Contracts and Chargebacks Seminar: Perspectives on Process Improvement" — October 15–16

Less than three weeks remain to register for HDMA's "Contracts and Chargebacks Seminar: Perspectives on Process Improvement." Taking place on October 15–16 in Wilmington, Del., the seminar will bring together professionals in the contracts and chargebacks sector to discuss current industry processes and challenges.

Agenda topics include:

"The 340B Landscape — Driving Program Integrity and Compliance in the 340B Program" with: Stephanie Trunk, Legal Counsel, Arent Fox LLP;
Marijo Bustos, Supervisor, Chargebacks, Fresenius Kabi, USA;
BJ Centers, Senior Director, Operations & Distribution Apexus/Prime Vendor Program; and,
Dr. Andrew L. Wilson, PharmD, Vice President, 340B Solutions, McKesson Corporation.


"EDI Q-and-A" with: Gail Jones, Business Analyst, Pharma Contract Administration, McKesson Corporation; and,
Susan Lowe, Principal, LoMac Consulting.


A "Managing Change with Team Building" presentation led by EJ Johnson, Director of Talent Development, AmerisourceBergen Corporation.
"Interactive Roundtables," offering an opportunity to discuss the 340B Refund Process (from both the manufacturer and distributor perspective); credit and rebills; and other topics.

The agenda also features distributor hosted roundtables, with table hosts and facilitators from AmerisourceBergen Corporation, H.D. Smith and McKesson Corporation.

As a reminder, the deadline to make reservations at the Hotel du Pont at the special HDMA group rate is tomorrow, Wednesday, October 1. For details, visit the seminar website.

Visit the seminar website for more information on the agenda. For registration questions, contact HDMA's Meetings & Conferences Department at (703) 885-0278. For program questions, contact Jo-Anne Torres.

{top of page}

Registration Continues for the Center's November 12–13 Specialty Seminar

Registration is under way for the Center for Healthcare Supply Chain Research's annual educational event, the Specialty Pharmaceutical Supply Chain Issues and Trends Seminar — taking place on November 12–13 at the Renaissance Arlington Capital View Hotel in Arlington, Va.

Program highlights include:

The potential impact of the Affordable Care Act (ACA) on the pharmaceutical supply chain, including changes in benefit design, the delivery system and involvement of consumers with Dan Mendelson, CEO & Founder, Avalere Health LLC.
An overview of what is in the pharmaceutical pipeline by disease state and drug characteristics with Ray Tancredi, RPh, MBC, CSP, Vice President, Specialty Pharmacy Development, Walgreens.
A panel discussion on cost-containment measures and how the supply chain will be impacted.
A new research study from the Center addressing learning opportunities from Europe in the commercialization of biosimilars and the market potential for biosimilars in the U.S., with insights provided by: Tom Moore, Marketing Director, US Value & Access, Amgen, Inc.;
Rich Tremonte, Vice President, Global Generic Pharmaceuticals, AmerisourceBergen Corporation;
Murielle Thinard-McLane, Vice President, Generics, McKesson Specialty Health;
Ray Tancredi, RPh, MBC, CSP, of Walgreens; and,
Bruce A. Feinberg, Vice President & Chief Medical Officer, Cardinal Health Specialty Solutions, Clinical Pathways, Cardinal Health Inc.


A dialogue facilitated by IMS' Vice President, Industry Relations, Doug Long on launching new specialty pharmaceuticals with: Chris Doerr, Senior Director, Trade Operations, TEVA Pharmaceuticals USA;
Thomas Doyle, Executive Vice President, Commercial Solutions, H. D. Smith Specialty Solutions; and,
Gayle Johnston, President, CuraScript Specialty Distribution, an Express Scripts Company.


A presentation on the potential impact of Accountable Care Organizations (ACOs) on the supply chain with Peter Weissberg, Associate Director, Client Strategist, Xcenda®, AmerisourceBergen.
A discussion by Michael Werner, Partner, Holland & Knight, to spotlight issues and insights relating to medical ethics in America and their effect on the supply chain.

For more information and to register, visit the Center's website, or contact Karen Ribler.

Hi Maggie,

 

I’ve attached the policy analysis that has been prepared on the Massachusetts legislation.  Note, that it is effective immediately (rather than late 2015 as you note), but there will be a host of rulemaking that will need to be done.  From a Policy / Government Affairs perspective, we’ll be actively engaged in the process.

 

Please note that there is still further analysis that needs to be done by our Legal and Regulatory teams before we assess potential benefit to our current portfolio (i.e. Exalgo & Xartemis) as well as MNK-155.  There is a school of thought that the language around ADT determination is so narrow that the data that we’ve (MNK) generated as part of the past submissions to the FDA would not be sufficient for the Drug Formulary Commission to make an “abuse deterrent” determination. 


As such, we should not engage with any customers around this.  We’ll keep all posted as more information is gathered, analysis prepared, and an official MNK position is developed around this legislation.  Further, I ask that this analysis not be shared beyond this group (above) and, especially, externally.

 

Happy to further discuss.  Hope all is well-


Best,


Derek

From: Glassman, Margaret

Subject: pending MA legislation



 

Hi Derek

I’m am in our Managed Markets group and have responsibility for some national health plans and the regional plans in New England and upstate NY. The Boston Globe ran an article on August 1st regarding the MA legislature’s approval on an opioid bill. There are several provisions in the bill related to preventing and treating substance abuse.

Specific to prescription meds, the legislation “seeks to encourage the use of certain kinds of painkillers that are less likely to be used inappropriately by addicts. Unless directed otherwise by a physician, pharmacists would be required to dispense drugs formulated to prevent abuse, such as those that cannot be crushed for injection or snorting. Insurers would be barred from charging higher copayments on those drugs”

The legislation doesn’t take effect until late 2015 but I’m wondering if we can leverage this with the payers in MA and possibly hospital systems. Also, I thought that CT had some bills pending on something similar but can’t find anything on the CT government website. Any ideas you may have on how I can approach payers and key thought leaders in the medical community would be much appreciated. Thanks in advance-

 

Best regards,

 

Maggie Glassman | Corporate Account Director

Mallinckrodt Pharmaceuticals

I want to again thank each of you for your participation and attentiveness during our meeting in Miami this week.  Now that we have been back in the field a couple of days, I thought it would be useful to review some of the key points of the meeting and more importantly the direction going forward in Q2.  To sum it up simply, we need to be BALANCED, have FOCUS, and make calls with FREQUENCY.  Let's take a closer look at each of those:



*         BALANCE:

o    With 4 products in our bag, we need to "Balance" our time in the field very carefully.

o    We received our product weighting, and Exalgo remains our Flagship product in all territories throughout the district.

o    While Exalgo is key to our success, we can't maximize our IC plan, Contest dollars or sales force ranking without successfully promoting the NSAID basket and SDP.

o    The "Call Planner" will help you to balance your time and allocate your call capacity throughout the month. We will review this document together on each field visit. Don't wait to work on your Call Planner.  Each of you should have this complete and start to implement on Monday.  You can make changes throughout the quarter as needed.

*         FOCUS:

o    It is very important that we focus our time and resources on our most important customers who can provide the biggest return on our investment.

o    Plan "focused" dinner/lunch programs planned around hyper targets. You will get more out of this valuable resource.  Get those programs scheduled ASAP!!!

o    Focus your field time on the top decile physicians within each market basket.

o    Use IMS to identify top prescribing physicians who accept plans where our products are covered

o    Deliver a calculated message based upon a solid pre-call plan.  What are we going to say to move the customer during this call?  What are we going to ask for as a result of the interaction?

o    Use the new "Pre-Call Planning" document to help develop a goal for each call.

*         FREQUENCY:

o    Frequency of calls on your top prescribers/targets drives results!!!!

o    Our top prescribers should be seen at least once per week. (or at the very least 3 times per month)

o    When we are in the office 3+ times in a month, hyper targets prescribe twice the amount of EXALGO than when we are there 2 times/month.  This is evidence that your efforts make a difference!

o    Frequency with top targets in all three market baskets is key to our success. Market research shows that one call per month does nothing.



We cannot afford to waste any calls.  We need to challenge our customers' perceptions of hydromorphone, challenge them to identify a patient for EXALGO, challenge the coverage perceptions and how they are dosing EXALGO.  We need to sell with passion, enthusiasm, and confidence in all of our calls whether it's selling Exalgo, Sumavel DosePro, Pennsaid, and/or Duexis!!  Remember, these products can change patients' lives for the better!  We need to challenge our customers to ask their migraine patients......."How are you really doing?" Does their current therapy relieve all of their headache types? What about the wake up or the throw up headaches?  Sumavel DosePro can significantly help these patients.  We need to hypertarget our prescribers for Duexis and get those prescriptions written.  We need to maintain and increase our Pennsaid business by targeting managed care plans where we have the access via IMS and selling on our Simon data comparing Pennsaid to oral diclofenac.



Q2 will be a defining quarter for this business and for each of you.  We need to show what we are made of and put our mark on FY13 during this quarter and showing why we are designating ourselves as the Southern Heat.  Let's turn up the heat on ourselves and more importantly our customers to get the job done.  I am here to help each of you meet and exceed your goals.  We've been given the tools and the direction to be successful, it's now our job to implement and use them in the field!  Let's get to it!!!!





Great Selling!!!

Re: [RxNews] Hydrocodone prescribing decline

The CDC's research shows a very close linear relationship between opioid sales and the rate of fatal overdoses
involving opioids, ( See, for example, Paulozzi U, Weisler RH, Patkar AA, A national epidemic of unintentional
prescription opioid overdose deaths: how physicians can help control it. The Journal of clinical psychiatry.
2011;72(5):589-592.) This relationship was suspected for years before the CDC finally produced solid evidence.
According to unpublished ARCOS data, in Florida in 20:10 there were 82,534.3 grams of oxycodone per100,000
population distributed for medical use. This was in the year BEFORE the anti-pill mill law took effect on July 1,
2011, That law prohibited docs from dispensing controlled substances from their offices (consequently putting
a quick end to pill mills) and imposed reporting requirements on wholesale drug distributors selling more than
5,000 dosage units per customer per month of controlled substances in the state.
In 2013, oxycodone sales in Florida for medical use were down to 2:1,614.43 grams per 100,000 population.
That's a 73.8 percent drop in market share in a very short period of time. Yes, there were some legitimate
complaints from patients, especially those who were previously treated at now closed pill mills. When seeking
new providers, they encountered problems either because their records were unavailable or unreliable or
because they were on very high regimens of opioids as a result of their treatment at the mill. There were likely
some legitimate patients inconvenienced by all this, especially those finding it difficult to fill prescriptions
because pharmacists under the new law could face criminal charges for the first time if they filled a fraudulent
prescription. Most of these problems seem to have resolved themselves as people became familiar with the
new regs.
It is not surprising to see that the prescribing of hydrocodone products decreased after the drug was moved to
C-Il status by FDA and DEA in October 2014. This drop in prescribing was forecasted by most analysts. I would
expect to see a corresponding decrease in abuse and mortality rates attributed to hydrocodone. In Florida,
where oxycodone distribution dropped 73.8 percent in less than two years, the number of oxycodone-caused
fatalities dropped 52.1 percent between 2010 and 2012 (from 1,516 in 2010 to 735 in 2012). This is a pretty
remarkable accomplishment in a field not knowing too many successes.
As we ponder these life-saving accomplishments, we should be mindful that pharmaceutical manufacturers
and wholesale distributors that buy these drugs in bulk and take title to them are losing market share when
prescribing is reduced, In response, they have been known to rile customers and the public by exaggerating
some of the aforementioned problems that some patients encounter after these regulatory changes. In some
cases, they have misrepresented alleged drug shortages as being caused by federal authorities and/or nonexistent federal regulations. The US Government Accountability Office studied some of these complaints last
year and found many of them to be the result of poor communications between the federal agency (DEA) and
the registrant community. (See: U.S. Government Accountability Office. Prescription Drugs: More DEA
Information about Registrants' Controlled Substances Roles Could Improve Their Understanding and Help
Ensure Access. 2015; http://www.gao.gov/products/GAO-15-471.)
John Coleman

Terry  

 

Below is a summation of the 5:30pm group. 2 PCPs (1 internist   geriatrics), 1 Physiatrist

Reaction to Messages

Dosing

Two physicians were most motivated by the message  two tablets, twice daily for fast-acting and long-lasting relief   felt it was the most succinct and to the point

The other physician liked the message about the 12 hour dosing not requiring their patients to watch the clock, chase their pain, etc   felt an emotional appeal to this message

pK

All respondents were motivated by messages related to the steady and sustained plasma concentrations with fewer peaks and troughs, again paired with the pK graph   Liked that it was concise and to the point and felt the graph was very helpful

Efficacy

One physician motivated by the message first and only (which tells them it is unique) .with immediate and extended release properties fast acting and long lasting- they found the fast acting and long lasting clever

Another liked the message about XARTEMIS XR lasting longer allowing the patients to focus on healing and recovery

The last physician connected to the more emotional messaging related to the Harris Poll statistic about the number of acute pain suffers have to wake in the night to dose

Patient type

Two were motivated by the message with XARTEMIS XR being suited for patients with pain throughout the day and night for whom you typically prescribe Percocet

The other physician was motivated by the message indicating the acute pain often lasts throughout the day and night and it is well suited to a product that is both fast acting and long lasting

Abuse

One physician was motivated by the message about XARTEMIS XR meeting 3 primary endpoints   although this caused a lot of questions related to the results

Another physician felt the message about receiving priority review was the most motivating

The last physician was most motivated by the message about HCPs can more responsibly prescribe XARTEMIS XR because it designed to offer longer duration of effect and reduce abuse potential for patients for patients and society   he connected very emotionally to this message

Misc. Message Comments

All the physicians seemed to refer to oxycodone/acetaminophen products as Percocet

Misc. Concept Comments

Really liked  Long on Relief- Short on Abuse  Branding element, but they felt the concept with just that element was not graphically interesting

Struggled with the  Paired against Pain  concept   did not connect with the deterrence component, it is not as well understood without the word abuse

Really liked the  Responsible Relief  tagline

Relief Extended is not easily understood   they do not get the 2

The concepts with the most stopping power were Relief Reinvented and Less is More (Both treatments were selected)

The concepts that were the most motivating were Less is More (crumpled cups treatment) and Two Needs One Script

Most motivating and differentiating concept was the long on abuse, short on relief with the reveal

Camille,
Per our conversations, customer has inquired about increasing the frequency of their Fentanyl orders or increasing the
quantity of their Fentanyl orders.
Further, they intend to purchase Hydromorphone powder as well.
Customer operates using a Retail Pharmacy DEA Registration.

Mallinckrodt interpretation of the regulations is as follows:

Retail Pharmacy
Compounds medications to fit the unique needs of the patient, as authorized by a prescription from physician.
The medications must be dispensed directly to a patient and not sent to the physician.
DEA does not  require  quota issuance for acquisitions by Retail Pharmacy registrants, distributions of CI and CII require
DEA 222 order forms.
Note: The Mallinckrodt business model does not include direct sales to Retail Pharmacy registrants.

Compounding Pharmacy
Compounds medications to fit the unique needs of the patient, as authorized by a prescription from physician.
Compounding pharmacy does not dispense medication to the patient but may send it directly to the prescribing physician
for office administration.
DEA requires Compounding Pharmacy registrants to be licensed within the category of Manufacturing registrants.
Manufacturing registrants require quota  for acquisitions of CI and CII controlled substances, distributions of CI and CII
require DEA 222 order forms.
Note: The Mallinckrodt business model accommodates sales to Compounding Pharmacy/Manufacturing registrants,
upon proof of current DEA registration license, provided they certify in writing that  the firm has available Procurement
Quota issued by DEA, adequate to cover the quantity of the specific sale.

To: Harper, Karen; Mannino, Tony; Ratliff, Bill; Hunter, Dave; Pokorny, Camille M
Subject: RE: Request Advice on Customer Order for Material to Prepare Reference Standard
Karen,

Last year (2008) I dispensed 63.5 grams of Codeine Phosphate reference standard for the analytical support of our
manufacturing of the bulk here in St. Louis and all the dosage forms in Hobart. So far this year (2009) I have dispensed 13


   grams. Last year Sherryl Ruder shipped one order for 200 milligrams to an external customer and had no internal requests for
Codeine Phosphate.

If I were to subdivide 1000 grams, that would last us almost 16 years at the rate that we used it in 2008. I must say that our
reference standard use is increasing, so that 1000 grams may only last maybe 10 years. That still is a very long time to store a
qualified reference. I also know that storing any controlled substance that long invites opportunities for diversion. So that
generally should be discouraged.

We use the manufacturing registration for our operation. When it is shipped to Hobart  it goes out under our manufacturing
registration and is transferred to Hobart's Analytical registration via their form 222.

It seems to me that if the customer is "manufacturing" a reference standard, it should be received into their manufacturing
registration. When it goes to their client to be used in the lab, that is when it should be transferred to analytical lab registration.

Ted
From: Harper, Karen
Sent: Friday, May 15, 2009 8:07 AM
To: Myrick, Ted
Cc: Pokorny, Camille M; Ratliff, Bill; Hunter, Dave
Subject: Request Advice on Customer Order for Material to Prepare Reference Standard
Ted
Controlled Substance Compliance and Security are working with Customer Service to determine the validity of a customer order
for 1 kg of Codeine Phosphate, within the scope of our Suspicious Order Monitoring Program.
Customer states their intended use is to "prepare a reference standard for a client who will use the material for testing activities".

Our concerns are:
The 1 kg quantity seems too large, does this exceed the quantity of API we would normally use internally to prepare reference
standards?
Does the intended use differ from the activity that you and Sherryl perform? Within Mallinckrodt, we use DEA Manufacturing
registration for the work you do in "making" ARS compounds, customer is requesting the material on an Analytical Lab DEA
registration.
Our regulatory interpretation is that use of Analytical Lab DEA registration is reserved for an entity that actually performs tests
on the material (example:
Gateway Medical Research obtains material on Analytical Lab DEA registration to perform clinical trial work)

Please comment and thank you.

INDICATION

EXALGO  (hydromorphone HCI) Extended-Release
Tablets (CII) is indicated for the management of
moderate to severe pain in opioid tolerant patients
requiring continuous, around-the-clock opioid
analgesia for an extended period of time.

IMPORTANT RISK INFORMATION

WARNING: ABUSE POTENTIAL,
LIFE-THREATENING RESPIRATORY DEPRESSION, and ACCIDENTAL EXPOSURE

Abuse Potential

EXALGO contains hydromorphone, an opioid agonist and a Schedule II controlled substance with an abuse liability similar to other opioid agonists, legal or illicit. Assess each patient s risk for opioid abuse or addiction prior to prescribing EXALGO. The risk for opioid abuse is increased in patients with a personal or family history of substance abuse (including drug or alcohol abuse or addiction) or mental illness (e.g., major depressive disorder). Routinely monitor all patients receiving EXALGO for signs of misuse, abuse, and addiction during treatment.

Life-threatening Respiratory Depression

Respiratory depression, including fatal cases, may occur with use of EXALGO, even when the drug has been used as recommended and not misused or abused. EXALGO is for use in opioid tolerant patients only. Proper dosing and titration are essential and EXALGO should be prescribed only by healthcare professionals who are knowledgeable in the use of potent opioids for the management of chronic pain. Monitor for respiratory depression, especially during initiation of EXALGO or following a dose increase. Crushing, dissolving, or chewing the tablet can cause rapid release and absorption of a potentially fatal dose of hydromorphone.

Accidental Exposure

Accidental ingestion of EXALGO, especially in children, can result in a fatal overdose of hydromorphone.



 


EXALGO is contraindicated in:
- Opioid non-tolerant patients. Fatal respiratory
  depression could occur in patients who are not
  opioid tolerant.

- Patients with significant respiratory depression

- Patients with acute or severe bronchial asthma in
  an unmonitored setting or in the absence of
  resuscitative equipment

- Patients with known or suspected paralytic ileus

- Patients who have had surgical procedures and/or
  underlying disease resulting in narrowing of the
  gastrointestinal tract, or have  blind loops  of the
  gastrointestinal tract or gastrointestinal obstruction

- Patients with hypersensitivity (e.g., anaphylaxis) to
  hydromorphone or sulfite-containing medications


 


EXALGO is indicated for opioid tolerant patients only. Patients considered opioid tolerant are those who are taking at least 60 mg oral morphine per day, 25 mcg transdermal fentanyl/hour, 30 mg oral oxycodone/day, 8 mg oral hydromorphone/day, 25 mg oral oxymorphone/day or an equianalgesic dose of another opioid, for a week or longer.


 


EXALGO is not intended for use as an as-needed analgesic and is not indicated for the management of acute or postoperative pain. It is contraindicated in patients who need management of mild pain or pain not expected to persist.


 


Avoid concurrent use of alcohol and EXALGO. Concurrent use of EXALGO with CNS depressants, including alcohol, increases risk of respiratory depression, hypotension, and profound sedation, potentially resulting in coma or death. EXALGO may impair the ability to drive a car or operate machinery.


 


Not intended in patients who have received MAO inhibitors within 14 days of starting EXALGO.


 


Use with caution and in reduced doses in older or debilitated patients, as well as patients with renal or hepatic insufficiency, Addison s disease, delirium tremens, myxedema or hypothyroidism, prostatic hypertrophy or urethral stricture, toxic psychosis. May aggravate convulsions in patients with convulsive disorders; may induce or aggravate seizures in some clinical settings. Consider use of an alternate analgesic in patients with severe renal impairment.


 


Respiratory depression, which occurs more frequently in elderly or debilitated patients, is the chief hazard with EXALGO.


 


Serious adverse events could also include hypotensive effects, GI effects, cardiac arrest from overdose and precipitation of withdrawal. Most common adverse events (>10%) seen in clinical studies (N=2474) were: constipation (31%), nausea (28%), vomiting, somnolence, headache, asthenia and dizziness.


 


Use EXALGO with extreme caution in patients susceptible to intracranial effects of CO2 retention.


 


Do not abruptly discontinue EXALGO.

The Statewide Public Affairs Team

{cid:6E90D38E-CF95-47AD-92A0-E26CD63E5D68}

 

Morning Update

Friday, June 10, 2016

 

Headlines:

Ride-booking bill in Albany still stuck in roadblock over insurance

Buffalo News

Though its plans to expand into New York have been watered down, the ride-hailing industry is leveling an all-out push for approval of the taxi-alternative transportation to upstate. The Senate and Assembly, however, are still apart over a key sticking point: how much insurance liability ride-hailing drivers must carry. Time is running out with next week’s scheduled end of session. It is a matter that has attracted the interest of transportation companies, trial lawyers, insurance firms, unions and disability groups. Here is the conflict: • Ride-hailing companies, led by giants Uber and Lyft, say consumers crave their services, and that the upstate economy and transportation choices will be bolstered by their presence. • Opponents, including upstate taxi companies, say job-creation claims are bloated, consumers will have fewer protections and cab companies will go out of business. http://goo.gl/5eYYVu

 

COR's big score: Why did a juicy job from NY state draw just one bidder?

Syracuse News

There's something odd about the way COR Development Co. faced no competition for a lucrative state contract to develop Central New York's nanotech projects. The contract was advertised and approved in a hurry. Other developers that might have fought for the job never knew about it. Instead, COR --€“ a major contributor to Gov. Andrew Cuomo's campaign -- was the only bidder. The deal has already brought the company $75 million in work funded by state taxpayers, with the potential for more. COR was selected in late 2013 as the state university's "strategic partner'' to develop and build high-tech economic development projects in Central New York. The five-year deal, which can be extended to 10 years, makes COR the preferred developer for all relevant projects. "That's a heck of a deal,'' said Michael P. Falcone, chairman and CEO of the Pioneer Companies, another prominent developer. "I kind of wish I had seen that ad.'' But the opportunity went unnoticed by Falcone and other leading Syracuse developers. The request for proposals was publicized less widely than many state procurement offers worth far less money. http://goo.gl/QP7Ejg

 

Cuomo releases recommendations to combat heroin, opioid abuse

Times Union

The Governor’s Heroin and Opioids Task Force, created last month, issued a report Thursday with 25 recommendations for combating the abuse of the illicit and prescription drugs in New York. The report follows a statewide listening tour by the Task Force, co-chaired by Lt. Gov. Kathy Hochul and state Office of Alcoholism and Substance Abuse Services Commissioner Arlene González-Sánchez. It comes as the legislative session is winding down to its final days. The Task Force was created in response to an epidemic of heroin and opioid abuse that has resulted in a rising number of deaths in recent years. A separate report released Thursday by state Comptroller Thomas DiNapoli showed deaths from heroin and prescription narcotic overdoses reached record highs statewide in 2014, and rose faster over the previous decade than in most other states in the nation. About 2,300 New Yorkers died in 2014 due to drug overdose. http://goo.gl/cJlN2W

 

Belmont Stakes Is Backdrop for Battle Over Racing

WSJ

The Belmont Stakes is set to anchor a festive day Saturday even as a fight brews in Albany for control of the New York Racing Association, the operator of the state’s top thoroughbred venues. For one day at least, the political battle may seem far off the radar at Belmont Park, where positive signs abound. In the clubhouse, most luxury seating areas have sold out. On the far side of the track, a new dormitory will improve living conditions for backstretch workers. And while Saturday’s crowd isn't expected to be as large as in years when a Triple Crown was possible, about 10,000 general-admission tickets were sold before consumers knew whether history was possible. These improvements have come about since 2012, when state lawmakers, in agreement with Gov. Andrew Cuomo, passed legislation that put the state in control of the racing association for three years. The goal was to make changes and tighten oversight before returning the organization to its previous status as a private nonprofit. Mr. Cuomo then secured a one-year extension of that control. http://goo.gl/LhSOgI

 

New York state Assembly plans on taking up child-sex abuse victims bill ‘next week’ before legislative session ends

Daily News

Despite criticism from those on both sides of the issue, the state Assembly still intends to take up a bill dealing with child sex abuse victims.“The plan is still to do the bill next week,” Assembly Democratic spokesman Michael Whyland said Thursday. “Nothing has changed.” Introduced Tuesday night, the bill designed to make it easier for victims to bring lawsuits was assailed by survivors for not going far enough while the Catholic Church opposes a provision that would allow for old cases to be revived. Whyland said he doesn’t expect any changes to the Assembly bill unless a deal on the issue is reached with Gov. Cuomo and the state Senate. “We’ll see how things progress,” he said. Whyland defended the bill. “It is a step forward and allows victims of sexual abuse to seek justice,” he said. Under the legislation, the five-year statute of limitation on felony criminal child sex abuse cases would start at age 23, up from 18. For civil cases, a person would have until their 28th birthday to bring a lawsuit against a predator, up from the current 23. The bill would also do away with a requirement that those abused in a public institution like a school must file a notice of intent to sue within 90 days of the incident. Instead, a person would have until their 28th birthday to bring cases regardless of whether the abuse occurred in a private or public institution. http://goo.gl/uMyKu6

New York City Mayor Bill de Blasio is in California through Sunday celebrating Chiara de Blasio’s graduation.

10 a.m. - “The Brian Lehrer Show” features de Blasio taking calls from listeners and discussing the budget agreement, increasing diversity in specialized high schools, the new citywide campaign on bathroom use and gender identity, and the presidential election, WNYC.

Due to the contract dispute between IMS and one of their primary pharmacy chains, our sales data has been impossible to verify until the dispute was resolved. During this period, the IMS Health projection methodology imputed the missing data. However, prescriber level accuracy depends upon the completeness of their sample and recently launched products such as EXALGO and PENNSAID are more sensitive to sample size fluctuations that usually leads to under-reporting and prescriber level variances.

 

The good news is that the data supplier relationship has been restored and IMS re-projected historical data was received last week. This data has been loaded into our systems and generally shows an increase in volume for January, February and to a lesser extent in March.  However, individual variances at the prescriber level could be positive or negative impacting your historical data, so don t be too alarmed when/if you notice changes.

 

As promised sales leadership has been working with Sales Operations to review the impact of the  supplemental  compensation plan that we mentioned during the National Sales Meeting. The supplemental plan combined with our original plan will help to insure the most equitable payout possible to the members of sales organization.  The decision to support a second perspective of our incentive plan was supported by the executive committee at Covidien and illustrates the support that you have from our internal team. By utilizing the better of the two plans for each sales person we will greatly increase the number of participants in the plan and nearly double the dollars paid.

 

Per the FY11 Pharmaceutical sector Terms and Conditions document, you are to receive communication regarding your FY11 Q1/Q2 SICP payout within 60 days of the end of the second quarter (May 31st). Since the IMS data was just received, your payout will be slightly delayed. We are currently estimating that payout will now happen on July 1st and lots of people are working very hard to make that date a reality. Further communication will follow immediately should that deadline be too aggressive. I m personally quite confident that you will find the wait worthwhile!

 

Given our overall performance that did not meet the sales forecast for either EXALGO or PENNSAID I hope that you will agree that it s now our turn to step up to the plate.  We have new sales tools, we have new contracts with more on the way and the EXALGO team just launched their new co-pay card today!  With a recently revised incentive compensation plan in place, NOW is the time to demonstrate our value to the organization.

 

 

Thanks again for your patience and your anticipated stellar sales contribution during the remainder of FY11.

 

Good selling!

 

Ron Wickline

Subject: Oxycodone Sales in Florida - Summary
As many of you have probably heard, Harvard Drug's license to handle controlled substances
was suspended this week. The predominate reason for the suspension was the sale of
Oxycodone in the state of Florida. Please see the attached article for additional information
and details.
http://www.freep.com/article/20100616/NEWS06/6160364/1322/DEA-suspends-license-
of-Livonia-distributor
Additionally, it came to our attention that Sunrise Wholesaler's DEA license was suspended pending further
investigation. Although the official reason for the suspension has not been named, we are under the
impression that it is also due to the sale of Oxycodone in the state of Florida.
The two wholesaler/distributor license suspensions led us to do a more in-depth analysis of Covidien's
Oxycodone sales in the state of Florida. We specifically focused on doctors' offices  and pain clinics. It
appears that Harvard and Sunrise were the dominate players in this market with over 50% of their total
sales coming from this market. HD Smith, Keysource and McKesson Onestop are next with only 3% to their
total sales coming from doctors' offices and pain clinics:
<<...>>
Karen Harper and team (internal Covidien investigators) will be working closely with the DEA regarding their
investigation of the distribution of Oxycodone in Florida and we will keep you apprised of further happenings.
A special thanks goes out to Vic Borelli, who was instrumental in notifying us of the  Harvard situation and
providing us with continuous news updates. Thank you for bringing to our attention.

Tricia,


FYI.  Message I sent to Debra Pasko at ASHP. 

 

I believe you had invited her based on your previous work experience.  Hopefully Debra will join our little band as we continue to drive access and patient safety forward.

Kevin

 

From: Webb, Kevin J
Sent: Friday, December 11, 2015 12:08 PM
To: 'dpasko@ashp.org'
Subject: Follow up from AfBPM Summit Meeting (Nov 12-13)



 

Debra,

 

On behalf of the Alliance for Balanced Pain Management (AfBPM), I would like to thank you for attending our recent Summit meeting held November 12-13 in Washington, DC.  Many of the points you raised during the work shop discussions were spot on regarding need to balance access to appropriate pain management with patient safety across the health care continuum, and the hospital/health system setting is of particular importance.

 

As you were leaving you had mentioned that the AfBPM would be a good fit with the ASHP.  The sole purpose of the AfBPM is to advance aligned coordination, singularity of message, and continuity in educating and empowering all stakeholders regarding responsible pain management. This includes the safe use, storage and disposal of pain medications.  The ASHP and the health-system pharmacist is crucial to this success, and we would be honored to have you as a member of the Alliance.

 

Attached is a brief slide deck that provides an overview, mission and structure of the Alliance for Balanced Pain Management.  After reviewing, let me know if you have any questions, or if would like to discuss in further detail.

 

For full disclosure I also wanted to make you aware that after the first of the year, management of the AfBPM will transition from Green Room Communications to a third-party, non-profit organization called the Alliance for Patient Access (AfPA).  This is a better long-term fit for the strategic direction and needs of the AfBPM, as the AfPA has the capabilities and capacity to guide the AfBPM to realize its full potential.  Over the next week I will be sending an announcement out the full membership, which I will copy you on, but I wanted to be completely transparent with you as you consider your decision.

 

Again, it was a pleasure meeting you, and look forward to your favorable reply.


Best regards,

Kevin

Subject: HDMA Weekly Digest, August 13: Kerlikowske to Leave ONDCP, Nominated as Commissioner of Customs and Border Protection
From: HDMA Weekly Digest <digest@hdmanet.org>
Date: Tue, 13 Aug 2013 13:41:26 +0000
To: eileen.spaulding@mallinckrodt.com


{HDMA Weekly Digest: A Newsletter for HDMA Members} 
{A Newsletter for HDMA Members} August 13, 2013 
  

 
   
In This Issue   
  Kerlikowske to Leave ONDCP, Nominated as Commissioner of Customs and Border Protection 
 Reminder: DEA Hosting October Conference for Distributors 
 CMS Releases Responses to FAQ on the Open Payments Act and Holds Conference Call for Physicians

{HDMA Trade Management Seminar} 
   
 {corner}  
{divider}

Kerlikowske to Leave ONDCP, Nominated as Commissioner of Customs and Border Protection

President Obama recently nominated the current director of the Office of National Drug Control Policy (ONDCP), R. Gil Kerlikowske, as Commissioner of U.S. Customs and Border Protection. If he is confirmed by the Senate, President Obama will nominate a new director of the ONDCP, who will coordinate drug-control activities and related funding across the federal government.

For more information, contact Allison Tuszynski.
{top of page}

Reminder: DEA Hosting October Conference for Distributors

As reported in last week's Weekly Digest, the DEA is hosting a Distributor Conference on October 22 at the Gaylord National Resort and Convention Center in National Harbor, Md. Due to space limitations, this DEA-organized conference invites two representatives from each distributor registrant to attend on a first-come, first-served basis.

An agenda is not yet available, but DEA intends to address such topics as drug and chemical trends, Automation of Reports and Consolidated Orders System (ARCOS) reporting, record-keeping requirements, and "suspicious orders" reporting.

If you plan to attend, register directly with the DEA. Further information and directions for online registration can be found through their website, or by contacting DEA directly at ODLL@usdoj.gov.

For more information, contact Anita Ducca.
{top of page}

CMS Releases Responses to FAQ on the Open Payments Act and Holds Conference Call for Physicians

The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) released responses to additional "Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)" last week. In response to FAQ 8980, CMS addresses the question of how distributors should report information in the "Product Indicator" data element. CMS stated that:

"Distributors that are considered applicable manufacturers because they hold title to a covered drug, device, biological or medical supply may report 'None' in the Product Indicator indicating that the payment or other transfer of value was not associated with any covered drugs, device, biological or medical supply if the payment or other transfer of value was related to the distributors full line of products, rather than any specific covered products."

Additionally, CMS hosted an August 8 conference call entitled, "Policy Updates on Payments and the Physician Resource Toolkit," which provided additional information for physicians on the Open Payments Act. View the PowerPoint presentation from the call; the audio recording and written transcript of the call will be posted here when available.

For more information, contact Kristen Freitas.
{top of page}

Distribution Center Challenge Update: AmerisourceBergen Hosts Alabama State Senator Jimmy Holley (R-31)


 
From Left: AmerisourceBergen's Dave Leverette, President, Oncology Supply, and Julie Eddy, Director, State Government Affairs; and State Senator Jimmy Holley (R-31). 

Alabama State Senator Jimmy Holley (R-31) visited AmerisourceBergen's Oncology Supply Center in Dothan, Ala., on July 18. AmerisourceBergen staff discussed a number of issues with the senator, including the challenges facing community oncology, Medicare reimbursement, compounding pharmacies and managed care systems. Senator Holley owns a compounding pharmacy with his son, who is a pharmacist in the community.

For more information on the Distribution Center Challenge, contact Jewelyn Cosgrove.

{top of page}

Learn Best Practices for Navigating Corporate Acquisitions and Divestitures at HDMA's Upcoming "Trade Management Seminar"

Geared toward individuals responsible for trade relations or account and vendor management, HDMA's "Trade Management Seminar" — September 23–24 at The Umstead Hotel in Cary, N.C. — will provide the opportunity to hear perspectives on building effective connections between distributors and manufacturers, solving key everyday problems and anticipating changes that may affect your company or one of your trading partners.

On Tuesday, September 24, Steve Noetzel, Director, Trade Accounts, Johnson & Johnson HealthCare Systems Inc.; and Dianne Pfahl, Vice President, Industry and Manufacturer Relations, Cardinal Health, Inc., will lead a session on, "The Angst of Acquisition." This session will present how product and corporate acquisitions or divestitures impact the supply chain, outline best practices for smooth transitions and but explore how to navigate these changes.

The full agenda is available through the HDMA website. For registration information, contact HDMA's Meetings & Conferences Department at (703) 885-0278.
{top of page}

FDA Withdraws OxyContin Approval

As noted in the April 23 Weekly Digest, FDA approved Purdue Pharma's reformulated OxyContin labeling changes and this week published a notice that the request for withdrawal of original formulation OxyContin was found to be not for reasons for safety and effectiveness. The FDA formally withdrew approval of original OxyContin; effective August 7, distribution of this product across states without an approved application is illegal.

For more information, contact Allison Tuszynski.

FDA approves 32 mg Why stock the 32 mg tablet?

 

 EXALGO 32 mg was the median effective dose in the pivotal trial.*1

 
 

 You may already be distributing multiple 16 mg tablets to patients.

 
*

 Mean effective dose was 37.8 mg.2

 

EXALGO TABLET STRENGTHS2

Tablets shown are not actual size.

START STOCKING EXALGO 32 MG TODAY!

REFERENCES: 1. Hale M, Khan A, Kutch M, Li S. Once-daily OROS hydromorphone ER compared with placebo in opioid-tolerant patients with chronic low back pain. Curr Med Res Opin. 2010;26(6):1505-1518.
2. EXALGO  Prescribing Information.

800-778-7898 | www.EXALGO.com

COVIDIEN, COVIDIEN with logo and Covidien logo are U.S. and internationally
registered trademarks of Covidien AG.
EXALGO is a registered trademark of Mallinckrodt LLC.
  2012 Mallinckrodt LLC, a Covidien company.  MK20164 September 2012

To ensure that you receive future email from EXALGO, add us to your address book.
If you no longer wish to receive email from EXALGO, unsubscribe now.

 INDICATION

EXALGO  (hydromorphone HCI) Extended-Release
Tablets (CII) is indicated for the management of
moderate to severe pain in opioid tolerant patients
requiring continuous, around-the-clock opioid
analgesia for an extended period of time.

IMPORTANT RISK INFORMATION

WARNING: ABUSE POTENTIAL,
LIFE-THREATENING RESPIRATORY DEPRESSION, and ACCIDENTAL EXPOSURE

Abuse Potential

EXALGO contains hydromorphone, an opioid agonist and a Schedule II controlled substance with an abuse liability similar to other opioid agonists, legal or illicit. Assess each patient s risk for opioid abuse or addiction prior to prescribing EXALGO. The risk for opioid abuse is increased in patients with a personal or family history of substance abuse (including drug or alcohol abuse or addiction) or mental illness (e.g., major depressive disorder). Routinely monitor all patients receiving EXALGO for signs of misuse, abuse, and addiction during treatment.

Life-threatening Respiratory Depression

Respiratory depression, including fatal cases, may occur with use of EXALGO, even when the drug has been used as recommended and not misused or abused. EXALGO is for use in opioid tolerant patients only. Proper dosing and titration are essential and EXALGO should be prescribed only by healthcare professionals who are knowledgeable in the use of potent opioids for the management of chronic pain. Monitor for respiratory depression, especially during initiation of EXALGO or following a dose increase. Crushing, dissolving, or chewing the tablet can cause rapid release and absorption of a potentially fatal dose of hydromorphone.

Accidental Exposure

Accidental ingestion of EXALGO, especially in children, can result in a fatal overdose of hydromorphone.

 

 

 EXALGO is contraindicated in:
- Opioid non-tolerant patients. Fatal respiratory
  depression could occur in patients who are not
  opioid tolerant.

- Patients with significant respiratory depression

- Patients with acute or severe bronchial asthma in
  an unmonitored setting or in the absence of
  resuscitative equipment

- Patients with known or suspected paralytic ileus

- Patients who have had surgical procedures and/or
  underlying disease resulting in narrowing of the
  gastrointestinal tract, or have  blind loops  of the
  gastrointestinal tract or gastrointestinal obstruction

- Patients with hypersensitivity (e.g., anaphylaxis) to
  hydromorphone or sulfite-containing medications



 
 

 EXALGO is indicated for opioid tolerant patients only. Patients considered opioid tolerant are those who are taking at least 60 mg oral morphine per day, 25 mcg transdermal fentanyl/hour, 30 mg oral oxycodone/day, 8 mg oral hydromorphone/day, 25 mg oral oxymorphone/day or an equianalgesic dose of another opioid, for a week or longer.



 
 

 EXALGO is not intended for use as an as-needed analgesic and is not indicated for the management of acute or postoperative pain. It is contraindicated in patients who need management of mild pain or pain not expected to persist.



 
 

 Avoid concurrent use of alcohol and EXALGO. Concurrent use of EXALGO with CNS depressants, including alcohol, increases risk of respiratory depression, hypotension, and profound sedation, potentially resulting in coma or death. EXALGO may impair the ability to drive a car or operate machinery.



 
 

 Not intended in patients who have received MAO inhibitors within 14 days of starting EXALGO.



 
 

 Use with caution and in reduced doses in older or debilitated patients, as well as patients with renal or hepatic insufficiency, Addison s disease, delirium tremens, myxedema or hypothyroidism, prostatic hypertrophy or urethral stricture, toxic psychosis. May aggravate convulsions in patients with convulsive disorders; may induce or aggravate seizures in some clinical settings. Consider use of an alternate analgesic in patients with severe renal impairment.



 
 

 Respiratory depression, which occurs more frequently in elderly or debilitated patients, is the chief hazard with EXALGO.



 
 

 Serious adverse events could also include hypotensive effects, GI effects, cardiac arrest from overdose and precipitation of withdrawal. Most common adverse events (>10%) seen in clinical studies (N=2474) were: constipation (31%), nausea (28%), vomiting, somnolence, headache, asthenia and dizziness.



 
 

 Use EXALGO with extreme caution in patients susceptible to intracranial effects of CO2 retention.



 
 

 Do not abruptly discontinue EXALGO.


 

See additional Important Risk Information, including boxed warning, in Full Prescribing Information and Medication Guide.

Subject: FW: Talking Points, Updating DEA on Mallinckrodt SOM Activities - Communication with Distributors
From: "spaulding, eileen l."
Date: Tue, 30 Nov 2010 14:04:36 -0600
To: "harper, karen"


Karen,
 
I spoke with DI Heather White - DEA Albany this morning regarding the attached talking points and she provided the following feedback:
DI White expressed concern about Mallinckrodt conducting on-site visits with these distributors as part of our SOM activities.  I explained in detail that this was an effort in due diligence and in no way would Mallinckrodt authorize/approve or give the impression of authorization as to their individual SOM programs, that it was simply another step in our process to ensure that our products were being handled appropriately all throughout the supply chain.

DI White reviewed the difference between excessive orders/purchase reports which were required by DEA in the past and a suspicious order.  Stated that excessive order reports are no longer required by DEA and that if an order is determined to be suspicious, we are not permitted to ship.  I stated that Mallinckrodt understood the difference and asked for an elaboration on what is considered "suspicious" of which her comment was 100,000 doses of Oxycodone to Florida in one month she would consider "suspicious", she did comment any further.

DI White gave indication that she was going to make some phone calls to her colleagues in the Cincinnati and St. Louis field division offices regarding the recent DEA initiative of "know you're customer's customer"


Should DI White contact me regarding this subject, I will be sure to keep you informed.

Eileen
