FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE
Date: June 15, 2010
Contact: Rich Isaacson
Number: (313) 234-4310

Michigan Pharmaceutical Supplier S Dea License Suspended
-Harvard Drug Group, LLC distributed 13 million doses of Oxy from 2008-2010

JUN 15 -- (Detroit, MI)   Robert L. Corso, Special Agent in Charge of the Detroit Field Division, Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) announced today the Immediate Suspension of the Federal Controlled Substance Registration of Harvard Drug Group, LLC.

Harvard Drug Group, LLC, based in Livonia, Michigan, has been the subject of a DEA investigation that alleges the company was selling large quantities of controlled substances to pharmacies, primarily in Florida. The investigation has revealed that several of Harvard s largest purchasers of oxycodone were engaged in schemes to dispense controlled substances based on prescriptions that were written for other than legitimate medical purposes. The investigation revealed that Harvard Drug Group, LLC, distributed over 13 million dosage units of oxycodone products to customers in the two year time frame between March 2008 and March 2010.

Robert L. Corso, stated,  Pharmaceutical companies have a responsibility to ensure that the drugs they sell don t end up in the hands of drug traffickers or businesses that are conducting their business illegally. Harvard Drug Group, LLC, should have known, based on the large, frequent quantities, that their customers were diverting oxycodone into arenas that were not legitimate. Today s action sends the message that the DEA is working hard to hold accountable those companies that are operating in a manner outside of federal law.

DEA s action suspends Harvard Drug Group, LLC s DEA Certificate of Registration in accordance with an Immediate Suspension Order and pursuant to Sections 303 and 304 of the Controlled Substances Act, Title 21, Sections 823 and 824. The DEA s investigation of Harvard Drug Group, LLC, has determined that the continued registration of this company constitutes an imminent danger to public health and safety.

Harvard Drug Group, LLC. received written notice of the factual and legal basis for this action. In addition, Harvard Drug Group, LLC will be given an opportunity for an administrative hearing within the next 60 days. After the hearing, the DEA Deputy Administrator will make a final decision on whether Harvard Drug Group, LLC registration should be permanently revoked. This decision will be published in the Federal Register.

Oxycodone is the generic name of an addictive prescription painkiller that is classified under federal narcotics laws as a Schedule II controlled substance. Oxycodone is typically legally prescribed to combat acute, severe pain for legitimate medical purposes. Accordingly, these prescriptions are usually for a modest number of pills to be taken over a short period of time.

This is an ongoing investigation. Please forward any questions to DEA Detroit Public Information Officer Rich Isaacson at (313) 234-4310.

From: Kelly A. Ryan
Sent: Tuesday, October 02, 2012 4:48 PM

Subject: Pharmacy Advisory Committee meeting summary

Hi all  

I covered the Medicaid Pharmacy Advisory Committee meeting today.  As is often the case, much of the meeting was either a reiteration of updates we are already aware of or discussion of issues from a very pharmacist-specific perspective, but there are always a few helpful tidbits that come out of the meetings.  Today was no exception here is a quick rundown, let me know if you have any questions or need more detail on any of the below (or anything else on the attached agenda):

BNE I-STOP update:

-          Some schedule changes from I-STOP will be effective on Nov 25 (these include the changes that were already made on the federal level and were just incorporated into state statute via I-STOP).  The biggies, hydrocodone to schedule II and tramadol to schedule IV, are effective February 23, 2013.  There will be further information and a set of Q&As posted on the BNE site shortly   I will monitor and circulate when this pops up.

o   One interesting point   when hydrocodone moves to schedule II, all outstanding refills will be immediately void, there is no transition time for existing scripts.

-          Members have been appointed to the I-STOP workgroup (I caught a couple of names only because Larry Mokhiber mentioned them during his separate update).  It is expected that the first workgroup meeting will be scheduled very shortly.  I caught the BNE representative off line and asked if the meetings will be public   her first response was no and then she said she didn t know.  It sounds like at least some members are representatives of state agencies so I m surprised it s not a public body   not sure if it s really our fight, but it would certainly be nice to monitor policy discussions that are going to directly impact regs and I-STOP implementation.

-          An interactive map re Rx disposal sites is up on the BNE website.  Further action on this item is on hold pending federal regulations (currently in progress) re drug disposal

Board of Pharmacy update:

-          Regs re pharmacists giving shingles vaccine will be published on an emergency basis tomorrow

-          Public sessions regarding the Limited English Proficiency Rx labeling law are being held (Albany on 10/11, NYC on 10/25)

EXALGO(r) (HYDROMORPHONE HCI) EXTENDED-RELEASE TABLETS (CII) DELIVERS TRUE ONCE-DAILY DOSING WITH STEADY PLASMA LEVELS AROUND THE CLOCK.

* EXALGO reaches steady-state concentrations in 3 to 4 days, reducing peaks and troughs

At steady state, once-daily EXALGO provides a more stable and consistent concentration than IR hydromorphone.1,2
[http://www.alertmarketing.com/email/JHCE/15840Covidien(Exalgo)MD_LG/w4/images/54477_covexa_e_md_alert2_lo8_04.jpg]

Once-daily EXALGO is available in 8 mg, 12 mg, and 16 mg tablets that can be used in combination to achieve the desired
dosing strength; tablets should be swallowed whole.

INDICATION
EXALGO is an extended-release oral formulation of hydromorphone hydrochloride indicated for the management of moderate to severe pain in opioid tolerant patients requiring continuous, around-the-clock opioid analgesia for an extended period of time.

IMPORTANT RISK INFORMATION
[http://www.alertmarketing.com/email/JHCE/15840Covidien(Exalgo)MD_LG/w4/images/54477_covexa_e_md_alert2_lo8_06t.jpg][http://www.alertmarketing.com/email/JHCE/15840Covidien(Exalgo)MD_LG/w4/images/54477_covexa_e_md_alert2_lo8_06m.jpg]

[http://www.alertmarketing.com/email/JHCE/15840Covidien(Exalgo)MD_LG/w4/images/54477_covexa_e_md_alert2_lo8_07.jpg]


WARNING: POTENTIAL FOR ABUSE, IMPORTANCE OF
PROPER PATIENT SELECTION AND LIMITATIONS OF USE

Potential for Abuse
EXALGO contains hydromorphone, an opioid agonist and a Schedule II controlled substance with an abuse liability similar to other opioid analgesics. EXALGO can be abused in a manner similar to other opioid agonists, legal or illicit. These risks should be considered when administering, prescribing, or dispensing EXALGO in situations where the healthcare professional is concerned about increased risk of misuse, abuse, or diversion. Schedule II opioid substances which include hydromorphone, morphine, oxycodone, fentanyl, oxymorphone and methadone have the highest potential for abuse and risk of fatal overdose due to respiratory depression.

Proper Patient Selection
EXALGO is an extended-release formulation of hydromorphone hydrochloride indicated for the management of moderate to severe pain in opioid tolerant patients when a continuous around-the-clock opioid analgesic is needed for an extended period of time. Patients considered opioid tolerant are those who are taking at least 60 mg oral morphine per day, 25 mcg transdermal fentanyl/hour, 30 mg oral oxycodone/day, 8 mg oral hydromorphone/day, 25 mg oral oxymorphone/day or an equianalgesic dose of another opioid, for a week or longer.
EXALGO is for use in opioid tolerant patients only.
Fatal respiratory depression could occur in patients who are not opioid tolerant.
Accidental consumption of EXALGO, especially in children, can result in a fatal overdose of hydromorphone.

Limitations of Use
EXALGO is not indicated for the management of acute or postoperative pain.
EXALGO is not intended for use as an as-needed analgesic.
EXALGO tablets are to be swallowed whole and are not to be broken, chewed, dissolved, crushed or injected. Taking broken, chewed, dissolved or crushed EXALGO or its contents leads to rapid release and absorption of a potentially fatal dose of hydromorphone.




[http://www.alertmarketing.com/email/JHCE/15840Covidien(Exalgo)MD_LG/w4/images/54477_covexa_e_md_alert2_lo8_08t.jpg][http://www.alertmarketing.com/email/JHCE/15840Covidien(Exalgo)MD_LG/w4/images/54477_covexa_e_md_alert2_lo8_08m.jpg]



*


EXALGO is also contraindicated in patients who:
- need management of mild pain or pain not expected
  to persist
- have significant impaired respiratory function including
  those with acute or severe bronchial asthma or hypercarbia
- have or are suspected to have paralytic ileus
- have narrowed or obstructed gastrointestinal tract
  including those from previous surgery or "blind loops"
  in the GI tract
- have known hypersensitivity to any components including
  hydromorphone hydrochloride and sulfites


*


Avoid concurrent use of alcohol and EXALGO. Concurrent use of EXALGO with CNS depressants, including alcohol, increases risk of respiratory depression, hypotension, and profound sedation, potentially resulting in coma or death. EXALGO may impair the ability to drive a car or operate machinery.


*


Not intended in patients who have received MAO inhibitors within 14 days of starting EXALGO.


*


Use with caution and in reduced doses in older or debilitated patients, as well as patients with renal or hepatic insufficiency, Addison's disease, delirium tremens, myxedema or hypothyroidism, prostatic hypertrophy or urethral stricture, toxic psychosis. May aggravate convulsions in patients with convulsive disorders; may induce or aggravate seizures in some clinical settings. Consider use of an alternate analgesic in patients with severe renal impairment.


*


Respiratory depression, which occurs more frequently in elderly or debilitated patients, is the chief hazard with EXALGO.


*


Serious adverse events could also include hypotensive effects, GI effects, cardiac arrest from overdose and precipitation of withdrawal. Most common adverse events (>10%) seen in clinical studies (N=2474) were: constipation (31%), nausea (28%), vomiting, somnolence, headache, asthenia and dizziness.


*


Use EXALGO with extreme caution in patients susceptible
to intracranial effects of CO2 retention.


*


Do not abruptly discontinue EXALGO

The moment is right for delivering the EXALGO  message.

News about the Opana  ER potential supply disruption is out. Physicians and pharmacists have received communication from Endo Pharmaceuticals about supply issues. We have followed up with e-mail alerts and direct mail that position EXALGO as a reasonable alternative to Opana ER to consider for opioid-tolerant patients.



Introduce your customers to Laverne.

We mentioned in a previous message that a new sales tool was in the works. Production of the  Laverne  patient profile was expedited since her story is perfect for sharing with customers who may be seeking alternatives for their Opana ER patients.



As a patient who is experiencing difficulty with her Opana ER regimen, Laverne represents a potential candidate for switching to EXALGO. With the supply disruption news, her situation is ideal for steering prescribers toward a conversation about EXALGO.



Here s how  Laverne  will help you:

  Laverne s medical and clinical history highlights her escalating pain and various side effects while on Opana ER

  The Hale study highlights the 50% reduction in mean pain intensity and contrasts median pain intensity change for EXALGO vs placebo

  Reduced peaks and troughs chart from the Moore study illustrates steady plasma concentrations over 24 hours and supports the once daily dosing

  The molecule matching story explains the logic behind switching to a dissimilar molecule

  Conversion information (remember C-A-T) plus a dosing conversion chart specifically for patients taking Opana ER familiarizes prescribers with steps for converting to EXALGO

  Managed care information overcomes perceived financial barriers to prescribing



Put our STAMP on it.

The Opana ER potential supply disruption message strategy has been on the fast track and it s critical to take advantage of this unique opportunity while you can. Since the Laverne profile was developed using the STAMP messaging flow, using STAMP for the core of your delivery (Situation-Trials-Appropriate Patient-Managed Care Coverage-Proper Conversion and Titration) is intuitive, just be sure to weave in the Opana ER potential supply disruption message.



Our objective is to move EXALGO from the last option to the first alternative. Endo s supply constraint provides us an incredible opportunity to do just that by establishing the clinical rationale for EXALGO for patients like Laverne, Tom and Eva.



Let this role-play video be your guide.

For ideas on how to capitalize on the Opana ER potential supply disruption, click here to view the role-playing video<https://www.compliancewire.com/Secure/login.aspx> created especially for the Laverne message. Watch this video to help you create a framework for a conversation. Then customize your message based on your knowledge of your customer.  Please note the video will be on Compliance Wire the site for three weeks.



Remember, you are providing a potential solution to what may be a frustrating problem for physicians and their opioid-tolerant patients. Use this opportunity to establish your commitment to supporting their needs.



Good selling!



The EXALGO Marketing Team

Subject: Summary: Reference Management Software/Product Bibliographies Meeting



 

Good afternoon,

 

It was nice to talk with you all today; I think it was a productive conversation.  Below I’ve included a summary of our discussion along with action items (in bold.)  Tina – we had one question about the approval process for a server-based reference management system; see point three below.

 

Meeting Objectives

·        Reference Management Software – Status Update (Lanham)

o   Requirements Document (R&D, Library Services, Medical Affairs)

o   Procurement RFP with Jenn Roberts

o   Dates for Vendor Capabilities Demonstration

·        Product Bibliography Development (Decker / Hendershot)

o   Identify Products

o   Develop Search Strategy and Bibliography Process

o   Evaluate Need for RSS Feeds / Alerts

 

 

Discussion summary and action items:

1.      Patrick will tie John and Alicia into the Acetaminophen IV alert which is currently distributed to PV.  Patrick will be the main contact for working with Global Med Affairs to develop search strategies/strings for GMA’s literature needs.

a.      There was discussion that search strategies need to be fairly broad; false positives are preferred over never knowing a piece of literature exists. 

b.      The question arose – who would vet the results?  Alicia was volunteered.

 

2.      Erin will forward the NERAC search information from Cadence to Patrick for his reference.

 

3.      Patrick will look into pricing for desktop copies of Reference Manager (RefMan) and EndNote.  Erin will purchase once she’s returned from vacation (July 23.)

a.      The strategy discussed:  get access to the needed software on John and Alicia’s computers, so they can start working with the Cadence literature.  After an unidentified period of time trying out/using both systems, a preference should be identified.  That preference will need to go through the proper channels for addition onto MNK servers.  The thought was that we could buy what is needed now, and then pursue the lengthier process of approvals for expanded licenses and server integration. 

b.      GMA’s preference and need for a robust, server-based reference management solution was discussed.  A solution such as EndNote or Reference Manager will better fit this need than RefWorks.

c.      Question for Tina:  Is an RFP process needed, or the IS Steering Committee review?  Or both?

 

4.      Erin will run a historical report of Reprints Desk Cadence orders; she now an administrator for the “Cadence” Reprints Desk account.  This is in an effort to find out if Cadence paid royalties on the est. 4000 articles.

 

5.      Erin will reach out to Jackie Evans-Shield to discuss MSL information needs, and how the library can support them.  Along those lines, we discussed a library presentation to MSLs, led by Patrick and/or Phyllis.

 

6.      John suggested that the library understand how Alicia uses the software PM Solutions and what it does.   

 

Please add anything I may have forgotten.

 

Thanks,

Erin

PREDICTABLE. RELIABLE. AVAILABLE.
ISN'T THAT WHAT PATIENTS WANT IN A CHRONIC PAIN MEDICATION?



EXALGO(r) (HYDROMORPHONE HCI) EXTENDED-RELEASE TABLETS (CII) DELIVERS TRUE ONCE-DAILY DOSING WITH STEADY PLASMA LEVELS AROUND THE CLOCK.

* EXALGO reaches steady-state concentrations in 3 to 4 days, reducing peaks and troughs

At steady state, once-daily EXALGO provides a more stable and consistent concentration than IR hydromorphone.1,2
[http://www.alertmarketing.com/email/JHCE/15840Covidien(Exalgo)MD_LG/w4/images/54477_covexa_e_md_alert2_lo8_04.jpg]

Once-daily EXALGO is available in 8 mg, 12 mg, and 16 mg tablets that can be used in combination to achieve the desired
dosing strength; tablets should be swallowed whole.

INDICATION
EXALGO is an extended-release oral formulation of hydromorphone hydrochloride indicated for the management of moderate to severe pain in opioid tolerant patients requiring continuous, around-the-clock opioid analgesia for an extended period of time.

IMPORTANT RISK INFORMATION
[http://www.alertmarketing.com/email/JHCE/15840Covidien(Exalgo)MD_LG/w4/images/54477_covexa_e_md_alert2_lo8_06t.jpg][http://www.alertmarketing.com/email/JHCE/15840Covidien(Exalgo)MD_LG/w4/images/54477_covexa_e_md_alert2_lo8_06m.jpg]

[http://www.alertmarketing.com/email/JHCE/15840Covidien(Exalgo)MD_LG/w4/images/54477_covexa_e_md_alert2_lo8_07.jpg]


WARNING: POTENTIAL FOR ABUSE, IMPORTANCE OF
PROPER PATIENT SELECTION AND LIMITATIONS OF USE

Potential for Abuse
EXALGO contains hydromorphone, an opioid agonist and a Schedule II controlled substance with an abuse liability similar to other opioid analgesics. EXALGO can be abused in a manner similar to other opioid agonists, legal or illicit. These risks should be considered when administering, prescribing, or dispensing EXALGO in situations where the healthcare professional is concerned about increased risk of misuse, abuse, or diversion. Schedule II opioid substances which include hydromorphone, morphine, oxycodone, fentanyl, oxymorphone and methadone have the highest potential for abuse and risk of fatal overdose due to respiratory depression.

Proper Patient Selection
EXALGO is an extended-release formulation of hydromorphone hydrochloride indicated for the management of moderate to severe pain in opioid tolerant patients when a continuous around-the-clock opioid analgesic is needed for an extended period of time. Patients considered opioid tolerant are those who are taking at least 60 mg oral morphine per day, 25 mcg transdermal fentanyl/hour, 30 mg oral oxycodone/day, 8 mg oral hydromorphone/day, 25 mg oral oxymorphone/day or an equianalgesic dose of another opioid, for a week or longer.
EXALGO is for use in opioid tolerant patients only.
Fatal respiratory depression could occur in patients who are not opioid tolerant.
Accidental consumption of EXALGO, especially in children, can result in a fatal overdose of hydromorphone.

Limitations of Use
EXALGO is not indicated for the management of acute or postoperative pain.
EXALGO is not intended for use as an as-needed analgesic.
EXALGO tablets are to be swallowed whole and are not to be broken, chewed, dissolved, crushed or injected. Taking broken, chewed, dissolved or crushed EXALGO or its contents leads to rapid release and absorption of a potentially fatal dose of hydromorphone.




[http://www.alertmarketing.com/email/JHCE/15840Covidien(Exalgo)MD_LG/w4/images/54477_covexa_e_md_alert2_lo8_08t.jpg][http://www.alertmarketing.com/email/JHCE/15840Covidien(Exalgo)MD_LG/w4/images/54477_covexa_e_md_alert2_lo8_08m.jpg]



*


EXALGO is also contraindicated in patients who:
- need management of mild pain or pain not expected
  to persist
- have significant impaired respiratory function including
  those with acute or severe bronchial asthma or hypercarbia
- have or are suspected to have paralytic ileus
- have narrowed or obstructed gastrointestinal tract
  including those from previous surgery or "blind loops"
  in the GI tract
- have known hypersensitivity to any components including
  hydromorphone hydrochloride and sulfites


*


Avoid concurrent use of alcohol and EXALGO. Concurrent use of EXALGO with CNS depressants, including alcohol, increases risk of respiratory depression, hypotension, and profound sedation, potentially resulting in coma or death. EXALGO may impair the ability to drive a car or operate machinery.


*


Not intended in patients who have received MAO inhibitors within 14 days of starting EXALGO.


*


Use with caution and in reduced doses in older or debilitated patients, as well as patients with renal or hepatic insufficiency, Addison's disease, delirium tremens, myxedema or hypothyroidism, prostatic hypertrophy or urethral stricture, toxic psychosis. May aggravate convulsions in patients with convulsive disorders; may induce or aggravate seizures in some clinical settings. Consider use of an alternate analgesic in patients with severe renal impairment.


*


Respiratory depression, which occurs more frequently in elderly or debilitated patients, is the chief hazard with EXALGO.


*


Serious adverse events could also include hypotensive effects, GI effects, cardiac arrest from overdose and precipitation of withdrawal. Most common adverse events (>10%) seen in clinical studies (N=2474) were: constipation (31%), nausea (28%), vomiting, somnolence, headache, asthenia and dizziness.


*


Use EXALGO with extreme caution in patients susceptible
to intracranial effects of CO2 retention.


*


Do not abruptly discontinue EXALGO

Subject: CONFIDENTIAL  Revised Document:  Project Oxygen DEA Regulations
From: "Harper, Karen" <karen.harper@mallinckrodt.com>
Date: Wed, 28 Sep 2016 08:41:49 -0500
To: "Lohman, Donald A" <donald.lohman@mallinckrodt.com>


 

Don,

I have conferred with Mark Caverly on Project Oxygen

Depending on the terms of the arrangement ---

 

MNK complete exit of the product line would lead to MNK surrender of annual quota for the product and removal of the drug code from MNK manufacturing DEA Certificate of Registration.

Upon further review of the DEA regulations, it has been determined that the requirements in 21CFR 1301.52 (complete ending inventory on the date of transfer, notification to DEA local office, etc.) are not applicable if MNK continues to maintain its registration to manufacture other CII products at the impacted facility.

Therefore, from the Controlled Substances Compliance perspective, no special recordkeeping is required and the exit of the business and shipment of the final inventory would be documented as a normal distribution only.

 

MNK continues manufacture of the product as contract manufacturer/toll manufacture

No changes to MNK quota process except the 3rd party would be required to provide sales forecasts to MNK as documentation of quota requirement.

MNK would retain the drug code on MNK manufacturing CEA Certificate of Registration.

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

Karen Harper  |  Sr. Manager, Controlled Substances Compliance Group

From: mcaverly@us.imshealth.com [mailto:mcaverly@us.imshealth.com]
Sent: Tuesday, September 27, 2016 3:41 PM
To: Harper, Karen
Subject: RE: CONFIDENTIAL MALLINCKRODT INQUIRY: Transfer of a Product Line Within the Mallinckrodt Portfolio to Another DEA Registrant



 

Hi Karen.  Sale or transfer of one or more controlled substance product lines from Hobart would not invoke 1301.52 if Hobart continues manufacturing of other controlled substance products.  The only issue you should explore is a modification of the existing DEA registration should the product transfer result in a discontinuance of a specific Schedule(s).  For example, if Hobart will no longer manufacture any Schedule II products after the transfer you should consider modifying the existing DEA registration and drop Schedule II.  Other actions, such as returning unused quota to DEA, should also be performed.  

 

DEA will require a modification request be made in writing to the local DEA office if in the middle of a registration cycle.  At renewal, you can just not check that box for the applicable Schedule.

 

Thanks,

Mark

 

From: Harper, Karen [mailto:Karen.Harper@mallinckrodt.com]
Sent: Tuesday, September 27, 2016 4:10 PM
To: Mark CAVERLY <mcaverly@us.imshealth.com>
Subject: CONFIDENTIAL MALLINCKRODT INQUIRY: Transfer of a Product Line Within the Mallinckrodt Portfolio to Another DEA Registrant



 

Mark,

Mallinckrodt is evaluating the possibility of transferring a segment of existing business (methadose liquid and methadone tablet) to a third party DEA registrant.

At such time of potential transfer, Mallinckrodt Hobart will discontinue manufacture of this product line but continue production of other controlled substances.

 

Mallinckrodt will retain its existing DEA Manufacturer Certificate of Registration at the Hobart facility for other products, so there is technically no termination of registration, no transfer of registration, no distribution upon discontinuance of business (except the exit of a segment of the business).

 

Don and I have been asked to explore the regulatory requirements around such a move.

Would the provisions of  1301.52 apply in this circumstance?                             

OR would the transaction simply be a distribution of product?

 

MODIFICATION, TRANSFER AND TERMINATION OF REGISTRATION
 1301.52 Termination of registration; transfer of registration; distribution upon discontinuance of business.

(d) Any registrant desiring to discontinue business activities altogether or with respect to controlled substance (by transferring such business activities to another person) shall submit in person or by registered or certified mail, return receipt requested, to the Special Agent in Charge in his/her area, at least 14 days in advance of the date of the proposed transfer (unless the Special Agent in Charge waives this time limitation in individual instances), the following information:
(1) The name, address, registration number, and authorized business activity of the registrant discontinuing the business (registrant-transferor);
(2) The name, address, registration number, and authorized business activity of the person acquiring the business (registrant-transferee);
(3) Whether the business activities will be continued at the location registered by the person discontinuing business, or moved to another location (if the latter, the address of the new location should be listed);
(4) Whether the registrant-transferor has a quota to manufacture or procure any controlled substance listed in Schedule I or II (if so, the basic class or class of the substance should be indicated); and
(5) The date on which the transfer of controlled substances will occur.
(e) Unless the registrant-transferor is informed by the Special Agent in Charge, before the date on which the transfer was stated to occur, that the transfer may not occur, the registrant-transferor may distribute (without being registered to distribute) controlled substances in his/her possession to the registrant-transferee in accordance with the following:
(1) On the date of transfer of the controlled substances, a complete inventory of all controlled substances being transferred shall be taken in accordance with Sec. 1304.11 of this chapter. This inventory shall serve as the final inventory of the registrant-transferor and the initial inventory of the registrant-transferee, and a copy of the inventory shall be included in the records of each person. It shall not be necessary to file a copy of the inventory with the Administration unless requested by the Special Agent in Charge. Transfers of any substances listed in Schedule I or II shall require the use of order forms in accordance with part 1305 of this chapter.
(2) On the date of transfer of the controlled substances, all records required to be kept by the registrant-transferor with reference to the controlled substances being transferred, under part 1304 of this chapter, shall be transferred to the registrant-transferee. Responsibility for the accuracy of records prior to the date of transfer remains with the transferor, but responsibility for custody and maintenance shall be upon the transferee.
(3) In the case of registrants required to make reports pursuant to part 1304 of this chapter, a report marked "Final" will be prepared and submitted by the registrant-transferor showing the disposition of all the controlled substances for which a report is required; no additional report will be required from him, if no further transactions involving controlled substances are consummated by him. The initial report of the registrant-transferee shall account for transactions beginning with the day next succeeding the date of discontinuance or transfer of business by the transferor-registrant and the substances transferred to him shall be reported as receipts in his/her initial report.

    I share your concern. 

    When we are talking about "release" are we talking about DDMAC submission? If that is it we should have been 
    able to submit to DDMAC, if the need was indicated as urgent, when all the submission documents were made 
    available to Penny by Marketing. If the DDMAC submission was held up and we could have done it faster then 
    how we all can improve that needs to be discussed and fixed. 

    If we are talking about "release" as the ability to have these panels manufactured and shipped to the sales force, 
    I, again, share your concern. Once we approve a piece it should be able to be manufactured. If that didn't 
    happen for some reason I apologize. The intent was that the approved table top graphics could not be USED by 
    the sales force until the memo was finalized, NOT that the pieces could not be printed. 

    If we are talking about "release" as the ability of the sales force to use a piece then there are two 
    components. The one that comes into play most often is DDMAC submission, which we have discussed 
    above. Unless implementation guides or memos are required, the sales force can use a piece, from our 
    perspective, the day after submission to DDMAC. If a memo is required to go along with the piece, all that is 
    necessary is that the memo be approved by PARC and sent to the sales force before the piece is 
    used. This approval is almost ALWAYS done on the fly, either electronically or as an unscheduled review 
    sandwiched into an already full meeting, very similar to what we did with the PENNSAID journal ad that we 
    received, I think, on Tuesday and that we approved at yesterday's packed meeting. 

    Kevin, we only ask for a memo when absolutely necessary but, frankly, our interpretation of the information we 
    were getting led us to believe there was flexibility in how the sales force could use a piece that we approved as 
    one contiguous unit. ..and we wanted some training (in the form of a memo) on how this graphic was to be 
    used. In fact, from our conversation today, that flexibility DOES exist as reps could, very easily, put the panels 
    together in any order and might only use one or two panels instead of the required 3 panels (giving us less than 
    required fair balance). Heck, the way I read Julie's memo, it was even theoretically possible, without some 
    instruction, that EXALGO and PENNSAID panels could accidentally be used together. 

    All this is with the backdrop of repeated Marketing pushback when I have asked for the simple language to be 
    placed on all panels of a multiple panel display: "Panel _ of. Only to be used in order and with the other 



                                                MNKOI 0004023123 

panels". I have seen this done a number of times in this industry at meetings where companies wanted to make 
sure that their materials were used as approved. As we did not have that we chose the fastest route: electronic 
review of a memo that explained how to use the pieces that we reviewed AND approved to be used in a particular 
way. The approval of this memo took place in about 90 minutes this morning, based on Penny's original e- 
mail. The approval of the memo was never intended to be an impediment to manufacturing the panels. It was 
always intended to be a required element of the training on how to properly use these pieces before they were 
used by the sales force. 

As I told you this morning, some of the need for the original discussion on this issue was due to PARC not 
completely understanding this table top graphic format and that a physical mockup might have been more 
helpful. My impression was that the pieces could be interchanged in some way but, frankly, I did not even get, 
for whatever reason, that the actual Marketing panels simply slid in and out of an existing three panel frame. 

So, if the production of the actual panels was held up then I apologize. We never intended that to be the 
case and I can't imagine a situation where PARC would ever hold up the production of Marketing materials until 
we had a related internal memo approved. However, we did intend that the USE of these graphics be dependent 
on the approval and dissemination of this internal memo, which we approved in a few minutes this 
morning. When the situation arises in the future, PARC will continue to require this as part of their approval for 
USE of pieces, but not production of those pieces. 

I share your frustration and apologize for any delay this has caused you and Marketing and will attempt to make 
sure we do a good job of servicing you guys, our customers, in the future. 

Have a good weekend. 


Dennis Nosco, PhD, RAC

First I would like to recognize the outstanding prescription demand you have generated in the most recent weeks.  We have just hit another all time high for EXALGO at 3,934 adjusted prescriptions for the week ending December 2, 2011.  Congratulations and great work!

Secondly, I wanted to update you on a new formulation of Opana ER.  The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) announced today that it has approved a new formulation of Opana(r) ER designed to be crush-resistant.  Endo plans to transition in 2012 from the original formulation to the new formulation, which utilizes the proprietary INTAC(tm)  technology owned by Grunenthal, a partner in the development of the product.  The new formulation will continue to be called Opana ER with the same dosage strengths, color and packaging and similar tablet size and shape.  Also, the FDA approval signifies that there is no significant difference in the rate and extent of absorption of the therapeutic ingredient between this new formulation and the original formulation of Opana ER.

Endo also announced that the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office will issue patent number 8,075,872 on Dec. 13, 2011.  The patent covers the new formulation of Opana(r) ER and is expected to provide protection until November 2023.  This new patent will be listed in the FDA's Orange Book with respect to the new formulation of Opana ER.
Because the new formulation of Opana ER still contains oxymorphone, a CII controlled substance, it remains a Schedule II opioid with all the attendant risks, specifically that the drug has a high potential for abuse. Use, misuse, or abuse of the drug may lead to physical dependence or addiction.  In addition, alteration of the tablet in any manner poses significant risks of overdose and death.  It has not been established that this new formulation of Opana ER is less subject to misuse, abuse, diversion, overdose, or addiction; therefore, there should be no claims or assertions made relative to the new formulation and its impact to abuse or tampering.
It is imperative that you continue to leverage the S.T.A.M.P. messaging.  We have received an unprecedented number of success stories about the impact this new message is having with your customers.  Specifically, continue to use the Patient Profiles to drive discussions centered on identifying  Appropriate patients for EXALGO and ensuring your physicians have a thorough understanding of Proper Conversion and Titration. Cc: Blumberg, Alan L
Subject: RE: Endo Health Solutions; Q2 2012 Earnings Call Summary

OK, let's level set here:

First, as far as I know OPDP NEVER approves promotional material.  They provide advisory comments.  If you take those comments and operate within them you have a safe harbor, at least until they tell you that they have changed their minds, which they sometimes do. Even in cases like accelerated review (I think this is the CFR type) where pre-submission of launch marketing materials is required, you don't get an approval or clearance, you just get advisory comments that you have to interpret.

The standard misnomer is that FDA "approves" or gives "pre-clearance" to marketing materials that are submitted to them.  That is very common with non-regulatory types and a basic mistake made in interpretation of what advisory comments mean.  I have even seen this mistake made when materials are just routinely submitted at time of first use.  In the latter case, people who don't know any better think that if you don't hear anything it means that FDA has 'approved' your material.  Even the terminology "pre-clearance" which people often use, is not appropriate.  So, Tammy's bullet below is probably just some executive mis-speaking.

Second, PARC has continued to encourage Marketing to submit materials for advisory comment.  In that regard we would like these materials to be PARC-approved so that we stand the best chance to make a good impression with OPDP.    Marketing has not been willing to do this but PARC constantly tries to get them to change their mind.

Third, we don't know what was in their marketing materials that OPDP reviewed.  If it is a simple statement of physical properties that might have gotten through OPDP.  If they tried to link those to treatment benefit or safety (read: abuse deterrence or overdose avoidance), I doubt that would have gotten through.

Fourth, PARC's position has been that if language is REMOVED from the draft PI during FDA review division review of the application, it would be difficult to market to that information.  There are many examples where physical properties of drugs have been marketed to where those properties or comparisons to other drugs properties, are not specifically called out in our labeling without ever having been removed in labeling negotiations.  You generally can't claim safety or efficacy benefits of these physical properties if they are not addressed in your PI but you can generally list those attributes and allow the reader to digest and interpret the meaning for themselves.  The comment below that Tammy put together is most likely that situation, i.e., that they are just listing the properties.  Note that we already list physical properties, some in comparison to other drugs where that data exists, for a lot of our products including EXALGO, Optiray and Optimark.  Doing this for Ruby or Zircon should not present any issues as long as it is done correctly and in the correct context.

From what I have read below I don't see anything new to consider.  If Debra thinks there is, I would be happy to have a meeting to discuss this.

Press Release: Mallinckrodt Receives Patent from U.S. Patent and Trademark Office
(Dow Jones and Company, Inc.) Feb 25 08:30 AM EST

Mallinckrodt Receives Patent from U.S. Patent and Trademark Office

U.S. Patent covers the release profile of XARTEMIS(TM) XR (oxycodone hydrochloride and acetaminophen) Extended-Release Tablets (CII) DUBLIN--(BUSINESS WIRE)--February 25, 2014--

Mallinckrodt (NYSE: MNK) today announced that it was granted a patent from the United States Patent and Trademark Office which contains composition claims directed to unique design, formulation, pharmacokinetic, and release characteristics of XARTEMIS(TM) XR. XARTEMIS XR (formerly known as MNK-795) is an investigational extended-release oral formulation of oxycodone and acetaminophen that has been studied with twice daily dosing for the management of acute pain in a post-surgical model. If approved, XARTEMIS XR will be the first oxycodone and acetaminophen combination medication specifically designed with immediate- and extended-release components. The patent, U.S. Patent Number 8,658,631, was issued on February 25, 2014.

The release profile of XARTEMIS XR combines Mallinckrodt-proprietary technology and Depomed's advanced Acuform(R) drug delivery technology. Between the Mallinckrodt and Depomed patent families, Mallinckrodt believes XARTEMIS XR will have strong patent protection for its novel features.

"XARTEMIS XR, a key driver in our near-term pipeline, represents an important component of our strategy to unlock continued potential and grow our branded specialty pharmaceutical portfolio," said Mark Trudeau, President and Chief Executive Officer, Mallinckrodt. "Mallinckrodt's patent, which includes the product's release profile, underscores our ability to effectively leverage our core formulation capabilities and partnerships."

Acuform is a registered trademark of Depomed.

ABOUT MALLINCKRODT:

Mallinckrodt is a leading global specialty pharmaceuticals business that develops, manufactures, markets and distributes specialty pharmaceutical products and medical imaging agents. The company's Specialty Pharmaceuticals segment includes branded and specialty generic drugs, and the Global Medical Imaging segment includes contrast media and nuclear imaging agents. Mallinckrodt has approximately 5,500 employees worldwide with sales in roughly 70 countries. The company's fiscal 2013 revenue totaled $2.2 billion. To learn more about Mallinckrodt, visit www.mallinckrodt.com.

Subject: The Hill Op-Ed: Elderly Risk and Opioids



 

Colleagues,

 

On Monday, July 13, 2015, the White House will host its official Conference on Aging, a once-a-decade summit that addresses policy strategy to meet the needs of America s elderly population.

 

We were successful in arranging to have the attached op-ed run in Friday s publication of The Hill, a key inside-the-beltway newspaper that is closely read by Members of Congress and Staff.  The op-ed draws attention to the health threats posed to the elderly by the use of opioids and calls for an alternative to opioids, such as intravenous acetaminophen.  The op-ed s call to action is for a broad discussion throughout the healthcare community on expanding options for treating pain in elderly patients, beginning with next week s White House Conference on Aging.

 

This is but one of several immediate steps we re taking to educate Members of Congress and Staff, as well as key patient groups, on alternatives to opioids, elevating the urgency of the issue so that it s top of mind in the context of the on-going national opioid debate.  We ll also be highlighting the op-ed to key congressional offices, including the two drug caucuses and the Senate Aging committee, and policy makers at the state level.

Subject: [RxNews] N Engl J Med    From 2010 through 2013,	there was a notable downturn in abuse of prescription opioids and a	coincident increase in abuse of heroin in the United States
From: Coolidge <coolidge@dakota2k.net>
Date: Thu, 12 Nov 2015 01:33:44 +0000
To: NADDI <rxnews@listserve.com>


http://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMc1505541



Correspondence

Shifting Patterns of Prescription Opioid and Heroin Abuse in the United States

N Engl J Med 2015; 373:1789-1790October 29, 2015DOI: 10.1056/NEJMc1505541

Share:
{Facebook}
{Tweet}
{Google+}
{LinkedIn}




Article
To the Editor:

From 2010 through 2013, there was a notable downturn in abuse of prescription opioids and a coincident increase in abuse of heroin in the United States.1 Given that there is some evidence of a relationship between the two trends (e.g., some persons who abuse prescription opioids switch to heroin for a number of reasons and drug interchangeability has been observed),2-4 we sought to examine this relationship more closely, including the validity of reports suggesting regional differences in the balance between prescription opioid and heroin abuse.5

Data on opioid abuse in the previous month were collected quarterly from January 1, 2008, through September 31, 2014, with the use of self-administered surveys that were completed anonymously by independent cohorts of 15,227 patients with opioid dependence, as defined by the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 4th edition, who were entering nonmethadone-maintenance treatment programs throughout the United States. Of these patients, 267 agreed to online interviews to gather qualitative information in order to amplify and interpret findings from the structured national survey.

Figure 1Figure 1National Rates of Abuse of Opioids in the Previous Month among 15,227 Respondents. shows the unadjusted rates of abuse of prescription opioids only, abuse of prescription opioids and heroin, or abuse of heroin only among respondents who reported such abuse in the previous month from 2008 through 2014. Rates of exclusive prescription opioid abuse remained stable from 2008 through 2010, at 70%, but then decreased steadily, with an average annual reduction of 6.1%, to less than 50% in 2014. Conversely, concurrent abuse of both heroin and prescription opioids in the previous month increased, with an average annual increase of 10.3%, from 23.6% in 2008 to 41.8% in 2014. Although the exclusive use of heroin was low in this population, it more than doubled from 2008 through 2014 (from 4.3% to 9.0%).

The national data obscure important regional differences (Fig. S1 in the Supplementary Appendix, available with the full text of this letter at NEJM.org). The Northeast showed the most striking shifts in patterns of abuse. The West followed closely behind, with concurrent heroin and prescription opioid abuse surpassing exclusive prescription opioid abuse in 2014. The Midwest and South followed similar trends, with the latter showing exclusive prescription opioid abuse to be more prevalent than in any other region.

These findings suggest that as prescription opioid use has waned, concurrent heroin abuse has increased, with important, distinct regional variations. The factors contributing to these evolving changes are not well established. However, in our exploratory qualitative online survey of a subgroup of 267 patients, among the 129 respondents who reported abusing prescription opioids prior to heroin use, 73.0% (92 of 126 respondents) primarily cited practical factors, such as accessibility and cost, when explaining their transition to heroin. Three of the 129 respondents did not provide an explanation for their transition to heroin.


Theodore J. Cicero, Ph.D.
Matthew S. Ellis, M.P.E.
Jessie Harney, M.S.

13:16 ET 6/20/11 [StreetAccount] PFE Preview of upcoming FDA decision on Pfizer/Pain Therapeutic's Remoxy (abuse-resistant formulation oxycodone) for moderate to severe pain ($20.20 -$0.06)

The PDUFA date for PFE/PTIE's class 2 NDA resubmission for Remoxy <https://www.streetaccount.com/biotech_search_productname.aspx?product_id=6018&searchtype=drug_names>  (extended release, abuse-resistant formulation oxycodone) for moderate to severe pain is 23-June. StreetAccount notes that the Street is generally expecting a delay to approval (Complete Response Letter) based on 3-May guidance provided by Pfizer. 

*	Background: 

	*	This FDA decision follows a December 2008 Complete Response Letter (CRL) and December 2010 resubmission, deemed a complete, class 2 filing in January. The CRL requested no new clinical trials, and sought additional non-clinical, later determined to be six-month stability data. The sponsor also took steps to strengthen the resubmission by completing a likeability study (positive topline results reported 25-Apr) and a pharmacokinetic trial in volunteers. 
	*	On May 16, 2011, the FDA met with members of the Industry Working Group (IWG) and other sponsors of Long Acting and Extended Release opioid drugs. The purpose of the meeting was to discuss the next steps in implementing A Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS) for these products through a single shared system. 

		*	According to the FDA.gov website: "We continue to work on the Medication Guide Template and expect to be able to provide it by June 24, 2011." 

			*	StreetAccount notes that this is coincidentally one day after Pfizer's 23-Jun PDUFA date. 

*	Approval issues: 

	*	Recall that Pfizer warned, on its Q1 earnings call on May 3, that it was working to address a specific issue in the manufacturing section of the Remoxy application, as well as to understand any potential implications of FDA's recent class-wide REMS announcement for extended release opioids. Pfizer stated that these issues could delay the timing of approval or the launch of REMOXY. 

*	Leveraged: 

	*	Pfizer (PFE), via its $3.6B acquisition of King Pharmaceuticals, has worldwide commercialization rights, ex-Australia and New Zealand. 
	*	Pain Therapeutics (PTIE) is entitled to receive a 20% royalty except for the first $1B in cumulative net sales, which royalty is set at 15%; outside the US, the royalty rate is flat 10%. 
	*	Durect Corporation (DRRX) is entitled to a royalty of 6-11.5% of sales, paid by PFE and through PTIE supplemental to the royalty above, for the use of its Oradur technology. 

*	Competition: 

	*	Branded Extended Release Opioid Products listed by the FDA include JNJ's Duragesic and Exalgo (the latter with COV), ENDP's Opana ER, several privately-owned, as well as King Pharmaceuticals' (now part of Pfizer) Avinza and Embeda. 
	*	StreetAccount notes that ACUR/PFE's Oxecta (formerly Acurox), approved on 17-Jun, is an immediate release opioid (as opposed to extended release). 

*	Recent sell-side research, commentary: 

	*	BOAML noted on 16-May the Remoxy PDUFA as one of several potentially positive catalysts for shares for PFE. 
	*	UBS noted on 4-May that a "manufacturing delay seems likely", echoing management's remarks but notably more focused on the former warning versus the REMS-specific warning. 
	*	Wells Fargo noted on 3-May management's expectation for delay, due to the two issues mentioned above. 
	*	Goldman Sachs on 3-May projected revenues 2011-2016 of $22M, $85M, $228M, $358M, $441M and $475M. 
	*	Oppenheimer noted on 21-April in an ENDP note the potential approval of Remoxy as a competing drug to the Opana franchise. 
	*	Jefferies noted on 13-April in an ENDP note that Endo's Opana should be in "excellent shape with managed care (even with Remoxy entry)". 

Shares of PTIE are trading +4.1% to $8.99 ahead of the FDA decision, and in sympathy to Friday's FDA approval of ACUR's Oxecta, +24%.

INDICATION

EXALGO(r) (hydromorphone HCI) Extended-Release Tablets (CII) is indicated for the management of moderate to severe pain in opioid tolerant patients requiring continuous, around-the-clock opioid analgesia for an extended period of time.

IMPORTANT RISK INFORMATION

WARNING: POTENTIAL FOR ABUSE, IMPORTANCE OF PROPER PATIENT SELECTION AND LIMITATIONS OF USE


Abuse Potential

EXALGO contains hydromorphone, an opioid agonist and a Schedule II controlled substance with an abuse liability similar to other opioid agonists, legal or illicit. Assess each patient's risk for opioid abuse or addiction prior to prescribing EXALGO. The risk for opioid abuse is increased in patients with a personal or family history of substance abuse (including drug or alcohol abuse or addiction) or mental illness (e.g., major depressive disorder). Routinely monitor all patients receiving EXALGO for signs of misuse, abuse, and addiction during treatment.

Life-threatening Respiratory Depression

Respiratory depression, including fatal cases, may occur with use of EXALGO, even when the drug has been used as recommended and not misused or abused. EXALGO is for use in opioid tolerant patients only. Proper dosing and titration are essential and EXALGO should be prescribed only by healthcare professionals who are knowledgeable in the use of potent opioids for the management of chronic pain. Monitor for respiratory depression, especially during initiation of EXALGO or following a dose increase. Crushing, dissolving, or chewing the tablet can cause rapid release and absorption of a potentially fatal dose of hydromorphone.

Accidental Exposure

Accidental ingestion of EXALGO, especially in children, can result in a fatal overdose of hydromorphone.


*

EXALGO is contraindicated in:



-

Opioid non-tolerant patients. Fatal respiratory depression could occur in patients who are not opioid tolerant.

-

Patients with significant respiratory depression

-

Patients with acute or severe bronchial asthma in an unmonitored setting or in the absence of resuscitative equipment

-

Patients with known or suspected paralytic ileus

-

Patients who have had surgical procedures and/or underlying disease resulting in narrowing of the gastrointestinal tract, or have "blind loops" of the gastrointestinal tract or gastrointestinal obstruction

-

Patients with hypersensitivity (e.g., anaphylaxis) to hydromorphone or sulfite-containing medications


*

EXALGO is indicated for opioid tolerant patients only. Patients considered opioid tolerant are those who are taking at least 60 mg oral morphine per day, 25 mcg transdermal fentanyl/hour, 30 mg oral oxycodone/day, 8 mg oral hydromorphone/day, 25 mg oral oxymorphone/day or an equianalgesic dose of another opioid, for a week or longer.

*

EXALGO is not intended for use as an as-needed analgesic and is not indicated for the management of acute or postoperative pain. It is contraindicated in patients who need management of mild pain or pain not expected to persist.

*

Avoid concurrent use of alcohol and EXALGO. Concurrent use of EXALGO with CNS depressants, including alcohol, increases risk of respiratory depression, hypotension, and profound sedation, potentially resulting in coma or death. EXALGO may impair the ability to drive a car or operate machinery.

*

Not intended in patients who have received MAO inhibitors within 14 days of starting EXALGO.

*

Use with caution and in reduced doses in older or debilitated patients, as well as patients with renal or hepatic insufficiency, Addison's disease, delirium tremens, myxedema or hypothyroidism, prostatic hypertrophy or urethral stricture, toxic psychosis. May aggravate convulsions in patients with convulsive disorders; may induce or aggravate seizures in some clinical settings. Consider use of an alternate analgesic in patients with severe renal impairment.

*

Respiratory depression, which occurs more frequently in elderly or debilitated patients, is the chief hazard with EXALGO.

*

Serious adverse events could also include hypotensive effects, GI effects, cardiac arrest from overdose and precipitation of withdrawal. Most common adverse events (>10%) seen in clinical studies (N=2474) were: constipation (31%), nausea (28%), vomiting, somnolence, headache, asthenia and dizziness.

*

Use EXALGO with extreme caution in patients susceptible to intracranial effects of CO2 retention.

*

Do not abruptly discontinue EXALGO.



See additional Important Risk Information, including boxed warning, in Full Prescribing Information<http://pharmaceuticals.covidien.com/workarea/downloadasset.aspx?id=2147483728> and Medication Guide<http://pharmaceuticals.covidien.com/workarea/downloadasset.aspx?id=2147483729>.

Russo's Pharmacy in Hagerstown is pictured on Thursday. David Russo, owner of Russo's Rx at 25 N. Cannon Ave., has been prohibited from dispensing drugs classified as controlled dangerous substances following allegations that he filled thousands of prescriptions for Oxycodone, OxyContin, methadone and other powerful painkillers written by two physicians whose licenses were subsequently suspended. (By Ric Dugan, Staff Photographer)

 
By DON AINES
 
dona@herald-mail.com
 
7:12 p.m. EDT, March 17, 2011
hm-pharmacist-can-no-longer-dispense-controlled-dangerous-substances-20110317 
A Hagerstown pharmacist has been prohibited from dispensing drugs classified as controlled dangerous substances following allegations that he filled thousands of prescriptions for Oxycodone, OxyContin, methadone and other powerful painkillers written by two physicians whose licenses were subsequently suspended.

The Maryland Board of Pharmacy voted on Dec. 22, 2010, to summarily suspend the license of David Russo, owner of Russo's Rx at 25 N. Cannon Ave.

"There has since been a consent agreement by which my license has been restored, but I cannot dispense controlled dangerous substances," Russo said Tuesday. However, Russo said he can dispense other prescribed medications. 



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Get the information you need fast. Sign up for our Breaking News alerts today. 
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------


No formal charges have been filed against him, and an evidentiary hearing will be scheduled during which he will present a defense to the allegations made by investigators with the pharmacy board, Russo said.

"We hope to have it resolved at that point," Russo said. He deferred specific questions to his attorney, but issued the following statement:

"Russo's Rx has always endorsed the American Academy of Pain Management's Patient Bill of Rights to insure access to medications prescribed for the treatment of chronic pain. We also do our best due diligence in the performance of our corresponding responsibility to mitigate abuse and diversion of controlled dangerous substances. We look forward to a hearing and the chance to defend ourselves."

"Certainly, Mr. Russo did fill prescriptions written by those two doctors and others," said his attorney, Richard Karceski of Towson, Md. "Every prescription written was legitimate .... There were no forgeries."

The investigative findings accompanying the suspension order cited Russo for "dispensing inappropriately large amounts of CDS prescribed by doctors known to engage in suspicious subscribing patterns."

The prescriptions were written in 2009 and 2010 by Dr. Nicola M. Tauraso, of Frederick, Md., and Silviu Ziscovici, of Rockville, Md., according to the investigative findings. 

The Maryland Board of Physicians summarily suspended Tauraso's license on Aug. 12, 2010, and Ziscovici's on Dec. 1, 2010, the report said.

Their licenses were suspended for prescribing high doses and large quantities of painkillers to mostly young people "who appeared healthy and did not appear to be in chronic pain or terminally ill," the Board of Pharmacy report alleged.

"It's not Dr. Russo's decision what to prescribe or how much," Karceski said. Those decisions were up to Tauraso and Ziscovici, both pain-management physicians, he said.



DEA investigated

Investigators from the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration met with Russo in January 2010 and questioned him about prescriptions written by the two doctors, Karceski said. 

Russo provided them with copies of the requested prescriptions, he said. 

Russo did not know what the investigation was about at that time and asked the DEA investigators if he should stop filling prescriptions from Ziscovici and Tauraso, Karceski said. The investigators told him he could continue to fill those prescriptions, he said.

Russo told inspectors he filled prescriptions for Tauraso's patients from Washington County, the report said. However, investigators alleged that Russo filled prescriptions for Tauraso's and Ziscovici's patients from other counties and states.

The telephone number for Tauraso's clinic was not in service, and there was no answer at the number for Ziscovici's practice.

 A Board of Physicians spokeswoman said Friday that the licenses of Tauraso and Ziscovici were still suspended.

From: Rod Hughes [mailto:rhughes@synchronyhc.com]
Sent: Friday, June 03, 2011 6:15 AM
To: Neuman, Herbert R
Cc: Morelli, Art ; Patrick, Jeffrey
Subject: Phase IV Study on Conversion of EX



 

I know we have been thinking a good deal about REMS and CARES but I wanted to suggest a Phase IV study that I think would be very important for EXALGO.


I believe that this study could be used to communicate the ideal dosing strategy and could perhaps lead to a potential label change with regard to the 50% reduction in calculated dose.


 


Randomize subjects into three conversion groups


                A. Converting from other long-acting/ER opioid without reduction in starting dose (ie, like nearly every EXALGO study but two)


                B. 25% reduction in starting dose (ie, like 301 and 302)


                C. 50% reduction in starting dose (ie, never been tested and may be associated with significant 


For each of the groups titration would occur (if necessary) in the same manner


 


We would have to discuss what to do about supplemental medication. The advantage of the study would be to test the conversion and titration according to the label which, as you know, includes no supplemental medication. 


 


Primary Outcome Measure:


Percentage of patients who achieve a stable dose of EXALGO 


                This can be stratified by previous opioid therapy and dose


 


Secondary Outcome Measures:


·         Duration of time and number of titration steps required to titrate patients to a stable dose of EXALGO 

o    Overall

o    Stratified by conversion group

o    Stratified by prior opioid therapy

·         Measures of opioid withdrawal syndrome COWS/SOWS

o    Overall

o    Stratified according to conversion group

o    Stratified according to prior opioid dose

·         Morphine equivalent of stable dose

o    Overall 

o    Stratified by conversion group

o    Stratified by prior opioid therapy

·         Change from baseline in the NRS, and measures of Brief Pain Inventory 

·         Use of supplemental analgesics

·         Adverse events (treatment emergent)

o    It would be especially important to assess symptoms associated with potential withdrawal and symptoms associated with potential over dosage (eg, sedation)

·         Number of patients at various risk level as assessed by the investigator (low, moderate, high - according to SOAPP or ORT)

o    including prior/current concerns with prescription opioid misuse, abuse and/or diversion 

·         Number of patients with aberrant behaviors (Current Opioid Misuse Measure [COMM®] score ≥ 9)

·         Number of patients with abnormal urine drug screening results 

The latter assessments would be done to document a low incidence of aberrant behaviors

From: Stauder, Nancy R
Sent: Tuesday, June 18, 2013 10:42 PM
To: Chinigo, Peter; Eyman, Dale B; Terifay, Terry W; Novak, Rod P; Webb, Kevin J; Collier, Ginger L
Cc: Von Rohr, Dawn M; Kaczmarek, Walt; Carchedi, Steve R; Hastings, Patrick; Haarmann, Annie; Brendel, Diane; Fischer, Meredith B; Phillips, Lynn; Abbett, Erica; Eaves, Nikki; Schooler, JoAnna S
Subject: Important Corporate Marketing Update: Launch Plans - Specialty Pharmaceuticals
Importance: High



 

Hello API, Brands and Generics marketing leaders,

 

Many of you have seen much of our Mallinckrodt Pharmaceuticals marketing launch plan in pieces to date, and many have contributed as we have asked for your support and guidance on meeting local needs along the way. Pat Hastings, Brand Manager, and I thank you for your collaboration and valuable contributions.

 

As we are now less than two very short weeks away from the official launch, it is important to share with you the detailed plan and tools you will receive to aid our efforts to effectively launch the new company brand, and promote broad awareness of and engagement with Mallinckrodt Pharmaceuticals. Please share this information broadly among your marketing and sales leadership teams so they are aware of the launch plans. The files are not to be shared externally prior to spin. (The text from this email is also contained in an attached file.)

 

Here is the comprehensive plan specifically applicable to the three Specialty Pharmaceuticals  businesses:

 

-       Corporate Brochure: Developed in English and translated into a number of other languages; copies of the brochure will be distributed each business based on numbers provided, including translations as requested for the API business. Each employee worldwide will also receive a copy of the brochure.

o    The first samples of the printed brochure have been received, and it looks great. Distribution of the English version will begin this week, with the translated versions sent out sometime next week.

o    An electronic version of the brochure has been developed, which can be used on iPads or iPhones, or emailed if desired (2MB file). The English version of the file will be shared next week with instructions for how to use on Apple devices. We can convert the other languages to similar electronic versions as needed.

 

-       Corporate Ad: For your businesses, the corporate ad will be utilized at the corporate level on a number of pain management web sites and print publications as chosen by your teams. Full placement details will be provided later this week.

o    All ad placements will begin on July 1 and run through December, 2013.

o    A sample of the digital ad that will be used is attached. (To view it, save the zip file to your desktop, extract the swf file further to your desktop, and open with Internet Explorer.)

o    The print ad, which has a bit more text, as well as the digital ad is available as desired for use commercially if desired beyond the placements we re making at the corporate level. The general ad is attached. Please contact Pat Hastings or me with artwork requests.

o    Other ad placements are also being implemented for the Global Medical Imaging business.

o    Work is also underway with your teams related to convention sponsorships as part of the corporate launch plan.

 

-       Customer Direct Mail/E-Mailer: The print version of this tool is a variation on the corporate print ad, with additional text added specific to each business. The e-mailer will likely be a variation of the digital ad. 

o    The print file is attached. Note there are three variations on the back side of the card, one for each of your businesses where the products are reflected in the closing paragraph. (This has had PARC approval.)

o    The Brands business will be using the print version only (details provided to you separately on printing/timing); Generics will use e-mailer for most customers with exception of Addiction Treatment, where print version will be used. API will have the option of either.

o    Customer letters will also be made available for use announcing the spin. (API already has theirs.)

 

-       Corporate Web Site : A fantastic new web site has been developed and will launch on June 30 as the most readily and frequently accessed face of the new company. Annie Haarmann, Digital and Social Media Manager, has led this effort with strong collaboration across all businesses.

o    There are two sections of the site    corporate  content and product content. There is a deliberate and distinct separation of the two sections; visitors will be alerted by a brief pop-up message that they are leaving corporate content and going to a promotional area of the site if they click on any product categories.

o    Note all micro-sites of any kind (e.g. EXALGO) have also been rebranded; those rebranded sites will go live at spin as well.

 

-       Mallinckrodt Pharmaceuticals Story Presentation: A PowerPoint presentation is in development for use at or near separation that will incorporate elements from the corporate brochure, financial data and other elements deemed appropriate.

 

-       Business Cards, Stationery, Name Tags: Last Friday the announcement was made that Smart Source was chosen as the U.S. source for these materials. There have admittedly been a few glitches in the process, but we have worked through them and you and your teams should be fully able to place orders through Smart Source now.

 

-       Company Launch Press Release: On Monday morning, July 1, a press release will be issued announcing the completed separation of Covidien and Mallinckrodt Pharmaceuticals. The release will be distributed via international wire services.

o    If any of you have specific trade publications that you would like to have the release sent to, please send your lists to Diane or to me, including contact names and email addresses, and we will compile a list to provide to Lynn Phillips, Media Relations Manager.

o    As a reminder, all media inquiries must be directed to Lynn.

 

Additional General Promotional Plans

-       Mark Trudeau external launch video is being produced and will appear on the new web site (linked from our YouTube page)

-       NYSE Bell-Ringing/Ads: On Monday morning (US time), Mark Trudeau and others will ring the opening bell on the New York Stock Exchange. As part of that event package, we have corporate banners that will appear outside the Exchange, along with billboards and other advertising in the New York City area

-       Billboards: In the St. Louis area, there will be strategically placed billboards in three spots around the area, as well as ad placements in Lambert St. Louis International Airport.

-       Newspaper ads have been placed for opening day or soon thereafter in St. Louis and other cities where we have a manufacturing presence.

-       Facility signage is being replaced to reflect the new brand at all sites around the world, with the majority being completed by spin.

-       Social Media: Our initial steps into these waters will begin with YouTube and Linked In, with additional avenues being explored further into the future. More details about the process to utilize social media for commercial purposes will be shared in mid-July

 

Pat and I will be working closely with each team to distribute the materials noted above, and you will be kept informed as they become available.

 

In addition, a separate message will be sent related to the official launch of www.mpbranding.com which is expected in the next couple of days, so stay tuned for that.

 

If anyone has questions about any of the information provided above, please let me know. Contact Pat or me with any brand-related questions or further needs.  It s an intense, exciting time to be part of Mallinckrodt as we prepare for the next stage in our evolution as a company and the launch of Mallinckrodt Pharmaceuticals!

 

Thanks,
Nancy

 

Nancy Stauder

Director, Communications

Cell: 314-409-5995

DEA Releases 2013 Drug Threat Assessment Summary

Posted: 20 Nov 2013 08:10 PM PST

By Karla L. Palmer – 

On Monday, November 18, 2013, DEA released the 2013 National Drug Threat Assessment Summary, which provides an assessment of the threat posed to the United States by trafficking and abuse of illicit substances and non-medical use of controlled prescription drugs.  The Summary also provides an analysis of the domestic drug situation during 2012 based on available law enforcement, intelligence, and public health data.  DEA took over responsibility for preparation of the Summary in June 2012 as a result of the closure of the National Drug Intelligence Center.  DEA considered both quantitative data from various sources (seizures, investigations, arrests, drug purity or potency, and drug prices; law enforcement surveys; laboratory analyses; and interagency production and cultivation estimates) and qualitative information (subjective views of individual agencies on drug availability, information on smuggling and transportation trends, and indicators of changes in smuggling and transportation methods). 

Highlights include the following:

§ The trafficking and abuse of illicit drugs continue to constitute a “dynamic and challenging” threat to the United States.

§ Controlled prescription drug abuse continues to be the United States’ fastest growing drug problem.  The rate of abuse of controlled prescription drugs remains high; abuse remains at a higher rate than any illicit drug except marijuana.  Pain relievers are the most common type of abused prescription drug, and are most commonly involved in overdose incidents. 

§ The availability of heroin continued to increase in 2012, likely due to high levels of heroin production in Mexico, and Mexican traffickers expanding into in the eastern and midwestern United States.  Some metropolitan areas observed an increase in heroin overdose deaths.  Reports reveal that many prescription opioid users have turned to heroin as a cheaper and/or more easily obtained alternative to prescription drugs. 

§ The trend of lower cocaine availability in the United States that began in 2007 continued through 2012.  

§ Methamphetamine availability is likely increasing because of sustained production in Mexico (the primary foreign source for the United States market) and continuing small-scale domestic production. 

§ Marijuana availability appears to be increasing because of sustained high levels of production in Mexico (the primary foreign source of United States supply) and increased domestic cultivation. 

§ The abuse of synthetic designer drugs has emerged as a serious problem in the United States.  The abuse of synthetic cannabinoids, such as “K2” and “Spice,” and synthetic cathinones, like “bath salts,” increased over the past few years, and “abusers have suffered severe consequences.”  Both state legislation and national scheduling of these drugs have helped to “mitigate the threat.”  DEA noted that the threat posed by synthetics most likely will continue to increase, in part because the chemical make-up of these drugs often differs by only one compound.  Thus as DEA exercises its scheduling authority to control certain substances, producers quickly change the chemical component of the newly banned substance to create a new one 

§ MDMA (ecstasy) is available in markets throughout the United States.  However, data suggest availability and abuse of the drug may have peaked.

Mike,

 

As we discussed last Friday, demand for API products manufactured at the St. Louis Plant is increasing significantly.

Carla and I have a meeting later this week with Nick Litzsinger and Marc Montgomery to line out how to capture opportunistic API business in quota requests so that we can offer our full support to these growth initiatives by obtaining quota appropriately.

 

Of utmost concern is the time that DEA is taking to process our quota requests currently.  As you can see from the chart below we have a number of quota increase letters pending, two of which are nine weeks old.

 

We have been told that our primary quota contact person has accepted a position outside of the Quota Unit and will be leaving that office within the next 90 days.  Historically, there has been a substantial learning curve associated with a change in this responsibility within DEA.

 

We have received unconfirmed rumors from a reliable source that DEA is reviewing the level of authority designation that has been granted to the Chief of the Quota Section in the past.  There is some indication that the power to sign quota grant letters has been elevated on an interim basis to a high ranking senior official.

 

Eric Evans has expressed a desire to meet with DEA and present our short term and longer term business strategies to the agency.

 

As an aside, we currently have requested a meeting with DEA Headquarters to discuss Suspicious Order Monitoring (proposed Mallinckrodt attendees are me, Pat Duft and Don Lohman).

 

Please let me know if you approve me setting up an internal meeting with Pat Duft and/or Tom Berry to evaluate the benefit of requesting a Quota discussion with DEA Headquarters and/or if you prefer to discuss with Pat and/or Tom directly.

Thanks, Hugh.


As Mario certainly knows, Exalgo will likely serve as an excellent reference for "market performance" of an otherwise highly-abusable opioid. Hydromorphone, embedded in PEO, demonstrated it was difficult at best for abusers to circumvent. As such, despite high payloads of "dilaudid" per tablet, Exalgo has witnessed quite low abuse rates, and much negative sentiment within the abuser forums.


In fact, the FDA refused to approve the 32mg dosage form until they witnessed the performance of the 8, 12 and 16mg dosages once commercially available. It was primarily based on the low-abuse profile of those strengths that supported the safety of the approval of the 32mg dosage.


I believe MNK's history of good stewardship along with the low abuse rate of Exalgo should be considered in decisions related to XXR. And by the way, Exalgo has about 200mg PEO per tablet, XXR has 322mg PEO per tablet.


Fingers crossed.


Thanks.

addition of the 32 mg tablet, along with the already approved
8, 12, and 16 mg tablets, you now have greater dosing flexibility.

Learn more about EXALGO.



The features of the added EXALGO 32 mg tablet include:

 

 Dosing flexibility. EXALGO 32 mg complements the already approved 8, 12, and 16 mg tablets.1

 
 

 Proven efficacy. EXALGO 32 mg was the median effective dose in the pivotal trial.*2

 
 

 Robust patient exposure. EXALGO 32 mg has been thoroughly tested in 14 clinical trials conducted in 2474 patients, with 1483 of these patients exposed to a dose of 32 mg or greater.3

 

* Mean effective dose was 37.8 mg.1

Additional EXALGO information available.

P.S. Learn about proper dosing and titration with
