Sending just to flag what's hot.  Not expecting you to read the details.

From: Schooler, JoAnna S
Sent: Monday, January 16, 2012 1:42 PM
To: Berry, Tom E; Edwards, Peter G; Giuliani, Michael; Harbaugh, Matthew; Haynes, Elaine E; Jansen, Joe; Mannebach, Mark; Neuman, Herbert R; Silver, David; Littlejohn, Stephen E; Harrell, Jamie; Stevens, Dirk E; Wirth, Christian; Von Rohr, Dawn M; Cano, David J (Human Resources); Cardetti, Lisa M (Lundergan); Kim, Stuart K.; Lohman, Donald A; Wuestner, Joe A; Collier, Ginger L; Saake, Lisa M; Mills, Sherice R; Williams, Jane L; Novak, Rod P; Terifay, Terry W; Wessler, Michael; Hasse, Debra C; Patrick, Jeffrey; Elsbernd, Brian D; Duft, Pat H; Troup, Cathy M; Budenholzer, Bob; Stauder, Nancy R; Phillips, Lynn
Cc: McBride, Timothy J.; Kalavritinos, Jack; Barranco, Nicole
Subject: Pharmaceuticals Public Affairs - Legislative Update - 1/16/12

1/16/12 - Pharmaceuticals Public Affairs - Legislative Update - Please note that new items and changes are highlighted.

Tamper Resistance Formulation (TRF) Substitution Bills - Throughout this legislative session we're continuing to track very similar bills that have been proposed in multiple states all of which prohibit pharmacists from substituting an opioid drug with "tamper resistance technology" with other non TRF products. Working with our colleagues in DC, we're currently keeping close tabs on TRF substitution bills in New Jersey, Tennessee, Ohio, New York, Georgia and Florida.


-       New Jersey - The NJ Assembly adjourned its 2010-2011 session and opened the 2012-2013 session as well this week. While the previously introduced House and Senate bills were not acted upon after they were assigned to the Health, Human Services Committees in the respective chambers. The new session opened with (S350) being introduced on Jan. 10 by the same sponsor Senator Linda Greenstein.  It was also assigned to the Health committee. We're tracking the Senate bill and staying on the lookout for a companion bill to be introduced in the House.

-       Tennessee - A bill (HB2567) was introduced on Jan. 13. No further action was taken, but we will monitor.

-       Ohio - The bill in Ohio (H373) was introduced on November 9, 2011, by a majority party member. It was referred to the Health and Aging committee, but it hasn't been scheduled for a hearing. The 2011 session adjourned without any action, but bills can be carried over to the 2012 session, which began on Jan. 2. As such, we're continuing to monitor this one.  No action occurred last week.

-       New York - A bill (S6062) was introduced on Jan. 4, the first day of the 2012 session. It has been assigned to the Health Committee. There was a bill introduced in the House (H7634) last May (5/11/11) and it was referred to committee, but there hasn't been a hearing on it. Bills can also be carried over from a prior session in NY, so we're monitoring these bills in both the House and Senate. No action occurred on these bills in NY last week.

-       Georgia - We've seen draft bill language that was being shopped through a contract lobbyist for Endo. The legislative session in GA began on Jan. 9.  This bill hasn't been introduced yet.

-       Florida - A standalone TRF substitution bill (S1364) has been pre-filed in Florida, but no further action has taken place on this week. This bill will follow up on the Pill Mill Bill that passed during the 2011 legislative session with the TRF substitution language taken out after our efforts to defeat the provision. Our consultants on the ground in Florida are watching the bill, but they believe it is doubtful that there will be much support for bills designed to add on to the provisions in the Pill Mill Bill in this session, as there will be a desire to allow the current legislation to take effect. They doubt the current TRF bill will get out of committee.  It appears that proponents of the bill (Endo, Pfizer) have likely made a strategic misstep by introducing it as a standalone bill. We've been told that when a bill is introduced and doesn't garner support in committee, language from it is prohibited from being used as an amendment to other bills that may see action later on in the session. We're tracking the bill to be sure that it stays off a committee agenda and will be ready to take action with our lobbyists to defeat it, if it does.

Prescription Monitoring Programs (PMP) - We're also tracking the establishment and refinements of PMP in various states.


-       Missouri - A bill establishing a PMP in Missouri has been introduced in the House (H1193). We're working with our Jefferson City consultants and our internal experts to tighten some of the language around who can access the information which is a concern that Sen. Robert Schaaf (District 34-St. Joseph) has expressed in the past as part of our effort to provide support for the bill throughout the legislative process. After hearing that Purdue Pharma has also expressed support for the bill, our consultants are working to keep close tabs on their activities.

-       New Jersey - New Jersey is launching its PMP more than five years after passing a law to start tracking prescription drug use.  Read more at the Washington Examiner: http://washingtonexaminer.com/news/2012/01/nj-launches-prescription-monitoring-program/2098951#ixzz1jeOfDkCp

-       New York - Attorney General Eric Schneiderman announced bipartisan support and law enforcement support for a bill that creates an on-line, real-time database to track the dispensing of prescription drugs. He unveiled the legislation last year, but he's announced plans to aggressively pursue it this year. NY's current PDMP requires pharmacists to report controlled substances dispensed at least once every 45 days. Along with establishing a real-time database, Schneiderman's I-STOP legislation requires practitioners to review a patient's controlled substances history in the system prior to prescribing, requires practitioners to report a prescription for controlled substances at the time of issuance, requires pharmacists to review the system to confirm the person presenting the prescription possesses a legitimate prescription prior to dispensing and requires the pharmacist to report dispensation of prescriptions.

-       Other states - We're working with various consultants on the ongoing tracking of PDMP-related legislation as well as changes in existing programs.

Federal - The FDA is taking the various User Fee Acts to Congress in preparation for passage before the end of the year.  There are Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee hearings scheduled in February. We're working with our colleagues in D.C. to monitor these hearings:


-       February 1 - PDUFA

-       February 7 - GDUFA and biosimilars

-       February 15 - MDUFMA
Please let me know if you have any questions or need additional information. We'll provide another update this week if there is new information to share. Have a good week.

Press Release

 
 
 

Mallinckrodt Agrees To Pay $35 Million Settlement for Failure To Report Suspicious Orders of Pharmaceutical Drugs and for Recordkeeping Violations

 

JULY 11 - (Washington, D.C.)   Mallinckrodt LLC, a pharmaceutical manufacturer and one of the largest manufacturers of generic oxycodone, agreed to pay $35 million to settle allegations that it violated certain provisions of the Controlled Substances Act (CSA) that are subject to civil penalties, Attorney General Jeff Sessions of the Justice Department and Acting Administrator Chuck Rosenberg of theDrug Enforcement Administration (DEA) announced today.

 

This is the first settlement of its magnitude with a manufacturer of pharmaceuticals resolving nationwide claims that the company did not meet its obligations to detect and notify DEA of suspicious orders of controlled substances such as oxycodone, the abuse of which is part of the current opioid epidemic. These suspicious order monitoring requirements exist to prevent excessive sales of controlled substances, like oxycodone in Florida and elsewhere. The settlement also addressed violations in the company s manufacturing batch records at its plant in Hobart, New York. Both sets of alleged violations impact accountability for controlled substances, and the compliance terms going forward are designed to help protect against diversion of these substances at critical links in the controlled substance supply chain. 

 

 In the midst of one of the worst drug abuse crises in American history, the Department of Justice has the responsibility to ensure that our drug laws are being enforced and to protect the American people,  said Attorney General Sessions.  Part of that mission is holding drug manufacturers accountable for their actions. Mallinckrodt s actions and omissions formed a link in the chain of supply that resulted in millions of oxycodone pills being sold on the street.  Thanks to the hard work of our attorneys and law enforcement, Mallinckrodt has agreed to do everything they can to help us identify suspicious orders in the future. And as a result of today's settlement, we are sending a clear message to drug companies:  This Department of Justice will hold you accountable for your legal obligations, and we will enforce our laws. I believe that will prevent drug abuse, prevent new addictions from starting, and ultimately save lives. 

 

 Manufacturers and distributors have a crucial responsibility to ensure that controlled substances do not get into the wrong hands,  said DEA Acting Administrator Chuck Rosenberg.  When they violate their legal obligations, we will hold them accountable. 

 

The government alleged that Mallinckrodt failed to design and implement an effective system to detect and report  suspicious orders  for controlled substances   orders that are unusual in their frequency, size, or other patterns. From 2008 until 2011, the U.S. alleged, Mallinckrodt supplied distributors, and the distributors then supplied various U.S. pharmacies and pain clinics, an increasingly excessive quantity of oxycodone pills without notifying DEA of these suspicious orders. Through its investigation, the government learned that manufacturers of pharmaceuticals offer discounts, known as  chargebacks,  based on sales to certain downstream customers.  Distributors provide information on the downstream customer purchases to obtain the discount.  The groundbreaking nature of the settlement involves requiring a manufacturer to utilize chargeback and similar data to monitor and report to DEA suspicious sales of its oxycodone at the next level in the supply chain, typically sales from distributors to independent and small chain pharmacy and pain clinic customers.

   

The government also alleged that Mallinckrodt violated record keeping requirements at its manufacturing facility in upstate New York. Among other things, these violations created discrepancies between the actual number of tablets manufactured in a batch and the number of tablets Mallinckrodt reported on its records. Accurate reconciliation of records at the manufacturing stage is a critical first step in ensuring that controlled substances are accounted for properly through the supply chain.

 

In addition to the significant monetary penalty, this settlement includes a groundbreaking parallel agreement with the DEA, as a result of which the company will analyze data it collects on orders from customers down the supply chain to identify suspicious sales. The resolution advances the DEA s position that controlled substance manufacturers need to go beyond  know your customer  to use otherwise available company data to  know your customer s customer  to protect these potentially dangerous pharmaceuticals from getting into the wrong hands. DEA s Memorandum of Agreement with Mallinckrodt also sets forth specific procedures it will undertake to ensure the accuracy of batch records and protect loss of raw product in the manufacturing process.

 

By entering into these agreements, elements of which Mallinckrodt is already implementing, the company is becoming part of the solution to this public health epidemic.

 

This lengthy investigation was led by DEA s Detroit Field Division on the suspicious order issues and the New York Field Division on the manufacturing record keeping issues.

 

U.S. Attorneys  Offices for the Eastern District of Michigan and the Northern District of New York, along with DEA Office of Chief Counsel and Diversion Control Division, led the civil settlement negotiations. The Criminal Division s Narcotic and Dangerous Drug Section (NDDS) also coordinated and assisted in negotiating the settlement.

Subject: Alert: Pharma. Law & Industry Report: Highlights
From: Bloomberg Government <alerts@bgov.com>
Date: Thu, 07 Dec 2017 15:00:34 +0000
To: derek.naten@mallinckrodt.com


{Bloomberg Government}  

 

 

Pharma. Law & Industry Report: Highlights

December 7, 2017 10:00AM ET | Bloomberg BNA


 

 

 

 

HIGHLIGHTS AND CONTENTS

1. Pharma Exec Prosecuted in Off-Label Case Won't Get New Trial

A pharmaceutical company founder's conviction for promoting off-label uses stands, as a federal appeals court found no error in his trial. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

2. Teamsters Health Plan Sues Opioid Manufacturers, Distributors

Opioid manufacturers and distributors are facing yet another suit over their marketing of the painkillers, this time from a Springfield, Mass.-based union health benefit plan. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

3. SCOTUS Seeks Government View in Fosamax Case

The U.S. Supreme Court asked the government Dec. 4 to weigh in on whether it should review a federal appeals court decision reviving some 500 Fosamax product liability suits against Merck & Co. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

4. Opioid Marketing Suits Sent to Federal Court in Ohio

Suits by states and local governments alleging Purdue Pharma LP and other makers of opioid painkillers contributed to an epidemic were sent to federal court in Ohio for consolidated proceedings. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

5. Court Won't Decide Perrigo Prilosec Generic Exclusivity Question

Perrigo Research & Development Co. lost a bid to have a court decide, after the FDA wouldn't, whether it needed to market a generic version of Prilosec now to avoid forfeiting a potentially lucrative exclusivity period. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

6. J&J, Bayer Ordered to Pay $28 Million in First Xarelto Loss

Johnson & Johnson and Bayer AG are responsible for a woman's injuries tied to the blood-thinning drug Xarelto and must pay almost $28 million in damages, jurors concluded in the companies’ first loss at a trial over the medicine. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

7. Compounding Pharmacy Fails to Boot False Claims Lawsuit

A compounding pharmacy the government says deliberately overcharged the federal health-care system for active duty military service members failed to end a lawsuit against it. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

8. Janssen Shielded by Mich. Law Despite Off-Label Risperdal Use

Michigan law immunizes Janssen Pharmaceuticals Inc. from liability in thirteen cases over side effects from the antipsychotic Risperdal, a Pennsylvania appellate court ruled. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

9. Aventis Wins Dismissal in Clomid Birth Defect Suit

Aventis Inc. won dismissal in federal district court of a birth defect suit linked to the prescription fertility drug Clomid. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

10. Opioid Lawyers Warned by Judge Cases Face ‘Serious’ Hurdles

States and local governments suing Purdue Pharma and other makers of opioid painkillers face “serious” legal hurdles that can derail their bids to reap a multibillion-dollar payout to cover the costs of a burgeoning drug epidemic, a federal judge said. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

11. Government Should Negotiate Drug Prices, Science Academy Says

The federal government should negotiate drug prices and allow for more flexible drug formularies, a national scientific organization said Nov. 30. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

12. Revisions to Anti-Bribery Law Enforcement Could Prove Significant

Recent revisions to the Justice Department's enforcement policy on the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act could be significant for companies deciding whether to voluntarily disclose wrongdoing under the anti-bribery statute. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

13. FDA Signals Review of Company Executive Liability Approach

The FDA wants to clarify when corporate officers should be held criminally responsible for company wrongdoing, the agency's top lawyer said. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

14. Growth of U.S. Health Spending Slows as Drug Prices Decelerate

Total U.S. health spending increased in 2016 but slowed compared with prior years, as Americans shelled out less on prescription drugs and the initial effects of increased Obamacare enrollment dwindled. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

15. FDA Seeks to Speed Approvals of Generic Drug-Device Combos

New FDA guidance will make it easier for generic companies to get drug-device combination products approved. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

16. More Money Needed to Tackle Opioid Crisis, Lawmakers Told

Federal agencies need funding through appropriations to address aspects of the opioid crisis such as research of alternative medication and oversight of insurance company compliance, witnesses said at a hearing on preventing, treating, and recovering from opioid abuse. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

17. States Want Continued Federal Funds to Fight Opioid Epidemic

States are providing more access to addiction treatment and putting more resources into prevention to fight the opioid epidemic, state officials testified before Congress Nov. 30. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

18. Lawmakers Open to New Ideas to Spur Drug, Device Innovation

Members of a key House panel indicated they're open to additional legislative action if necessary to speed new medicines to patients. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

19. Once-Monthly Opioid Addiction Injection Cleared for U.S. Sales

Efforts to combat the opioid epidemic killing thousands of Americans each year got a boost from U.S. regulators with the approval of a first-of-its-kind monthly treatment for addiction to opiates including pills and heroin. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

20. Forget Amazon. Health Companies Really Want to Be UnitedHealth

As the specter of Amazon.com Inc. looms over the health-care industry, it's easy to see the tech giant's threat as a major factor behind the megadeal between CVS Health Corp. and Aetna Inc. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

21. Who's Next? CVS-Aetna Deal Could Start a Health Takeover Run

CVS Health Corp.’s deal to buy insurer Aetna Inc. for about $67.5 billion could be just the start of a new wave of health-care takeovers. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

22. Pharmacy Making Intravenous Drugs Hit With FDA Warning

A New Jersey compounding pharmacy making intravenous drug products received an FDA warning letter for problems that included insanitary manufacturing conditions. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

23. CVS to Buy Aetna for $67.5 Billion, Remaking Health Care Sector

CVS Health Corp. will buy Aetna Inc. for about $67.5 billion, creating a health-care giant that will have a hand in everything from insurance to the corner drugstore. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

24. Newer Birth Control Pills Don't Lower the Risk of Breast Cancer

Newer birth control drugs developed to replace those tied to cancer risk were thought to improve safety for the women who took them. It turns out they didn't, according to a massive new study. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

25. Express Scripts CEO Open to Insurer Deal, Ties with Amazon

Express Scripts Holding Co.’s chief executive said he's open to a deal with a health insurer or partnering with Amazon.com Inc. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

26. U.S. Drug Approval Helps Push Biocon Shares to Fresh Record

Shares of Biocon Ltd. extended a record after U.S. regulators approved its competing version of Roche Holding AG's blockbuster breast cancer drug Herceptin. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

27. Frayed Gasket Delaying Astra's ZS-9 Shows Pharma M&A Perils

When AstraZeneca Plc paid $2.7 billion for an experimental drugmaker in 2015, it had its sights set on a potential blockbuster medicine. Instead, it got a Texas factory riddled with defects and two scathing reviews from U.S. regulators rejecting the treatment. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

28. Biotech Eyes Tax Revamp as Next Chance to Shake Its Recent Woes

Biotechnology investors who saw their portfolios stumble after a late-summer bull run may refocus on a key reason that the group took off: the U.S. tax overhaul and repatriation. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

29. Bayer's Ready to Spend on Its Transformation to Cancer Company

Bayer AG is ready to spend more money on deals and research that will help make it into a cancer company as the company's blockbuster blood-thinner Xarelto nears the final years of its patent life. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

30. CVS Said to Near $65 Billion-Plus Deal for Insurer Aetna

CVS Health Corp. is nearing an agreement to acquire health insurer Aetna Inc. for more than $65 billion, according to a person familiar with the negotiations, in a deal that could reshape the pharmacy and health insurance industries. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

31. A Deadly Drug Cocktail Shines a Light on an AstraZeneca Blockbuster

The last time John Nebinger spoke to his son Bradley was about thirty minutes after midnight on March 15, 2010. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

32. Minnesota Mulls Per-Pill Fee to Counter Opioid Abuse

Pharmaceutical companies would have to pay fees to sell opioids in Minnesota under a bill expected to be introduced in 2018. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

33. This Company Is Ready to Flood the U.S. with Cheap HIV Drugs

Among the coconut plantations and beaches of South India, a factory the size of 35 football fields is preparing to churn out billions of generic pills for HIV patients and flood the U.S. market with the low-cost copycat medicines. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

34. Canada Proposes Tougher Reviews of New Drug Prices

Canada proposed changes to its pricing controls for patented medicines that are projected to lower net drug costs for provincial health plans by C$1.8 billion ($1.2 billion) per year. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

35. Drug Companies from Glaxo to J&J Pledge to Make U.K. Investments

GlaxoSmithKline Plc, Johnson & Johnson, Merck & Co., and AstraZeneca Plc are among more than two dozen global pharmaceutical companies pledging to invest funds in the U.K. as part of a multi-billion-pound effort to spur the country's health-care industry. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

36. European Drug Regulator's Brexit Move Sparks Concern at Genmab

The Brexit-induced relocation of the European medicines regulator to Amsterdam may slow product approvals, hurting some drugmakers, Genmab A/S Chief Executive Officer Jan van de Winkel said. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

37. Richter Falls as Liver Cases Prompt Review of Flagship Product

Shares in Gedeon Richter Nyrt., eastern Europe's largest drugmaker, plunged after cases of serious liver injuries prompted the review of one of its flagship products. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

38. 50,000 New Drug Tests Among Brexit Worries for Pharma Companies

Global drugmakers from Johnson & Johnson to AstraZeneca Plc warned that potential trade and regulatory hurdles may burden them with a host of additional costs after Britain leaves the European Union. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

Feds raid a pair of pain clinics in city
By KATE HOWARD
Publication: Florida Times-Union (Jacksonville)
Date: Friday, July 30 2010
ID_Web_horizontal_sml_white
You are viewing page  1

Nearly all of the patients at a North Jacksonville pain clinic raided Thursday were p rescribed the same remedy: the
highly addictive pain killer oxycodone, the anti-anxiety medicine Xanax and a muscle relaxer called Soma. And the
unassuming clinic, tucked away in a West 48th Street strip mall, did a staggering business.
Florida Department of Health records show that 611,000 oxycodone pills were dispensed  by Duval Wellness Center
in April and May alone.
The clinic and its owner, 78-year-old osteopathic physician Donald W. Hall, were issu ed a cease and desist order
Wednesday by the health department.
About 10 a.m. Thursday, FBI and DEA agents and Jacksonville
police burst into the clinic and First Coast Pain and Urgent Care on
Normandy Boulevard, also owned by Hall.
No charges have been brought and no arrests were made in the
months-old investigation, federal officials said.
The targeted businesses are among a growing number of pain
management clinics registered in Jacksonville - with the number
jumping from less than 50 in March to about 60 today.
"Pill mills" have been largely viewed as a South Florida problem. But
as crackdowns and moratoriums on the pain clinics grew more
intense in Broward County and nearby towns, many clinic owners opened shop farther no rth.
Steve Cole, spokesman for the U.S. Attorney's Office, said the Jacksonville investigation focused on the two clinics.
"We've had similar investigations like this throughout the Middle District of Florida, looking into pain clinics that may
be dispensing prescription drugs illegally," he said. "Florida has had a problem with  that. So we obviously are looking
in all the major cities to see if and where there are problems."
FBI spokesman Jeff Westcott said he couldn't reveal any details about the investigati on or the dozen search warrants
executed Thursday.
About 99 percent of the 8,000 prescriptions issued by Duval Wellness in April and May  were identical: oxycodone,
Xanax and Soma, according to the health department. The state inspected the facility's medical records in early June
and also found that they had been operating as a pain clinic without state authorizat ion.
Hall, who has been practicing medicine for 40 years, couldn't be reached for comment.
A neighbor of Hall's, Pat Collins, said she saw lots of police activity at Hall's Lak e City home early Thursday.

Important OxyContin(r) Update

On April 17th, the FDA ruled on OxyContin stating:

*         The FDA has determined that the benefits of original OxyContin no longer outweigh its risks and that original OxyContin was withdrawn from sale for reasons of safety or effectiveness.

*         Accordingly, the agency will not accept or approve any abbreviated new drug applications (generics) that rely upon the approval of original OxyContin.

*         The reformulated version of OxyContin has abuse-deterrent properties.

*         New labeling was approved which indicates that the reformulated product has physical and chemical properties that are expected to make abuse via injection difficult and to reduce abuse via the intranasal route (snorting).

The OxyContin label changes include:

*         Statements supporting the reformulated version's abuse deterrent properties (section 9.2 of the OxyContin PI).

o   "OxyContin is formulated with inactive ingredients intended to make the tablet more difficult to manipulate for misuse and abuse."

*         Results of several physical and chemical tablet manipulation studies (crushing, dissolving, syringing, etc.) as well as clinical studies of drug "liking" of intranasally administered OxyContin.

*         Statement supporting that, like other opioid agonists, OxyContin can still be abused and is subject to misuse, addiction and criminal diversion.

What This Means to You:
Background on the physical characteristics of the EXALGO(r) tablet:
While we cannot make claims concerning abuse potential, physicians may be interested to know about the physical properties of EXALGO:

*         Hard outer shell

*         Formation of large particles when drug is crushed

*         Clumping of drug with exposure to water when crushed

Specific direction regarding this market news:

*         Do not proactively discuss this announcement with your customers.  Your primary sales focus should remain conveying WHO EXALGO is appropriate for, WHY it could be a good choice for those patients and HOW to properly convert and titrate patients.

*         If the physician asks specifically if EXALGO is abuse deterrent:

o   Ensure the physician understands that EXALGO cannot claim abuse/tamper resistance, but there are physical properties to the tablet of which they should be aware.

o   "Doctor, while we do not have FDA approved labeling concerning abuse potential, you may be interested to know that EXALGO has a hard outer shell that is difficult to crush, and if crushed it forms large particles.  Also, it clumps when exposed to water when crushed.  Of course, it is important to keep EXALGO out of the hands of inappropriate patients.  However, let's discuss an appropriate patient for EXALGO like the Elaine patient.  This is a patient you likely see multiple times a day who may benefit from the true 24-hour dosing EXALGO provides."

o   Refer them to Medical Affairs as we have a standard response letter and studies to provide further information.

The EXALGO Marketing & Training Team

May 10, 2012 I By Don Frances<http://www.scpr.org/about/people/staff/don-frances/>
[httP://media.scpr.org/assets/images/commentbg.png]0<http://www.scpr.org/blogs/news/2012/05/10/6054/authorities-raid-panorama-city-medical-clinicarre/#disqus_thread>

A pile of Oxycodone pills
A raid on a medical clinic in Panorama City yesterday resulted in 70 arrests, including of physicians,
for allegedly operating an illegal Oxycontin prescription ring or "pill mill ."
Wednesday morning's raid on the Roscoe Van Nuys Medical Clinic included the arrest of Dr. Manuel Sison,
the clinic's medical director, who is also a physician at the L.A. County Jail, CBS
reports<http://losangeles.cbslocal.com/2012/05/09/agents-raid-doctors-van-nuys-office-in-allegedprescription-drug-ring/>.
During the raid, authorities from county, state and federal agencies found 42 patients in the clinic -more than the clinic plausibly could have been taking on for legitimate medical concerns, agents told
CBS.
According to wire service reports<http://northridge.patch.com/articles/northridge-woman-among-70arrested-in-pill-mill-raids#photo-9882148>, the clinic at 8121 Van Nuys Blvd. was raided by the Health
Authority Law Enforcement Taskforce, or HALT, consisting of authorities from the FBI, the L.A. County
Sheriff's Department, the state Department of Justice, the DEA, the IRS and the county Department of
Health and Human Services. A description of the task force<http://lasheriff.org/divisions/detective/major_crimes/mjrcrm.html> by the Sheriff's Department says that it
"investigates Medi-Cal fraud, counterfeit and illegal distribution of pharmaceuticals and the illegal
practice of medicine and dentistry."
Also arrested among the doctors, patients and clinic staff was the clinic's manager, 52-year-old Aida
Hawatmeh of Northridge. Several other doctors and clinic staff remain under investigation in the case,
authorities said.
A "pill mill" is a place where drug dealers and addicts can pay hundreds of dollars for prescriptions -usually for the powerful narcotic painkiller

MNKOI 0001309367

 Oxycontin/Oxycodone<http://drpullen.com/oxycontinvsoxycodone> -- without ever being examined by a doctor.
The illegal operations can pull down many thousands of dollars a day. Authorities said Roscoe Van Nuys
Medical Clinic was shut down once before for operating as a pill mill, but reopened later under different
doctors.

From: National Rx Drug Abuse & Heroin Summit <no-reply@rx-summit.com>

To: kevin.webb@mallinckrodt.com



Not rendering correctly? View this email as a web page here.

 

 

 

        Volume 7 Issue 16                                                                                                           August 24, 2017

The largest national collaboration for those impacted by Rx drug abuse & heroin use.
-----


-----



 

 

{         Summit Website         }


{  Call for Presentations }

 {       Refer a Friend       }


Educational Advisor:





 

 

 In This Issue:

At least 17 states limiting painkiller prescriptions
7-fold spike seen in opioid-linked fatal car crashes
Opioid overdose ICU admissions, death rate increasing
Police try new database for documenting overdoses




 

 
Summit Spotlight

 

 

 
Register Now for the 2018 National Rx Drug Abuse & Heroin Summit! Lowest Rates Now Available!


 

 



 


 

 
April 2   5, 2018 | Hyatt Regency Atlanta


The National Rx Drug Abuse & Heroin Summit is where solutions are formulated, stakeholders convene, and change begins. It is the annual gathering for stakeholders to discuss what s working in prevention and treatment. Notable speakers in past years have included President Barack Obama in 2016 and U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Secretary Tom Price in 2017. Be part of the international discussion on addressing the opioid crisis by attending the 2018 National Rx Drug Abuse & Heroin Summit in Atlanta.

{     Register Now     }




 

 
Top Stories in the News Disclaimer: Articles and links within articles do not necessarily reflect the views or opinions of the National Rx Drug Abuse & Heroin Summit or Operation UNITE.



 

 

 
At least 17 states enacting limit on length of painkiller prescriptions
Katie Zezima, The Washington Post States are enacting strict limits on the number of powerful prescription painkillers doctors can prescribe, a move that many believe will help fight the opioid crisis but has raised alarms among some physicians. At least 17 states have enacted rules to curb the number of painkillers doctors can prescribe. Some, including Arizona, Connecticut, Delaware, Massachusetts, New Jersey and Ohio, have passed laws limiting the duration of initial opioid prescriptions to five or seven days. Others are passing dosage limits. In Kentucky, a law went into effect last month capping opioid prescriptions for acute pain to three days.


{Read More}
-----
7-fold spike seen in opioid-linked fatal car crashes
Steven Reinberg, HealthDay News In yet another sign of just how deadly the U.S. opioid epidemic has become, researchers report a sevenfold increase in the number of drivers killed in car crashes while under the influence of prescription painkillers. Prescriptions for drugs such as oxycodone (OxyContin), hydrocodone (Vicoprofen) and morphine have quadrupled, from 76 million in 1991 to nearly 300 million in 2014, so it's no surprise these medications are playing a growing role in highway deaths, the Columbia University researchers said.

{Read More}
-----
Opioid overdose ICU admissions, death rate increasing
Salynn Boyles, MedPage Today Deaths associated with opioid overdoses in hospital intensive care units nearly doubled over a seven-year period from 2009 and 2015, and the costs of treating overdose victims in the ICU has skyrocketed, researchers report. The average cost of caring for an opioid overdose patient in the ICU increased by 58% from $58,500 to $92,400, according to a retrospective analysis of hospital billing records from 162 hospitals in 44 states. Admissions to ICUs linked to opioid overdoses increased by 34% at the hospitals from January of 2009 to September 2015, according to the analysis appearing online in Annals of the American Thoracic Society.

{Read More}
-----
Police try out new database for documenting opioid overdoses
Jennifer McDermott, Associated Press Police in Massachusetts are testing a new database for documenting opioid overdoses they hope will help departments share information in real time and get people into treatment. It works like this: When a department is called to an overdose, it's recorded in the system. The system then alerts the department to do a follow-up outreach visit. Within 24 hours of a nonfatal overdose, a non-uniformed officer and recovery coach will go to the person's house to discuss treatment and offer resources to their family.

{Read More}

Why stock the 32 mg tablet?

 

 EXALGO 32 mg was the median effective dose in the pivotal trial.*1

REFERENCES: 1. Hale M, Khan A, Kutch M, Li S. Once-daily OROS hydromorphone ER compared with placebo in opioid-tolerant patients with chronic low back pain. Curr Med Res Opin. 2010;26(6):1505-1518.

To ensure that you receive future email from EXALGO, add us to your address book.
If you no longer wish to receive email from EXALGO, unsubscribe now.

 INDICATION

EXALGO  (hydromorphone HCI) Extended-Release
Tablets (CII) is indicated for the management of
moderate to severe pain in opioid tolerant patients
requiring continuous, around-the-clock opioid
analgesia for an extended period of time.

IMPORTANT RISK INFORMATION

WARNING: ABUSE POTENTIAL,
LIFE-THREATENING RESPIRATORY DEPRESSION, and ACCIDENTAL EXPOSURE

Abuse Potential

EXALGO contains hydromorphone, an opioid agonist and a Schedule II controlled substance with an abuse liability similar to other opioid agonists, legal or illicit. Assess each patient s risk for opioid abuse or addiction prior to prescribing EXALGO. The risk for opioid abuse is increased in patients with a personal or family history of substance abuse (including drug or alcohol abuse or addiction) or mental illness (e.g., major depressive disorder). Routinely monitor all patients receiving EXALGO for signs of misuse, abuse, and addiction during treatment.

Life-threatening Respiratory Depression

Respiratory depression, including fatal cases, may occur with use of EXALGO, even when the drug has been used as recommended and not misused or abused. EXALGO is for use in opioid tolerant patients only. Proper dosing and titration are essential and EXALGO should be prescribed only by healthcare professionals who are knowledgeable in the use of potent opioids for the management of chronic pain. Monitor for respiratory depression, especially during initiation of EXALGO or following a dose increase. Crushing, dissolving, or chewing the tablet can cause rapid release and absorption of a potentially fatal dose of hydromorphone.

Accidental Exposure

Accidental ingestion of EXALGO, especially in children, can result in a fatal overdose of hydromorphone.

 

 

 EXALGO is contraindicated in:
- Opioid non-tolerant patients. Fatal respiratory
  depression could occur in patients who are not
  opioid tolerant.

- Patients with significant respiratory depression

- Patients with acute or severe bronchial asthma in
  an unmonitored setting or in the absence of
  resuscitative equipment

- Patients with known or suspected paralytic ileus

- Patients who have had surgical procedures and/or
  underlying disease resulting in narrowing of the
  gastrointestinal tract, or have  blind loops  of the
  gastrointestinal tract or gastrointestinal obstruction

- Patients with hypersensitivity (e.g., anaphylaxis) to
  hydromorphone or sulfite-containing medications



 
 

 EXALGO is indicated for opioid tolerant patients only. Patients considered opioid tolerant are those who are taking at least 60 mg oral morphine per day, 25 mcg transdermal fentanyl/hour, 30 mg oral oxycodone/day, 8 mg oral hydromorphone/day, 25 mg oral oxymorphone/day or an equianalgesic dose of another opioid, for a week or longer.



 
 

 EXALGO is not intended for use as an as-needed analgesic and is not indicated for the management of acute or postoperative pain. It is contraindicated in patients who need management of mild pain or pain not expected to persist.



 
 

 Avoid concurrent use of alcohol and EXALGO. Concurrent use of EXALGO with CNS depressants, including alcohol, increases risk of respiratory depression, hypotension, and profound sedation, potentially resulting in coma or death. EXALGO may impair the ability to drive a car or operate machinery.



 
 

 Not intended in patients who have received MAO inhibitors within 14 days of starting EXALGO.



 
 

 Use with caution and in reduced doses in older or debilitated patients, as well as patients with renal or hepatic insufficiency, Addison s disease, delirium tremens, myxedema or hypothyroidism, prostatic hypertrophy or urethral stricture, toxic psychosis. May aggravate convulsions in patients with convulsive disorders; may induce or aggravate seizures in some clinical settings. Consider use of an alternate analgesic in patients with severe renal impairment.



 
 

 Respiratory depression, which occurs more frequently in elderly or debilitated patients, is the chief hazard with EXALGO.



 
 

 Serious adverse events could also include hypotensive effects, GI effects, cardiac arrest from overdose and precipitation of withdrawal. Most common adverse events (>10%) seen in clinical studies (N=2474) were: constipation (31%), nausea (28%), vomiting, somnolence, headache, asthenia and dizziness.



 
 

 Use EXALGO with extreme caution in patients susceptible to intracranial effects of CO2 retention.



 
 

 Do not abruptly discontinue EXALGO.


 

See additional Important Risk Information, including boxed warning, in Full Prescribing Information and Medication Guide.

Subject: [RxNews] OXY EXPRESS
A worrisome new kind of drug dealer is gaining a toehold in Georgia after fleeing crackdowns in
surrounding states, setting up in bedroom communities northwest of Atlanta along 1-75 to serve customers
near and far.
So-called "pill mills" are illegally selling prescription drugs in Georgia. Police say it's no
coincidence that the first bust of a suspected pill mill - the kind of illicit pain clinics that have
proliferated in South Florida - occurred last month in Cartersville, the seat of Bartow County. Nor that
a Cherokee county house served as a distribution site for a counterfeit prescription drug operation.
The counties are along the superhighway that brings drug seekers in droves from Kentucky, Tennessee, west
Virginia and Ohio to pill mills in Florida along a route that has come to be known as the "oxy Express,"
after the powerful and highly addictive prescription painkiller oxycodone. oxycodone and its brand names
oxycontin and Roxycodone are sometimes called "hillbilly heroin" because of their popularity in
Appalachian states.
Georgia lawmakers have been slower than neighboring states to try to deter prescription drug abuse
through means such as a statewide database to track prescriptions or tough regulations for pain clinics.
As a result, recent high-profile indictments and arrests illustrate the extent to which prescription
forgery rings, counterfeit prescription pushers and illicit pain clinics have sprung up in the Peach
State.
• In May, 11 people were indicted on federal charges of conspiring to forge oxycodone prescriptions and
trafficking in oxycodone. The alleged ringleader, Kristen Noelle Goduto, 27, of Marietta, and alleged
conspirators from Acworth, Canton and Braselton manufactured prescriptions and recruited others to pass
them at pharmacies across metro Atlanta. The ring obtained more than 10,000 tablets they intended to sell
on the streets, according to the federal indictment.
• Federal , state and local authorities raided Atlanta Medical Group clinic in Cartersville a month ago in
the first takedown of a suspected pill mill in Georgia. A few weeks later on June 29, the clinic
financiers, who are from Vero Beach, Fla., were arrested on federal drug and money laundering charges.
Federal agents removed close to $600,000 in cash from two homes in Florida as part of the raid.
• Cherokee county drug investigators searched a house in Woodstock in January 2010 and seized 100,000
prescription pills including the anti -anxiety drug Xanax, the erectile dysfunction drugs viagra and
Cialis and the diet drug phentermine. Many were counterfeit drugs imported from China. The resident,
Robyn Phillip Henderson, 34, has pleaded guilty to charges related drug trafficking in federal court.
Combating prescription drug abuse has become a top priority for the office of Sally Quillian Yates, U.S.
attorney for the Northern District of Georgia.
"As shown by last week's federal indictment charging the owners and staff of a pill mill in Cartersville,
our drug prosecutors are bringing larger and more sophisticated cases to focus on the largest sources of
abused painkillers, and we'll continue to bring these cases until the epidemic subsides," Yates said.
Phillip Price, who heads the Cherokee Multi -Agency Narcotics Squad, shifted two of his 10 detectives to
prescription drug investigations last year after observing the uptick in those cases. when one of them,
Investigator Nate Luca, began introducing himself to local pharmacies, he was startled at how much
prescription forgery was going unreported. Pharmacists handed over folders of information on suspicious
customers they had been collecting for months.
"Every pharmacy had a folder that was 2 inches thick," he said.
There is little to prevent patients who are doctor-shopping or forging prescriptions from going from
pharmacy to pharmacy to score drugs. Georgia lawmakers this year passed a law to create a prescription
drug monitoring program, an electronic database that would track how prescriptions are dispensed, but no
funding was allocated.
Rick Allen, director of the Georgia Drugs and Narcotics Agency, said he has applied for a federal grant
to fund the database, which would cost between $400,000 and $1.2 million. Even if the state gets the
grant, it will probably be 2013 or later before the database is online.
Prescription medications can be more deadly than heroin, meth and cocaine when abused. Nationally, there
has been a tenfold increase in prescription drug-related deaths over the past four decades, according to
the centers for Disease Control and Prevention. In Georgia, six times more people died from prescription

MNKOI 0001471861

 drug overdoses in 2009 than from all other illegal drugs, accounting for 87 percent of drug-related
deaths.
Among the people who suffered untimely deaths was Brandi Lynn Kanthak, 24, of Cartersville, who died Feb.
25, 2010, from an overdose of the painkiller Demerol. Unbeknownst to her parents and husband, she would
crush the pills to negate the time-release formula and inject them, said her mother, Barbara Pruitt. The
once-promising nursing student who worked at a medical clinic went into respiratory failure one day and
never revived.
"She had so much ahead of her," Pruitt said. "And she was so smart, and she could do anything. It's just
a sad thing."
"Doctor-shopping" and forging prescriptions are prime ways people get their fix. Another avenue is pill
mills, such as the one raided in Cartersville last month. Unlike legitimate pain clinics, they prescribe
large doses of painkillers with little to no screening of patients.
Allen used to keep a count of how many pain clinics were operating in the state. The tally went from
about five last year to about 50 earlier this year. But within the past few months, there have been two
to three new ones opening each week.
"They are all over the place," Allen said. "We can't even keep up with them anymore. We quit trying."
There are at least 10 pain clinics currently operating in Cherokee county, according to Price. Five years
ago, the county didn't have any.
Now as many as five to six calls per day come in to Mid-City Pharmacy in Canton from people asking
whether it fills oxycodone prescriptions, owner and pharmacist Billy Cagle said. Many of the requests are
coming from out-of-state customers and unfamiliar clinics.
"The pain clinics that we are familiar with that are local, we take care of," Cagle said. "But you've got
some people coming from Tennessee and from Florida, and from some of the pain clinics we are not familiar
with. We turn them down."
Pill mills are likely to keep moving into Georgia because it has no operational prescription drug
monitoring database, unlike its neighbors. And new legislation in Tennessee and Florida that took effect
July 1 is aimed at making it more difficult for pain clinics to operate in those states. The new laws
state only doctors can own pain clinics. They require the physicians to be board-certified in pain
management. And they prohibit convicted felons from ownership
All of which are "no-brainers" to Rusty Grant, who supervises the Canton Regional Drug Enforcement Office
of the Georgia Bureau of Investigation. And yet, according to law enforcement officials, no state
legislators have proposed similar measures in Georgia.
Grant said pain clinics with Florida owners started moving into his 28-county region in northwest Georgia
more than a year ago in anticipation of the crackdown in the Sunshine State.
"They didn't wait for July 1," Grant said. "They went ahead and made the move to get up here as quickly
as they could."

Thank you, Tunde.  The issue at its core is actually pretty straight forward, but when it started to get complicated I let you know right away.  I believe working with Michael Baker as I indicated will gain us a fairly efficient path forward.  (I should acknowledge at some point, this excellent suggestion actually came from Lawrence).

 

However, as I mentioned, this specific issue is reflective of some larger concerns Lawrence and I share regarding commercial influence on scientific matters.  I’ve attached another correspondence that seems to reflect a similar concern.

 

We may want to set aside some time in addition to our scheduled 1 on 1, but since that is probably the next time you have available, perhaps we can start the conversation then and decide if we need more time.

 

Best regards,

John

John,

 

I am only getting bits and pieces of this issue. Let’s discuss after the weekend so I could get the full picture.

-Tunde-

Hello Tunde.

 

I’ve copied you on a chain of emails that reflects some provocative comments from our commercial colleagues about an important Letter to the Editor that we have been working on.  I will follow up shortly with more information, but wanted to make you aware of this situation that threatens to spiral.  I’ve copied in Lawrence, with whom I’ve spoken about this, as this situation is symptomatic of some important and larger issues regarding commercial influence in scientific communications as well as R&D project development. 

 

Best regards,

John

 

John Decker, PhD

Dear all,

 

Given the numerous concerns expressed by our commercial colleagues over the draft response I circulated, and the importance of this document, it seems to me the most efficient and effective next step will be to engage an external medical writer to draft the next response.  If there are no objections, I propose to engage Michael Baker in this capacity, who has extensive experience with this product and its related communications.

 

Thank you, and best regards,

John

 

John F. Decker,  PhD l Director, Global Scientific Communications

Cc: Mathews, Michael; Dutcher, Bonni; Patel, Monica; Devarakonda, Krishna; Zimmerman, Thomas
Subject: RE: APS Letter to the Editor re_Chou.docx



 

Team:

 

I agree 100% with Christy’s comments and concerns.  We need to be consistent in our response to this article as we are with how our MSL team handles this with supportive data in the field.  Not doing this would be a disservice to the brand and a biased response according to one person’s understanding of a KOL response.  I understand that there are deadlines and limitations to how we can respond but the current response is not appropriate.   

 

Regards,

 

Jen Williams, BSN, MBA, CPHQ, Lean Six-Sigma Greenbelt

Marketing Director, Market Access & Quality Lead-Acute Care

Mallinckrodt Pharmaceuticals

675 McDonnell Blvd (301-3 West)

Hazelwood, MO 63042

jennifer.williams@mallinckrodt.com


 

From: Hill, Lawrence
Sent: Friday, March 25, 2016 8:30 AM
To: England, Christina; Decker, John F
Cc: Mathews, Michael; Dutcher, Bonni; Patel, Monica; Devarakonda, Krishna; Zimmerman, Thomas; Williams, Jennifer
Subject: RE: APS Letter to the Editor re_Chou.docx



 

John,

 

Since your response is a very specific piece to address a narrow point to a targeted audience, how can we address the larger and broader points Christy makes? 

 

I mean, it may be that many of her points go beyond what you are trying to do here, but they are relevant for the larger issues facing Ofirmev.  What would be the best way to promulgate them?  This is your wheelhouse and I would trust your opinion on this.

 

I agree that the limitations on the length of this response may prevent us from developing her themes adequately, and we risk diluting the specific message you are trying to make if we attempt to make too many points in one concise letter . . . .  

 

Lawrence

(314) 654-3631 (desk)

(314) 239-8105 (mobile)


 

From: England, Christina
Sent: Thursday, March 24, 2016 2:55 PM
To: Decker, John F
Cc: Mathews, Michael; Dutcher, Bonni; Patel, Monica; Devarakonda, Krishna; Hill, Lawrence; Zimmerman, Thomas; Williams, Jennifer
Subject: RE: APS Letter to the Editor re_Chou.docx



 

Hi John,

 

I had the opportunity to go through the letter.  I think it is a really really good start, but we can definitely make it stronger before sending.

 

Please see my comments in the attached.  These are all very critical points to include.  We should keep the letter focused on the evidence and point to their lack of consideration for patient safety and not ask rhetorical or emotional questions.  They cannot promote MMA, whose whole goal is to reduce opioids, and then in the same document disregard the evidence across 4 studies that show clinically meaningful difference in opioid consumption vs. oral APAP.  In doing this, they are disregarding the entire point of MMA, which is to maintain adequate analgesia by reducing opioids.  They are better off not making a recommendation on route of administration than making this one, it is in clear disregard for patient safety.   That should be our ask, to reverse their recommendations or at a minimum remove their comparative comment and leave it to the provider to decide route of administration.

 

Mike and Jen, please find time to review this and see if you have anything to add.

 

Thank you and please let me know if you have any questions related to my comments in the attached.

 

Christy

 

Christy England, MPH

Brand Marketing Lead/Director, Hospital Acute Care Division

Mallinckrodt Pharmaceuticals

9920 Pacific Heights Blvd, Suite 150

San Diego, CA 92121

P: (314) 654-5392

F: (314) 654-5391


 

From: Decker, John F
Sent: Thursday, March 24, 2016 11:48 AM
To: England, Christina
Cc: Mathews, Michael; Dutcher, Bonni; Patel, Monica; Devarakonda, Krishna; Hill, Lawrence; Zimmerman, Thomas
Subject: APS Letter to the Editor re_Chou.docx



 

Hi Christy,

 

I’ve attached the draft response to the APS Guidelines that is nearly finalized, as we discussed today.  You indicated there are pharmacodymanic data being used by the field directly comparing IV vs Oral in a the classic pharmacodynamics sense (ie, comparing pain control rather than a proxy measure such as reduced opioid consumption), and I mentioned that I have not seen this.  I’m copying in Bonni as the field representative, as well as Krishna and Lawrence, with whom I vetted this response, so we are all on the same page. 

 

We received an early draft of this Letter to the Editor based on the SRL, but neither the response nor the SRL had PD data.  The closest was the Bollinger study, but this is supportive of the argument in this reply: that reduced opioid consumption is a valid *proxy* for pharmacodynamics evidence of analgesia (rather than a SPID or other measure of pain, typically vs placebo).   This version of the reply goes considerably beyond the SRL, to focus on the argument sketched out above. 

 

If there are PD data comparing IV vs Oral acetaminophen, I have not seen it.  As I mentioned today, this was the specific challenge to me from Dr. DeLeon Cassasola and Dr. Viscusi.  I would be grateful if you could please direct me to those data, or if someone else can do so, I would most welcome it and we will revise the response to include this additional information. 

 

Thank you for your comments to help us make this the response the best it can be. 

 

Best regards,

 

John

 

 

John F. Decker,  PhD l Director, Global Scientific Communications

> FDA NEWS RELEASE

•> For Immediate Release: April 16, 2013
> Media Inquiries: Morgan Liscinsky, 301-796-0397;
morgan.liscinsky@fda.hhs.gov<mailto:morgan.liscinsky@fda.hhs.gov>
> Consumer Inquiries: 888-INFO-FDA
•> FDA approves abuse-deterrent labeling for reformulated OxyContin
> Agency will not approve generics to original OxyContin
•> The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today approved updated labeling for Purdue Pharma L.P.'s
reformulated OxyContin (oxycodone hydrochloride controlled-release) tablets. The new labeling indicates
that the product has physical and chemical properties that are expected to make abuse via injection
difficult and to reduce abuse via the intranasal route (snorting).
•> Additionally, because original OxyContin provides the same therapeutic benefits as reformulated
OxyContin, but poses an increased potential for certain types of abuse, the FDA has determined that the
benefits of original OxyContin no longer outweigh its risks and that original OxyContin was withdrawn
from sale for reasons of safety or effectiveness. Accordingly, the agency will not accept or approve any
abbreviated new drug applications (generics) that rely upon the approval of original OxyContin.
•> The FDA approved the original formulation of OxyContin in Dec. 1995. The product was abused, often
following manipulation intended to defeat its extended -release properties. Such manipulation causes the
drug to be released more rapidly, which increases the risk of serious adverse events, including overdose
and death. In April 2010, the FDA approved a reformulated version of OxyContin, which was designed to be
more difficult to manipulate for purposes of misuse or abuse. Purdue stopped shipping original OxyContin
to pharmacies in August 2010.
•> "The development of abuse-deterrent opioid analgesics is a public health priority for the FDA," said
Douglas Throckmorton, M.D., deputy director for regulatory programs in the FDA's Center for Drug
Evaluation and Research. "While both original and reformulated OxyContin are subject to abuse and misuse,
the FDA has determined that reformulated OxyContin can be expected to make abuse by injection difficult
and expected to reduce abuse by snorting compared to original OxyContin."
•> The FDA has determined that the reformulated product has abuse-deterrent properties. The tablet is more
difficult to crush, break, or dissolve. It also forms a viscous hydrogel and cannot be easily prepared
for injection. The agency has determined that the physical and chemical properties of the reformulated
product are expected to make the product difficult to inject and to reduce abuse via snorting. However,
abuse of oxycontin by these routes, as well as the oral route, is still possible. The reformulated
product also may reduce incidents of therapeutic misuse, such as crushing the product to sprinkle it onto
food or to administer it through a gastric tube. When FDA finds that a new formulation has abuse
deterrent properties, the agency has the authority to require generics to have abuse-deterrent properties
also
•> The agency review of this issue included an analysis of the following:
•> *
Citizen petitions requesting that the agency determine whether original OxyContin was voluntarily
withdrawn from sale for reasons other than safety or effectiveness;
> •
Comments submitted to the public dockets associated with these petitions;
> *
Information concerning original and reformulated OxyContin and the withdrawal of original
OxyContin;
> *
Clinical data, peer-reviewed literature, and other information concerning postmarketing adverse
events associated with original OxyContin, reformulated OxyContin, and other extended -release oxycodone
products.

MNKOI 0000602323

 > Postmarketing assessments of the impact of reformulated OxyContin on abuse are ongoing, and the FDA
will update its evaluation of the effects of reformulated OxyContin on abuse as new data become
available.
•> The FDA, together with other public health agencies, continues to encourage the development of abusedeterrent formulations of opioids and believes that such products will help reduce prescription drug
abuse. At the same time, the FDA remains committed to ensuring that patients with pain have appropriate
access to opioid analgesics.

Subject:Suspicious Order Monitoring Processes
Attachments:Amerisource Bergen: Suspicious Call Report, Puchase Order Inquiry; RE: ABC Orlando FL  Oxy
Shipment - Covidien Order 70125597; ABC PO 046203576
Hi Heather,

I just wanted to take a moment and let you know of some situations that we have had recently with one of our customers,
AmerisourceBergen in Orlando FL. Due to the shortage of Oxycodone in the market, Mallinckrodt is being extra sensitive to
possible diversion issues that may occur.

Within the past week AmerisourceBergen Orlando has contacted us twice regarding suspicious orders that they have received
regarding Oxycodone shipments. Attached are e-mails for your review of us being notified by AmerisourceBergen Orlando
that they have received as suspicious call about an upcoming Oxycodone shipment and what we are doing to ensure the
safety and security of our shipments when we are made aware of such a circumstance.

Basically as part of our suspicious order monitoring process when notified by the customer that they have an indication of a
possible diversion issue, we are "walking" the shipment through the transportation system and monitoring it through senior
FedEx security at each touch point to ensure adequate delivery to our customer.

Notes: On the 1st e-mail last dated 3/5/09 confirming receipt of shipment where the customer says "not the Oxycodone 30",
we did not ship Oxycodone 30 as it is currently backordered, only the Oxycodone/Acetaminophen 5/325mg Tablets were
shipped. On the 2nd e-mail originally dated 3/6/09 in which AmerisourceBergen is stating that a consumer advised them that
they obtained their phone number from the Manufacturer, Mallinckrodt never supplies any customer information to anyone
over the phone (other than law enforcement inquiries regulated through our Legal Depa rtment).

This is just an FYI for you to know what Mallinckrodt is doing on our end of the supply chain.

Biopharmaceutical Good Distribution Practices Summit, March 18-20, 2013, Bethesda, MD   If one syringe goes missing in your distribution chain, you could be facing a total recall. FDA, EU Likely to Increase Use of Special Designations to Speed Approvals in 2013, Tufts Says
U.S. and EU regulators hope to increase the use of special designations, such as fast track, priority review and accelerated approval, to speed approvals of drugs for non-cancer diseases that are rare and/or life-threatening, according to a new Tufts report. Regulators want to approve these products at the same levels oncology drugs enjoyed between 2007 and 2011.
Drug Industry Daily

Court Dismisses Endo Suit, Opens Door to Generic Opana ER
A Washington, D.C., district court judge has thrown out Endo Pharmaceuticals  bid to prevent generic companies from producing the opioid drug Opana ER. In March, the company pulled its oxymorphone extended-release drug off the shelves and replaced it with a new formulation it says is crush-resistant and harder to snort.
Generic Line

Pharma Codevelopment Soaring, FDA Guidance Stalling
A new report by healthcare investment bank Leerink Swann trumpets the benefits of codevelopment partnerships and acquisitions (P&A): improved market performance, reduced R&D inefficiencies and healthy product pipelines. The number of biopharma acquisitions in 2012 (nine) surpassed 2011 (six) and that trend is likely to continue as companies have spent less in aggregate on P&A over time, the report states.

Teva Pharmaceutical plans to boost work in women s health beyond fertility as it narrows its branded-drug focus amid competition to its best-selling medicine, CEO Jeremy Levin said.

The growth of Indonesia s pharmaceutical industry in 2013 is projected to be not as strong as in last year due to expected rise in production cost, an industry leader said.

China will cut prices of about 400 drugs for respiratory diseases, fever and pain by up to 20 percent from February, in a move to make medicines, including some products from Pfizer, GlaxoSmithKline and Novartis, more affordable.

In digital and mobile health, policy is changing at the federal level, cultural attitudes about wellness are evolving and new forms of technology are transforming the way patients relate to their bodies and the way clinicians practice medicine, blogger Rich Meyer writes. Venture capital funding of digital health grew dramatically in 2012 with investors funneling 46 percent more money and making 56 percent more deals in healthcare. Just thought I should let you know that Keysource Medical has had their DEA license revoked as of June 10. See the
news release below from the DEA.

News Release [printer-friendly version]
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE
June 10, 2011
Contact: Rich Isaacson
Number: (313) 234-4310
Cincinnati Pharmaceutical Supplier's DEA License Suspended
Keysource Medical distributed 48 million doses of oxycodone products to Florida pharm acies
JUN 10 - DETROIT- Robert L. Corso, Special Agent in Charge of the Detroit Field Division, Drug  Enforcement
Administration (DEA) announced today the immediate suspension of the federal controlled substance Registration of
Keysource Medical, a wholesale supplier of pharmaceuticals.
Keysource Medical, based in Cincinnati, Ohio, has been the subject of a DEA investigation that alleges the company was
selling large quantities of controlled substances to pharmacies, primarily in Florida. The investigation has revealed that
several of Keysource Medical's largest purchasers of oxycodone were engaged in schemes to dispense controlled
substances based on prescriptions that were written for other than legitimate medical  purposes. The investigation
revealed that Keystone Medical distributed approximately 48 million dosage units of oxycodone products to customers in
Florida over a two year time between November of 2008 and November of 2010.
 Pharmaceutical companies have a responsibility to ensure that the drugs they sell don't end up in the hands of drug
traffickers or businesses that are conducting their business illegally,  said Corso.  Prescription drug abuse in Florida,
southern Ohio and northern Kentucky has risen to epidemic proportions, and Keysource Medical, should have known
based on the large, frequent quantities, that their customers were diverting oxycodone into arenas that were not
legitimate. This action is another reminder that the DEA is working hard to hold accountable those companies who
choose to operate outside the law.
DEA's action suspends Keysource Medical's DEA Certificate of Registration in accordance with an Immediate
Suspension Order and pursuant to Sections 303 and 304 of the Controlled Substances Act, Title 21, Sections 823 and
824. The DEA's investigation of Keysource Medical has determined that the continued registration of this company
constitutes an imminent danger to public health and safety.
Keysource Medical received written notice of the factual and legal basis for this action. In addition, Keysource Medical
will be given an opportunity for an administrative hearing within the next 60 days. After the hearing, the DEA Deputy
Administrator will make a final decision on whether Keysource Medical's registration should be permanently revoked.
This decision will be published in the Federal Register.
Oxycodone is the generic name of an addictive prescription painkiller that is classified under federal narcotics laws as a
Schedule II controlled substance. Oxycodone is typically legally prescribed to combat  acute, severe pain for legitimate
medical purposes.

BOSTON ?

A pair of pharmacies in Quincy and Norwood have been shut down by the

Massachusetts Board of Registration in Pharmacy following charges of
regulatory violations.
The pharmacies are co-owned by Dorchester resident Son Dinh and Christopher
Le of Stoughton.
The Quincy pharmacy, CarePro, had been granted a license to operate less
than eight months before it was officially suspended. The Norwood pharmacy,
Medi-Son, has had a license since the end of 2010.
Both Dinh and Le have been served with summary suspensions of their
pharmaceutical licenses. As Administrative Hearing Consul Beverly Cogut noted at
Dinh?s administrative hearing on Monday, summary suspensions are issued when
a ?continued threat to public health, safety or welfare? is believed to
have been found.
William Frisch, an investigator with the Office of Public Protection, said
at the hearing that he first visited CarePro in April, accompanied by his
partner and two agents from the federal Drug Enforcement Administration.
During the visit, Frisch said, he observed a number of violations of
pharmacy board regulations including a number of suspicious prescriptions for 30
mg tablets of the narcotic oxycodone for out-of-state patients. The
prescriptions, according to Frisch, originated from a pain center in Fort
Lauderdale, Fla.
Frisch also described deficiencies in the pharmacy?s record -keeping,
particularly regarding inventories and records of Schedule II drugs like
oxycodone. In one instance, Frisch said he found a vial of Ketamine that had come
from Medi-Son to fill a prescription without documentation that, according
to Dinh, had been misplaced.
Schedule II drugs include substances that the federal government holds to
have medical value, but have a high potential for abuse and addiction.
Although CarePro?s license to operate was not immediately suspended
following Frisch?s visit, the Norwood pharmacy, Medi-Son, was served with a
cease-and-desist order following a separate visit from the Office of Public
Protection investigators the previous day.
Then, during a follow-up visit to Medi-Son in May, investigators allegedly
found several prescriptions ? including one for Ritalin, also a Schedule II
drug ? that appeared to have been filled by CarePro.
Through his attorney, Dinh contends he had attempted to follow up the
investigator?s April visit with changes to his pharmacy?s policies, and was
simply the victim of opaque state pharmacy regulations.

Our highway interdiction team that is attached to the Warren County Drug Task Force in SW Ohio, intercepted a vehicle
returning from Florida to Columbus, Ohio. During the stop our drug canine (Kilo) detected the odor of marijuana, mostly
because they were smoking it in the vehicle! The dog alert prompted a search and in addition to 400 hits of heroin, two
baggies that contained 1,050 OxyContin 80mg. tablets. The interesting part of this is that the OxyContin is the old
formulation, with the indicia "OC" on the tablets.
Most of you are aware that Purdue reformulated OxyContin and began marketing the new product in August 2010, with
the vast majority of the old product gone by the end of 2010 in retail pharmacies. So how do these fine folks have
$100,000 worth of OxyContin that has been discontinued two years ago was the question. Although they indicated they
had been doctor shopping across the state of Florida, it was determined that the mastermind in this case had just
recently been paroled from prison after a several year stay, and this OxyContin had been stashed until he got out.
This was a great stop for our team which is made up of the Ohio State Highway Patrol (Simms) and the Warren County
Sheriff's Office (Lewis), working under the umbrella of the drug task force.

Suspect visited 38 pharmacies, 54 MDs

Kelley Noyes, a teacher from Naples, Fla., was arrested Tuesday and charged with 25 counts of fraud. Subject: FW: FYI from Pharmalot - "Walgreens And A Secret Checklist For Pain Reliever Prescriptions"
From: "Harper, Karen" <karen.harper@mallinckrodt.com>
Date: Thu, 10 Oct 2013 19:19:26 -0500
To: "Brian Rucker (brian.rucker@ipcrx.com)" <brian.rucker@ipcrx.com>


 

 

 

Karen Harper  |  Sr. Manager, Controlled Substances Compliance Group

Mallinckrodt Pharmaceuticals

675 McDonnell Blvd.

Hazelwood, MO 63042

T: 314.654.1868  |  M: 314.401.1573

This information may be confidential and/or privileged.  Use of this information by anyone other than the intended recipient is prohibited.  If you receive this in error, please inform the sender and remove any record of this message.

 

 

 

 

http://www.pharmalive.com/walgreens-and-a-secret-checklist-for-pain-reliever-prescriptions

As regulators, legislators and physicians grapple with ways to mitigate the ongoing abuse and misuse of prescription painkillers, there are unintended consequences   some patients are having a harder time obtaining needed medications. The latest indication is a secret check list that the Walgreens pharmacy chain is requiring its pharmacists to use to weed out prescriptions that may be suspect, according to a report by WTHR, an Indianapolis television station.

Called the Good Faith Dispensing Policy (here it is), the effort comes shortly after the drug-store chain agreed to pay a record $80 million in civil penalties for violating its license and the rules that govern how prescription painkillers are distributed (back story). The deal stemmed from an investigation that began at a Walgreen s warehouse and pharmacies in Florida and extended to other locations around the country.

The settlement prompted some other large pharmacy chains to tighten their oversight of prescribing practices over concerns that federal officials will widen their probes. CVS, for instance, scoured a database to identify questionable prescribing (read this). The Walgreen s policy also arrives as the FDA announced plans to require class-wide safety labeling changes and new post-market study requirements for all extended-release and long-acting opioid analgesics (look here).

These moves are designed to thwart what many public health and law enforcement officials describe as an epidemic of deaths and accidental addictions due to the rising use of these medicines. Three years ago, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention noted that the increase in overdose deaths in the US paralleled a 300 percent increase since 1999 in the sale of prescription painkillers (read this).

Consequently, the US Senate Finance Committee last year began a probe into the promotional efforts by drugmakers (read here). Meanwhile, a recent study found that the use of opioid painkillers may have rocketed over the years, but the beneficial effect these controversial prescription drugs have actually had on pain treatment appears to have been inconsequential. And the use of safer alternatives   specifically, non-opioid analgesic painkillers that do not include opioids   was essentially flat (more here).

For its part, Walgreen s is not discussing its policy with customers. But its pharmacists are required to use a checklist each time a customer presents a prescription for one of several powerful narcotics, including Oxycodone, Fentanyl and Opana, among others, according to WTHR. But some customers are finding it difficult to obtain a prescription.

In response the American Medical Association and the American Academy of Pain Management tell WTHR that they have begun tracking consumer complaints. Consider one woman who asked not to be named. She was Oxycodone for blood clots in her legs, but was turned away by a Walgreens (WAG) pharmacist without providing an explanation, other than to say he was following the new policy.

 He said,  We suggest you take it to CVS. At this point, we re just feeding an addiction.  He was very loud and it was right in the open when he basically called me an addict. At that point, I was just so upset I left,  she tells WTHR.  I ve been going to the same Walgreens for eight years. All I wanted was the same medication from the same doctor for the same medical condition, and they refused with no warning. 

The practice angers Deborah Peel, who founded the Patient Privacy Rights Foundation.  This is really outrageous,  she tells the TV station.  It s simply wrong for people not to know they are being evaluated in this fashion. If Walgreens wants to really offend its customers and prescribing physicians, this is the way to do it: have a secret policy and force people to comply with it and not tell them what it is  Everyone who has a pain prescription is being treated as a suspected criminal. We need programs that target the abusers, that don t treat everyone as an abuser. 

Meanwhile, Jackie Rowles, a certified registered nurse anesthetist at Meridian Pain Group in Carmel, Indiana, says the questions that Walgreens pharmacists may ask healthcare providers can be problematic. For instance, the expected length of treatment may be unknown and a particular drug may not be within the standard of care if prescribed off-label.

But the new policy does not surprise former Walgreens pharmacy technician Maryanne Ryan, who tells WTHR that the practices that led to the $80 million in penalties was not confined to Florida.  In our store, no prescriptions were ever turned down. We had a reputation that we were the store that would  fill anything,  so we saw suspicious prescriptions all the time. Even when we d raise red flags, our pharmacy managed didn t care. He told us to fill them anyway. 

  I saw very few things changes when this came out, other than people were being inconvenienced. The truth is a lot of bad prescriptions still get approved because the pharmacy manager s bonus is based on the amount of scripts that get filled,  she tells WTHR. And she adds that the policy is applied inconsistently, depending upon the decisions of the pharmacy staff on duty.

As for Walgreens, the chain issued a statement to WTHR that says, in part:  Our policy does not require prescriber contact for every prescription. We firmly believe that addressing prescription drug abuse will require all parties   including leading the community, physicians, pharmacies, distributors and regulators   to play a role in finding practical solutions to combating abuse while balancing patient access to critical medication.  You can read the rest of the statement at the bottom of theWTHR story.

STORY ENDS HERE

 



Sent from my iPad
