DEA Suspends Controlled-Substance License of Another Cardinal Health Distribution Center
DUBLIN, Ohio (AP) -- The government has suspended the medical products and services company's license to distribute
controlled substances from its Lakeland, Fla., distribution center effective Dec. 10, the company said Friday.
The suspension follows a similar action announced last week against Cardinal's Washington state distribution
ADVERTISEMENT
center amid an investigation of a customer's online sales of the prescription painkiller hydrocodone, commonly
known by the brand name Vicodin.
That suspension went into effect Monday after a U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration order said Cardinal's distribution center
in Auburn, Wash., supplied the drug to a pharmacy that allegedly dispensed excessive amounts based on illegitimate
prescriptions from Internet pharmacies.
Cardinal spokesman Jim Mazzola on Friday said the Florida center's suspension is related to the same matter. The company is
working with the DEA to resolve the issue and is taking steps that guard against distribution to pharmacies "engaged in

Pete & Jane,

Attached is the revised McKesson VIP model and a separate file containing just the summary of the latest proposal (without all the data and calculations).  This takes the model that Karen reviewed and approved over the weekend and makes minor modifications as we discussed yesterday, including:

1.      Removal of APAP/Codeine from the compliance tiers.  Due to our supply issues, they have not been coming anywhere close to the original trend, and it is likely that we've even lost a portion of the volume.  Growth is pretty unrealistic at this point.
2.      Inclusion of a column showing current run rate for the compliance families.  This allows a comparison to where they were trending based upon March data (pulled for the original model), and shows that they've already achieved about half of the growth we are targeting in total.
3.      A modification of the compliance targets to provide two levels, which they had asked for in June.  The first level is clearly within reach and has lower payouts than the previous version, and the upper level has higher targets and, in some cases, slightly higher payouts.  The full analysis (on the "7-9-12 Level 1" and "7-9-12 Level 2" tabs) shows that both of these two options now give us 40% or more in standard margin, up from the 39.5% we had in the one-level version we started with yesterday.  And, the first level gives McKesson an 18.2% overall payout, while the second level (still attainable, I think) gives 19.5%, right in the middle of where they wanted to be.

Pete, I did not include sales by product family for the last VIP period anywhere...I can't remember if you said you did want that for sure, but if you do, I can send that to you separately.

I am copying Karen on this since there are minor tweaks since yesterday, but I hope those won't be a problem since we are now better off in terms of margin for both new compliance target levels.  Karen, please advise if you do have concerns.

Thanks, and let me know if you have questions.
Kevin

The FDA has approved the EXALGO  (hydromorphone HCl) Extended-Release Tablets (CII) 32 mg tablet for use in
appropriate opioid-tolerant chronic pain patients. With the
addition of the 32 mg tablet, along with the already approved

The features of the added EXALGO 32 mg tablet include:

Additional EXALGO information available<http://whatcounts.jobson.com/t?r=12&c=0&l=2982&ctl=547BA:B5F526631F6058485DD7F585132E82E093B8F18DA1535B1F&>.

INDICATION

EXALGO  (hydromorphone HCI) Extended-Release
Tablets (CII) is indicated for the management of
moderate to severe pain in opioid tolerant patients
requiring continuous, around-the-clock opioid
analgesia for an extended period of time.

IMPORTANT RISK INFORMATION

WARNING: ABUSE POTENTIAL,
LIFE-THREATENING RESPIRATORY DEPRESSION, and ACCIDENTAL EXPOSURE

Abuse Potential

EXALGO contains hydromorphone, an opioid agonist and a Schedule II controlled substance with an abuse liability similar to other opioid agonists, legal or illicit. Assess each patient s risk for opioid abuse or addiction prior to prescribing EXALGO. The risk for opioid abuse is increased in patients with a personal or family history of substance abuse (including drug or alcohol abuse or addiction) or mental illness (e.g., major depressive disorder). Routinely monitor all patients receiving EXALGO for signs of misuse, abuse, and addiction during treatment.

Life-threatening Respiratory Depression

Respiratory depression, including fatal cases, may occur with use of EXALGO, even when the drug has been used as recommended and not misused or abused. EXALGO is for use in opioid tolerant patients only. Proper dosing and titration are essential and EXALGO should be prescribed only by healthcare professionals who are knowledgeable in the use of potent opioids for the management of chronic pain. Monitor for respiratory depression, especially during initiation of EXALGO or following a dose increase. Crushing, dissolving, or chewing the tablet can cause rapid release and absorption of a potentially fatal dose of hydromorphone.

Accidental Exposure

Accidental ingestion of EXALGO, especially in children, can result in a fatal overdose of hydromorphone.



 


EXALGO is contraindicated in:
- Opioid non-tolerant patients. Fatal respiratory
  depression could occur in patients who are not
  opioid tolerant.

- Patients with significant respiratory depression

- Patients with acute or severe bronchial asthma in
  an unmonitored setting or in the absence of
  resuscitative equipment

- Patients with known or suspected paralytic ileus

- Patients who have had surgical procedures and/or
  underlying disease resulting in narrowing of the
  gastrointestinal tract, or have  blind loops  of the
  gastrointestinal tract or gastrointestinal obstruction

- Patients with hypersensitivity (e.g., anaphylaxis) to
  hydromorphone or sulfite-containing medications


 


EXALGO is indicated for opioid tolerant patients only. Patients considered opioid tolerant are those who are taking at least 60 mg oral morphine per day, 25 mcg transdermal fentanyl/hour, 30 mg oral oxycodone/day, 8 mg oral hydromorphone/day, 25 mg oral oxymorphone/day or an equianalgesic dose of another opioid, for a week or longer.


 


EXALGO is not intended for use as an as-needed analgesic and is not indicated for the management of acute or postoperative pain. It is contraindicated in patients who need management of mild pain or pain not expected to persist.


 


Avoid concurrent use of alcohol and EXALGO. Concurrent use of EXALGO with CNS depressants, including alcohol, increases risk of respiratory depression, hypotension, and profound sedation, potentially resulting in coma or death. EXALGO may impair the ability to drive a car or operate machinery.


 


Not intended in patients who have received MAO inhibitors within 14 days of starting EXALGO.


 


Use with caution and in reduced doses in older or debilitated patients, as well as patients with renal or hepatic insufficiency, Addison s disease, delirium tremens, myxedema or hypothyroidism, prostatic hypertrophy or urethral stricture, toxic psychosis. May aggravate convulsions in patients with convulsive disorders; may induce or aggravate seizures in some clinical settings. Consider use of an alternate analgesic in patients with severe renal impairment.


 


Respiratory depression, which occurs more frequently in elderly or debilitated patients, is the chief hazard with EXALGO.


 


Serious adverse events could also include hypotensive effects, GI effects, cardiac arrest from overdose and precipitation of withdrawal. Most common adverse events (>10%) seen in clinical studies (N=2474) were: constipation (31%), nausea (28%), vomiting, somnolence, headache, asthenia and dizziness.


 


Use EXALGO with extreme caution in patients susceptible to intracranial effects of CO2 retention.


 


Do not abruptly discontinue EXALGO.


See additional Important Risk Information, including boxed warning, in Full Prescribing Information<http://whatcounts.jobson.com/t?r=12&c=0&l=2982&ctl=54A39:B5F526631F6058485DD7F585132E82E093B8F18DA1535B1F&> and Medication Guide<http://whatcounts.jobson.com/t?r=12&c=0&l=2982&ctl=54A3A:B5F526631F6058485DD7F585132E82E093B8F18DA1535B1F&>.

Heather,

To advise your office of an incident in which Rockledge, FL Police Department forwarded to Mallinckrodt tablets supplied by a confidential informant with similar marking to Mallinckrodt Oxycodone 30 mg. that "did not work".

Mallinckrodt preliminary test results indicate the material is counterfeit.

From:   Herman, Cliff 
Sent:   Tuesday, October 12, 2010 4:29 PM
To:     Ratliff, Bill; Harper, Karen
Subject:        Update on mystery "Oxycodone 30 mg" tablets

Hi Karen and Bill,

After preliminary investigation by CAR using non-destructive methods, we can state without doubt that the tablets received from Hobart did not originate from Mallinckrodt.

The markings on the mystery tablet are very similar, but when examined under a microscope they are clearly not identical to Mallinckrodt tooling used for 30 mg Oxycodone tablets.
The mystery tablets are made of completely different ingredients when compared with the Mallinckrodt Oxycodone 30 mg tablet.
The mystery tablets do not appear to contain any oxycodone (this will be confirmed this week).
The mystery tablets are slightly larger than Mallinckrodt Oxycodone 30 mg tablets.





 

As I mentioned, these tests were non-destructive. Over the next couple of days, we will be running the validated analytical method to test for the presence of oxycodone.

We currently suspect that the unknown tablets contain some type of drug and we are working to identify that drug is and will provide a report to you later this week.

Hope that this helps answer your questions.

To:  'rxnews@listserve.com'
Subject:  [RxNews] 498-count indictment was unsealed today charging 53 defendants in a multimillion dollar drug conspiracy
Attach:  ATT1780851.txt

Included in the indictment are Dr. Norman Werther, of Horsham, pharmacist Ihsanullah

 Sean  Maaf, of Northeast Pharmacy in Philadelphia, and alleged drug trafficker William

Stukes, of Philadelphia. According to the indictment, Stukes and his alleged drug trafficking

organization recruited large numbers of pseudo patients and then transported them to Dr.

Werther s medical office for fake examinations. These  patients  paid an office visit fee, usually

$150, to the office staff and Werther would write prescriptions for those  patients  to obtain

oxycodone-based drugs without there being a medical need for the prescription. The  patients

were then driven to various pharmacies to have their prescriptions filled, including Northeast

Pharmacy where Maaf would fill the prescription. The drugs were then turned over to Stukes or

his drivers. Stukes and his organization would allegedly sell the narcotics to numerous drug

dealers, who are also named in the indictment, who would also then resell the drugs on the street.

It is estimated that between September 2009 and July 2011, the Stukes drug trafficking

organization earned more than $5 million through these illegal prescriptions and that the

defendants unlawfully acquired and distributed over 200,000 pills containing oxycodone.


The complete press release can be accessed here:


http://www.justice.gov/usao/pae/News/2011/Aug/werther_release.pdf


Kim

Subject:  DEA Suspicious Order Quantities


I wanted to advise all of you that we re working with Security and the DEA Compliance Group (Bill Ratliff and Karen Harper) to develop procedures to insure we maintain compliance with the DEA requirement that we report any suspicious order quantities and/or patterns to them.   In light of the recent developments with McKesson, a good deal of focus is being placed on this project.

Briefly, if an order is deemed  peculiar  by a customer service rep based on a set of guidelines currently being developed, it will be placed on hold and the DEA compliance group (Bill Ratliff and Karen Harper) will be advised.  DEA Compliance will then conduct a more in-depth investigation and determine if the situation warrants notification to the DEA.  If the order is deemed appropriate, customer service will be notified and the order will be released from hold status for shipment.   If the outcome of the investigation supports that the order is in fact   suspicious  it will not be shipped and the local DEA office will be notified.   I would expect that we also develop a means of communication to the business group any time an order is placed on hold for reasons of peculiarity by the Customer Service Group.   Updates regarding the status of specific orders should be forwarded as well as the  peculiar order  proceeds through the review process.

Preliminary processes are in development and I m in the process of determining/evaluating how best to identify deviations from the norm based on the type of businesses we service as well as the products being purchased.  Criteria that is well suited for an AT Clinic may be too stringent for a Distributor.  Each class of customer (clinics, distributors, wholesalers, etc.) will be handled based on the merits of the business segment they support.  Any anomalies that support what we term as a  peculiar  order will be forwarded to the DEA compliance group for further investigation prior to it being turned over to the DEA.

As these respective formulas are developed, I will share them with you along with a sampling of data used to support the validity/effectiveness of the assumptions used in developing same.   At first pass, the formula might look like this:

-        Customers will be separated into their respective class of business (distributors, wholesalers, clinic, hospitals, retail, etc)

-        Add purchase quantities, by product (all Oxy products and again by individual skus) for the last 12 months for all customers within the same class of business for any controlled substances

o      Customer s with multiple  ship to  locations should have their total aggregated at the  sold to  level; but also reviewed at the  ship to  level

-        Add customer months for every record used in the above total (months within the last 12 that customer purchases of the item were not zero)

-        Divide total quantity purchases by the total customer months

-        Then multiply by the factor below to give the maximum mount that the customer can order per month before showing up on the suspicious order report.

o      Factor = 2 for C-II Controlled Substances

o      Factor = 4 for C-III, IV and V

Once the myriad aspects of this project are refined, selective excess order quantity business rules may require adjustment.

In addition to order quantities by product, we hope to also develop criteria for orders that deviate from normal ordering patterns and/or from usual order frequency (not yet sure how to capture this; hope to identify an algorithm that will support parsing through the data to identify patterns, frequency, etc.)  A report will be generated daily (at a minimum) but hope to eventually have the systems in place so customer service receives a  real time  flag when an order violates one of our parameters and will flag the order as peculiar.

The group is working on other indicators that might be used in evaluating whether or not a customer should be reported as  peculiar .  The Sales force will play a key role in this process by verifying the customer s physical site and operations ring true with the type of business they purport to run.  The DEA Compliance group is in the process of discussing this aspect with management on the Sales side of the business.

If you have any questions, please let me know.  This process is in preliminary stages so we may not have answers to all the questions that may come up, but those questions might also be food for thought in furthering the breadth of this project.

Regards,

INDICATION

EXALGO  (hydromorphone HCI) Extended-Release
Tablets (CII) is indicated for the management of
moderate to severe pain in opioid tolerant patients
requiring continuous, around-the-clock opioid
analgesia for an extended period of time.

IMPORTANT RISK INFORMATION

WARNING: ABUSE POTENTIAL,
LIFE-THREATENING RESPIRATORY DEPRESSION, and ACCIDENTAL EXPOSURE

Abuse Potential

EXALGO contains hydromorphone, an opioid agonist and a Schedule II controlled substance with an abuse liability similar to other opioid agonists, legal or illicit. Assess each patient s risk for opioid abuse or addiction prior to prescribing EXALGO. The risk for opioid abuse is increased in patients with a personal or family history of substance abuse (including drug or alcohol abuse or addiction) or mental illness (e.g., major depressive disorder). Routinely monitor all patients receiving EXALGO for signs of misuse, abuse, and addiction during treatment.

Life-threatening Respiratory Depression

Respiratory depression, including fatal cases, may occur with use of EXALGO, even when the drug has been used as recommended and not misused or abused. EXALGO is for use in opioid tolerant patients only. Proper dosing and titration are essential and EXALGO should be prescribed only by healthcare professionals who are knowledgeable in the use of potent opioids for the management of chronic pain. Monitor for respiratory depression, especially during initiation of EXALGO or following a dose increase. Crushing, dissolving, or chewing the tablet can cause rapid release and absorption of a potentially fatal dose of hydromorphone.

Accidental Exposure

Accidental ingestion of EXALGO, especially in children, can result in a fatal overdose of hydromorphone.



 


EXALGO is contraindicated in:
- Opioid non-tolerant patients. Fatal respiratory
  depression could occur in patients who are not
  opioid tolerant.

- Patients with significant respiratory depression

- Patients with acute or severe bronchial asthma in
  an unmonitored setting or in the absence of
  resuscitative equipment

- Patients with known or suspected paralytic ileus

- Patients who have had surgical procedures and/or
  underlying disease resulting in narrowing of the
  gastrointestinal tract, or have  blind loops  of the
  gastrointestinal tract or gastrointestinal obstruction

- Patients with hypersensitivity (e.g., anaphylaxis) to
  hydromorphone or sulfite-containing medications


 


EXALGO is indicated for opioid tolerant patients only. Patients considered opioid tolerant are those who are taking at least 60 mg oral morphine per day, 25 mcg transdermal fentanyl/hour, 30 mg oral oxycodone/day, 8 mg oral hydromorphone/day, 25 mg oral oxymorphone/day or an equianalgesic dose of another opioid, for a week or longer.


 


EXALGO is not intended for use as an as-needed analgesic and is not indicated for the management of acute or postoperative pain. It is contraindicated in patients who need management of mild pain or pain not expected to persist.


 


Avoid concurrent use of alcohol and EXALGO. Concurrent use of EXALGO with CNS depressants, including alcohol, increases risk of respiratory depression, hypotension, and profound sedation, potentially resulting in coma or death. EXALGO may impair the ability to drive a car or operate machinery.


 


Not intended in patients who have received MAO inhibitors within 14 days of starting EXALGO.


 


Use with caution and in reduced doses in older or debilitated patients, as well as patients with renal or hepatic insufficiency, Addison s disease, delirium tremens, myxedema or hypothyroidism, prostatic hypertrophy or urethral stricture, toxic psychosis. May aggravate convulsions in patients with convulsive disorders; may induce or aggravate seizures in some clinical settings. Consider use of an alternate analgesic in patients with severe renal impairment.


 


Respiratory depression, which occurs more frequently in elderly or debilitated patients, is the chief hazard with EXALGO.


 


Serious adverse events could also include hypotensive effects, GI effects, cardiac arrest from overdose and precipitation of withdrawal. Most common adverse events (>10%) seen in clinical studies (N=2474) were: constipation (31%), nausea (28%), vomiting, somnolence, headache, asthenia and dizziness.


 


Use EXALGO with extreme caution in patients susceptible to intracranial effects of CO2 retention.


 


Do not abruptly discontinue EXALGO.

THURSDAY, OCTOBER 18, 2012

You are invited to participate in the upcoming National
Broadcast Event "Important Considerations in Customizing
Pain Management: Patient Selection and Dosing Strategies."
The expert faculty panel will cover the following information:

 

 Establish a rationale for choosing a long-acting
extended-release opioid

 
 

 Define proper patient selection

 
 

 Explore dosing conversion and titration strategies

 
 

 Improve prescriber-patient communication to help
facilitate successful treatment outcomes

 

PROGRAM DETAILS



 See the Program Chair, Michael Brennan, MD, describe the importance of this educational event.

 


 
Important: At the conclusion of the video, you will be
directed to the Registration website. If you are in the
Eastern or Central time zones please use NEbroadcast for
your invitation code. If you live in the Mountain or Pacific time zones, please use WTbroadcast for your invitation code.
If you are unable to make it to a meeting site, you also can
view the event from your home computer.

 

This interactive program will be broadcast to 60 venues
throughout the United States on Thursday, October 18th,
and will include a complimentary dinner at each venue.
The first live broadcast begins at 7:30 PM EST; a second live
broadcast will begin at 9:30 PM EST.

SEATING IS LIMITED REGISTER TODAY!

RSVP today using one of the following methods:

1.

 Online at: www.HLXBroadcast.com. If you are in the

your invitation code. If you live in the Mountain or Pacific
time zones, please use WTbroadcast for your invitation code.

 
2.

 Call: 800-111-0467.

 
3.

This event is promotional; there are no certified continuing medical education credits approved for this presentation. Covidien proudly adheres to the Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers Association Code for Interactions with Healthcare Professionals. Attendance must be limited strictly to healthcare professionals. Spouses and other guests cannot be accommodated. Thank You.

Expert Faculty Panel

Michael Brennan, MD (Program Chair)

Fairfield, CT

Charles E. Argoff, MD, PhD

Albany, NY

Joseph Shurman, MD

San Diego, CA

In addition to a live Question and Answer session with the
nationally recognized faculty, there will be robust post-event discussion at each venue led by a local faculty speaker.

 


800-778-7898 | www.EXALGO.com

COVIDIEN, COVIDIEN with logo and Covidien logo are U.S. and internationally registered trademarks of Covidien AG. EXALGO is a registered trademark of Mallinckrodt LLC.
  2012 Mallinckrodt LLC, a Covidien company.  MK20185 October 2012

 INDICATION

EXALGO  (hydromorphone HCI) Extended-Release
Tablets (CII) is indicated for the management of
moderate to severe pain in opioid tolerant patients
requiring continuous, around-the-clock opioid
analgesia for an extended period of time.

IMPORTANT RISK INFORMATION

WARNING: ABUSE POTENTIAL,
LIFE-THREATENING RESPIRATORY DEPRESSION,
and ACCIDENTAL EXPOSURE

Abuse Potential

EXALGO contains hydromorphone, an opioid agonist and a Schedule II controlled substance with an abuse liability similar to other opioid agonists, legal or illicit. Assess each patient s risk for opioid abuse or addiction prior to prescribing EXALGO. The risk for opioid abuse is increased in patients with a personal or family history of substance abuse (including drug or alcohol abuse or addiction) or mental illness (e.g., major depressive disorder). Routinely monitor all patients receiving EXALGO for signs of misuse, abuse, and addiction during treatment.

Life-threatening Respiratory Depression

Respiratory depression, including fatal cases, may occur with use of EXALGO, even when the drug has been used as recommended and not misused or abused. EXALGO is for use in opioid tolerant patients only. Proper dosing and titration are essential and EXALGO should be prescribed only by healthcare professionals who are knowledgeable in the use of potent opioids for the management of chronic pain. Monitor for respiratory depression, especially during initiation of EXALGO or following a dose increase.
Crushing, dissolving, or chewing the tablet can cause rapid release and absorption of a potentially fatal dose of hydromorphone.

Accidental Exposure

Accidental ingestion of EXALGO, especially in children, can result in a fatal overdose of hydromorphone.

 

 

 EXALGO is contraindicated in:

- Opioid non-tolerant patients. Fatal respiratory
  depression could occur in patients who are not
  opioid tolerant.

- Patients with significant respiratory depression

- Patients with acute or severe bronchial asthma in
  an unmonitored setting or in the absence of
  resuscitative equipment

- Patients with known or suspected paralytic ileus

- Patients who have had surgical procedures and/or
  underlying disease resulting in narrowing of the
  gastrointestinal tract, or have  blind loops  of the
  gastrointestinal tract or gastrointestinal obstruction

- Patients with hypersensitivity (e.g., anaphylaxis) to
  hydromorphone or sulfite-containing medications


 
 

 EXALGO is indicated for opioid tolerant patients only. Patients considered opioid tolerant are those who are taking at least 60 mg oral morphine per day, 25 mcg transdermal fentanyl/hour, 30 mg oral oxycodone/day, 8 mg oral hydromorphone/day, 25 mg oral oxymorphone/day or an equianalgesic dose of another opioid, for a week or longer.



 
 

 EXALGO is not intended for use as an as-needed analgesic and is not indicated for the management of acute or postoperative pain. It is contraindicated in patients who need management of mild pain or pain not expected to persist.

 
 

 Avoid concurrent use of alcohol and EXALGO. Concurrent use of EXALGO with CNS depressants, including alcohol, increases risk of respiratory depression, hypotension, and profound sedation, potentially resulting in coma or death. EXALGO may impair the ability to drive a car or operate machinery.

 
 

 Not intended in patients who have received MAO inhibitors within 14 days of starting EXALGO.

 
 

 Use with caution and in reduced doses in older or debilitated patients, as well as patients with renal or hepatic insufficiency, Addison s disease, delirium tremens, myxedema or hypothyroidism, prostatic hypertrophy or urethral stricture, toxic psychosis. May aggravate convulsions in patients with convulsive disorders; may induce or aggravate seizures in some clinical settings. Consider use of an alternate analgesic in patients with severe renal impairment.

 
 

 Respiratory depression, which occurs more frequently in elderly or debilitated patients, is the chief hazard with EXALGO.

 
 

 Serious adverse events could also include hypotensive effects, GI effects, cardiac arrest from overdose and precipitation of withdrawal. Most common adverse events (>10%) seen in clinical studies (N=2474) were: constipation (31%), nausea (28%), vomiting, somnolence, headache, asthenia and dizziness.

 
 

 Use EXALGO with extreme caution in patients susceptible to intracranial effects of CO2 retention.

 
 

 Do not abruptly discontinue EXALGO.


 

See additional Important Risk Information, including boxed warning, in Full Prescribing Information and Medication Guide.

Subject: HDMA Weekly Digest, May 14: Safeguarding America's Pharmaceuticals Act of 2013 Introduced
From: HDMA Weekly Digest <digest@hdmanet.org>
Date: Tue, 14 May 2013 15:50:50 +0000
To: steven.becker@covidien.com


{HDMA Weekly Digest: A Newsletter for HDMA Members} 
{A Newsletter for HDMA Members} May 14, 2013 
  

 
   
In This Issue   
  Safeguarding America's Pharmaceuticals Act of 2013 Introduced 
 Legislators Send Letter to FDA on Hydrocodone-Combination Product Rescheduling 
 California Board of Pharmacy Establishes E-Pedigree Committee, Announces June Meeting 

   Florida DWDAC to Hold Conference Call 
 Original Formulation of Opana ER Can Stay on
Market — FDA 
 DEA Hosting Manufacturer/Importer/Exporter Conference 

  
     

 
   
{HDMA 2013 Business and Leadership Conference} 
   
 {corner}  
{divider}

Safeguarding America's Pharmaceuticals Act of 2013 Introduced

Reps. Bob Latta (R-Ohio) and Jim Matheson (D-Utah) introduced the Safeguarding America's Pharmaceuticals Act of 2013 (H.R. 1919) on May 9. The bill reflects the legislative discussion draft on pharmaceutical supply chain safety and traceability that was marked up May 7 by the House Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health. During the markup, legislators discussed wholesaler licensure standards, federal preemption of state pedigree laws, returns processing and verification and the migration to unit-level serialization and traceability. Members on both sides of the aisle urged bipartisan cooperation and supported the process moving forward with patience and collaboration.

The House Energy and Commerce Committee scheduled a full committee markup of H.R. 1919 for May 14 at 4:00 p.m. in room 2123 of the Rayburn House Office Building, which will continue into a legislative markup on May 15 at 10:00 a.m. Additional details are available through the committee website.

For more information, contact Liz Gallenagh.
{top of page}

Legislators Send Letter to FDA on Hydrocodone-Combination Product Rescheduling

Senators Mark Kirk (R-Ill.), Joe Manchin (D-W.Va.) and a bipartisan, bicameral group of legislators sent a March 9 letter to FDA Commissioner Margaret Hamburg urging the agency to take action on rescheduling hydrocodone combination products. This letter is a follow up to one sent earlier this year imploring the FDA to act quickly on the FDA Advisory Committee's recommendation.

In addition to Senators Kirk and Manchin, the letter also was signed by Senators Jay Rockefeller (D-W.Va.), Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.), Dianne Feinstein (D-Calif.), Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.), Bill Nelson (D-Fla), Marco Rubio (R-Fla) and Representative Vern Buchanan (R-Fla).

Additional details, including the text of the letter, are available in the press release.

For more information, contact Jewelyn Cosgrove.
{top of page}

California Board of Pharmacy Establishes E-Pedigree Committee, Announces June Meeting

The California Board of Pharmacy established a separate E-Pedigree Committee, which will focus solely on matters pertaining to the implementation of California's e-pedigree law. The next meeting is set for June 24 in Sacramento. An agenda will be released 10 days prior to the meeting.

For more information, contact Liz Gallenagh.
{top of page}

Florida DWDAC to Hold Conference Call

The Florida Drug Wholesale Advisory Council (DWDAC) is hosting a conference call on May 16 at 9:30 a.m. (EDT). The agenda and meeting materials will be posted prior to the call and may be accessed here. The DWDAC provides input to the Division of Drugs, Devices and Cosmetics.

For more information, contact Dan Bellingham.
{top of page}

Original Formulation of Opana ER Can Stay on Market — FDA

On May 10, FDA responded to a petition filed by Endo Pharmaceuticals Inc., and concluded that the original formulation of Opana ER (oxymorphone hydrochloride) Extended-Release Tablets should not be be withdrawn from the market for reasons of safety or effectiveness. For further information, see the FDA website.

For more information, contact Allison Tuszynski.
{top of page}

DEA Hosting Manufacturer/Importer/Exporter Conference

DEA is hosting a national two-day Manufacturer/Importer/Exporter Conference on Tuesday, June 18 and Wednesday, June 19 in National Harbor, Md. The conference will present federal laws and regulations that affect the pharmaceutical and chemical manufacturing, importing, and exporting industry and tiscuss practices to prevent diversion while minimizing the impact on legitimate commerce. In addition, topics such as quotas, year-end reporting, ARCOS reporting, import/export permits and declarations will be discussed.

Registration is available on a first-come, first-served basis. Further information, including an agenda and a registration form, can be found on the DEA website.

For more information, contact Anita Ducca.

From: Kazemi, Kian L
Sent: Friday, July 19, 2013 1:47 PM
To: Williams, Jane L
Subject: McKesson Request for Verbiage Changes



 

Hi Jane,

 

McKesson is asking that we make the following verbiage changes to our fentanyl patch price revision for OneStop.  I am okay with the first one.  We are in the A slot, and there are 3 players in an AC slot.  Thus, we are not awarded on a “sole” basis.  However, we are in the primary position, and we do get the ROFR opportunity.  On the second one, I will need some guidance on how we want to handle this.  I believe we keep pushing for it.  If it becomes a major issue, then maybe we have to back off.  I believe Ginger said the other day that we have been getting pushback from other customers on this verbiage.  McKesson stated they would work with us on how we handle items in this situation (remove from the program, put in an AC slot, etc.), but that they can’t have a complete blanket exclusion from fees, etc..  This language has obviously been in our agreements with McKesson for a while and there has never been an issue.  Not sure why that has changed now.  I will be talking to Mayosh, Amber and Mike on Tuesday regarding legacy methylphenidate, so I can also ask about this change as well.  Lastly, they want to remove the clauses in # and #4 below because they are in our other agreements already.  I know we discussed changing our OneStop Supplier Agreement so that these clauses are included and don’t have to be put in any subsequent letter, but that has not been done yet.  With that said, why do we have to have it included here when it was included in the original letter signed by both parties?  We are just amending the pricing structure here.

 

In any case, what are your thoughts on these items?  Thanks.

 

1.      Mallinckrodt LLC will remain McKesson’s sole primary incumbent supplier of the Product and will be given the

opportunity to “meet or beat” any written, bona fide competitive bid for this Product that is received by McKesson.  Remove the word “sole”.

2.      Notwithstanding any other provision of this agreement or the existing contract, Mallinckrodt LLC’s ability to supply the Products may be subject to regulatory agency restrictions on quota impacting Manufacturing and product availability. In the event such restrictions are imposed, no rebates shall be paid for such restricted Product that has not shipped and no other penalties shall apply during the period during which such restrictions are in effect with respect to such Product.  Remove this verbiage.

3.       Customer represents and warrants that it has in place a suspicious order monitoring program as required by 21 C.F.R. § 1301.74(b). Customer agrees that upon written request, it will allow company, at company’s expense, to audit Customer’s suspicious order monitoring program.

4.       McKesson has the sole obligation to timely, fully, and accurately report all product discounts and rebates to Medicaid, Medicare and/or third party payers in accordance with all applicable federal and state laws and regulations. McKesson shall sell the contracted Products it is buying from Mallinckrodt LLC under this agreement to end user pharmacy customers only. In no event shall McKesson sell Mallinckrodt LLC’s products to any other party, including, without limitation, wholesalers/distributors or warehousing entities that distribute and or resell product. All chargeback submissions not complying with the aforementioned will be denied. McKesson shall purchase all Mallinckrodt LLC’s products directly from Mallinckrodt LLC.

In preparation for today's DRT  around the 32mg "Sizzle" discussion....some food for thought.....


*         We have mentioned a possible tactic with Nurse Educators...could be a pretty cool option for field sales to have dedicated Nurse Educators in each region to bring into offices for lunch and learns around education on appropriate use


*         Accountable care is still much talked about with not much meat on the bone yet. I'm not sure if drug spend is included, as an ACO contract is a payment option between insurers and providers for medical costs. So far, insurers are still using P4P type incentives to rein in drug spend (needing to meet local generic rate of prescribing, sticking to formulary meds)...I do believe we have benefits around bringing accountable care to the Managed Care audiences for the patients and looking to create in a HEDIS measure with NCQA for Monitoring Patients on  Pain Meds/Abuse Deterrent methodologies

Subject : Message from Mark - Pharmaceuticals' Portfolio of Businesses - April 9, 2012
Attachments : image001.png; image002.jpg; image003.jpg; image004.jpg


        [cid:image001.png@01CD1672.C82A9890]






"Message from Mark" is a monthly series that features business topics of particular interest and importance to Pharmaceuticals President Mark Trudeau. This month's topic focuses on Pharmaceuticals' portfolio of businesses.

[Mark_Trudeau_FP.jpg]One of the reasons I found the opportunity to become the President of Pharmaceuticals so compelling is its strong and broad portfolio of businesses. Each of our businesses - Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients, Specialty Generics, Specialty Pharmaceuticals, and the Nuclear Medicine and Contrast Media arms of Imaging - complement each other and play an important role in the growth strategy for the new Mallinckrodt.

Once we're an independent company, our investors will ask how we intend to grow. They will want to know both our short-term goals and what we have in the pipeline to potentially ensure a return on their investments in the future. This is why being a portfolio of businesses puts us in a position of strength. We have the right balance of businesses that generate cash for short-term expectations and others that have the potential to meet investors' expectations for generating long-term growth.

It's no secret the Nuclear Medicine and Contrast Media businesses produce a lot of cash. Investors will expect us to use that cash for growth investments, but this doesn't mean we will look to Imaging only to generate cash. Instead, we're looking for growth in all of our businesses:


*         Contrast Media & Delivery Systems (CMDS) is one of the world's leaders in prefilled syringes and it also provides us a global footprint in high growth markets.



*         Nuclear has opportunities with its unique distribution, vertical integration and enhanced customer recognition programs to grow its Technetium-99m generator business in the U.S and Europe, Middle East and Africa (EMEA).  We can also explore opportunities with other radiopharmaceuticals.



*         Specialty Pharmaceuticals' two key branded pain products, EXALGO(r) (hydromorphone HCI) Extended-Release Tablets, (CII) and PENNSAID(r) (diclofenac sodium topical solution) 1.5% w/w, directly support our growth by laying the foundation for future products in the space.


*         Specialty Generics submitted six Abbreviated New Drug Applications (ANDAs) last fiscal year to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), and we're actively looking to submit more to generate value. We believe the business' exceptional reformulation and vertical integration capabilities will continue to open opportunities for future growth.



*         API grew last year and continues to generate value, especially as we execute on Project Pinnacle at the St. Louis plant. Customers value our stable supply of controlled raw material and our quality in a highly regulated environment. API products operate in intensely competitive markets where this is a differentiator.

Our short-term growth opportunities are evident. Now we need to focus on our long-term plans to ensure our investors trust we're going to have healthy, sustainable, ongoing business growth. It's a challenging, but wonderful, opportunity to focus on building our product pipeline and expand into new markets. This is an exciting time in the history of this company, and our continued success will depend on the active engagement of each and every one of us.

[MALCOV v2.jpg]

[RxNews] Mandatory Prescriber Training

The issue of mandatory training for opioid prescribers is again in the news after a joint meeting last week of the
FDA's Drug Safety and Risk Management Advisory Committee and its Anesthetic and Analgesic Drug
Products Advisory Committee once again recommended it. This suggestion was first raised by these committees
in July 2010 when they were discussing whether a proposed REMS that FDA had put forward then was an
appropriate approach to the problem of opioid abuse.
The vote in 2010 was 25 to ten, with the majority saying that the FDA's proposal was insufficient. In discussing
the vote, the notion of training opioid prescribers was suggested. Dr. John Jenkins, Director, Office of New
Drugs, Center for Drug Evaluation and Research, agreed with the panelists but said that prescriber training — as
a REMS requirement — would require congressional action.
Dr. Jenkins indicated that the DEA, being the only federal agency authorized to register prescribers of
controlled substances, might be able to require such training as a condition for new or continued prescriber
registration.
The Controlled Substances Act gives the Attorney General broad authorization "to promulgate rules and
regulations and to charge reasonable fees relating to the registration and control of the manufacture,
distribution, and dispensing of controlled substances." [21 USC 821] Assuming that the Attorney General
could, by rulemaking, add training to the list of conditions already required for DEA registration, the larger
question remains as to whether such training would have the desired effect of reducing the abuse of opioids.
Thus far, there has been no "needs assessment" showing, for example, that the problem of opioid abuse results
from a lack of training on the part of prescribers. While it stands to reason that some infrequent prescribers of
opioids might benefit from specialized training, many regular prescribers of opioids probably already know as
much as they need to know about these drugs and the patients using them. For them, the benefits of mandatory
training would be marginal at best.
We can expect to hear more about this recommendation in the coming months. Training, after all, is the plain
vanilla universal solution for just about any problem and generates little opposition. In this regard, whether it
will have much of an effect in reducing opioid abuse remains unknown.
John Coleman

Thanks Lisa.

These orders hit the "threshold limit". I will probably butcher this, but here goes:

The report is looking at the previous 18 months of orders (product specific) for an average. It is them
multiplied by 3. this is called the "target average qty", which is an acceptable amou nt. Keep in mind
they are measured by molecule of the product family and not on skus.
The "target average qty" for hydromorphone is 106, actual order qty is 149 (again this is measured by
molecule)
The "target average qty" for morphine is 960, actual order qty is 1392 (molecules again)

This is not a very technical way of describing the process, but it is how I understand it.

This is just one of several formulas used on the report.

Hope this helps.

INDICATION

EXALGO(r) (hydromorphone HCI) Extended-Release Tablets (CII) is indicated for the management of moderate to severe pain in opioid tolerant patients requiring continuous, around-the-clock opioid analgesia for an extended period of time.

IMPORTANT RISK INFORMATION

WARNING: POTENTIAL FOR ABUSE, IMPORTANCE OF PROPER PATIENT SELECTION AND LIMITATIONS OF USE


Abuse Potential

EXALGO contains hydromorphone, an opioid agonist and a Schedule II controlled substance with an abuse liability similar to other opioid agonists, legal or illicit. Assess each patient's risk for opioid abuse or addiction prior to prescribing EXALGO. The risk for opioid abuse is increased in patients with a personal or family history of substance abuse (including drug or alcohol abuse or addiction) or mental illness (e.g., major depressive disorder). Routinely monitor all patients receiving EXALGO for signs of misuse, abuse, and addiction during treatment.

Life-threatening Respiratory Depression

Respiratory depression, including fatal cases, may occur with use of EXALGO, even when the drug has been used as recommended and not misused or abused. EXALGO is for use in opioid tolerant patients only. Proper dosing and titration are essential and EXALGO should be prescribed only by healthcare professionals who are knowledgeable in the use of potent opioids for the management of chronic pain. Monitor for respiratory depression, especially during initiation of EXALGO or following a dose increase. Crushing, dissolving, or chewing the tablet can cause rapid release and absorption of a potentially fatal dose of hydromorphone.

Accidental Exposure

Accidental ingestion of EXALGO, especially in children, can result in a fatal overdose of hydromorphone.


*

EXALGO is contraindicated in:



-

Opioid non-tolerant patients. Fatal respiratory depression could occur in patients who are not opioid tolerant.

-

Patients with significant respiratory depression

-

Patients with acute or severe bronchial asthma in an unmonitored setting or in the absence of resuscitative equipment

-

Patients with known or suspected paralytic ileus

-

Patients who have had surgical procedures and/or underlying disease resulting in narrowing of the gastrointestinal tract, or have "blind loops" of the gastrointestinal tract or gastrointestinal obstruction

-

Patients with hypersensitivity (e.g., anaphylaxis) to hydromorphone or sulfite-containing medications


*

EXALGO is indicated for opioid tolerant patients only. Patients considered opioid tolerant are those who are taking at least 60 mg oral morphine per day, 25 mcg transdermal fentanyl/hour, 30 mg oral oxycodone/day, 8 mg oral hydromorphone/day, 25 mg oral oxymorphone/day or an equianalgesic dose of another opioid, for a week or longer.

*

EXALGO is not intended for use as an as-needed analgesic and is not indicated for the management of acute or postoperative pain. It is contraindicated in patients who need management of mild pain or pain not expected to persist.

*

Avoid concurrent use of alcohol and EXALGO. Concurrent use of EXALGO with CNS depressants, including alcohol, increases risk of respiratory depression, hypotension, and profound sedation, potentially resulting in coma or death. EXALGO may impair the ability to drive a car or operate machinery.

*

Not intended in patients who have received MAO inhibitors within 14 days of starting EXALGO.

*

Use with caution and in reduced doses in older or debilitated patients, as well as patients with renal or hepatic insufficiency, Addison's disease, delirium tremens, myxedema or hypothyroidism, prostatic hypertrophy or urethral stricture, toxic psychosis. May aggravate convulsions in patients with convulsive disorders; may induce or aggravate seizures in some clinical settings. Consider use of an alternate analgesic in patients with severe renal impairment.

*

Respiratory depression, which occurs more frequently in elderly or debilitated patients, is the chief hazard with EXALGO.

*

Serious adverse events could also include hypotensive effects, GI effects, cardiac arrest from overdose and precipitation of withdrawal. Most common adverse events (>10%) seen in clinical studies (N=2474) were: constipation (31%), nausea (28%), vomiting, somnolence, headache, asthenia and dizziness.

*

Use EXALGO with extreme caution in patients susceptible to intracranial effects of CO2 retention.

*

Do not abruptly discontinue EXALGO.



See additional Important Risk Information, including boxed warning, in Full Prescribing Information<http://pharmaceuticals.covidien.com/workarea/downloadasset.aspx?id=2147483728> and Medication Guide<http://pharmaceuticals.covidien.com/workarea/downloadasset.aspx?id=2147483729>.

Extended-Release Hydromorphone Shows Safety, Efficacy for Sustained Pain Control
Nancy A. Melville
October 22, 2009 (Phoenix, Arizona)   An extended-release form of the opioid drug hydromorphone (Exalgo, Neuromed Pharmaceuticals) provides effective and safe therapy for chronic moderate to severe lower back pain, according to a phase 3 study presented here at the American Association of Pain Management 20th annual clinical meeting.
Although similar in efficacy to the opioid morphine, hydromorphone offers an advantage in the treatment of pain in the elderly and patients with problems with renal clearance of drugs because it lacks the active metabolites that are present in morphine, said Douglas Gourlay, MD, director of the Pain and Chemical Dependency Division, Wasser Pain Centre, Mount Sinai Hospital in Toronto, Ontario.
"Morphine is often considered a poor choice for the elderly or people who are renally impaired because of the active metabolites, but hydromorphone offers an advantage, in that it's a relatively clean molecule, so it's often preferred," said Dr. Gourlay, who was not involved in the study. "It's a potent opioid with nice, clean kinetics."
The double-blind study involved 268 patients with mild to severe lower back pain who were randomized into 2 groups of 134 patients each to receive either extended release hydromorphone or placebo for 12 weeks. The patients recorded pain intensity scores on an 11-point Likert Numeric Rating Scale. Results were presented at the meeting by Arifulla Khan, MD, medical director and principal investigator of Northwest Clinical Research Center in Bellevue, Washington.
The results showed significant improvements in changes in mean pain intensity scores from baseline to week 12 between the hydromorphone group (median, 0.2) and the placebo group (median, 1.6; P < .0001).
Adverse events reported by the hydromorphone group were similar to those of other oral opioids, including drug withdrawal syndrome (7.5%), constipation (6%), nausea (3%), and headache (3%).
An extended-release hydromorphone product made its way to the American marketplace briefly under the name Palladone, but the product was voluntarily withdrawn in 2005 by maker Purdue Pharma after a US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) advisory issued a warning of potentially fatal adverse effects related to dose dumping when combined with alcohol.
Joanna Schooler, a spokesperson for Neuromed, said that data provided to the FDA indicate that Exalgo is not subject to dose dumping.
"In vitro studies have shown that alcohol in various concentrations does not alter the extended-release properties or pharmacokinetic profile of Exalgo," she said.
The benefits of a controlled-release formulation of hydromorphone are 2-fold; it offers improved steady pain control and serves as a deterrent for abuse, Dr. Gourlay noted.
"There is clearly a population of patients who struggle with withdrawal-mediated pain resulting from the waxing and waning of drug levels from medication taken over the course of a 24-hour period, and the ultimate effect is that their pain is amplified," he said.
"The idea with the controlled release is to not only reduce the tendency toward multiple doses required throughout the day, but also to give increased stability and have a lower incidence of that withdrawal-mediated pain."
The steady delivery of the drug also eliminates the highs and lows that make the drug susceptible to abuse.
"Drugs that rapidly cross over the blood brain barrier and that peak quickly and fall off quickly tend to be drugs with higher abuse liability, so the theoretical advantage of a controlled-release delivery system is that the reward associated with taking the drug is less intense and will hopefully have a lower abuse liability," he said.
The study received funding from Neuromed Pharmaceuticals. Dr. Gourlay has disclosed no relevant financial relationships.

Survey Objective/Goal:

·         In partnership with Mallinckrodt, Inflexxion developed an Internet Survey to obtain information that would further characterize opioid abuse and abuse specific to Exalgo among members from drug discussion forums,. This survey was intended to complement analyses from the ASI-MV and WIS: Internet monitoring studies, as a supplemental informational analysis to add further context to and understand drug abusers perceptions of Exalgo as an option for abuse.

·         Survey contained 4 sections (A-Demographics, B-General Opioid Use, C-Opioid Perceptions/Knowledge of Products,  D-Specific Opioid Product Use)

·         The target recruitment was 300-500 respondents, with 300 at the lower end for total number of completions.



Survey Duration:

·         Survey was posted on Bluelight.ru on November 14, 2014 through January 20, 2015  (9 weeks total)

·         Inflexxion held weekly conference calls with the website moderators to monitor and increase the number of completions from respondents

·         Responses remained low throughout the initial launch of the survey with efforts made with the website moderators for increased participation and completions



Survey Response:

·         Total number of respondents = 274

·         Total respondents who completed survey = 169

·         Total number respondents partial  = 105  (most of partial respondents dropped out at section B)

·         3 Reported use of Exalgo (1 survey completion, 2 partial completion)

·         35 Reported no use of Exalgo, however had heard of Exalgo
Conclusions

·         The unusually low sample and survey response does not allow meaningful analysis and any analysis of current data will be difficult to interpret land likely not be persuasive to the FDA Options

·         Pause any further action on the current survey and survey analysis

·         Revise survey to only questions of relevance and re-launch later with intention to increase response/sample size

From: Zook, David R. [mailto:Dave.Zook@FaegreBD.com]

To: Webb, Kevin J
Subject: Aetna embraces medication to combat opioid crisis



 

Aetna is going all in on medication-assisted treatment in response to the opioid epidemic, according to a letter CEO Mark Bertolini is sending today to a handful of Democratic senators. Bertolini highlights three goals the insurer hopes to achieve by 2022:

Reduce inappropriate opioid prescriptions by 50%.
Increase by 50% the number of opioid addicts treated with medication-assisted treatment and other evidence-based treatments.
Increase the number of enrollees with chronic pain who use alternative pain treatments by 50%.

Go deeper: Aetna's embrace of medication-assisted treatment is a sharp contrast from some insurers' previous reluctance to cover the approach, which Bob Herman covered for Modern Healthcare. It also follows Tom Price's controversial comment saying medication-assisted treatment is "substituting one opioid for another."

But Aetna has already worked to make medication more available: Earlier this year, it removed all pre-authorization requirements for certain products and put them on a preventive medicine list that reduces cost-sharing for patients.

 ORANGE PARK, Fla. -- Two doctors were arrested Wednesday and charged in connection to the investigation of Total Medical
Express, an Orange Park that the Clay County Sheriff's Office calls a "pill mill."
The business was raided in March 2011 on suspicion of prescription fraud and operating an unregistered pain clinic. Several
customers and the office manager were arrested then on various charges.
Adla Adi, 72, of Ponte Vedra, turned himself in on charges of owning or operating an nonregistered pain management clinic.
Terry Howard, 58, was picked up by U.S. marshals in Orlando on the Clay County warrant.
According to the arrest warrant, Adi and Howard admitted to being the only doctors who saw patients during certain days at the
business, and the only ones in the business on those days authorized to write prescriptions.
Investigators said the business was attracting drug dealers and users from across the region.
"Prescription fraud is quickly becoming the scourge of many communities and our goal is to stop its impact on Clay County by
holding accountable the doctors who are the very source of the problem," said Clay County Sheriff Rick Beseler. "Not only did
we arrest the customers of the 'pill mill,' but now also the doctors themselves. Arrests made at the physician level are a rare and
important step for local law enforcement."
Adi posted $250,003 bond and was released. Howard is being held in a correctional facility in Seminole County and is scheduled
to appear before a judge on the Clay County charge on Thursday.

Mallinckrodt Announces Agreement with Xanodyne to Purchase Roxicodone(r)


[cid:image005.jpg@01CD8137.15700660]As part of our ongoing effort to grow the business through acquisitions, licensing and co-promotion activities, I am delighted to announce that Mallinckrodt has acquired Roxicodone(r) (oxycodone hydrochloride tablets (USP) in 5, 15 and 30 mg dosage strengths.  Roxicodone is an immediate release formulation of oxycodone indicated for the management of moderate to severe pain where the use of opioid analgesic is appropriate.



In our agreement with Xanodyne Pharmaceuticals, we acquired all the rights to the Roxicodone New Drug Application (NDA).  This acquisition complements our existing portfolio of opioids and leverages our pain management experience.  We will immediately begin the sale and distribution of Roxicodone.

READ FURTHER FOR COVIDIEN'S PRESS RELEASE ANNOUNCEMENT.





Mallinckrodt Announces Agreement with Xanodyne to Purchase Roxicodone(r)


HAZELWOOD, MO - August 23, 2012 - Mallinckrodt, the Pharmaceuticals business of Covidien<http://www.covidien.com/> (NYSE: COV), today announced that it has entered into an agreement with Xanodyne Pharmaceuticals to purchase Roxicodone(r) (oxycodone hydrochloride tablets USP) in 5, 15 and 30 mg dosage strengths. Roxicodone, currently marketed in the United States, is an immediate release formulation of oxycodone indicated for the management of moderate to severe pain where the use of an opioid analgesic is appropriate. With this agreement, Mallinckrodt acquires all rights to the Roxicodone New Drug Application (NDA).  No financial details were disclosed.



"We are excited about this agreement as it complements our existing portfolio of opioids and leverages our pain management expertise," said Mark Trudeau, President, Pharmaceuticals. "More importantly, we are committed to safe and effective use of all of our products along with ensuring access for all patients in need of pain treatment."



Mallinckrodt is the largest U.S. supplier of opioid pain medications and among the top 10 generic pharmaceuticals manufacturers in the U.S., based on prescriptions.  Its branded portfolio includes EXALGO(r) (hydromorphone HCl) Extended-Release Tablets (CII) and PENNSAID(r) (diclofenac sodium topical solution) 1.5% w/w.  Mallinckrodt is also one of the world's leading producers of bulk acetaminophen.



Covidien announced last December that the Company planned to spin off Mallinckrodt into a stand-alone company, a process that is expected to be completed in mid-2013.



IMPORTANT RISK INFORMATION



About ROXICODONE


Roxicodone tablets are contraindicated in patients with known hypersensitivity to oxycodone, or in any situation where opioids are contraindicated. This includes patients with significant respiratory depression (in unmonitored settings or the absence of resuscitative equipment) and patients with acute or severe bronchial asthma or hypercarbia. Oxycodone hydrochloride tablets are contraindicated in any patient who has or is suspected of having paralytic ileus.


Serious adverse reactions that may be associated with Roxicodone tablets therapy include: respiratory depression, respiratory arrest, circulatory depression, cardiac arrest, hypotension, and/or shock.  Common adverse events that may be associated with Roxicodone tablets therapy include:  nausea, constipation, vomiting, headache, pruritus, insomnia, dizziness, asthenia, and somnolence.


About EXALGO


INDICATION

EXALGO(r) (hydromorphone HCI) Extended-Release Tablets (CII) is indicated for the management of moderate to severe pain in opioid tolerant patients requiring continuous, around-the-clock opioid analgesia for an extended period of time.

WARNING: ABUSE POTENTIAL, LIFE-THREATENING RESPIRATORY DEPRESSION,
and ACCIDENTAL EXPOSURE
Abuse Potential

EXALGO contains hydromorphone, an opioid agonist and a Schedule II controlled substance with an abuse liability similar to other opioid agonists, legal or illicit. Assess each patient's risk for opioid abuse or addiction prior to prescribing EXALGO. The risk for opioid abuse is increased in patients with a personal or family history of substance abuse (including drug or alcohol abuse or addiction) or mental illness (e.g., major depressive disorder). Routinely monitor all patients receiving EXALGO for signs of misuse, abuse, and addiction during treatment.

Life-threatening Respiratory Depression

Respiratory depression, including fatal cases, may occur with use of EXALGO, even when the drug has been used as recommended and not misused or abused. EXALGO is for use in opioid tolerant patients only. Proper dosing and titration are essential and EXALGO should be prescribed only by healthcare professionals who are knowledgeable in the use of potent opioids for the management of chronic pain. Monitor for respiratory depression, especially during initiation of EXALGO or following a dose increase. Crushing, dissolving, or chewing the tablet can cause rapid release and absorption of a potentially fatal dose of hydromorphone.

Accidental Exposure

Accidental ingestion of EXALGO, especially in children, can result in a fatal overdose of hydromorphone.



*         EXALGO is contraindicated in:

-   Opioid non-tolerant patients. Fatal respiratory depression could occur in patients who are not opioid tolerant.

-   Patients with significant respiratory depression

-   Patients with acute or severe bronchial asthma in an unmonitored setting or in the absence of resuscitative equipment

-   Patients with known or suspected paralytic ileus

-   Patients who have had surgical procedures and/or underlying disease resulting in narrowing of the gastrointestinal tract, or have "blind loops" of the gastrointestinal tract or gastrointestinal obstruction

-   Patients with hypersensitivity (e.g., anaphylaxis) to hydromorphone or sulfite-containing medications



*         Serious adverse events could also include hypotensive effects, GI effects, cardiac arrest from overdose and precipitation of withdrawal. Most common adverse events (>10%) seen in clinical studies (N=2474) were: constipation (31%), nausea (28%), vomiting, somnolence, headache, asthenia and dizziness.





About PENNSAID

PENNSAID is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug ("NSAID") indicated for the treatment of signs and symptoms of osteoarthritis of the knee(s).

[cid:image015.png@01CD8100.AE9006B0]


WARNING: CARDIOVASCULAR AND GASTROINTESTINAL RISK

Cardiovascular Risk

* Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) may cause an increased risk of serious cardiovascular thrombotic events, myocardial infarction, and stroke, which can be fatal. This risk may increase with duration of use. Patients with cardiovascular disease or risk factors for cardiovascular disease may be at greater risk.

* PENNSAID is contraindicated in the perioperative setting of coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery.

Gastrointestinal Risk

* NSAIDs cause an increased risk of serious gastrointestinal adverse events including bleeding, ulceration, and perforation of the stomach or intestines, which can be fatal. These events can occur at any time during use and without warning symptoms. Elderly patients are at greater risk for serious gastrointestinal events.





PENNSAID is also contraindicated in patients:

-     With known hypersensitivity to diclofenac sodium or any other component of PENNSAID.

-     Who have experienced asthma, urticaria, or allergic-type reactions after taking aspirin or other NSAIDs. Severe, rarely fatal, anaphylactic-like reactions have been reported in these patients.



Anaphylactoid reactions may occur in patients without prior exposure to PENNSAID. NSAIDs can cause serious skin adverse events such as exfoliative dermatitis, Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS), and toxic epidermal necrosis (TEN), which can be fatal.

The most common treatment-related adverse events in patients receiving PENNSAID were application site skin reactions including dry skin (32%), contact dermatitis characterized by skin erythema and induration (9%), contact dermatitis with vesicles (2%) and pruritus (4%). In a long term safety study, contact dermatitis occurred in 13% and contact dermatitis with vesicles in 10% of patients, generally within the first 6 months of exposure, leading to a withdrawal rate for an application site event of 14%. Other common adverse events greater than placebo include: dyspepsia (8%), abdominal pain (6%), flatulence (4%), diarrhea (4%) and nausea (4%).


ABOUT COVIDIEN



Covidien is a leading global healthcare products company that creates innovative medical solutions for better patient outcomes and delivers value through clinical leadership and excellence. Covidien manufactures, distributes and services a diverse range of industry-leading product lines in three segments: Medical Devices, Pharmaceuticals and Medical Supplies. With 2011 revenue of $11.6 billion, Covidien has 43,000 employees worldwide in more than 65 countries, and its products are sold in over 140 countries. Mallinckrodt, the Pharmaceuticals business of Covidien, manufactures active pharmaceutical ingredients, including bulk acetaminophen, opioid pain medications, nuclear and contrast media diagnostic agents. Sales in 2011 were $2.0 billion.  Please visit www.covidien.com<http://www.covidien.com/> to learn more about our business.



EXALGO is a registered trademark of Mallinckrodt LLC.  PENNSAID is a registered trademark of Nuvo Research Inc.  Roxicodone is a registered trademark of Xanodyne Pharmaceuticals, Inc.

FIVE MIAMI PHARMACIES ORDERED TO STOP OPERATING
 - Two year multi-agency investigation identifies pill mill scam -


TALLAHASSEE   The Florida Department of Health (DOH) today suspended five pharmacy permits, immediately ordering the pharmacies and the entire staff to cease operations, based on investigative findings in partnership with the United States Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA) that the pharmacy owner and its pharmacists dispensed controlled substances, other than in the course of the professional practice of pharmacy.

 Florida s law enforcement and public health leaders remain committed to our ongoing effort to end the criminal distribution of prescription drugs, and I thank them for their great work,  said Governor Rick Scott.   Removing the sources of these drugs is essential to saving lives and stopping this scourge on our communities.

Four of the five Miami pharmacies are owned by Aiman Aryan, a licensed pharmacist. The pharmacies operate under the business name of Robert s Drug Store and are responsible for purchasing more than 1.6 million pills of oxycodone-based medications starting January 1 through June 30, 2011.

 The severity of this epidemic cannot be overstated,  said Dr. Farmer.  DOH is committed to suspending and revoking the licenses of unscrupulous practitioners and pharmacies who inappropriately prescribe highly addictive controlled substances to patients, with the hopes of stopping countless senseless deaths in our state.

Further investigative efforts revealed that the pharmacies had  recruiters  who would pick up Medicare  patients  and drive them various doctor s offices who would write a prescription to the patient for a controlled substance without a legitimate medical purpose and without performing a physical examination of the patient. After obtaining the prescription, the patient was transported to one of the four Robert s Drug Stores to have the prescription filled.  The recruiters paid the patients $600 for their medications that usually consisted of 720 pills per patient. When the prescription was brought to one of the Robert s Drug Stores, Mr. Aryan would pay the recruiters in cash for bringing patients to his pharmacies to have prescriptions filled.

The four pharmacies owned by Aryan also worked under the business names of Pharmacy One Inc. and Izz & Sons, Inc.

At the same time today, Pharmalife Consultant Inc., was also issued an emergency suspension order mandating the pharmacy permit be suspending after an investigation revealed that the pharmacy filled over 150 fraudulent prescriptions accounting for 23,500 oxycodone pills.

The ESOs were issued as a result of investigative assistance provided by the Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA), US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), United States Attorney s Office, Miami-Dade Police Department and the Broward County Sheriff s Office.


View the complete Order listed above on DOH s Online Newsroom at http://newsroom.doh.state.fl.us/category/healthcare-licensing/ <http://newsroom.doh.state.fl.us/category/healthcare-licensing/> .

Emergency suspension or restriction orders are not considered final agency action but are imposed as specified by section 456.074, Florida Statutes, for serious violations relating to the commission of crimes, standard of care, drug use, or for student loan defaults. The subject is entitled to a hearing before final action is taken by a regulatory board or by DOH.

To learn more about the Florida Department of Health visit www.doh.state.fl.us <http://www.doh.state.fl.us> .

###

The mission of the Florida Department of Health and Medical Quality Assurance (MQA) is to protect and promote the health of all residents and visitors in the state through organized state and community efforts, including cooperative agreements with counties. Working in conjunction with 22 boards and six councils, MQA regulates six types of facilities and more than 40 healthcare professions. MQA evaluates the credentials of all applicants for licensure, issues licenses, analyzes and investigates complaints, inspects facilities, assists in prosecuting practice act violations, combats unlicensed activity and provides credential and discipline history about licensees to the public.

Southeast Region Sales Team,

Thanks to all of you who responded to the request for EXALGO successes and best practices. Our District Manager representing the region on the EXALGO Field Advisory Council, Jerry Robinson, has pulled together a few gems in the message below. PLEASE take the time to read this and hopefully find some ideas that may help you in expanding your EXALGO business.

At our POA meeting in April, I showed you that our weekly script count had grown from around 600/week in early January to over 1,000/week by the end of March. Well, another three months have passed since that meeting and we are still hovering around 1,000/week. We need to move EXALGO up in our success algorithm!

Here's to a great selling week.

Bill

                                                                                                                                [Final-REVISED-2.0-Logo-DK-blue.png]

        [cid:image003.jpg@01CD5DBB.97694AE0]




Southeast Region:

As we enter the final quarter of 2012 we can all look back at the hard work we have put into selling Exalgo and are really beginning to see our "fair share" of successes.  Let's not forget we still have one quarter left to expand on these successes.  I wanted to take a moment of your time to share some of these successes with everyone and highlight the hard work, persistence, thinking outside the box and never give mentality demonstrated within the Southeast Region.  Because, after all, you need all the above to be successful in selling Exalgo.

We have a great message with Exalgo and utilizing the OROS more often can help differentiate ourselves from the competition.  Chris Clark utilizes the INSPIRE message very well below and is now being used in other Districts as well:

"One thing I have found effective, especially with PCP's, is relating the combination of hydromorphone and OROS to become Exalgo with the experience they had with Ritalin and its abuse as a QID drug and its combination with OROS to become Concerta. I tell them that this changed the ADHD landscape forever and the fact that they don't call Concerta -> Ritalin ER  -( I must give Chris Clark credit here) - ... I emphasize using the PK values located in the MSA of Dilaudid and Exalgo that OROS is innovative in the pain market and that Exalgo is NOT Dilaudid ER. I ask them which PK profile do they want their chronic opioid tolerant pain patients on long term."

It's an understatement to say persistence and  a never give up mentality are needed to sell Exalgo.  These two qualities are critical for Covidien Representatives.  Lisa Wimberly and Nikki Ziegenhirt provide some great examples of this in their successes below.  It's not too hard to wonder why they are ranked numbers 4 and 10 on the April Rank Report respectively.  Keep up the nice efforts!

"I had spoken to you before about Dr. Vilasuso, who  I've been calling on for over a year now and never could get him to commit to trying Exalgo.  He has always been hesitant about hydromorphone and its potency.  I was able to use the new PK data in the Master Sales Aid to get into a great discussion with him on our last call. I specifically  showed him the PK chart with the IR hydromorphone in comparison to the different strengths for Exalgo.  I truly believe that this changed the way he viewed Exalgo and told me he was going to put his first patient on it.  We went over the dosing and conversion chart, in order to ensure the patient would receive the correct dose.  I went to his office to follow up with him and he informed that the patient was stable with 32mg of Exalgo  and she was doing great.  He followed the dosing and titration properly JHe is excited about the results and is looking to convert several new patients."

"I have recently had success with a specialty that I originally thought didn't have much potential.  As I was looking over my Leap Frog and IMS data, I noticed that quite a few of my Internal Med/Family Practice physicians were writing more long-acting pain meds than I had realized.  When we first launched Exalgo I would present it if it was part of the call plan but I didn't really feel they had a strong need for a medication like Exalgo (my mistake).  To be honest,  I didn't sell it with as much passion as I did when talking to a pain physician.  I have since realized that many internal med/family practice physicians do have a strong need for Exalgo with their patient population.  Many of these physicians treat people who have had chronic pain for years but aren't complicated cases.  Due to their close relationship, both the patient and physician are more comfortable not referring out .  These types of patients are ideal for Exalgo since they are well-known, compliant , stable patients.  Since I have opened my eyes to this missed opportunity and targeted them with the same enthusiasm as my pain physicians I have had many successes.  I currently have 5 internal/primary care physicians writing Exalgo on a regular basis.  I have 2 more that I think will start prescribing Exalgo within the next few weeks.  Several scripts a month from 5 or 6 physicians can really make a difference at the end of the quarter!!!  I thought you might want to pass this on because maybe others in our district have been overlooking these "diamonds" like I had."

And finally, thinking outside the box leads to new ideas for everyone to stay in front of our competition.  Kim McCoy provide a great example for National Pain Awareness Month (which is September).  So, let our planning begin!!


"Here is an idea.  Since September is National Pain Awareness month, (I know it's July but some offices get booked up quickly)  Make those lunches all about Cares Alliance and focused on the patients, physicians and staff.  Bring in the patient cards and resource portfolio,  order the kits early from smart source and show how we want to partner with them.   Discuss challenges they may be facing.  I have heard from staff many issues including:  Lack of patient information, reimbursement issues, how to overcome QL issues, etc.  This is also a good time to get EEIFs out.  Really  go all out for the offices,  use our Exalgo lunch kits and really make it an event.  We will be remembered and since Oct - Dec can be tough months why not do something to differentiate ourselves and give Exalgo a little more top of mind awareness as well."



Thanks to everyone for sharing their successes with Exalgo.  Your hard work is starting to pay off and we are beginning set some new highs with the brand.  Keep up the nice efforts!!





Jerry Robinson
