7.5 mg... and IV morphine 10 mg is about equal to IV 
hydromorphone 1.5 mg. 
   For patients not tolerant to opioids, recommend starting 
with no more than 2 to 4 mg of oral hydromorphone every 4 to 6 
hours. ..or 1 to 2 mg of IV hydromorphone every 4 to 6 hours. 
   Caution to use even lower doses in elderly patients, or 
those with renal or hepatic insufficiency. 
   Exalgo (hydromorphone extended-release) will be the only 
once- daily oral product on the market... coming this June. 
   It's already sold in Europe and Canada as Jurnista. 
   Pailadone was the first hydromorphone ER. But it was 
taken off the market because alcohol caused the drug to release 
too fast. 
   Explain that Exalgo has a new osmotic delivery system 
that's not compromised by alcohol. 
   It's hoped that delayed absorption will lead to a slower 
onset of drug liking and lower peak of euphoria ... but this 
isn't proven. 
   Watch for potential errors.. .save Exalgo for chronic 
therapy in opioid-tolerant patients. It's NOT for acute pain. 
   Watch that hydromorphone immediate-release isn't given 
instead of Exalgo extended-release. This could be life- 
threatening. 
   Tell patients not to worry if they see the empty shell or 
ghost tablet in their stool.

should get the same therapeutic effect as the old tablets.

updated chart, Equianalgesic Dosing of Opioids for Pain

		To: #MKG - Pharma Field Sales
		Cc: Harrell, Jamie; Novak, Rod P; Webb, Kevin J; Grelle, Edward G; Patterson, Mike E; Kast, Mike; Lierman, Jennifer A; Albonico, Lisa A; Rausch, Ryan; Crandall, Margaret A
		Subject: Oxecta
		

		Field Sales Force -

		As a follow up to the voicemail message I left last week, below is some additional information relative to the newest entrant in the pain space -Oxecta.

		On June 20th, Pfizer Inc. and Acura Pharmaceuticals Inc. announced the marketing approval from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) of OXECTA (oxycodone HCl, USP) Tablets CII. OXECTA is an immediate-release oral formulation of oxycodone HCl indicated for the management of acute and chronic moderate to severe pain where the use of an opioid analgesic is appropriate.

		Oxecta is available in two dosing strengths 5mg and 7.5mg of oxycodone HCl.  Currently, generic oxycodone immediate release tablets are available in 5mg, 10mg, 15mg, 20mg and 30mg strengths.  The recommended dosing interval for Oxecta is every 4 to 6 hours, similar to other immediate release oxycodone products.  The Oxecta label does indicate it is not amenable to crushing and dissolution; however, it also states the product may be abused by crushing, chewing, snorting or injecting the product.  

		Also, caution is advised when initiating oxycodone treatment, including Oxecta, in patients currently taking or discontinuing CYP3A4 inhibitors or inducers.  
		Remember unlike Exalgo or hydromorphone, oxycodone is metabolized through the CYP450 system.

		Oxecta peak plasma concentrations occur on average within 1.2 to 1.4 hours of the first dose.  Thereafter, oxycodone concentrations fall with an average terminal half-life ranging between 3-4 hours.  Oxecta is bioequivalent with other oxycodone immediate-release tablets with no differences identified in the time to peak exposure (tMax) and terminal elimination half-life (T ½) of oxycodone between administration of Oxecta and the other oxycodone immediate-release tablets.  

		In a double-blind, active-comparator, crossover study in 40 non-dependent recreational opioid users, "drug liking" responses and single-dose safety of crushed OXECTA tablets were compared with Other crushed immediate-release Oxycodone tablets when subjects self-administered the drug intranasally.  The presence of sequence effects resulted in questionable reliability of the second period data. First period data demonstrated small numeric differences in the median and mean drug liking scores, lower in response to OXECTA than immediate-release oxycodone. Thirty percent of subjects exposed to OXECTA responded that they would not take the drug again compared to 5% of subjects exposed to immediate-release oxycodone. Study subjects self-administering OXECTA reported a higher incidence of nasopharyngeal and facial adverse events and a decreased ability to completely insufflate two crushed tablets within a fixed time period (21 of 40 subjects). The clinical significance of the difference in drug liking and difference in response to taking the drug again reported in this study has not yet been established.

		There is no evidence that OXECTA has a reduced abuse liability compared to immediate-release oxycodone.
		
		In conclusion, Oxecta is another immediate release oxycodone product, with a minimal range of doses.  While it may appear to have physical properties unique to immediate release oxycodone products, it has no approved claims pertaining to tamper resistance or abuse deterrence.  

		It is critical you continue to message to the unique benefits of hydromorphone, as well as the showcase how the OROS technology has transformed the hydromorphone in Exalgo.  Remember if a patient is unable to tolerate a generic oxycodone product, why would a physician select Oxecta as the next choice?  In fact, arguably Exalgo would be the most logical selection for these opioid tolerant chronic pain patients.  It is more potent, the moiety or active ingredient is dissimilar to oxycodone (unlike another oxycodone product or oxymorphone) and it has good product access, especially given the new co pay card and some of our recent Managed Care wins. 

		As important, our competitive advantage is the physician has you as a resource for Exalgo! 
		
		If you have any questions regarding the product, please do not hesitate to contact me.

		Take care and good selling.

Subject: RE: OptiSource Compliance - July
From: "Block, Jennifer M (Bullerdick)" <jennifer.block@mallinckrodt.com>
Date: Wed, 12 Aug 2015 13:54:39 +0000
To: "Cardetti, Lisa M" <lisa.cardetti@mallinckrodt.com>


Regarding Methadone – not sure how the RLD is impacting this.  Let’s discuss when you get a chance.

 

Also, did they say anything about HB-APAP, that family is very low as well.

 

Thanks!

 

From: Cardetti, Lisa M
Sent: Tuesday, August 11, 2015 12:12 PM
To: Longenecker, Jacob; Block, Jennifer M (Bullerdick); Elmore, Sylvia A (Aubuchon)
Cc: Kazemi, Kian L; Montgomery, Marc
Subject: RE: OptiSource Compliance - July



 

I have received feedback from OptiSource on the below listed products:

 

·        Dextro IR:

o   Issue: Price

o   Suppliers: MNK and Aurobindo, DP

o   DN Price direction: 5mg MNK $32, Aurobindo $23,

§  similar on 10mg, Aurobindo is ~28% lower

o   Recommendation/Comments: no action. Aurobindo only has 2% of the market, so we should not pick up the volume from them.

·        Fentanyl Patch:

o   Issue: Price & Preference

o   Suppliers: Apotex (low price to compensate for size of patch), Mylan (preference), Sandoz (price), DP

o   DN Price direction: 25mg MNK $11.40, Apotex $8.80

o   Recommendation/Comments: McKesson has the highest DN of all 3 wholesalers, an option would be to go to 10% higher than McKesson, it would put our DN at $8.80 (Apotex price). I know we have not wanted to compete against their price due to patch size in the past, however, if we are wanting to pick up volume, that is what we would need to do with this account.  Apotex currently only has 12% market share, we have 23%, so we may want to leave this one alone.

·        Methadone:

o   Issue: Price and RLD? (Our RLD is Dolophine, Roxane is listed as Methadone – could this be impacting anything – how they search for product by RLD? Why are they different?)

o   Suppliers: MNK, Roxane, Ascend, MNK listed as primary, but we are highest on 10mg

o   Contract Price: 10mg MNK $23.50, Roxane $20, Ascend more than half our price – based on feedback from NCM, sell price is $8.70 (getting 4x our volume at this price)

o   Recommendation/Comments: I understand we are standing our ground against Ascend price, however, I would ask that we look further into the RLD on this product.

·        Methylphenidate OS

o   Issue: they are looking into this, still had Breckenridge as primary. Need to go back to see how they responded on ROFR.

·        Methylphenidate ER

o   Issue: Volume decline and Price

o   Suppliers: MNK 10mg (exclusive but Y/Y volume has declined), Upstate 20mg Metadate product comp

o   DN Price: MNK $400, Upstate $60

o   Recommendation/Comments: no action, KVK-Tech has not approached them to add to contract. Can’t do anything with Metadate pricing in market.

·        Methylphenidate IR

o   Issue: Price

o   Suppliers: Sun, Sandoz, Upstate: DP, MNK secondary

o   DN Price: all others are in low $20s, MNK $36, Upstate sell price is $31.05

o   Recommendation/Comments: no action with a new entrant unless Qualitest approaches another customer of ours and we need to pick up more share

·        Morphine ER – biggest upside opportunity

o   Issue: Price

o   Suppliers: Rhodes primary, MNK secondary. Rhodes has not been willing to give this up. Met ROFR price when we decreased

o   Price: our contract price is lower (which is why we have seen a slight increase in volume, but Rhodes has a much lower dead net and members are supposed to purchase primary position knowing that there is more on the back end rebates off Contract price). I estimated what Rhodes DN price MIGHT be based on their sell prices in the market (using our Contract to DN % of 28%). If these are their prices, they align with ABC DN price, which is ~5-18% higher than McKesson OS).



o   Recommendation/Comments: Rhodes has 45% of the market, would like to revisit this to try for 50/50 split with Rhodes.

 

If we decide to be more aggressive on these prices, it would trigger ROFRs, however, there is so much upside potential in volume with this group. I will call to discuss these with you individually.

 

Thank you,

Lisa

HDA to Testify before Senate HELP Committee on Drug Pricing

The Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions (HELP) has called upon representatives from pharmaceutical supply chain organizations to testify at an October 17 hearing entitled, "The Cost of Prescription Drugs: How the Drug Delivery System Affects What Patients Pay, Part II." HDA Senior Vice President, Government Affairs and General Counsel, Liz Gallenagh, will testify on the role of distributors in the pharmaceutical supply chain. The hearing will take place at 10:00 a.m. in 430 Dirksen Senate Office Building. 

A full list of scheduled witnesses includes: 

Lori M. Reilly, Executive Vice President, Policy, Research & Membership, Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America, Washington, D.C. 
Chester "Chip" Davis, Jr., President and Chief Executive Officer, Association for Accessible Medicines, Washington, D.C.
Elizabeth A. Gallenagh, Senior Vice President Government Affairs and General Counsel, Healthcare Distribution Alliance, Arlington, Va. 
Mark Merritt, President and Chief Executive Officer, Pharmaceutical Care Management Association, Washington, D.C. 
Thomas E. Menighan, BSPharm, MBA, ScD(Hon.), FAPhA, Executive Director and Chief Executive Officer, American Pharmacists Association, Washington, D.C.

For more information, contact Jewelyn Cosgrove.

{http://sv-ecs-public.hdma.net/ct.asp?id=05E056CB629792E42653956641A55658620AD0C39D4420F41AB6F12E8B2E21E9A80FDA83F57C2719B23467006FA6F6BB27F48FC1B560FEE01A5AEBA6CEE7EDF1&ct=4aeUswAAAAA%3d}


One Month Remains to Register for the 2017 Blockchain Pre-Seminar Workshop and the Traceability Seminar

A short time remains to register for the November 8 Blockchain Pre-Seminar Workshop (hosted in partnership with IEEE) and HDA’s 2017 Traceability Seminar (November 8–10) in Washington, D.C. The pre-seminar workshop will provide attendees a look in to blockchain technology and how it can be applied to traceability in the pharmaceutical supply chain, while the Traceability Seminar will educate registrants on a variety of traceability topics and how they relate to DSCSA implementation efforts.

Register for the seminar and the workshop. For registration help or questions, contact HDA’s Meetings and Conferences at (703) 885-0278.  

{http://sv-ecs-public.hdma.net/ct.asp?id=05E056CB629792E42653956641A55658620AD0C39D4420F41AB6F12E8B2E21E9A80FDA83F57C2719B23467006FA6F6BB27F48FC1B560FEE01A5AEBA6CEE7EDF1&ct=4aeUswAAAAA%3d}

Congressional Hearings on the Opioid Crisis

Senate HELP Committee Discusses Federal Response to the Opioid Crisis

The Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions (HELP) Committee held a hearing last week (October 5) on "The Federal Response to the Opioid Crisis."  There were a range of questions about treatment, research, prescribing issues, concerns with illicit fentanyl and funding for addressing opioids, among others. It was noted that this is the first in a series of hearings on opioids. The next hearing will be in November (no date has been announced); the hearing will focus on state and local perspectives, exploring the challenges they face and the successes they have had in addressing the epidemic.

House Energy and Commerce Committee to Host Hearing on Opioids

The Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee is holding a "Member Day" tomorrow, Wednesday, October 11 at 10:15 a.m. to allow members both on and off the committee the opportunity to testify about the opioid epidemic.  

For more information, contact Jewelyn Cosgrove.

{http://sv-ecs-public.hdma.net/ct.asp?id=05E056CB629792E42653956641A55658620AD0C39D4420F41AB6F12E8B2E21E9A80FDA83F57C2719B23467006FA6F6BB27F48FC1B560FEE01A5AEBA6CEE7EDF1&ct=4aeUswAAAAA%3d}

Administration Names Acting DEA Administrator

Robert Patterson has been named Acting Administrator of the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA). Patterson is a career DEA Special Agent, having served with the agency since 1988. He had been serving, in effect, as Acting Deputy Administrator since late last year. An acting deputy administrator has not been named.

For more information, contact Ruth Miller.

{http://sv-ecs-public.hdma.net/ct.asp?id=05E056CB629792E42653956641A55658620AD0C39D4420F41AB6F12E8B2E21E9A80FDA83F57C2719B23467006FA6F6BB27F48FC1B560FEE01A5AEBA6CEE7EDF1&ct=4aeUswAAAAA%3d}

New Member Spotlight: Domino Amjet, Inc.

{http://sv-ecs-public.hdma.net/ct.asp?id=05E056CB629792E42653956641A55658620AD0C39D4420F41AB6F12E8B2E21E9A80FDA83F57C2719B23467006FA6F6BB27F48FC1B560FEE01A5AEBA6CEE7EDF1&ct=4aeUswAAAAA%3d}     HDA recently welcomed Domino Amjet, Inc. as a service provider member. Based in Gurnee, Ill., Domino has become the global solution provider for all product identification needs — including UDI and track and trace — for the most significant brands in the life science sector. Whether it’s serialized or variable printing, product marking or date coding, Domino Amjet and its products are a proven solution.

 

For more information, visit the company’s website or contact Paul Hammond, President.

{http://sv-ecs-public.hdma.net/ct.asp?id=05E056CB629792E42653956641A55658620AD0C39D4420F41AB6F12E8B2E21E9A80FDA83F57C2719B23467006FA6F6BB27F48FC1B560FEE01A5AEBA6CEE7EDF1&ct=4aeUswAAAAA%3d}

USP Announces Intent to Delay Chapter on Handling Hazardous Drugs

The United States Pharmacopeia (USP) has announced that it intends to delay the effective date of its General Chapter <800> Hazardous Drugs—Handling in Healthcare Settings until Dec. 1, 2019. The chapter, which relates to drugs identified by NIOSH as hazardous, describes standards that healthcare personnel, pharmacies, hospitals, physicians’ offices, and veterinarians should use to promote patient safety, worker safety, and environmental protection. Several states have discussed adopting the chapter into their requirements. The chapter does not impose requirements on wholesale distributors.

For more information, contact Ruth Miller.

{http://sv-ecs-public.hdma.net/ct.asp?id=05E056CB629792E42653956641A55658620AD0C39D4420F41AB6F12E8B2E21E9A80FDA83F57C2719B23467006FA6F6BB27F48FC1B560FEE01A5AEBA6CEE7EDF1&ct=4aeUswAAAAA%3d}

DEA to scrutinize hospital pharmacists for opioid monitoring

Julia Talsma, Content Channel Director

Publish Date: SEP 03,2014
When it comes to preventing opioid abuse and misuse, hospital pharmacists are under the same pressures as those in the community setting.

Both groups have the legal duty to ensure that prescriptions for controlled substances are for legitimate medical needs, and both are required to have procedures in place to minimize the risk of employee theft or diversion, according to a report published online in the American Journal of Health-System Pharmacy.

Labels, orders, and treatment

One area where it is important for pharmacists to keep current is that of labeling standards for opioids, as they are subject to change. For example, in September 2013, FDA issued new labeling for long-acting and extended-release opioids, requiring that these drugs be used only for severe pain by patients needing continuous daily treatment over the long term and for whom alternative treatments are not adequate.

In addition, ?Health-system pharmacists must remain vigilant for questionable orders of prescriptions. As individuals who abuse drugs find it more difficult to obtain opioids from retail pharmacies, they may turn to emergency departments and outpatient pharmacies to obtain these medications,? wrote Daniel J. Cobaugh, PharmD, vice president of ASHP Research and Education Foundation, Bethesda, Md., and his colleagues in their article, ?The opioid abuse and misuse epidemic: Implications for pharmacists in hospitals and health systems,? scheduled for publication in the September 15 issue.

Related news: Higher rates of hospitalization seen in opioid prescribing by multiple providers

Record-keeping requirements are extremely important in hospital pharmacies, and policies should be in place to ensure that orders and prescriptions are complete and accurate. Pharmacists working in the hospital setting should also be aware of the restrictions on opioids for maintenance or detoxification of drug-addicted patients.

?The basic rule is that only an opioid treatment program registered with DEA is permitted to use an opioid drug to maintain or detoxify an opioid-addicted individual,? the authors wrote. ?However, hospital staff is permitted to provide opioid maintenance or detoxification therapy to a patient as an incidental adjunct to medical or surgical treatment of conditions other than addiction, thereby allowing a hospitalized addicted person to avoid the risk of withdrawal while being treated for some other condition.

In addition, hospital staff can provide opioids to an addicted patient with intractable pain, such as the case of a cancer patient who has become addicted to these medications.


Prevention of drug diversion

Policies and procedures should be in place to prevent or minimize the risk of hospital staff theft or diversion of opioids.

The risk of diversion is particularly problematic in the case of prefilled syringes or single-use vials of controlled substances when the physician orders a smaller dose than the syringe or vial contains.

?A nurse could carry an empty sterile vial in a pocket and, instead of destroying excess drug, inject it into the vial; this pattern could be repeated several times throughout the shift,? diverting a large amount of a controlled substance that could be hard to trace, Cobaugh and colleagues wrote.

Directors of pharmacy should be aware of these risks and institute policies and procedures to minimize the potential of employee theft or diversion of these drugs, the authors said.

Overall, pharmacists working within a health system can play a vital role in identifying opioid toxicity and in preventing inappropriate prescribing of these controlled substances and diversion of these painkillers.

DEA Compliance Procedure   No:
Subject:  Revision No.:
 Draft 4 Published 07/15/08
Identification and Review of Peculiar Orders  Effective Date:

Controlled Substance Suspicious Order Monitoring Program  Supersedes Date:
NEW
 Page No.:
1  of 4

Originator: Security:
Karen Harper
Corporate Logistic  Documentation Coordinator:


PURPOSE:
This procedure formally outlines the internal criteria and standards to identify, capture,
investigate, report suspicious orders to the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) prior to
shipment.
SCOPE:
Applies internally to Covidien Customer Service Group, Information Services Group, DEA
Compliance, and Security for monitoring of controlled substance orders received electronically
or manually, bulk or finished dosage products, for all active customer accounts from order
placement to shipment.
REFERENCES:
_  Title 21 CFR 1301.74(b)
The registrant shall design and operate a system to disclose to the registrant suspicio us orders of
controlled substances. The registrant shall inform the Field Division Office of the Administration
in his area of suspicious orders when discovered by the registrant. Suspicious orders include
orders of unusual size, orders deviating substantially from a normal pattern, and orders of
unusual frequency.
OVERVIEW:
DEA cannot/will not tell a DEA registrant if an order is legitimate and/or if an order should be
shipped.  It is fundamental for sound operations that DEA registrants take reasonable measures
to identify their customers, understand the normal and expected transactions typically conducted
by those customers, and, consequently identify those transactions that are suspicious in nature.
The Procedure for Identification and Review of Peculiar  Orders, Suspicious  Order Monitoring
Program, is designed for compliance by developing systems to:
 Identify, capture, and hold orders that meet Peculiar Order criteria


   QSP 00.00  Rev  TITLE  2  of 4

Investigate Peculiar Orders and release for shipment if authorized after review by
Security and DEA Compliance
Elevate  Peculiar Orders to the level of Suspicious Order based upon investigation
results and notify DEA   [per CFR21 1301.74(b)].
DEFINITIONS:
Peculiar Order   A controlled substance order that meets an internal, established criteri a
that will be placed on hold  pending further review by DEA Compliance.
Suspicious Order  A Peculiar Order that has been reviewed by DEA Compliance and
Security  and has been elevated to DEA reporting status.
REPORTS REQUIRED
_  Do Not Ship List
RESPONSIBILITIES:
Customer Service Representative
Perform the following activities for each controlled substance order:
1. Verify that the account is in good standing
 a. Reference the  Do Not Ship List  file on the Shared Drive.
2. Assure that the order is valid
 a.  Verify that the customer has provided a complete order
3. Check customer DEA registration status
 a. Current customer DEA registration certificate is to be on file  in Customer
  Service department
 b. DEA registration suspension/revocations can be checked by calling DEA
  Compliance group who will refer to DEA webpage, Registration Validation
  Link
4. For CI and CII controlled substance orders
 a. Verify customer has provided a DEA 222 form
b. Obtain a  Certificate of Available Procurement Quota  fro m customers using a
Manufacturing registration DEA 222 Form
c. Obtain a  Statement of Intended Use  from customers using a Research,
Compounding Pharmacy, or Analytical Lab registration DEA 222 Form
 I. Forward the  Statement of Intended Use  to DEA Compliance
5. Review the order based on the criteria above and identify order as  Peculiar  if there are
any exceptions
6. Forward  Peculiar  order information to Customer Service Manager and Security
Director

Customer Service Manager


   QSP 00.00  Rev  TITLE  3  of 4


1.  Review the IS system  generated Peculiar Order Report which lists orders that meet the
criteria established in this procedure
a. Annotate the report with applicable explanation that authorizes shipment of
Peculiar Orders that deviates from normal order pattern, size, frequency such as
trade show sales, etc.
b. Manually release orders in the order entry system that are authorized to  ship
c.. For orders that have no applicable explanation for deviation from normal order
pattern, size, frequency, the order will remain on hold pending further
investigation by the business group and Security/DEA Compliance.
d.. Upon completion of review, forward the annotated Peculiar Order  Report to
Security/DEA Compliance for record retention per Company policy
2. Maintains  the Do Not Ship List on the Shared drive by updating for any customer for
which shipment has been cancelled based on suspicious order criteria.


Information Service Department


1.  Programs and publishes the order entry generated Peculiar Order Report which lists
orders that  meet the criteria as follows:
a.  Orders in excess of 2X the amount of product ordered during the previous fiscal
year andYTD average by customer, by sku.
b. Orders that appear on the Peculiar Order Report will be placed on hold
automatically within the order entry system
c. The Peculiar Order Report exempts orders from the 20? largest customers in each
customer category (Wholesalers, Distributors).


Security Director  and DEA Compliance
1. Investigates Peculiar Orders that have no applicable explanation for deviation from
normal order pattern, size, frequency
2. Consults with the business group as part of the Peculiar Order investigation
3. Reviews Peculiar Orders for correlation to  DEA webpage  Drugs of Concern Listing
4. Responsible for DEA reporting of orders that have been  escalated from Peculiar Order
status to Suspicious Order status
5. Maintains files of Peculiar Order Reports and Suspicious Order Investigation
documentation per Mallinckrodt/Covidien per Covidien Record Retention Policy
6. Responsible for training internal customers on this procedure.


  QSP 00.00  Rev  TITLE  4  of 4

MCKESSON AGREES TO PAY RECORD $150 MILLION SETTLEMENT FOR FAILURE TO REPORT SUSPICIOUS ORDERS OF PHARMACEUTICAL DRUGS
 
JAN 17 - (Washington, DC)   McKesson Corporation (McKesson), one of the nation s largest distributors of pharmaceutical drugs, agreed to pay a record $150 million civil penalty for alleged violations of the Controlled Substances Act (CSA), the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) announced today.
 
The nationwide settlement requires McKesson to suspend sales of controlled substances from distribution centers in Colorado, Ohio, Michigan and Florida for multiple years. The staged suspensions are among the most severe sanctions ever agreed to by a DEA-registered distributor. The settlement also imposes new and enhanced compliance obligations on McKesson s distribution system.
 
In 2008, McKesson agreed to a $13.25 million civil penalty and administrative agreement for similar violations. In this case, the government alleged again that McKesson failed to design and implement an effective system to detect and report  suspicious orders  for controlled substances distributed to its independent and small chain pharmacy customers  i.e. orders that are unusual in their frequency, size, or other patterns. From 2008 until 2013, McKesson supplied various U.S. pharmacies an increasing amount of oxycodone and hydrocodone pills, frequently misused products that are part of the current opioid epidemic.
 
The government s investigation developed evidence that even after designing a compliance program after the 2008 settlement, McKesson did not fully implement or adhere to its own program. In Colorado, for example, McKesson processed more than 1.6 million orders for controlled substances from June 2008 through May 2013, but reported just 16 orders as suspicious, all connected to one instance related to a recently terminated customer. 
 
"This groundbreaking resolution is tough and appropriate and underscores our commitment to hold accountable all DEA registrants, including those who distribute controlled substances," said DEA Acting Administrator Chuck Rosenberg.  "DEA is committed to fighting the opioid epidemic with all of the tools at our disposal."
 
In addition to the monetary penalties and suspensions, the government and McKesson agreed to enhanced compliance terms for the next five years. Among other things, McKesson has agreed to specific, rigorous staffing and organizational improvements; periodic auditing; and stipulated financial penalties for failing to adhere to the compliance terms. Critically, the settlement will require McKesson to engage an independent monitor to assess compliance   the first independent monitor of its kind in a CSA civil penalty settlement.
 
This was a multi-district investigation that involved the following DEA Field Divisions:  Boston Field Division, Chicago Field Division, Denver Field Division, Detroit Field Division, Miami Field Division, New Jersey Field Division, San Francisco Field Division, St. Louis Field Division, and Washington Division Office. The following U.S. Attorneys  Offices participated in the case: Central District of California, Eastern District of California, District of Colorado, Middle District of Florida, Eastern District of Kentucky, Northern District of Illinois, District of Massachusetts, Eastern District of Michigan, District of Nebraska, District of New Jersey, Northern District of West Virginia, and Western District of Wisconsin.
 
U.S. Attorneys  Offices for the District of Colorado and the Northern District of West Virginia, along with DEA s Office of Chief Counsel and its Diversion Control Division, led the civil settlement negotiations.  DEA s Denver, Detroit and Miami Field Divisions and its Washington Division Office led the administrative and civil investigation. The U.S. Department of Justice Criminal Division s Narcotic and Dangerous Drug Section (NDDS) also coordinated and assisted in negotiating certain portions of the settlement. Assistant United States Attorneys Amanda Rocque (Colorado) and Alan McGonigal (NDWV) represented the United States in the civil penalty investigations and negotiations.  Associate Chief Counsel Lee Reeves and Senior Attorneys Dedra Curteman, Dana Hill and Krista Tongring represented DEA in the investigations and negotiations. Trial Attorneys Harry Matz and Kirtland Marsh were involved for NDDS.

New York State EDI Report Requirements

Manufacturers and distributors located within New York State must transmit information from all controlled substances sales. Manufacturers and distributors located outside of New York State must transmit information only from controlled substances sales to DEA registrants located within New York State. Reverse distributors must transmit information from the return of controlled substances from DEA registrants located within New York State. Transfers of controlled substances between licensees authorized to distribute controlled substances are not required to be reported

FDA's CDER Unveils Plans for 2O16 Guidance Documents I RAPS

Note abuse deterrent guidance for generic drugs are in the plan.
FDA's CDER Unveils Plans for 2016 Guidance ➢ocuments
Regulatory Focus
By Zachary Brennan
1/22/2016
http://www. raps.org/Regul atoryFocus/News/2016/01/22/23952/FDA%E2%80%99s-CDER-Unveils-Plans-for2016-Guidance-Documents/
The guidance agenda for the next fiscal year from the US Food and Drug
Administration's (FDA) Center for Drug Evaluation and Research (CDER)
reveals a lot of new advice on generics, pharmaceutical quality, off-label
communications and other recommendations carried over from 2015, particularly
on the implementation of the Drug Supply Chain Security Act (DSCSA).
The 15 categories of guidance documents planned for 2016 range from
advertising (including a potentially controversial one on communications on
unapproved, unlicensed or uncleared uses of approved, licensed or cleared human
drugs, biologics, animal drugs and medical devices) to clinical (meta-analysis on
randomized controlled trials) to safety (new guidance on post-market reporting for
biologics and vaccines).
The total of 102 planned guidance documents is slightly higher than the 90 CDER
planned to release in 2015 and considerably more than what was planned
for 2014 and 2013.
And included on both 2015 and 2016 lists: The same three biosimilar guidance
documents (on interchangeability, labeling and statistical approaches for
evaluating similarity data), one on Internet, social media and promotional
labeling, one on pregnant women in clinical trials and one on multiple endpoints
in clinical trials, among others.
As for generic drug companies, FDA will release new draft guidance on: "General
Principles for Evaluating Abuse-Deterrent Properties of Generic Solid Oral
Opioid Drug Products," "Three-Year Exclusivity Determinations for Drug

MNKOI 0001644104

 Products," and "Updating ANDA Labeling After the Marketing Application for
the Reference Listed Drug Has Been Withdrawn."
Also included in this year's list are new guidance plans for different types of
treatment, including those for ulcerative colitis (also included in 2015's list),
revised guidance on allergic rhinitis products and exocrine pancreatic
insufficiency drugs.
On the DSCSA implementation front, which has already begun, FDA plans six
guidance documents, all except one (Field Alert Submissions) of which were
included in 201.5's list:
-Annual Reporting by Prescription Drug Wholesale Distributors and Third-Party
Logistics Providers;
-Products Eligible for Grandfather Status;
-Standards for the Interoperable Exchange of Information for Tracing Certain
Human, Finished Prescription Drugs;
-The Product Identifier for Human, Finished, Prescription Drugs;
-Verification Systems for Prescription Drugs;
-Waivers, Exceptions and Exemptions from Product Tracing Requirements; and
-Field Alert Report Submissions.

On 4/26/12, I spoke with Ed Hazewski, Director of Corporate Security, Amerisource Bergen (ABC) regarding Food City and specifically about the three DEA Registrations listed below. He advised he is well aware of the three Food City Pharmacies that are buying inordinate amounts of Oxycodone 30mg tablets and that he was in the three stores two weeks ago. Also, the Food City hired a retired DEA employee, Matt Murphy to assist them in bringing their program in line. Further, he advised that the three pharmacies have one clinic "Bearden (ph)" that is driving the large numbers. The problem, Ed explained, is the size of Food City as an ABC customer and the fact this is only three of the Food City Pharmacies. He has been told to try to bring them in line.

At that point, I advised Ed that based on the unusually large orders of oxy 30mg tablets, Mallinckrodt is considering putting them on the restricted charge back list. Ed advised that ABC has discussed the same thing, but they would rather fix the problem, if possible. I explained the similarity of Food City and the Cardinal issue with CVS in Florida and Ed advised that had also been discussed internally. Ed advised the problem started when a former Director of Food City brought in another distributor (Masters but name not mentioned) to supply additional oxy 30mg tablets to the three pharmacies being discussed. Initially, ABC was unaware of the additional distributor, but began to see their orders for oxy 30mg drop. The then Director advised he was merely dispersing the volume. Eventually, that Director was dismissed and since that time Ed and his group has been working with the three pharmacies.

In addition, Ed advised they are in the process of breaking out oxy 30mg tablets from the rest of the oxy family to give them a better picture and early warning that orders are out of line.

Based on what we now know, I see little exposure to Mallinckrodt/Covidien because of the smaller amounts of oxy 30mg that we are supplying. That being said, the similarity to the Cardinal CVS issue in Florida cannot be ignored. My recommendation is to bring this before the SOM committee to discuss. My personal opinion, put them on the restricted charge back list.

                                 From: Saake, Lisa M

                                 To: Morelli, Art; Hasse, Debra C; Kim, Stuart K. ; Darton Jr., Eddie L; Neuman, Herbert R 
                                 Subject: Pink Sheet Article- Embeda, Oxycontin Might Get Abuse-Deterrent Claims With Post-Marketing Trials- 
                                 FDA Advisory committee meeting Oct 21st and 22nd 


                                 Note the reference to post-marketing studies intended to be epidemiological or 
                                 observational in nature- Lisa 


                                 Embeda, Oxycontin Might Get Abuse-Deterrent Claims With Post-Marketing 
                                 Trials 








Confidential — Subject to Agreed Protective Order MNK_TNSTA07233924 

  A two-day, joint meeting of FDA's Anesthetic and Life Support Drugs and Drug Safety and Risk Management 
  advisory committees will consider the design of post-marketing studies for Purdue Pharma's Oxycontin and 
  King Pharmaceuticals' Embeda to determine if their product-specific properties intended to discourage misuse 
  and abuse are effective. 

  Both Oxycontin (oxycodone hydrochloride controlled-release) and Embeda (morphine sulfate extended-release 
  with a sequestered naltrexone hydrochloride inner core) are approved for management of moderate to severe 
  pain when a continuous, around-the-clock opioid analgesic is needed for an extensive period. 

  The post-marketing studies are intended to be epidemiological or observational trials to assess the drugs' known 
  serious risks as well as whether their abuse deterrent properties "actually result in a decrease" of abuse and 
  misuse as well as curtailing their potential consequences - addiction, overdose and death, according to FDA. 

  FDA is happy to see the development of potentially safer opioids, but the agency has been loathe to give the 
  products a claim for abuse deterrence, since simply engineering the pills not to be enjoyed doesn't prove they 
  will work that way, and a controlled trial couldn't ethically have misuse as a endpoint. 

  The advisory committee meeting, set for Oct. 21 and Oct. 22 in Gaithersburg, Md., is a signal, though, that the 
  agency may consider allowing different kinds of data to support risk reduction language in the label. 

  Getting The Message Out With A REMS 
  Having an abuse reduction claim or even just robust data in labeling would be a great benefit for either product, 
  particularly as the agency may be pushing all sponsors to shift their promotional efforts to a risk and education 
  message as part of a potential class-wide Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy for long-acting and extended- 
  release opioids. 

  In July, the agency issued a proposed REMS for long-acting opioids, to consist of a MedGuide, requirements 
  for drug sponsors to provide prescriber education, requirements for educational sheets to be offered to patients, 
  and a program and timetable for assessing the plan's effectiveness ('FDA's Guide To Mitigating Risks Of Long- 
  Acting Opioids,' The Pink Sheet, July 5, 2010). 

  But the Anesthetic and Life Support Drugs and Drug Safety and Risk Management advisory committees voted 
  against approval of the FDA proposal by 10-25 on July 22. Panel members cited concerns that prescriber 
  participation in the educational programs would be voluntary rather than mandatory. 

  The panel also considered an industry proposal for an opioids REMS during that meeting, suggesting that if 
  prescriber education be mandatory, implementation be through either a third-party industry-wide registry or a 
  Drug Enforcement Administration registry that would require approval by Congress. Industry participants 
  indicated they probably would prefer the latter option ('If Opioid REMS Mandates Prescriber Training, Firms 
  May Ask DEA For Help,' The Pink Sheet, Aug. 2, 2010).

John, I think this looks really good. Only recommendation would be to further distill this down into a clear executive summary that organizes the objective, outcomes and recommendations into as succinct as possible message so that it cannot be missed. The rest of the slides contain a lot of great detail for those that want to dig further, but for the large number of those viewing this, the key takeaways should be right up front.

Commercial colleagues,

I want to make you aware of a recent FDA request for an analysis of the available data (Clinical development and post marketing) for the incidence of allergic reactions (Anaphylaxis, Anaphylactoid, Urticaria, Angioedema, etc.) associated with Exalgo. They have indicated they believe this is attributable to an excipient, Sodium Metabisulfite (See agency letter of request below). It is my understanding that sodium metabisulfite is a component of the HM active ingredient rather than the OROS technology (Phil, please correct if I am mistaken). preliminary search of the Adverse Events Reporting System (AERS) also identified cases
suggesting allergic reactions.

formulation, we request the following:

summarized in tabular form by preferred term, giving the number of cases and incidence
for each treatment arm. Please present data from randomized controlled trials separately
from open label trials.

Hi BJ,

 

Hope all is well.

 

Since you were not able to be there in person today, I wanted to give
you my perspective on the day. Overall take away: we are on to something
unique and innovative in this space.

 

First and foremost, all of what I am going to relate was made possible
by Bill's strong relationships in the account, meeting prep, logistical
execution and strategic account planning. As we both know, when all
these things are in place, the execution flows and we look good.

 

The presentation was in 4 basic parts:

 

1)     Bill nicely set it up, provided an overview of the agenda and
framed the approach we were about to take ( 5 min).

2)     Karrie provided a very succinct overview of Exalgo pharmacology
with appropriate emphasis on aspects relevant to this audience: e.g.
true QD, CYP insights, rationale for opioid rotation, dose dumping,
co-morbidities. Her presentation separated validity from relevance very
well. She handled questions with aplomb. ( about 25 mins)

3)     I presented the Exalgo REMS, the Exalgo REMS performance data,
and a CARES Alliance review. This was not REMSology 101, but an inside
view of REMS operations, and how we could work together to enhance
appropriate prescribing and safe use among their member prescribers and
patients. We also pitched some unique collaborative projects we can
discuss later.( 25 mins). Preston created a new deck and it is strong.

4)     Bill then did a crisp wrap-up and close.( 5 min)

 

There was one theme that Bill uncovered and briefed us on during  the
weeks leading to the meeting: Medimpact believes they have sufficient
opioids( LAO's and IR's) on their formulary to adequately treat pain,
and that adding another LAO will increase overall opioid use. To address
this Karrie emphasized that the rotation of tolerant patients does not
mean more opioid use, it promises better analgesia and/or fewer AEs.
That didactic element dovetailed nicely with all that we are doing in
the safe use area. Clearly, Exalgo and all that we offer with it, is a
solution, not part of the societal problem, and we are working to keep
it that way.

 

We had handouts and examples of many CARES tools, our posters on Tamper
Resistance and RxFMEA, and all were taken. When we mentioned we were
working with pain specialists like Joe Shurman, MD at Scripps San Diego,
and Mark Wallace, MD at UCSD we scored big. Bill's main contact wrote
these names down. I am sure he will check references.

 

It went well, and it can be even more focused and honed on customer
needs and concerns. I recommend we sit face to face and plan v2.0 off
this experience. Teamwork is a beautiful thing.

 

Leading the Science of Safety,

Art

I already spent some time (about two weeks) on this trying to find out what’s wrong with my system or my sample preparations since we have good relationship with Mallinckradt for so many years and this type of issue didn’t happen before.  But no matter what I checked (checked with manufactures’ method or other methods), the Codeine Methyl Ether peak still shows the same retention time as that of Codeine N-Oxide USP standard (I don’t think we can question USP reference standard at this time).   When checked with the Mallinckrodt’s method (method found in DMF of codeine phosphate), all other impurities show comparable results with the document recorded in the DMF (the same order of the retention times for all the impurities of codeine phosphate such as Morphine comes out first, followed by 10-Hydroxycodeine, Codeine-N-Oxide, Codeine, Norcodeine and Codeinone) except the Codeine Methyl Ether.   We would like to address this issue ASAP.   Would you please help us to approach this?

 

Thank you very much.

 Procedure
Subject:  Revision Date:
Identification and Review of Peculiar Orders  03/28/11
Mallinckrodt Controlled Substance Suspicious Order Monitoring
Program

Originator: Page 1 of 4
Karen Harper
Senior Manager, Controlled Substance Compliance


PURPOSE:
In accordance with U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) regulations 21 CFR
1301.74(b), Mallinckrodt has an obligation to inform DEA of suspicious orders.
This procedure outlines the Identification and Review of Peculiar Orders component o f the
Mallinckrodt Suspicious Order Monitoring Program.
APPLIES TO:
Controlled Substance Customer Service Representatives and Managers
Information Service Group
Finance &Administration
Suspicious Order Monitoring Leadership Team
Commercial Group
Controlled Substance Compliance
Security  Director
OVERVIEW:
DEA communication to industry assigns shared responsibility for maintaining appropriate
safeguards against diversion to all registrants.
The Mallinckrodt Controlled Substance Procedure for Identification and Review of Peculiar
Orders, Suspicious  Order Monitoring Program, is designed to:
Define the internal criteria for detecting Peculiar Orders that require further review
Elevate  Peculiar Orders to the level of Suspicious Order as needed, based upon
investigation results, and notification to  DEA  accordingly


   C/S Comp  Identification and Review of Peculiar Orders  2  of 5
3.0  Controlled Substance Compliance Suspicious Order Monitoring Program

DEFINITIONS:
Peculiar Order:  Mallinckrodt direct customer controlled substance order that meets an
internal, established criteria  of 3X the average amount of product ordered
during the previous 12  months by DEA reporting class

Suspicious Order  A Peculiar Order that has been investigated by Finance, Security  Director,
Controlled Substance Compliance without resolution and is elevated to
DEA reportable status
REPORTS REQUIRED
_  Peculiar Order Report
_  Returned 222 Excel Spreadsheet
RESPONSIBILITIES:
Customer Service Representative
Perform the following activities for each controlled substance order:
1. Verify that the account is in good standing  by reviewing the  Do Not Ship List  file on
the Shared Drive

2. Assure that the order is valid  by completing an evaluation and verification of an order to
determine  that the customer has provided a complete order

3. For CI and CII controlled substance orders
 a. Verify customer has provided a complete DEA 222 form
b. Confirm that DEA 222 Purchaser address agrees with customer DEA registration
license
 c. Review the DEA 222 form for any unusual entries  or anomalies
d. Return the 222 form to the customer if it is unacceptable, enter returned 222
information in the  Returned 222 Excel Spreadsheet report
e. Forwards the Returned 222 Excel spreadsheet to Controlled Substance
Compliance monthly
f. Obtain a  Certificate of Available Procurement Quota  from bulk API  customers
using a Manufacturing Registration DEA 222 Form
g  Obtain a  Statement of Intended Use  from customers using a Research,
Compounding Pharmacy, or Analytical Lab registration DEA 222 Form

4. Review the order based on the criteria above and  refer to Controlled Substance
Compliance for additional inve stigation as required

Information Services Department


   C/S Comp  Identification and Review of Peculiar Orders  3  of 5
3.0  Controlled Substance Compliance Suspicious Order Monitoring Program


1.  Programs and publishes the Peculiar Order Report which lists dosage and API orders that
meet the criteria as follows:
a.  Orders in excess of 3X the average amount of product ordered during the previous
12 months  by customer, by DEA reporting class. The algorithms have been
established to identify whether a customer is deviating from a normal order
pattern, and/or increasing in frequency


Finance & Adminstration

1.  Review the IS system generated Peculiar Order Report which lists orders that meet the
established criteria

2.  Annotate Peculiar Order Report accordingly if Finance & Administration review
authorizes shipment with no further investigation, include signature and date reference for
notations

 2a. At the written direction of the Suspicious Order Monitoring Leadership Team,
Peculiar Order investigation is adjusted to address individual
product/order/customer circumstances as needed based upon specific diversion
trends
3a. If input from Commercial Group is required  in the course of Finance &
Administration Peculiar Order review, obtain documentation from Commercial
Group in support of review conclusion

3. Maintains files of Peculiar Order reports and investigation findings for those Pec uliar
Orders that do not require further investigation

1. Refer Peculiar Orders that warrant further investigation to Controlled Substance
Compliance or Security  Director

Commercial Group

Responds to Finance & Administration Group inquiries related to Pec uliar Order Report
investigation. Responses may include recommendations to approve Peculiar Orders for shipment
based upon market knowledge such as receipt of new customer supply agreements or other
justification

Suspicious Order Monitoring Leadership Team

1. Collaborates with Security and Controlled Substance Compliance to adjust Peculiar
Order review based on diversion trends
2.
Consults with Security and Compliance in Monthly Meetings to provide oversight and
guidance for all aspects of the Suspicious Order Monitoring Program


   C/S Comp  Identification and Review of Peculiar Orders  4  of 5
3.0  Controlled Substance Compliance Suspicious Order Monitoring Program


Controlled Substance Compliance

1. Investigates  Peculiar Orders that have no applicable explanation for deviation from
normal order pattern, size, and frequency, in conjunction with Security Director  upon
referral from Finance & Administration

2. Consults with the Commercial Group  as part of the peculiar order investigation, in
conjunction with Security Director

3. Reviews Peculiar Orders for comparison to DEA webpage  Drugs of Concern Listing ,
in conjunction with Security Director

4. Responsible for reporting to DEA Peculiar Orders that have been investigated and further
defined as Suspicious Orders, in conjunction with Security Director

5. Maintains files of Peculiar Order reports and investigation findings for those Peculia r
Orders that have required further investigation, in conjunction with Security Director

6. Responsible for training internal customers on this procedure, in  conjunction with
Security Director

7. In conjunction with Security, responsible for training internal  stakeholders on this
procedure

Security Director
1. Investigates  Peculiar Orders that have no applicable explanation for deviation from
normal order pattern, size, and frequency, in conjunction with Controlled Substance
Compliance

2. Consults with the  Commercial Group as part of the peculiar order investigation, in
conjunction with Controlled Substance Compliance

3. Reviews Peculiar Orders for comparison to DEA webpage  Drugs of Concern Listing ,
in conjunction with Controlled Substance Compliance

4. Responsible for reporting to DEA Peculiar Orders that have been investigated and further
defined as Suspicious Orders, in conjunction with Controlled Substance Compliance

5. Maintains files of Peculiar Order reports and investigation findings for those Peculiar
Orders that have required further investigation, in conjunction with Controlled Substance
Compliance


  C/S Comp  Identification and Review of Peculiar Orders  5  of 5
3.0  Controlled Substance Compliance Suspicious Order Monitoring Program


6. Responsible for training internal customers on this procedure  in, conjunction with
Controlled Substance Compliance


7
In conjunction with Controlled Substance Compliance, responsible for training internal
stakeholders on this procedure

Revision History

03/29/11
Added Revision History section to  document future changes to this procedure

Good afternoon CEPOP Participants   The  CEPOP Salutes  initiative is underway. We would like to share with you the invitation below (and attached) for the initial CEPOP Salutes national webinar on August 15th.  Please forward to colleagues who may be interested in this subject matter.

Matt

CEPOP Salutes: Hospital Networks Lead Efforts
to Reduce Opioid-Related Injuries

Monday, August 15, 2016

1:00pm   2:30pm EDT

 


Please join the Collaborative for Effective Prescription Opioid Policies for a national webinar highlighting the efforts of Hospital Engagement Networks (HENs) in improving pain management and avoiding opioid-related adverse events and injuries. Members from the Hospital & Healthcare Association of Pennsylvania and the Michigan Health & Hospital Association Foundation Keystone Center will present on their sentinel efforts to help reverse the opioid epidemic.

 

 

To register for the webinar, please visit: CEPOP Salutes Registration Portal.

 

 

For more information, please contact Matthew Rubin at matthew.rubin@faegrebd.com.

 

 

Launched in January of 2015, the Collaborative for Effective Prescription Opioid Policies (CEPOP) engages diverse stakeholders behind a comprehensive and balanced public policy strategy to reduce prescription opioid abuse and promote treatment options, both for those living with chronic pain and confronting addiction.  CEPOP has 70 active participants and has involvement from patient and family advocacy, provider, public health, dispensing, distribution, and manufacturing organizations.

MNK's political liason team is working with an individual who puts together graphical presentations to make complex problems comprehensible to people with short attention spans.

Moore, Keith (Clinical) 2:29 PM

LOL!!

Herman, Cliff 2:29 PM

Seriously, we are using photos and I would also like a couple (3-4) representative PK curves demonstrating what PK looks like in terms of blood levels.

From: Patrick, Jeffrey
Sent: Thursday, December 09, 2010 1:08 PM
To: Wickline, Ronald P; Novak, Rod P
Cc: Neuman, Herbert R; Meyer, Jay E; McGowan, Gavin J; Kisinger, Connie ; Wessler, Michael
Subject: FW: Label Language - Converting to Exalgo



Sales and Marketing Colleagues,

 

Please see the email I sent to Herb following a discussion we had on potential educational needs for physicians on issues surrounding the conversion process of patients on other opioids to Exalgo. The Exalgo label excerpts that I included below provide treating physicians with information that is pertinent to the management of the opioid rotation process to Exalgo, however, there are questions regarding physicians awareness of these additional elements of the label, as they are located somewhat deeper in the label and there is likelihood that physicians may not have thoroughly read these elements as a result.

 

We believe that some, if not many, physicians may be utilizing only part of the conversion recommendations (the general recommendation for dose reduction of 50%) and they may not necessarily be implementing other elements as described in the label to ensure the process is managed thoroughly and safely. There may be educational needs for the physicians on the aspect of the opiate deficit that is created by the employing the recommended dose reduction which can lead to withdrawal symptoms, which is why it may be important to utilize other steps that are described in the label language, such as monitoring rescue medication usage. Additionally, the importance of understanding the pharmacokinetics of Exalgo is pertinent to the conversion and titration aspect, which may result in the requirement of supportive rescue medication and physician evaluation of patients  response and side effects, until the patient is at steady-state on Exalgo. Finally, as the label language suggests, there is no single fixed conversion ratio that will suitably address the needs of all patients and physicians might benefit by being apprised of alternative conversion options, such as that employed in the pivotal 301 study published by Hale et al, which utilized a 25% dose reduction and the proceeded with titration.  

 

An idea we had was to consider developing a leave-behind educational card, with  Considerations for Conversion to Exalgo  that would utilize the label language elements on conversion and titration (such as those included below) and provide physicians with a succinct review of the FDA recommendations for the process of conversion to and titration of Exalgo. However, if the sales force already cover these elements or have an educational piece of this nature, there is no need to be redundant.

 

We look forward to your thoughts and input on this subject.

 

Thank you.

 

jtp

 

From: Patrick, Jeffrey
Sent: Wednesday, December 08, 2010 6:38 PM
To: Neuman, Herbert R
Cc: Patrick, Jeffrey
Subject: Label Language - Converting to Exalgo



 

Herb,


 


Appropriately, the FDA wrote the label language to aid and direct physicians in their efforts to convert patients to Exalgo. However, they did not suggest that there is one fixed process that will satisfy all patients converted. The following EXALGO label excerpts point to the need for the prescribing physician to utilize their clinical judgement as well as close communication to best manage patients in the conversion process:


 


In the selection of the initial dose of EXALGO, give attention to the following:

? the daily dose, potency, and specific characteristics of the opioid the patient has been taking previously;

? the reliability of the relative potency estimate used to calculate the equivalent hydromorphone dose needed;

? the patient's degree of opioid tolerance;

? the age, general condition, and medical status of the patient;

? concurrent non-opioid analgesics and other medications, such as those with Central Nervous System (CNS) activity [see Drug Interactions (7)];

? the type and severity of the patient's pain;

? the balance between pain control and adverse effects;

? risk factors for abuse, addiction, or diversion, including a prior history of abuse, addiction, or diversion

 

In general, start EXALGO therapy by administering 50% of the calculated total daily dose of EXALGO (see conversion ratio table below) every 24 hours. The initial dose of EXALGO can be titrated until adequate pain relief with  tolerable side effects has been achieved. The following table provides approximate equivalent doses, which may be used as a guideline for conversion.

? The conversion ratios and approximate equivalent doses in this conversion table (Table 1) are only to be used for the conversion from current oral opioid therapy to EXALGO. No fixed conversion ratio is likely to be satisfactory in all patients, especially in patients receiving large opioid doses.

Individualization of Dosage

? Once therapy is initiated, assess pain relief and other opioid adverse reactions frequently.

? Titrate patients to adequate analgesia with dose increases not more often than every 3 to 4 days, in order to attain steady-state plasma concentrations of hydromorphone at each dose.

? As a guideline, consider dosage increases of 25% to 50% of the current daily dose of EXALGO for each titration step.

? If more than two doses of rescue medication are needed within a 24 hour period for two consecutive days, the dose of EXALGO may need to be titrated upward.

? Administer EXALGO no more frequently than every 24 hours.

During periods of changing analgesic requirements, including initial titration, maintain frequent contact between physician, other members of the healthcare team, the patient and the caregiver/family.

 

I believe these are educational points for all discussions related to patients who have Exalgo prescribed for them.

 

jtp

Hello All,

 

As you know, following a meeting Art and I had with David Brushwood at APS, I have been talking with David regarding a potential pilot program with the VIGIL tools.  Pharmacists have become increasing integrated into the care of patients with pain, however, unlike physicians in pain practice, pharmacists are not accustom to having tools for assessment and documentation.  As a result, pharmacists will likely not readily adapt them into their practices without better understanding the potential benefits.  A pilot study and subsequent publications in pharmacy journals will help to validate the tools and increase awareness. 

 

As a next step, David has suggested a focus group session with 5-6 community retail pharmacists in order to  evaluate how best to implement the VIGIL tools as part of Cares Alliance, as well as discuss and gather the important data and observational outcomes for a pilot study with the tools.

 

We discussed the types of data to be gathered in order to better understand what are reasonable expectations in a retail setting and  how the tools might work to improve the quality of pharmacy care in a retail setting, specifically related to dispensing medications to patients with pain.  A sample of some of the areas to understand from this group would be:

 

-how often are pharmacists asking for ID when dispensing an opioid

-who is typically picking up the opioid (patient, family member, friend..)

-how often are pharmacists consulting with the MD when there is ambiguity (e.g., two extended release or two short acting opioid prescriptions, refill too early, rapid dose escalation, etc)

-how often is the first presented opioid prescription for a dose that exceeds 60 mg morphine equivalents per day

-how often is an opioid prescription changed to something else as a result of a pharmacist intervention

 

Please let me know your thoughts on ‘if and how’ we could support this next step.  Also let me know if you have questions and / or want additional information. 

 

Angela

The American Telemedicine Association has identified a valid access to care issue for patients who suffer with chronic
pain who require ongoing opiate therapy.
Instead of Telemedicine, we have our stable pain patients examined, monitored and medically maintained by a
Prescribing Pharmacist who is more accessible/local to the patient than his Pain Management specialist. At VeraPharm,
we think our solution to this problem is safer for both the patient and his community. (VeraPharm.biz)
Under a strict protocol from a pain management specialist, VeraPharm pharmacists may prescribe pain medications to
stable patients for whom access to their Pain Management Specialist is problematic. This system helps protect the
patient, his community, and his prescriber from the potential issues that may arise with chronic pain. Under the
protocol, patients may be seen by their local VeraPharm pharmacist if:
*The patient has an intractable pain diagnosis
*the patient has been stable on medication and therapy for at least a year
*the patient has not shown aberrant behaviors
*the patient's condition has not changed
*the patient is not ill from other causes
*the patient has a significant other who can monitor their daily functionality and medication use and report
responsibly
If any of the above conditions change, the Pain Management: specialist is immediately contacted.
At a monthly, IN-PERSON office visit, the Prescribing Pharmacist examines and interviews both patient and significant
other, The pharmacist: monitors for aberrant behaviors, checks for ADE. and other functionality, and may make minor

MNKOI 0004243891

 changes to the pain patient's medication regime. Patients are not pre--warned about toxicology screening. The patient's
chart: information is then sent to the Pain Management specialist who reviews it in a timely manner per legal
requirements. Both the physician and pharmacist have full access to the patient's chart at all times,
At VeraPharm, patients get a hands-on visit with a qualified pharmacist. Telemedicine may be the best choice for some
pain patients, but, where possible, and in-person visit with a VeraPharm pharmacist is often a better choice.
VeraPharm.biz

 On-site visits for all controlled substance customers

Posted: Monday,

December 23, 2013 10:59 am

Ohio Attorney General Mike DeWine is once again urging the U.S. Food and
Drug Administration (FDA) to require manufacturers of generic prescription
pain relievers to develop tamper-resistant versions of their products.
Attorney General DeWine joined 41 other state and territorial attorneys
general today in sending a second letter to the FDA requesting the
requirement. Attorney General DeWine was one of 48 attorneys general who signed a
similar letter sent to the FDA in March.

?Adding new physical and chemical features to prescription opioids can
deter abuse and reduce misuse and accidental death,? said Attorney General
DeWine. ?By making the generic versions of prescription pain pills harder to
abuse, we can prevent addiction and save lives.?
In their letter, the attorneys general thanked the FDA for their recent
efforts to require abuse-deterrent formulations for branded opioid drugs.
However, they also urged the FDA to go even further by ensuring that generic
opioids, like their branded counterparts, have abuse-deterrent properties.
According to the FDA, ?Abuse-deterrent formulations target the known or
expected routes of abuse, such as crushing in order to snort or dissolving in
order to inject, for the specific opioid drug substance in that
formulation.?
?Accordingly, the undersigned State Attorneys General respectfully request
that the FDA provide clear and fair regulatory standards for the
incorporation of abuse-deterrent technologies into generic opioids,? reads the
National Association of Attorneys General (NAAG) letter.
Attorneys general across the country remain in the national forefront in
combating prescription abuse by sponsoring prescription drug-take back
efforts, spearheading legislative and law enforcement initiatives in their
respective jurisdictions, and mandating state level prescription drug monitoring
programs.
In addition to Attorney General DeWine, attorneys general from the
following states/territories signed the NAAG letter: Alabama, Arizona, Arkansas,
Colorado, Delaware, Florida, Georgia, Guam, Hawaii, Idaho, Illinois,
Indiana, Iowa, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan,
Minnesota, Mississippi, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, Nevada, New Hampshire, New
Jersey, New Mexico, North Carolina, North Dakota, Oregon, Pennsylvania,
Rhode Island, South Carolina, South Dakota, Texas, Utah, Vermont, Washington,
West Virginia and Wisconsin.

INDICATION

EXALGO  (hydromorphone HCI) Extended-Release
Tablets (CII) is indicated for the management of
moderate to severe pain in opioid tolerant patients
requiring continuous, around-the-clock opioid
analgesia for an extended period of time.

IMPORTANT RISK INFORMATION

WARNING: ABUSE POTENTIAL,
LIFE-THREATENING RESPIRATORY DEPRESSION, and ACCIDENTAL EXPOSURE

Abuse Potential

EXALGO contains hydromorphone, an opioid agonist and a Schedule II controlled substance with an abuse liability similar to other opioid agonists, legal or illicit. Assess each patient s risk for opioid abuse or addiction prior to prescribing EXALGO. The risk for opioid abuse is increased in patients with a personal or family history of substance abuse (including drug or alcohol abuse or addiction) or mental illness (e.g., major depressive disorder). Routinely monitor all patients receiving EXALGO for signs of misuse, abuse, and addiction during treatment.

Life-threatening Respiratory Depression

Respiratory depression, including fatal cases, may occur with use of EXALGO, even when the drug has been used as recommended and not misused or abused. EXALGO is for use in opioid tolerant patients only. Proper dosing and titration are essential and EXALGO should be prescribed only by healthcare professionals who are knowledgeable in the use of potent opioids for the management of chronic pain. Monitor for respiratory depression, especially during initiation of EXALGO or following a dose increase. Crushing, dissolving, or chewing the tablet can cause rapid release and absorption of a potentially fatal dose of hydromorphone.

Accidental Exposure

Accidental ingestion of EXALGO, especially in children, can result in a fatal overdose of hydromorphone.



 


EXALGO is contraindicated in:
- Opioid non-tolerant patients. Fatal respiratory
  depression could occur in patients who are not
  opioid tolerant.

- Patients with significant respiratory depression

- Patients with acute or severe bronchial asthma in
  an unmonitored setting or in the absence of
  resuscitative equipment

- Patients with known or suspected paralytic ileus

- Patients who have had surgical procedures and/or
  underlying disease resulting in narrowing of the
  gastrointestinal tract, or have  blind loops  of the
  gastrointestinal tract or gastrointestinal obstruction

- Patients with hypersensitivity (e.g., anaphylaxis) to
  hydromorphone or sulfite-containing medications


 


EXALGO is indicated for opioid tolerant patients only. Patients considered opioid tolerant are those who are taking at least 60 mg oral morphine per day, 25 mcg transdermal fentanyl/hour, 30 mg oral oxycodone/day, 8 mg oral hydromorphone/day, 25 mg oral oxymorphone/day or an equianalgesic dose of another opioid, for a week or longer.


 


EXALGO is not intended for use as an as-needed analgesic and is not indicated for the management of acute or postoperative pain. It is contraindicated in patients who need management of mild pain or pain not expected to persist.


 


Avoid concurrent use of alcohol and EXALGO. Concurrent use of EXALGO with CNS depressants, including alcohol, increases risk of respiratory depression, hypotension, and profound sedation, potentially resulting in coma or death. EXALGO may impair the ability to drive a car or operate machinery.


 


Not intended in patients who have received MAO inhibitors within 14 days of starting EXALGO.


 


Use with caution and in reduced doses in older or debilitated patients, as well as patients with renal or hepatic insufficiency, Addison s disease, delirium tremens, myxedema or hypothyroidism, prostatic hypertrophy or urethral stricture, toxic psychosis. May aggravate convulsions in patients with convulsive disorders; may induce or aggravate seizures in some clinical settings. Consider use of an alternate analgesic in patients with severe renal impairment.


 


Respiratory depression, which occurs more frequently in elderly or debilitated patients, is the chief hazard with EXALGO.


 


Serious adverse events could also include hypotensive effects, GI effects, cardiac arrest from overdose and precipitation of withdrawal. Most common adverse events (>10%) seen in clinical studies (N=2474) were: constipation (31%), nausea (28%), vomiting, somnolence, headache, asthenia and dizziness.


 


Use EXALGO with extreme caution in patients susceptible to intracranial effects of CO2 retention.


 


Do not abruptly discontinue EXALGO.


See additional Important Risk Information, including boxed warning, in Full Prescribing Information<http://whatcounts.jobson.com/t?r=12&c=0&l=2982&ctl=54A39:B5F526631F6058485DD7F585132E82E093B8F18DA1535B1F&> and Medication Guide<http://whatcounts.jobson.com/t?r=12&c=0&l=2982&ctl=54A3A:B5F526631F6058485DD7F585132E82E093B8F18DA1535B1F&>.

[RxNews] Tenncare Investigation
ATT1762079.txt

CLINTON - When the next-door pharmacy one day ran out of the pain pills that Dr. Delvin Littell prescribed, his patients made a
run on a nearby Food City pharmacy in Oliver Springs.
Within two hours, 840 OxyContin pills were dispensed there, Anderson County prosecutor Sandra Donaghy said Monday.
Between October 2004 and Feb. 1, 2007, TennCare paid more than $2.3 million for pain pill prescriptions written by Littell,
according to a TBI affidavit.
Littell, 76, now retired, pleaded guilty to TennCare fraud and reckless endangerment in Anderson County Criminal Court.
The pleas followed an investigation by the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation that spanned two years.
Littell, a Deer Lodge resident, operated the now-closed Oliver Springs Walk-In Medical Clinic in the same Tri-County Boulevard
building as Riddle Drugs.
TennCare patients would pay cash for OxyContin and hydrocodone they were prescribed by Littell and then sell the pain pills in
the clinic's parking lot, according to Donaghy.
State Sen. Randy McNally and Oliver Springs Mayor Ed Kelley, now deceased, told the TBI in spring 2005 that they had
received complaints about drug activity outside the pharmacy and clinic, according to the TBI affidavit.
Littell's patients came from as far away as Kentucky and Virginia. Some would be in and back out of his clinic in 30 minutes,
pain pill prescriptions in hand, the affidavit states.
Six TennCare patients who obtained prescriptions for narcotics from Littell were arrested in 2005-06 for selling drugs, the filing
states. The TBI also received reports of overdoses and thefts that involved Littell's patients, according to the affidavit.
Littell's pleas netted him a two-year prison sentence for TennCare fraud and an 11-month, 29-day sentence for reckless
endangerment, to be served at the same time. But the sentences were suspended, and he was instead placed on probation
and ordered to pay $5,200 in fines.

Ginger,

Please find below information on Oxy as requested. There are a lot of moving parts, but let me know if you would like to discuss
the below further.

 Backorders were low in June.
o  Have some orders kicked out of the system for being on backorder too long?Yes , there have been a total of
297 orders to date that have been cancelled due to expired 222 forms, in which the customer had to
re-order. The value of the lost sales is ~$8.8M (based on June ASP), assuming that the order was not
placed again (which it most likely was).

Item Description Cancelled Orders
OXYCODONE HCL 5MG TABS
055201 73
USP

055262 38
USP
OXYCODONE HCL 15MG TABS
851501 77
USP
OXYCODONE HCL 30MG TABS
853001 109
USP
Total  297

o  Was this partly due to timing of product shipped to wholesalers being too late to sell to pharmacies? This was
due to us allocating product to priority customers while on backorder as well as those customers that
were cut off but still ordering product. Only 10 of these cancelled orders were direct ship priority
customers; the rest were wholesalers and distributors (mainly distributors).
 Are we shipping everything we get in stock?Yes , however, we keep minimal inventory on hand for direct ship
customers depending on the next expected release date.
 Are the chargebacks dropping? Yes, it appears that within the past several months (starting in Jan), the 3 month
average has been slowly decreasing by ~4%. Oxy 15 and 30 are driving the decrease, Oxy 5 remains steady.

o  What end customers drove this?McKesson  OneStop is contributing a lot to the decrease in chargebacks
on the 15 and 30mg. The attached file shows the breakdown of key drivers based on past 3 month
average compared to the previous 3 month avg. Rite Aid is driving a lot of the inconsistency of OneStop
demand. For example, for the 30mg, during the months of Oct - Dec, they ordered ~15K bottles/month
through OneStop and for the past few months they are back to 0.


o  Is it any particular wholesaler at issue more than others?McKesson  OneStop as mentioned above.
o  Are we supplying distributors all that they need?No , we are still not supplying Optisource fully. Once we
start supplying all of the distributors, the wholesaler demand may slow. This would also increase our
distribution in hopes to regain the end users back. However, we are still allocating product to
distributors when we are in a safe inventory position until the next release.
 I keep hearing we will have ongoing issues
o  Is that based on forecast which is above demand? I think we are still playing catch-up for the most part
along with trying to fully understand the increase in wholesaler's demand (whether it  is true demand or
not). According to the chargebacks we have lost business at the end user due to backorders. The

Thanks for the specific information Holt.  Can you provide any more information in relation to my questions below in red?

 

Gus, please work with the CTM and respond ASAP. . .

 

Holt, the next time you are in Hampton, please set up some time with me!  I haven’t really gotten to know you yet and I am keen to strengthen the relationshipship with our field representatives who know our investigators . . .
