From: Miller, Holt W
Sent: Thursday, October 20, 2016 3:40 PM
To: Decker, John F; Rodriguez, Domingo
Cc: Otulana, Tunde; Hill, Lawrence; Cortes, Robert
Subject: RE: IT Hydromorpone Investigator concerns



 

Thank you, John.

During my meeting this morning with Dr Saulino, he articulated, in order of importance, the following frustrations around our Hydromorphone study:

1)      There appears to me no leadership for this study….no point person.  “Who is running this study.”  He would like to have a single, identified individual with whom he can interface as needed. I’m confused by this since the protocol has the contact individuals listed.  Who do you think he means?

2)      There have been no investigator meetings in 3 years and there have been no conference calls in 2 years.  What do you think his expectation is regarding this?  I mean, except for the oncology trial we have conducted that had a data safety monitoring board with some of the lead investigators, we do not normally have regular conference calls with the investigators.  Our communication channel is typically between the in-house clinical trial manager and the site’s study coordinator.  Communication with the actual investigator occurs on an as-needed basis, usually because of a safety incident.

3)      There have been no abstracts for this study.  Yes, that is correct.  There have been no publication efforts for this program.  As you know, this is driven primarily by the med affairs strategic agenda.  

4)      There is no consistency of protocol.  He has had 8 study monitors and each seems to bring in their own set of protocols.  For example:  Patient required pump replacement secondary to end of life pump.  Was told by one study monitor that this was okay and not a documentable adverse event and then was told after the surgery by another study monitor that this was indeed a documentable adverse event.  I can understand this concern.

5)      Just yesterday, Dr Saulino met with his institution and was told, due to the volume of issues with this study, that the IRB may significantly restrict his investigator status resulting in a loss of other, unrelated studies he is currently involved with.  This he indicated he feels he can mitigate.  This is a serious comment.  Did he happen to mention what issues are of concern to the IRB? 

6)      In conclusion, Dr Saulino indicated that if this study is going to be discontinued, then discontinue it.  If it’s going to be modified, then stop this study and start over.  Just don’t let it keep limping along as it is.  The study has been enrolling relatively steadily; I’m confused why he characterizes it as limping along.  The last patient visit will occur in about April of next year and then the submission will go in.

 

I do think the next step from us would be someone reaching out to Dr Saulino.  He indicated that email will be the best course for this action.  Please, let me know if you would like his email address.  Yes, reaching out to him is clearly necessary. 

 

Thank you,

 

Holt Miller

Market Development Manager

Gablofen

Mallinckrodt Intrathecal Therapies

St. Louis, MO

M: 224-234-7978

www.Gablofen.com


 

From: Decker, John F
Sent: Thursday, October 20, 2016 11:24 AM
To: Rodriguez, Domingo <Domingo.Rodriguez@mallinckrodt.com>
Cc: Otulana, Tunde <Tunde.Otulana@mallinckrodt.com>; Hill, Lawrence <Lawrence.Hill@mallinckrodt.com>; Miller, Holt W <Holt.Miller@mallinckrodt.com>; Cortes, Robert <Robert.Cortes@mallinckrodt.com>
Subject: IT Hydromorpone Investigator concerns



 

Hi Domingo,

 

I got a call from Holt, who just met with Dr. Saulino, one of our IT-H investigators. Holt let me know that Dr. Saulino is very upset with the way that Mallinckrodt is managing this clinical trial and related communications.  Holt, can you please share some of Dr. Saulino’s concerns that he shared with you?

 

I spoke with Tunde and Lawrence, so they are aware, and both wanted me to share this with you.

 

I’d also like to mention that we (several folks from MNK, including Tunde) will be meeting with another IT-H investigator, Dr. Oscar deLeon Cassasola, at ASRA.  Krishna will be presenting our phase 1 Ofirmev data there.  Oscar is the outgoing president of ASRA (being followed by Gene Viscusi).   They were both authors on the recent APS guidelines, which were very unfavorable to Ofirmev.  My point is that our Investigators are also very influential KOLs and Authors, and not necessarily for one brand.   Oscar specializes in cancer pain, and is a passionate supporter of intrathecal hydromorphone.  Ofirmev is only of passing interest to him- but he can be very influential in how others perceive it, and Mallinckrodt.

 

I realize there are many factors at play, and I know I don’t see all the pieces.  I’m simply passing along a message, and letting you know of the potential implications from my perspective.  And I’d really like to know if there is something I can do to help.

 

Lawrence indicated you would be in the office next week, and I will be out on PTO from Oct 22 to Nov 9- so I wanted to share this information, and open this channel of communication promptly.

 

Best regards,

John

 

John F. Decker,  PhD l Director, Global Scientific Communications
Mallinckrodt Pharmaceuticals
Perryville III Corporate Park | 53 Frontage Road | Third Floor
P. O. Box 9001 | Hampton, NJ 08827-9001

    "leonard, john"
Cc: "nicholl, harry",

I agree,  This also points out valuation issues with material that is not 100% such as the opium and morphine Bitartrate and Sulfate solutions.

Thanks

Gary

_____________________________________________
From:   Nelson, Lee 
Sent:   February 14, 2008 6:30 PM
To:     Wilkening, Gary; Leonard, John
Cc:     Nicholl, Harry; Treadaway, Joan; Harper, Karen; Wynne, Mike F; Stewart, Bill
Subject:        RE: Simple and Complex Quota models

Gary,

Hydrocodone is mid-level complex.  It has only one input - Codeine - and one output - 1582 hydrocodone bitartrate.  It is a good example of straight-line production with short recycles.

Morphine has everything you mentioned below, but has 2 quotas, raw materials from 3 countries, 5 charging points, 7 isolated intermediates, multiple assay intermediate (M&C), and besides 2 sales products is converted to 6 other synthetic products.  Also after it is converted, there are derivative streams which come back into inventory and need their own WIP.

Opium/CPS receipts are simple, but they have multiple assays and 19 year-end reports.

Maybe Morphine and Opium/CPS should be added as Extra Complex!

Lee

_____________________________________________
From:   Wilkening, Gary 
Sent:   February 14, 2008 3:43 PM
To:     Nelson, Lee; Leonard, John
Cc:     Nicholl, Harry; Treadaway, Joan; Harper, Karen; Wynne, Mike F; Stewart, Bill
Subject:        RE: Simple and Complex Quota models

John Leonard and I talked and if you have not picked a complex item, you may want to use Hydrocodone.

Hydrocodone Alkaloid (6282) gets made from Codeine.
There are waste streams from the process that contain Hydrocodone Alkaloid and affect Quota.
Hydrocodone Alkaloid has a recycle stream that goes to another process that gets converted to another product 3959 (Recovered Hydrocodone Alkaloid).

A portion of this gets reprocessed back into 3959 because the impurities are too high to process forward.  This process is done in Building 235 and 6&7.

Hydrocodone Alkaloid is converted to Hydrocodone Bitartrate which has a conversion factor to adjust it back to Alkaloid.

There is also a recycle stream from this which goes back to be recovered as Hydrocodone Alkaloid Code 3959.

There may also be other items that I am missing.

Thanks

Gary




_____________________________________________
From:   Nelson, Lee 
Sent:   February 14, 2008 1:51 PM
To:     Leonard, John
Cc:     Nicholl, Harry; Treadaway, Joan; Wilkening, Gary; Harper, Karen; Nelson, Lee; Wynne, Mike F; Stewart, Bill
Subject:        Simple and Complex Quota models

John,

You have the meeting set for Monday 2/18 which is a vacation day.
 << File: DEA St. Louis Quota model.xls >>
The simple manufacturing quota model is 3221 Aminonitrile.

This product has only one step, one use, no WIP and is very seldom reworked.

Quota procedure
Add all R and PR Receipt transactions
Add Issue transactions only if the work order code is the same as the charging code.
        3221 --> 3221

The net is quota consumed

MC9382 - step 1
Batch Records
6.110 - Aminonitrile Drying
6.120 Rework of Aminonitrile.
Quota: QC9254 Methadone Intermediate

Sincerely,
Lee Nelson

Dear AfBPM Responsible/Safe Use Working Group Members:
Thank you for your participation in our call on Thursday, October 15. We appreciate your time and efforts.

AfBPM Responsible/Safe Use Working Group Call Recap
Participants: Shaina Smith (U.S. Pain Foundation); James Appleby and Trish D'Antonio (The Gerontological
Society of America); Wade Delk (American Society for Pain Management Nursing); Lisa Winstel (Caregiver
Action Network); Marcia Lee Taylor (Partnership for Drug-Free Kids); Kevin Webb and Rhonda Sciarra
(Mallinckrodt); Green Room

•

•

•

Access survey officially closed on October 5 with 833 completed responses; trends and key takeaways
remain the same as previously reported, most notable that while opioids have been most commonly
recommended by HCPs for the management of pain they have also been the most difficult to access;
results currently being weighted by survey experts
On the first day of the Summit (Thurs, November 12), KWebb will open Summit and Green Room will
introduce speakers, which will be followed by speaker presentations, review of current literature on pain
management, working/networking lunch and Working Group breakouts
o In terms of speakers we are currently looking at Dr. Howard Koh for responsible/safe use
(involved with recent National. Action. Plan for Adverse Drug Event Prevention) and Dr.
Nalamachu for access; UPDATE: following 10/15 Working Group call Lynn DeBar notified
Green Room that she is unavailable to speak at the Summit due to scheduling
Group discussed potential AfBPM tactics:
o LWinstel: The transition of care is important as not everyone is close to their hospital in terms of
distance; caregivers need to better understand how to take care of their loved ones once they are
home; a discharge protocol for properly managing pain would be useful with instructions for the
caregiver included
o TD'Antonio: It's important to integrate caregivers into the entire discharge process and equip
them with the right tools
o WDelk: Is there a way to capture what pain management medication can potentially do and their
side-effects, including information about opioids and alternatives to seek relief?

MNKOI 0001017680

 •

•
•
•
•

•

WDelk shared the Checklist at a meeting last month and noted it was very well-received
and copies were requested
o MTaylor: Sports injuries are critical with regard to pain management and important to note that
often parents allow their children to manage their own pain/medication; need to consider
addressing concept of people managing their medicine and ensuring a responsible caregiver is
available to manage process, keep medication in a safe place, etc.
o JAppleby: Communication to patients and caregivers about the affects of opioids on other
systems in the body is important, e.g.,opioid-induced constipation (OIC), particularly for the
aging population; could be included as part of the discharge plan
o LWinstel: One of the more difficult topics to speak about is intimacy and how OIC can affect it
o KWebb: All of the ideas discussed have merit as we think through under the context of
continuing to ensure patient safety and not doing anything that would prevent access to
appropriate pain management; important to remember that we don't want to go too far down one
path; need to factor in empowerment of the patient and caregiver to have conversations with
healthcare professionals and continue to focus on individualized patient care; could also
highlight what about opioids patients needs to know when they are leaving the hospital with
these medications
o JAppleby: Patients and caregivers are likely not asking all of the right questions about pain
management in advance of surgical procedures, accidents, etc., and some patients have to
remember they are high-risk
o KWebb: There is currently a receptive environment due to the National Pain Strategy and other
initiatives re: individual patient care and patient safety; if we can advance a tool that allows us to
tap into this already-receptive audience we may get more traction
Any members with additional tactics/initiatives for consideration, please send them to
gsherman@greenroompr.com
Like last year, we are considering inviting non-Alliance members to attend and participate in the
Summit; a memo will be forthcoming week of 10/19 with additional information (completed)
It's critical that all AfBPM members RSVP to the Summit (via the invitation that went on 10/7) by
10/21; hotel accommodations must be secured by 10/23
In terms of media activities a press release will be issued by AfBPM on 11/17 and trade and consumer
media outreach will ensue; if AfBPM members have media contacts/established relationships with either
trade or consumer media outlets please email gshermanqD,greenroompr.com with the information so that
we can add these folks to our media lists
Dr. Nalamachu, who work with the Alliance for Patient Access, authored a blog post on behalf of
AfBPM which has been submitted to FormularyWatch blog; acceptance status is pending

CVS probed in alleged loss of painkillers

CVS Caremark Corp. could face as much as $29 million in fines for allegedly losing track of hydrocodone pills at four California stores. They may have been sold on the black market.

CVS Caremark Corp. could face as much as $29 million in fines for allegedly losing track of prescription painkillers at four of its California stores, from which authorities said thousands of pills may have been sold on the black market. Doug Kolk reports

By David Lazarus

March 10, 2014, 7:25 p.m.

{CVS Caremark Corporation}CVS Caremark Corp. could face as much as $29 million in fines for allegedly losing track of prescription painkillers at four of its California stores, from which authorities said thousands of pills may have been sold on the black market.

Officials at the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration and the California Board of Pharmacy told me Monday that more than 37,000 pills were apparently taken from CVS stores in Modesto, Fairfield, Dixon and Turlock.

Meanwhile, CVS pharmacists in Southern California said they've been instructed by the drugstore chain to get their paperwork in order so that no other prescription meds are found to be missing.

David Lazarus

{Description:}Photo: 

Have a consumer question? Ask Laz

Casey Rettig, a special agent in the DEA's San Francisco office, said warrants were served on the four California CVS stores last May. She declined to comment further because the agency's investigation is still open.

Virginia Herold, executive officer of the state Board of Pharmacy, which licenses and oversees all drugstores in California, said each of the missing pills   all painkillers, such as {Vicodin (drug)} Vicodin   could have a street value of as much as $10.

Lauren Horwood, a spokeswoman for the U.S. attorney's office in Sacramento, said CVS faces 2,973 possible violations of the federal Controlled Substances Act for alleged discrepancies between the company's records and its inventory of prescription drugs.

The maximum fine for these violations could be $29 million, she said.

Horwood said CVS has yet to respond to a letter sent last month by her office. The letter outlines the alleged violations and seeks more information from the company.

Officials, requesting anonymity because of the sensitivity of the matter, described the loss of painkillers as a big problem throughout the pharmacy business.

In some cases, the drugs have gone missing because pharmacists "self-medicate," they said. But in most cases, the officials said, lower-level pharmacy workers, such as technicians, have made off with the drugs and then sold them to others.

Such thefts typically come to light after pharmacies perform routine inspections of their inventory. They're required by law to report any missing meds within 14 days of discovery.

According to formerly sealed affidavits submitted as part of the DEA's application for search warrants, an investigator for the agency, Brian Glaudel, said the Sacramento district office became aware in late 2012 of losses of numerous {Hydrocodone (drug)} hydrocodone tablets from CVS stores in the region.

Hydrocodone is a narcotic painkiller sold under various brand names, including Vicodin and Norco.

The pending investigations stem from a case involving a CVS store in Rocklin, northeast of Sacramento.

Glaudel said CVS notified officials in December 2012 that a pharmacy worker in the Rocklin store was seen hiding a bottle of hydrocodone in her pants.

The worker subsequently admitted to CVS managers that she had stolen more than 20,000 hydrocodone tablets, Glaudel said.

The worker was arrested and charged with embezzlement, he said. It's unclear whether the stolen hydrocodone was recovered in the Rocklin case.

Glaudel said DEA investigators went over records for other CVS stores in the area and found more than 16,000 hydrocodone tablets missing from the Turlock store, 11,000 from the Fairfield store and almost 5,000 each from the Modesto and Dixon stores.

Michael DeAngelis, a CVS spokesman, said the investigations are aimed at "assuring compliance with state and federal requirements for administrative record keeping related to invoices and inventory for controlled substances."

Subject:

Amendment offered on Mandatory Training and expected on the Floor to CARA

Opioid Abuse Bills Advance as Democrats Complain About
Funding
The Senate Judiciary Committee on Thursday advanced a pair of bills intended to address the prescription drug abuse epidemic
as Democrats complained that money to fund the response won't be included. Some suggested the legislation was an anemic,
response to a crisis that in 2014 claimed nearly 30,000 lives due to overdoses.
"We passed larger bills to address swine flu and Ebola, even though we did not have Ebola in the United States," said
Sen. Patrick J. Leahy,
th.e committee's ranking member. "This, we do have in the United States, every community
does."
One measure (S 524), by Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.1., and Rob Portman, R-Ohio, would provide financial assistance to state
efforts including such as prescription drug monitoring programs. The bill would also increase access to drugs that can
counteract the effect of opioids and prevent overdoses, as well as expand prevention and treatment efforts.
A second bill (S 483), by Orrin G. Hatch, R-Utah, would instruct the Drug Enforcement Agency and the Department of Health
and Human Services to collaborate ou strategies to prevent prescription drug abuse while ensuring that patients who
legitimately need the drugs can still access them.
Both bills were cleared. by voice vote and will likely be taken up by the full Senate after the President's Day recess. A.ntonia
Ferrier, a spokesperson for Majority Leader Mitch McConnell, R-IKy., said the senator "is very pleased with the Judiciary
committee's action on such a critical, bipartisan piece of legislation."
Despite an abundance of Democratic support for the bill by Whitehouse and Portman, some expressed frustration that the bill
only authorizes new funding and doesn't actually allocate the funds.
"We have to walk the walk, not talk the talk. To just authorize money and not actually put money to spend will do nothing to
resolve the crisis," said Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y.
When the measures reach the floor Democrats are expected to make a push to include legislation, introduced byjearme
Shaheen, D-N.H., that would provide $600 million in emergency supplemental funding to address heroin and opioid abuse.
Following the Judiciary markup, Schumer, Shaheen and other Democratic senators expressed support for the intent of the
V,Whitehouse-Portman bill and elaborated on the need for more funding.
"We're glad that passed, but that's not the whole answer, because what's really needed are he .resources,"Shaheen said.

MNKOI 0001640076

 Schumer declined to say whether Democrats would filibuster the bill when it comes to the floor. "We're going to fight hard to
get the funding on the floor, and we'll cross that bridge when we come to it," he said.
Two other ❑emocrats, Edward J. Markey of Massachusetts and Joe Manchin HI of West Virginia, have placed holds on the
nomination of Robert Califf to lead the Food and Drug Administration over that agency's approvals of prescription opioid
drugs.
Last week the FDA announced plans to overhaul its opioid approval policies, including requiring independent advisory
committee to evaluate those drugs that aren't manufactured to prevent abuse. Markey believes drugs with abuse-deterrent
formulations must also receive the extra scrutiny from an advisory committee,
"Abuse-deterrent opioids is an oxymoron," Markey said. "Whether an opioid is abuse-deterrent or not hasn't prevented tens of
thousands of people who have had their wisdom teeth removed or experienced lower back pain from getting addicted to these
painkillers. nn
During the markup, Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., tried to offer an amendment to the Portman-Whitehouse bill that would
require prescribers of opioid. painkillers and other controlled substances to undergo mandatory training in safe practices. He
was told such a requirement fell outside of the committee's jurisdiction.
Markey hopes to revive the provision during floor debate, "We have to have the debate on that amendment, on the floor of the
United States Senate, on prescriber education," he said.

MNKOI 0001640077

DEA establishes production limits for painkillers, with some drugs set for big increases

In a U.S. Federal Register notice, the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration released a list of dozens of schedule I and II controlled substances that will be subject to production quotas in 2015. Regulatory Focus reported 22 of the drugs will see an increase in their quotas next year, and 10 will see a decrease in their allowed production limits. Several painkiller drugs including codeine for sale, oripavine and oxymorphone for conversion will see large increases in 2015. The article said phenylacetone, thebaine and codeine for conversation will see large decreases in 2015.

Regulatory Focus (09/5/2014), Read the Federal Register notice (09/8/2014)

From: e-MD/alert <emdalert@alertmarketingmail.com>

{e-M.D./alert } 
{e-M.D./alert  Providing important information to healthcare professionals since 1976} {e-M.D./alert } 
{e-M.D./alert } 

The FDA has approved the EXALGO  (hydromorphone HCl) Extended-Release Tablets (CII) 32 mg tablet for use inappropriate
opioid-tolerant chronic pain patients. With the addition of the 32 mg tablet, along with the already approved 8, 12, and 16 mg dosing strengths, you now have greater dosing flexibility.

Learn more about EXALGO.

The features of the added EXALGO 32 mg tablet include:

 

 Dosing flexibility. EXALGO 32 mg complements the already approved 8, 12, and 16 mg tablets.1

 
 

 Proven efficacy. EXALGO 32 mg was the median effective dose in the pivotal trial.*2

 
 

 Robust patient exposure. EXALGO 32 mg has been thoroughly tested in 14 clinical trials conducted in 2474 patients, with 1483 of these patients exposed to a dose of 32 mg or greater.3

 

* Mean effective dose was 37.8 mg.1

Additional EXALGO information available.

P.S. Learn about proper dosing and titration with
once-daily EXALGO.

REFERENCES: 1. EXALGO  Prescribing Information. 2. Hale M, Khan A, Kutch M, Li S. Once-daily OROS hydromorphone ER compared with placebo in opioid-tolerant patients with chronic low back pain. Curr Med Res Opin. 2010;26(6):1505-1518. 3. Data on file. Mallinckrodt Inc.

800-778-7898 | www.EXALGO.com

COVIDIEN, COVIDIEN with logo and Covidien logo are U.S. and internationally
registered trademarks of Covidien AG.
EXALGO is a registered trademark of Mallinckrodt LLC.
  2012 Mallinckrodt LLC, a Covidien company.  MK20158 September 2012

 

  

INDICATION

EXALGO  (hydromorphone HCI) Extended-Release
Tablets (CII) is indicated for the management of
moderate to severe pain in opioid tolerant patients
requiring continuous, around-the-clock opioid
analgesia for an extended period of time.

IMPORTANT RISK INFORMATION

WARNING: ABUSE POTENTIAL,
LIFE-THREATENING RESPIRATORY DEPRESSION,
and ACCIDENTAL EXPOSURE

Abuse Potential

EXALGO contains hydromorphone, an opioid agonist and a Schedule II controlled substance with an abuse liability similar to other opioid agonists, legal or illicit. Assess each patient s risk for opioid abuse or addiction prior to prescribing EXALGO. The risk for opioid abuse is increased in patients with a personal or family history of substance abuse (including drug or alcohol abuse or addiction) or mental illness (e.g., major depressive disorder). Routinely monitor all patients receiving EXALGO for signs of misuse, abuse, and addiction during treatment.

Life-threatening Respiratory Depression

Respiratory depression, including fatal cases, may occur with use of EXALGO, even when the drug has been used as recommended and not misused or abused. EXALGO is for use in opioid tolerant patients only. Proper dosing and titration are essential and EXALGO should be prescribed only by healthcare professionals who are knowledgeable in the use of potent opioids for the management of chronic pain. Monitor for respiratory depression, especially during initiation of EXALGO or following a dose increase. Crushing, dissolving, or chewing the tablet can cause rapid release and absorption of a potentially fatal dose of hydromorphone.

Accidental Exposure

Accidental ingestion of EXALGO, especially in children, can result in a fatal overdose of hydromorphone.

 

 

 EXALGO is contraindicated in:

- Opioid non-tolerant patients. Fatal respiratory
  depression could occur in patients who are not
  opioid tolerant.

- Patients with significant respiratory depression

- Patients with acute or severe bronchial asthma in
  an unmonitored setting or in the absence of
  resuscitative equipment

- Patients with known or suspected paralytic ileus

- Patients who have had surgical procedures and/or
  underlying disease resulting in narrowing of the
  gastrointestinal tract, or have  blind loops  of the
  gastrointestinal tract or gastrointestinal obstruction

- Patients with hypersensitivity (e.g., anaphylaxis) to
  hydromorphone or sulfite-containing medications


 
 

 EXALGO is indicated for opioid tolerant patients only. Patients considered opioid tolerant are those who are taking at least 60 mg oral morphine per day, 25 mcg transdermal fentanyl/hour, 30 mg oral oxycodone/day, 8 mg oral hydromorphone/day, 25 mg oral oxymorphone/day or an equianalgesic dose of another opioid, for a week or longer.



 
 

 EXALGO is not intended for use as an as-needed analgesic and is not indicated for the management of acute or postoperative pain. It is contraindicated in patients who need management of mild pain or pain not expected to persist.

 
 

 Avoid concurrent use of alcohol and EXALGO. Concurrent use of EXALGO with CNS depressants, including alcohol, increases risk of respiratory depression, hypotension, and profound sedation, potentially resulting in coma or death. EXALGO may impair the ability to drive a car or operate machinery.

 
 

 Not intended in patients who have received MAO inhibitors within 14 days of starting EXALGO.

 
 

 Use with caution and in reduced doses in older or debilitated patients, as well as patients with renal or hepatic insufficiency, Addison s disease, delirium tremens, myxedema or hypothyroidism, prostatic hypertrophy or urethral stricture, toxic psychosis. May aggravate convulsions in patients with convulsive disorders; may induce or aggravate seizures in some clinical settings. Consider use of an alternate analgesic in patients with severe renal impairment.

 
 

 Respiratory depression, which occurs more frequently in elderly or debilitated patients, is the chief hazard with EXALGO.

 
 

 Serious adverse events could also include hypotensive effects, GI effects, cardiac arrest from overdose and precipitation of withdrawal. Most common adverse events (>10%) seen in clinical studies (N=2474) were: constipation (31%), nausea (28%), vomiting, somnolence, headache, asthenia and dizziness.

 
 

 Use EXALGO with extreme caution in patients susceptible to intracranial effects of CO2 retention.

 
 

 Do not abruptly discontinue EXALGO.


 

See additional Important Risk Information, including boxed warning, in Full Prescribing Information and Medication Guide.

News Release [printer-friendly version]
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE
June 10, 2011
Contact: Rich Isaacson
Number: (313) 234-4310
Cincinnati Pharmaceutical Supplier's DEA License Suspended
Keysource Medical distributed 48 million doses of oxycodone products to Florida pharm acies
JUN 10 - DETROIT- Robert L. Corso, Special Agent in Charge of the Detroit Field Division, Drug  Enforcement Administration
(DEA) announced today the immediate suspension of the federal controlled substance Registration of Keysource Medical, a
wholesale supplier of pharmaceuticals.
Keysource Medical, based in Cincinnati, Ohio, has been the subject of a DEA investigation that alleges the company was selling
large quantities of controlled substances to pharmacies, primarily in Florida. The investigation has revealed that several of
Keysource Medical's largest purchasers of oxycodone were engaged in schemes to dispense controlled substances based on
prescriptions that were written for other than legitimate medical purposes. The investigation revealed that Keystone Medical
distributed approximately 48 million dosage units of oxycodone products to customers in Florida over a two year time between
November of 2008 and November of 2010.
 Pharmaceutical companies have a responsibility to ensure that the drugs they sell don't end up in the hands of drug traffickers or
businesses that are conducting their business illegally,  said Corso.  Prescription drug abuse in Florida, southern Ohio and
northern Kentucky has risen to epidemic proportions, and Keysource Medical, should have known based on the large, frequent
quantities, that their customers were diverting oxycodone into arenas that were not legitimate. This action is another reminder
that the DEA is working hard to hold accountable those companies who choose to operate outside the law.
DEA's action suspends Keysource Medical's DEA Certificate of Registration in accordance with an Immediate Suspension Order
and pursuant to Sections 303 and 304 of the Controlled Substances Act, Title 21, Sections 823 and 824. The DEA's investigation
of Keysource Medical has determined that the continued registration of this company constitutes an imminent danger to public
health and safety.
Keysource Medical received written notice of the factual and legal basis for this action. In addition, Keysource Medical will be
given an opportunity for an administrative hearing within the next 60 days. After the  hearing, the DEA Deputy Administrator will


   make a final decision on whether Keysource Medical's registration should be permanently revoked. This decision will be
published in the Federal Register.
Oxycodone is the generic name of an addictive prescription painkiller that is classified under federal narcotics laws as a Schedule
II controlled substance. Oxycodone is typically legally prescribed to combat acute, severe pain for legitimate medical purposes.

Hi Tina,

      I hope that you are doing well:) I have a question that was brought to my attention from a physician yesterday as an objection. I think that I handled it as best as could be although he was still somewhat questioning. I thought that he was sending out a " smokescreen" until someone else brought it up..Today a PA called me due to a patient's XR script having to be switched due to the patient's concern over the same issue.. On our coupons and literature there is a very pronounced disclaimer regarding risk of abuse, death etc.. This is language that patient's and HCPs are familiar with regarding opioids.. What is articulated a little different that " put off" the physician and now patient is the language regarding how death can occur even if taken as prescribed and after other medicines basically are not adequate.. I understand what this means as someone can obviously die even if taking as prescribed due to various other variables.. Also I and most HCPs understand that an acute opioid is generally written after or when an NSAID etc will not suffice. The language though is strung together in a way though that HCPs have not seen with other opioids.. As for the patient the PA and physician "broke it all down" for them but the death even if taken as prescribed scared them.. I looked at all opioid leave behinds/ coupons as well as Zohydro's warnings and disclaimers and could not find anything like. They were all similar to Exalgo which breaks down for ex why risk of death or abuse.. I am just curious and would like feedback if this comes up again as to why our wording is a little different.. Although  it is saying the same thing as others it is in a more succinct and different manner that can be perceived as, " I risk dying if taking this even as prescribed and it should be last resort". My HCP thought that the language made him appear more liable if someone abuses etc and at a detriment if ever sued because it states clearly that can die and use other medicines first. I get it but what is the reason that our language is "different".. ? I know that they have " tightened" up on opioid labeling but again ours is unique.Sorry if provided too much info. Hopefully it makes sense.. Thanks so much!

Rachel

States fight 'tourists' trafficking painkillers 
Published July 08, 2012 

Associated Press 

LEBANON, Ohio - As he sat in the doctor's office, ex-boxer and weightlifter Gerald Dixon explained that 
years of sports had left him in pain, especially his hands •Redacted-PII 

After a. eursa.ry. examination at the clinic in West Palm Beach , Fla. , Dixon 
  *Redacted - PII - and a plan to return to his Ohio home and sell them on the street. 
The trips made by Dixon and others like him - authorities dub them "prescription" or "drug" tourists - 
have complicated the challenges investigators face trying to stem the flow of painkillers, whose 
prevalence have made drug overdoses the leading cause of accidental death in dozens of states including 
Ohio, Florida, Kentucky and Utah, surpassing car crashes. 

Dixon, 52, a drug dealer for most of his adult life, had recently discovered a new angle on an old 
profession. By driving to Florida just once a month and acquiring a bagful of pain pills - legally and 
illegally - he could earn tens of thousands of dollars. 

The only thing the medical clinics that Dixon visited in Florida cared about was the money, he said. A 
diagnosis for severe pain was easy to obtain. 

"It's all about cash, cash, cash," Dixon said during a prison interview in April with The Associated 
Press. "You go, you pay the money, and they're going to come back and say, 'Yeah, you're right, you was 
hurt. 

Prescription tourists thwart local efforts to combat the illegal sale of painkillers and to treat addicts 
by bringing huge volumes of drugs in from outside. Cracking down on the trade also requires complicated 
prosecutions crossing multiple state lines. 






                                          MNKOI 0005999417 

These tourists are based in a variety of states, but investigators in Kentucky, Ohio and West Virginia - 
where authorities have already cracked down on local pill mills - are among the busiest trying to track 
trips to Florida, Georgia and elsewhere. 

The lucrative business involves drug dealers dispatching underlings like Dixon to states with numerous 
pill mills where they load up on painkillers, then return to sell the drugs to addicts willing to pay as 
much as $100 a pill, or as much as 10 times the drugstore price. 

Florida for years was a popular destination because of its virtually unregulated pain clinic industry, 
which provided easy access to thousands of painkillers marketed under names like OxyContin, vicodin and 
Percocet. 

As Florida cracks down on its pill mills, the clinics have migrated to states like Georgia, which had 
practically none three years ago and now has as many as 150, said Richard Allen, director of the Georgia 
Drugs and Narcotics Agency. 

Runners - another term for people like Dixon or addicts sent to buy pills and take them home - are coming 
from as close as Kentucky and Tennessee and as far away as Arizona and Nebraska, Allen said. 

"They're like a swarm of locusts," he said. "Once they have a scrip, they'll hit every pharmacy in the 
state trying to get them filled." 

In eastern Kentucky, several residents arrested in 2009 in a massive drug sweep had visited the 
Lauderhill Medical Clinic in Oakland Park, Fla. U.S. Attorney Kerry Harvey estimates that nine of every 
10 patients at the clinic are from Kentucky. He prosecutes about five dozen cases a year involving 
prescription drugs. 

At West Virginia's Huntington Tri-State Airport, authorities have dubbed low-cost flights to Florida 
aboard Allegiant Air the OxyExpress. The airline isn't accused of wrongdoing, and spokeswoman Jessica 
Wheeler says it hasn't been approached by authorities. 

In Tennessee, strict laws governing pain clinics force drug dealers out of state for supplies, using 
Interstate 75 to bring pills back from Florida or move them farther north, said Kristin Helm, spokeswoman 
for the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation. 

Ohio has prosecuted several prescription tourists in recent months, with a federal judge in December 
sentencing Christopher Thompson of suburban Columbus to 15 years in prison for leading a scheme involving 
more than a dozen other people who traveled from Ohio to Florida, obtained and filled prescriptions for 
oxycodone and other drugs, and mailed the pills back to central Ohio for illegal distribution. 

"The effect is the same effect as if they were coming out of our own pain clinics," said Aaron Haslam, 
who directs Ohio's anti-painkiller abuse efforts in the state's attorney general's office. "We have 
overdoses all over the state of Ohio because of it." 

Defendants in one southern Ohio case brought back drugs worth $50,000 on the street in one trip, Haslam 
said. 

Authorities have fought back with extensive crackdowns in Florida against pill mills and with 
prosecutions in states like Kentucky, Ohio and West Virginia of both drug tourists and the Florida 
doctors who wrote prescriptions. State medical boards also regularly discipline or revoke the licenses of 
doctors who overprescribe painkillers. 

Florida is finally seeing a drop in pill mills and doctors prescribing painkillers after enacting a 2011 
law toughening penalties against doctors and clinics engaged in prescription drug trafficking. 

Still, such a stance has consequences. A group sued the state in 2010 over the pill mill crackdown. one 
of the doctors, Paul Sloan, owner of Florida pain management clinics in Fort Myers and Sarasota, says 
that there's no question that some doctors and clinic owners were doing bad things, but that the state 
has overreacted. 

"We're dealing with a war on legitimate medications that's being dealt with like we're all cartels and 
drug lords," he said. 

Doctors in that lawsuit defended disbursing prescriptions to patients who paid cash, saying uninsured 
patients with chronic pain relied on pain pills for relief because they often couldn't afford more 
expensive procedures or services. 

Posing as such a patient can serve a prescription tourist well. 

Dixon said he traveled to West Palm Beach for about seven months in 2008, visiting clinics and picking up 
prescriptions and pills over a two or three-day period. Dixon never visited more than one doctor, but 
soon was also buying pills from people he met on the streets in deals arranged in motels. 

"Once you get to motels down there, it's just like a Wal-Mart or Kmart or Kroger store for drugs, pills, 
whatever," Dixon said. "Once you get in that clique, they will find you." 

He said it was not uncommon to see pills offered from bulging 50-pound dog food bags filled with the 
prescriptions. 




                                          MNKOI 0005999418 

Dixon was arrested in 2008 returning from what would turn out to be his last trip, set up, he says, by a 
fellow drug dealer. He had 6,000 pills hidden in a false exhaust system he'd installed beneath the car. 
He is serving a four-year sentence for drug trafficking charges. Although painkillers are a legal drug, 
it's against the law for anyone but a doctor or pharmacist to dispense them. 

Crackdowns like Florida's may be driving prescription tourists to states like Georgia, Haslam said. 

"We're squeezing a balloon," he said. "And as you squeeze the balloon, the air in the balloon goes 
someplace else."

Subject: Oxycodone and Morphine Hobart Procurement Quota: DEA Telephone Conversation Notes 10/15/10 a.m.



Michael Morley (DEA Washington DC Quota Section) called in response to the second voicemail left for him this morning.
 
I asked that he communicate DEA rationale in only granting 6% of Mallinckrodt's most recent Oxycodone Hobart procurement quota request (quantity requested 3,800 kg AA, quantity granted 218 kg AA).
Mr. Morley indicated that, in general, DEA is restricting the amount of Oxycodone in the supply chain due to current diversion and abuse trends.  DEA is limiting quantities of Oxycodone to that necessary to meet legitimate demand.  DEA would have granted a small percentage of additional Oxycodone procurement quota due to DEA assessment that the supply chain has sufficient inventory.
In doing so, DEA reviews IMS data to determine how much Oxycodone is being sold out of the supply chain and compares that quantity to how much Oxycodone manufacture has been authorized by procurement quotas.  Additionally, DEA receives estimates from FDA in terms of how much the market is expected to change in a given year.  Example:  FDA believes that Oxycodone market will increase by a  certain % or decrease by a % or if FDA will be withdrawing or granting approval to products.
 
I asked Mr. Morley if the same rationale was applied to Mallinckrodt's Morphine procurement quota increase request (800 kg. AA request was denied with zero granted by DEA) and he indicated that the same supply chain inventory review would have been conducted, HOWEVER, Morphine is under less scrutiny than Oxycodone.  He indicated that he was not at liberty to discuss in detail DEA's zero Morphine grant to Mallinckrodt.
 
I inquired as to the status of Mallinckrodt Hobart pending procurement request for 400 kg of Methylphenidate and the reply was that "the request is currently under review".
 
I stated that Mallinckrodt is gravely concerned about going into a backorder situation on pain products and potential market disruption due to supply shortage.  Further, Mallinckrodt sent an additional quota request for 3,900 kg AA Oxycodone procurement quota to DEA by FedEx yesterday, to be followed by another request for increased Morphine procurement quota that Mallinckrodt is currently assembling.
Mr. Morley replied that all registrants are entitled to resubmit quota requests if additional justification data becomes available. 
 
I told Mr. Morley that it was of utmost importance that we receive DEA expedited review of yesterday's Oxycodone procurement quota increase submission within the next two weeks to avoid backorder.
Mr. Morley flatly stated "that will not happen" because today is the close of the Federal Register 2011 Initial Proposed Manufacturing Aggregate and that he plus one other person in the quota section will be out of the office on annual leave all of next week.
 
Mr. Morley acknowledged receipt of e-mail copy sent yesterday to Dr. Sannerud, Section Chief, requesting an immediate meeting in Washington DC but could not speculate as to whether a meeting will be granted.
 
In closing, I thanked Mr. Morley for calling back and discussing the situation; and informed Mr. Morley that the Oxycodone and Morphine quota issues have been escalated to the most senior levels of executive management within Mallinckrodt and that we will be escalating the matter within DEA. 
 
The conversation was very matter of fact but not unpleasant.
 
Next step:  Karen Harper will call Dr. Sannerud's office today in an attempt to arrange a meeting at DEA Headquarters
 
Nothing further.

Research Update

 
Mallinckrodt plc

 
This morning, Mallinckrodt announced a three year distribution agreement with Amneal (private) on generic Suboxone (for the maintenance treatment of opioid dependence) sublingual tablets. Terms of the deal were not disclosed. While we don t believe this announcement will have a material impact to our estimates, the much larger market opportunity is tied to Reckitt Benckiser s Suboxone sublingual film, which we estimate has annual sales in excess of $1 billion. We believe the market opportunity with Suboxone sublingual tablets is much smaller (~$70-$75 million), with two generic players (Actavis and Amneal). According to Source Healthcare Analytics prescription data, as of the end of July, Actavis and Amneal each held a 45-47% share in the Suboxone tablet market, with Reckitt Benckiser s branded product holding the remaining share. Our analysis of the prescription market suggests that Reckitt has effectively transferred approximately 85% of Suboxone prescriptions over to its sublingual film.

 

Between now and year-end, we think investors will focus on three upcoming events; 1) the potential release of additional details on MNK-795 (an abuse deterrent formulation of an acetaminophen/opioid combination product) at the upcoming Pain Week Medical Conference in Las Vegas, NV on September 4-7, 2) the Company s planned release of F 14 financial guidance by the end of October, and 3) an FDA decision on the approvability of MNK-795 potentially by year end. Our F 14-F 16 estimates include MNK-795 revenues of $25 million, $75 million, and $120 million, respectively.

 

Investment Summary   SELL/$34PT. We maintain our SELL rating and $34PT, which we arrive at via a 7.1x multiple on our 2013 EBITDA estimate of $382 million, and a P/E multiple (11.6x our CY13 EPS estimate of $2.92). MNK shares currently trade at 14.7x our CY13 EPS estimate of $2.92, and 18.8x our CY14 EPS estimate of $2.28. On average, we believe MNK shares are trading at a 53% premium to its peers on a forward P/E multiple basis. Based on our expectations for MNK to face additional competition on several of its key pharmaceutical products (generic Concerta, and Exalgo) in the second half of 2013, we believe F 14 revenue could fall approximately (4.6%) vs. F 13, with EPS dropping to $2.27 (21% YOY) in F 14.  New Strategies in Prescription Opioid Abuse Deterrence Measurement

The webinar will address some of the most pressing current issues pertaining to Abuse Deterrent Formulations (ADFs) of prescription opioids:

   How does the broader environment affect the likelihood that a given product will or will not demonstrate abuse deterrence?

   How to measure abuse deterrence when a product doesn't have a non-ADF precursor?

   What to do when measuring the abuse of a product with minimal or low market share?

These are some of the challenges that will be faced by manufacturers, regulators and public health authorities as new products are brought to market and seek ADF labeling.

Folks, we are looking for your input on the draft below. After a meeting today in my office, we are recommending an approach similar to what I have described below to meet our speaker program needs with a more limited team of speakers than originally requested.  Thanks in advance for your assistance and your understanding.
 
Draft:
 
To: Field Sales Management Team
 
" This message is intended to update you on the progress that is being made to develop speakers for both Pennsaid and Exalgo. After a few internal complications, under the direction of Jackie Kim in Medical Affairs, we are back on an accelerated track to meeting our goal of having 100 qualified and trained speakers for both Pennsaid and Exalgo. However, all of these speakers will not be immediately available at launch. The goal of Medical Affairs is that we will have approximately 50 speakers for each product, ready to be utilized immediately after launch.
 
Given this slight delay, we have a cross functional team working together internally to best address your most immediate needs for speaker programs. We have several different approaches being considered that we think will help your district level efforts. The first approach will be to arrange pre-established programs in our major metropolitan areas, utilizing the expertise of The Selva Group, the vendor who is currently managing speaker bureau logistics. These programs will have an assigned speaker with invitations that can be delivered by multiple representatives to help populate a program for 20-25 healthcare professionals. Your representatives will not need to worry about any of the logistics except for ensuring a strong audience. Jackie is working with Selva to establish a method in which they will handle all program-related expenses, including the necessary compliance reporting documents.   
 
Another initiative will be based on your ability to determine speaker opportunities for what I call "pre-planned" groups. We know that certain groups of physicians, PAs, NPs, and various city or regional medical associations have regular monthly or quarterly meetings with an audience of 25-50 clinicians in attendance. When the audience is appropriate for our product and the group is looking for a speaker, we can take advantage of this type of group meeting  without burdening our representatives to build an audience. In this case the vendor might only need to coordinate the payment to the speaker, but Jackie and her team can customize the approach to meet your needs.
 
Maximizing our speakers early will help us with our launch success and having larger venues delivers our message to more potential prescribers faster. As more speakers get trained we will be better positioned to address the individual territory level programs. While we will still be able to handle a select number of individual territory requests at launch, our internal capabilities will not be at full speed until late May.
 
The direction that you should take from this message is to start identifying "pre-planned" group meeting opportunities now. Where the audience is appropriate and the speaker need exists, we will make every effort to get you a qualified and recognized speaker. Through your Regional Directors we will begin to identify the best "metropolitan markets" for a speaker program that can be coordinated by our national vendor, but you will be responsible for generating the audience. We will work with you closely to coordinate preferred dates and or restaurant locations.
 
That's it for now, more details will be available at the managers meeting and of course, if you have any questions at all, please contact your Regional Director or Jackie Kim in Medical Affairs. We are dedicated to your launch success and know that your success is our success. We will do everything possible to help you and your district have a positive experience with these speaker programs.  
 
Ron Wickline

Press Release

 
 
 

MCKESSON AGREES TO PAY RECORD $150 MILLION SETTLEMENT FOR FAILURE TO REPORT SUSPICIOUS ORDERS OF PHARMACEUTICAL DRUGS

 

JAN 17 - (Washington, DC) – McKesson Corporation (McKesson), one of the nation’s largest distributors of pharmaceutical drugs, agreed to pay a record $150 million civil penalty for alleged violations of the Controlled Substances Act (CSA), the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) announced today.

 

The nationwide settlement requires McKesson to suspend sales of controlled substances from distribution centers in Colorado, Ohio, Michigan and Florida for multiple years. The staged suspensions are among the most severe sanctions ever agreed to by a DEA-registered distributor. The settlement also imposes new and enhanced compliance obligations on McKesson’s distribution system.

 

In 2008, McKesson agreed to a $13.25 million civil penalty and administrative agreement for similar violations. In this case, the government alleged again that McKesson failed to design and implement an effective system to detect and report “suspicious orders” for controlled substances distributed to its independent and small chain pharmacy customers– i.e. orders that are unusual in their frequency, size, or other patterns. From 2008 until 2013, McKesson supplied various U.S. pharmacies an increasing amount of oxycodone and hydrocodone pills, frequently misused products that are part of the current opioid epidemic.

 

The government’s investigation developed evidence that even after designing a compliance program after the 2008 settlement, McKesson did not fully implement or adhere to its own program. In Colorado, for example, McKesson processed more than 1.6 million orders for controlled substances from June 2008 through May 2013, but reported just 16 orders as suspicious, all connected to one instance related to a recently terminated customer. 

 

"This groundbreaking resolution is tough and appropriate and underscores our commitment to hold accountable all DEA registrants, including those who distribute controlled substances," said DEA Acting Administrator Chuck Rosenberg.  "DEA is committed to fighting the opioid epidemic with all of the tools at our disposal."

 

In addition to the monetary penalties and suspensions, the government and McKesson agreed to enhanced compliance terms for the next five years. Among other things, McKesson has agreed to specific, rigorous staffing and organizational improvements; periodic auditing; and stipulated financial penalties for failing to adhere to the compliance terms. Critically, the settlement will require McKesson to engage an independent monitor to assess compliance – the first independent monitor of its kind in a CSA civil penalty settlement.

 

This was a multi-district investigation that involved the following DEA Field Divisions:  Boston Field Division, Chicago Field Division, Denver Field Division, Detroit Field Division, Miami Field Division, New Jersey Field Division, San Francisco Field Division, St. Louis Field Division, and Washington Division Office. The following U.S. Attorneys’ Offices participated in the case: Central District of California, Eastern District of California, District of Colorado, Middle District of Florida, Eastern District of Kentucky, Northern District of Illinois, District of Massachusetts, Eastern District of Michigan, District of Nebraska, District of New Jersey, Northern District of West Virginia, and Western District of Wisconsin.

 

U.S. Attorneys’ Offices for the District of Colorado and the Northern District of West Virginia, along with DEA’s Office of Chief Counsel and its Diversion Control Division, led the civil settlement negotiations.  DEA’s Denver, Detroit and Miami Field Divisions and its Washington Division Office led the administrative and civil investigation. The U.S. Department of Justice Criminal Division’s Narcotic and Dangerous Drug Section (NDDS) also coordinated and assisted in negotiating certain portions of the settlement. Assistant United States Attorneys Amanda Rocque (Colorado) and Alan McGonigal (NDWV) represented the United States in the civil penalty investigations and negotiations.  Associate Chief Counsel Lee Reeves and Senior Attorneys Dedra Curteman, Dana Hill and Krista Tongring represented DEA in the investigations and negotiations. Trial Attorneys Harry Matz and Kirtland Marsh were involved for NDDS.

Originator: Security:

PURPOSE:
Establish a procedure to identify and report controlled substance suspicious orders  to the Drug
Enforcement Administration
SCOPE:
Applies to establishing a new controlled substance customer account and subsequent shipment of
all controlled substance orders to new or established customers.
REFERENCES:
Title 21 CFR 1301.74(b)
The registrant shall design and operate a system to disclose to the registrant suspicious orders of
controlled substances. The registrant shall inform the Field Division Office of the Administration
in his area of suspicious orders when discovered by the registrant. Suspicious  orders include
orders of unusual size, orders deviating substantially from a normal pattern, and orders of
unusual frequency..
DEFINITIONS:
Peculiar Order   A controlled substance order that meets and internal, established criteria
that will be placed on  hold  pending further review by DEA Compliance.
Suspicious Order  A controlled substance Peculiar Order that has been reviewed by DEA
Compliance and Security that will not be shipped and will be reported to
the Drug Enforcement Administration.


   QSP 00.00  Rev 1  TITLE  2  of 3


RESPONSIBILITIES:
Credit Department or Customer Data Integrity Group
Perform Dun & Bradstreet information check on new controlled substance customers to
determine credit worthiness.
Refer  the new customer account to Security Director or DEA Compliance if the new account has
no historical or financial information available or if the data shows liens, lawsuits, or other
information which might raise suspicions as to the legitimacy  of the new account company.
Conduct periodic checks on our  existing customers if they ve been put on credit hold two times
in the previous 12 months.
Field Sales
Completes Site Survey Checklist for New Controlled Substance Customers (Attachment A)
Customer Service Representative
Completes Controlled Substance Order Checklist (Attachment B) and refers orders that meet the
Peculiar Order criteria to DEA Compliance and Security Director for review
Customer Service Manager
Obtains a daily report from the order entry system that highlights orders deviating in qua ntity
from an established order pattern calculation to determine if order quantity fits Peculiar Order
criteria and refers to DEA Compliance and Security Director for review
Security Director
Provides Site Survey Checklist for New Controlled Substance Customers to be completed by
Field Sales
Reviews results of Site Survey Checklist for New Controlled Substance Customers and provides
authorization to proceed with new customer account set-up
In conjunction with DEA Compliance, reviews controlled substance or ders that have been
identified as Peculiar Orders by Customer Service and makes the ship or do not ship decision
Reports orders deemed Suspicious to the Drug Enforcement Administration
DEA Compliance
Provides updated  Drugs of Concern  listing to Customer  Service quarterly
Provides Controlled Substance Order Checklist to Customer Service


  QSP 00.00  Rev 1  TITLE  3  of 3

In conjunction with Security Director, reviews controlled substance orders that have been
identified as Peculiar Orders by Customer Service and makes the ship or do not ship decision
Reports orders deemed Suspicious to the Drug Enforcement Administration.
Maintains a file at the St. Louis Plant Site for record retention of Suspicious Order Monitoring
documents and reports.

Study Illustrates Need for Better Patient/Provider Communications on Opioid Therapy

A new study published online in the Annals of Emergency Medicine found that patients seen in the emergency department for acute pain expressed a desire for better communication from physicians about their pain management options, along with discussion of the risks of opioid dependence. The study was conducted via semi-structured open-ended telephone interviews of patients discharged from the emergency department at the Hospital of the University of Pennsylvania during a 4 month period in 2014. The subjects revealed several themes related to opioid dependence including 1) fear of developing dependence or addition; 2) worries about following prescribed dosing preventing the possibility of addiction; 3) relying on media and other individuals as a source of information about opioids; and 4) awareness of physicians  need to balance patients  pain management needs and safe opioid prescribing guidelines.

This is the crux of the issue to me, coming in new to the conversation.  Without knowing the history of prior conversations with Cardinal, I was wondering why (and if) we felt that the Force Majeure language in the contract would not apply to Quota situations. It gives some examples but states "including, without limitation", so I didn't see why Quota should be excluded simply because wasn't explicitly mentioned.  Also, this interpretation of Force Majeure is certainly not unique to this contract.  The basic definition  of Force Majeure include 1) an event or effect that cannot be reasonably anticipated or controlled (Merriam-Webster.com), and 3) an unexpected and disruptive event that may operate to excuse a party from a contract (Dictionary.com).  To me, Quota would seem to fall under these (again, without being privy to specific content of any prior conversations with Cardinal regarding the intent behind our contract clause).

Bottom line, it appears to me that there is enough language in the contract to justify Quota as valid reason to deny per Force Majeure.  But if Cardinal continues to disagree, how willing are we to continue to fight for it?

DEA Suspends Cardinal Health Distribution Facility: Cannot Sell Controlled Substances for Two Years

  

On May 15 the DEA announced a settlement agreement with Cardinal Health, a pharmaceutical wholesale distributor that suspends for two years its ability to sell controlled-substance medications from its Lakeland, Florida, distribution facility. In the agreement, Cardinal admits that its due diligence efforts for some pharmacy customers and its compliance with an earlier agreement signed in 2008 for similar violations at the same facility were, in certain respects, inadequate. The obligations of the agreement remain in full force and effect for a period of five years unless DEA agrees in writing to an earlier termination.The current settlement agreement also includes a signed Administrative Memorandum of Agreement whose terms apply to all Cardinal's 28 registered distribution facilities.

 

On February 3 of this year, DEA's Miami Field Division served an Immediate Suspension Order (ISO) against Cardinal Health's distribution center in Lakeland, Florida, alleging that this distribution center failed to maintain effective controls against the diversion of controlled substances, specifically oxycodone. It was not DEA's first action against Cardinal's Lakeland facility. In December 2007, DEA issued an ISO at the location as a result of its distribution of hydrocodone to 'rogue' internet pharmacies. That action, and similar actions at other Cardinal Health facilities across the United States, resulted in a $34 million fine.  Click here to read DEA's full press release.  

 

 

Information for Members on Electronic Prescribing of Controlled Substances   


Attached please find information forwarded by Surescripts related to electronic prescribing of controlled substances.  Given that it has been over two years since the DEA issued its interim final rule that allows the electronic prescribing of controlled substances, Surescripts is sharing the information here that lists those states in which prescribers reportedly are utilizing DEA-compliant systems.  

OIG Issues Report on Questionable Part D Billing 



 

 

The Office of Inspector General of the United States Department of Health and Human Services (OIG) recently issued a report on retail pharmacies with questionable Medicare Part D billing. Medicare Part D is a voluntary prescription drug benefit available to Medicare beneficiaries that went into effect on January 1, 2006. Since that time, the OIG and others have raised concerns about Part D billing. In several reports, OIG found that the program has limited safeguards in place and is vulnerable to fraud, waste, and abuse.

 

Moreover, recent cases have illustrated a variety of alleged fraud schemes by pharmacies. For example, one pharmacist who owned 26 pharmacies was charged with health care fraud and drug diversion. The pharmacist allegedly paid physicians to write prescriptions that were medically unnecessary and to direct patients to fill them at his pharmacies, which purportedly billed $37.7 million to Medicare.

 

In this report, OIG examined the Part D billing patterns of 59,000 retail pharmacies during 2009, which amounted to nearly 1 billion prescriptions. Through the study, investigators revealed contrasts between normal pharmacy practices and potential criminal behavior. Overall, the report found a pattern of questionable claims at 2,637 pharmacies around the country, including one pharmacy in Kansas that billed Medicare for more than 1,000 prescriptions for two patients in a single year. In total, Medicare paid $5.6 billion in possible fraudulent billings that year.  A copy of the report is found here.

b)     McKesson was hired to create a database showing which entities (distributors, retailers, physicians, patients) have completed the requirements to be eligible to handle / write scripts, etc for the Fentanyl oral product. (McKesson will bill us for this service).

c)     As of that date, Mallinckrodt's responsibility will be to ensure any customer ordering the product directly from us has met the requirements to distribute the product. Therefore, we must access the website and verify the customer's eligibility prior to shipping the product.

d)     The distributor (and retailer) must then verify (again by accessing the website) their customer's eligibility before forwarding the product.

e)     There does not appear to be any requirement to capture number of units shipped to any location. Therefore, there would be no need for us to capture EDI 867 (sales tracings) data from any distributor. (Note: an EDI 867 is reporting from a wholesaler / distributor providing all units they shipped to all customers, regardless of price charged. Currently, Pharma does not include this data in our systems, however, other business units do include it. If a decision was made to include within the Pharma data, several downstream implications would need to be considered, including, sales comp, government reporting and Suspicious Order Monitoring), not to mention the incremental customers that would be required to be added).

If I have the facts correct above, can Kathy Weiss or Debbie Digby reach out to Cardinal and ask why they believe we need to receive the EDI 867?

Subject: Couple of Discussion Topics - Deck of Truth notes Obstacles/Barriers & COVIDIEN/GSW 360 evaluation tool
From: "Gunn, Edward" <egunn@gsw-w.com>
Date: Fri, 01 Apr 2011 12:45:49 -0500
To: "wessler, michael"


When: Monday, April 04, 2011 10:00 AM-10:30 AM (GMT-05:00) Eastern Time (US & Canada).
Where: TBD - teleconference 
 
Note: The GMT offset above does not reflect daylight saving time adjustments.
 
*~*~*~*~*~*~*~*~*~*
 
I ll call you, Mike.
 
Mike:
 
It was really good to see you yesterday.  I know you have a lot going on but I am requesting about 30 minutes of your time to discuss the following topics:
 
          Deck of Truth   follow up (Obstacles/Barriers below)
          CRM   COVIDIEN/GSW 360 evaluation tool   (Attached is a draft tool in development) 
o   Review 
   Joint effort between GSW NY & C
   Draft at starting point
   Corporate behaviors   GSW & COVIDIEN   how the tool could potentially support both needs
   Timing of team feedback from COVIDIEN
 
Deck of Truth Obstacles/Barriers Discussion
 
Below is the list of Barriers/Obstacles that were discussed at the end of our meeting.  Please insure that I have captured them correctly, and if not, make any adjustments necessary. I have taken a stab at placing them in order of EXALGO success priority, but as discussed, we will need for your team to confirm.  Ultimately we can put 2-3 obstacles/barriers into our inVentiv network now.  Others we are happy to put through a little later.
 
          Limited Sales Training Support
o   Presently within COVIDIEN, Sales Training is a shared service.  This has resulted in an internal brand weakness for EXALGO due to a physical lack of resources for the branded personal sales organization. inVentiv Health support will focus on the advancement of field force training -  for new and experienced sales representatives.
          Effective Conversion & Titration to EXALGO
o   When converting patients from an existing opioid product to EXALGO, the labeling currently directs HCPs to sum the total daily dose of the patient s existing opioid and multiple that dose by listed conversion ratios to calculate the approximate oral hydromorphone equivalent.  The labeling then directs, in general terms, that the HCP should administer 50% of the calculated total daily dose of EXALGO every 24 hours. The initial dose of EXALGO can then be titrated to adequate pain relief with tolerable side effects.  The direction of administration of 50% of the dose for EXALGO is resulting in patients  pain being under-treated, or in some cases opioid withdrawal due to physician inexperience with conversion of these type of opioids, especially in those patients on a large dose of their existing opioid.  InVentiv Health partners will look to give guidance on how to better communicate the conversion to EXALGO in various communication channels.
          Repositioning hydromorphone
o   A significant strategy for EXALGO.  Most HCPs have a current perception of hydromorphone through experience with IR hydromorphone (q4-6hr), or Dilaudid. Historically IR hydromorphone has been seen as a very effective pain reliever but also highly abused/diverted in its oral formulation.  An internal brand weakness for EXALGO is physicians  feeling that because of the strength, potency, and abuse potential of hydormorphone, EXALGO should be used significantly later in their treatment algorithm. InVentiv Health partners will look to give guidance on how to better communicate the effectiveness and safety of once-daily EXALGO while allaying concerns surrounding abuse in various communication channels.
          Identify the EXALGO patient
o   EXALGO is indicated for use in only opioid tolerant patients requiring continuous, around-the-clock opioid analgesia for an extended period of time. The indication is very broad and theoretically, any opioid tolerant chronic pain patient is a candidate for EXALGO.  Since several ER opioid analgesic products have been on the market before EXALGO, we know that HCPs have established prescribing habits of 1st, 2nd, 3rd, etc. line products that they are comfortable using. In this type of situation, the brand needs to identify the patient profile that offers the best opportunity, or scenario, for which EXALGO would be an optimal choice of treatment. InVentiv Health partners will help identify the types of patient profiles Best suited for successful conversion to EXALGO.
          EXALGO   New 32mg strength launch (Coverage/Pricing)
o   Because EXALGO was limited to 8, 12, and 16 mg strengths, the lack of a higher strength dose has left the brand at a disadvantage when patients are converted from their existing higher dose opioid to EXALGO.  Patients are having to take multiple dosage strengths to get to the optimal daily dose.  With current monthly limitations on CII opioids this creates hassles for physicians and patients. The addition of a 32 mg strength will help reduce the number of EXALGO pills a patient will need to consume once-daily. It will also offer the brand the opportunity to adjust their pricing strategy. InVentiv Health partners will investigate launch strategies for the 32 mg dose, and pricing strategies for the existing line of dosage strengths to optimize managed care coverage.
 
When you have the opportunity, please let me know when would be a good time to chat on Friday, 4/1, or Monday, 4/4.
 
Best,
 
Ed

Thanks Karen!

On Mar 28, 2014, at 10:04 AM, "Karen Moore" <karenm@moorecommgroup.com> wrote:


March 28, 2014

By HEALTH NEWS FLORIDA STAFF

On both Florida coasts, the toll of oxycodone continues, as a doctor is arrested and clinic owners are convicted.

 

The Boca Raton Police arrested Dr. Harry Kesten, 47, owner of Quick Test Labs in Delray Beach, after he tried to buy $300 worth of oxycodone pills, the South Florida Sun Sentinel reports. Police used an undercover informant to tape a phone conversation, then set up the fake buy.

 

In the recorded call, according to the arrest report, Kesten said he could falsify drug test results and make fake labels for prescription bottles.

 

Meanwhile in Tampa, in a case that took years to bring to trial, a jury convicted the operators of First Medical Group pain clinic of trafficking in oxycodone as well as conspiracy, the Tampa Bay Times reports.

 

Those who were convicted after five days of jury deliberation were clinic owners Jorge Gonzalez-Betancourt, 53, and Michele Gonzalez, 37, both of Tampa, and manager was Maureen Altman, 58, of Lakeland.

 

The clinic's physician, Dr. Kimberly Daffern, died in 2011 before the case went to trial. As the Times reports, he was accused of prescribing 1 million oxycodone pills in three months.

 

Even though the clinic attracted hordes of customers from as far as Ohio and Kentucky, it took years of investigation for years before prosecutors felt there was enough evidence to go to trial.

 

It is notoriously difficult to prosecute drug cases involving prescription drugs. Last month, the three-month-long trial of a Palm Beach County physician and pharmacist ended in acquittal. Dr. Timothy Sigman and pharmacist Peter Del Toro had been charged with dealing in human growth hormone, testosterone and anabolic steroids.

 

 

Karen B. Moore, CPRC, APR | CEO and Founder
Moore Communications Group

> 
> As a follow up from our discussion last week on field coaching feedback- Here's Kirk's quick summary plan for success in the Pittsburgh area with his people.  Thanks
>

> 
> -----Original Message-----
> From: Dumont, Kirk E
> Sent: Tuesday, June 24, 2014 11:00 AM
> To: Rago, Jay M
> Subject: FW: Success stories in Pittsburgh area 
> 
> Jay, listed below is what we are trying to do to grow our business in a challenging  manage care environment in the Pittsburgh and surrounding areas.
> 
> 1. Planning and preparation - Focus on physician offices that have favorable manage care coverage for our products - Highmark (open lives 70%) / Caremark  -  We will review our IMS Data and our Physician Map Tool  ( we utilize our IMS data more often). We steer away from UPMC and Gessinger physician offices that have a large percentage of their patients with these manage care companies. We spend a lot of time reviewing our IMS data, so we can build an effective call routing action plan for our territories.
> 
> 
> 2. Territory & Time management - These are key ingredient toward success - we need to make sure that we are effectively and efficiently working our territories, so we are getting quality face time with or key targets that have favorable manage care coverage for our products. When we are reviewing our IMS data together, the reps are amazed of the potential and opportunity there is in their territories for XXR and Pennsaid, even though UPMC makes up for about 31% of their Percocet and Hydrocodone combos meds prescribed in their territories!!! We try to look for the positives in each territory - we focus on where we can grow our business daily.
> 
> 3.Confirmation - once we do our due diligence with the data, we will confirm the information at the physician offices with the key insurance person in the office, not the physician!!!! Once we have confirm our fact finding adventure (positive / negative - leave the building), we will move forward influencing the physician to prescribe our products to their patients focusing on their Highmark / Caremark patients. We will emphasize that UPMC and Gessinger will not pay for XXR and Pennsaid unless you complete a step/edit or PA. Then we will repeat it again about UPMC to the physician & staff, but sure enough the first patient they prescribe XXR or Pennsaid for, is a UPMC patient.
> 
> 4.Educating the physician & Office staff - when we convinced our providers to prescribe our products, we need to educate them on In Network and Out of Network pharmacies for Highmark and UPMC. If a Highmark patient tries to fill their prescription at a CVS pharmacy which is Out of Network for Highmark, the pharmacist will charge the patient cash price for our products, but if they would go across the street to a Rite-Aid, Giant Eagle, Wal-Mart or Sam's Club they would pay the around $10.00 or $20.00 co-pay!!!!Additionally, we supply the physicians /staff, what pharmacies (addresses and telephone numbers) that are currently stocking XXR in their area.
> 
> Kirk
