DEA Compliance Procedure   No:
Subject:  Revision No.:
 Draft 3  published 06/02/08
Controlled Substance Suspicious Order Monitoring  Effective Date:

 Supersedes Date:
NEW
 Page No.:
1  of 5

Originator: Security:
Karen Harper
Corporate Logistics: Documentation Coordinator:


PURPOSE:
Establish a procedure to identify and report controlled substance suspicious orders  to the Drug
Enforcement Administration  (DEA) prior to shipment.  DEA cannot/will not tell a DEA
registrant if an order is legitimate and/or if an order should  be shipped. It is fundamental for
sound operations that DEA registrants take reasonable measures to identify their customers,
understand the normal and expected transactions typically  conducted by those customer, and,
consequently identify those transactions that are suspicious in nature. SCOPE:
Applies to establishing a new controlled substance customer account and subsequent shipment of
all controlled substance orders to new or established customers.
REFERENCES:
Title 21 CFR 1301.74(b)
The registrant shall design and operate a system to disclose to the registrant suspicious orders of
controlled substances. The registrant shall inform the Field Division Office of the Administration
in his area of suspicious orders when discovered by the registrant. Suspicious orders include
orders of unusual size, orders deviating substantially from a normal pattern, and o rders of
unusual frequency..
DEFINITIONS:
Peculiar Order   A controlled substance order that meets an  internal, established criteria
that will be placed on hold  pending further review by DEA Compliance.
Suspicious Order  A Peculiar Order that has been reviewed by DEA Compliance and
Security that will not be shipped and will be reported to the Drug
Enforcement Administration.


   QSP 00.00  Rev 1  TITLE  2  of 5


RESPONSIBILITIES:
Credit Department
Performs  Dun & Bradstreet  and/or other information checks  on new controlled substance
customers to determine credit worthiness.
Refers  the new customer account to Security Director or DEA Compliance if the new account
has no historical or financial information available or if the data shows liens, lawsuits, or other
information which might rais e suspicions as to the legitimacy of the new account company.
Conducts  periodic checks for existing accounts. Notifies Security Director or DEA Compliance
of any customer credit concerns.
Field Sales
Completes Site Survey Checklist for New Controlled Substance Customers (Attachment A)
Conducts an on-site visit including taking photographs inside and out for review  by Security
Director and DEA Compliance Manager.

Customer Service Representatives
Bulk Narcotics Customer  Service Representatives will  perform the following activities for each
order entered:
Verify that the customer has a valid DEA Registration certificate
Assure that the customer has provided a DEA 222 form for CI and CII substances
Obtain a  Certificate of Available Procurement Quota  from cus tomers using a Manufacturing
Registration DEA 222 Form
Obtain a  Statement of Intended Use  from customers using a Research or Analytical Lab
Registration DEA 222 Form  for quantities of >500 grams of material
Forward the  Statement of Intended Use  to DEA  Compliance for review
Designate an order as  Peculiar  if the customer fails to provide the appropriate documentation
above.
Forward Peculiar Order  information to Customer  Service Manager and Security Director

Dosage Customer Service Representatives will  perform the following activities for
_________________need clarification, orders for all new Retail or Wholesale accounts may be
reviewed, Retail Chain Pharmacies may be exempted.
- Verify that the customer has a valid DEA registration certificate
- Insure the customer has provided a properly executed DEA 222 form for CI and
CII substances


   QSP 00.00  Rev 1  TITLE  3  of 5

- Flag orders that deviate from the norm in terms of quantity ordered, frequency of
order and/or pattern of normal order  placement, CSR s will evaluate the
circumstances of the order. This evaluation should be based on their knowledge
of the specific customer and the industry in which the customer operates  and
should the circumstances deviate from the norm, upon completi on of the order,
place same on hold and notify Security and the Customer Service Manager.
___________________

If Dosage Customer Service representatives are contacted by a new customer asking that an
account be set up  and the interview process yields questionable results, the CSR will obtain the
following information from the customer and forward the information in an e-mail to the
Director of Security (Bill Ratliff) as well as the Customer Service Manager. In addition to the
pedigree information listed below, the CSR should recap the circumstances of the conversation
which caused them to question the authenticity of the caller and/or business.
- Contact s name, address and phone
- Name of business
- Type of business
- DEA License number
Customer Service Manager
Obtains a Peculiar Order Daily Report from the order entry system  forwarded to a group mail
box  that highlights orders that are unusually large, unusually frequent, and/or deviating in
quantity from an established order pattern.

Annotates  the Peculiar Order Report if there is a valid business reason for an order of unusually
large, unusually frequent, and/or deviating in quantity from an established order pattern.
Forward the Peculiar Order Report to Security Director/DEA Compliance.

Customer Service Manager will maintain a  Do Not Ship List  of customers to whom Covidien
has ceased distribution due to suspicious activity.

For Bulk Narcotics, an order will be deemed to be Peculiar if the order quantity is double the
amount of product ordered during the previous fiscal year and YTD average by sku, by
customer.

For Dosage Narcotics, an order will be deemed to be Peculiar if the order quantity exceeds the
result of a formula based on the class of business in which the business operates  (AT clinics,
distributors, wholesalers, hospitals, retailers, etc).  This is only until such time as we re able to
develop a method for the system to flag these orders real time    .???

- Proposed  Preliminary  Dosage Formula:


   QSP 00.00  Rev 1  TITLE  4  of 5

- Add purchase quantities, by product (all Oxy products and again by individual
skus) for the last 12 months for all customers within the same class of business for any
controlled substances
o  Customer s with multiple  ship to  locations should have their total
aggregated at the  sold to  level; but also reviewed at the  ship to  level
- Add customer months for every record used in the above total (months within
the last 12 that customer purchases of the item were not zero)
- Divide total quantity purchases by the total customer months
- Then multiply by the factor below to give the maximum mount that the
customer can order per month before showing up on the suspicious order
report.
o  Factor = 2 for C-II Controlled Substances
o  Factor = 4 for C-III, IV and V
These factors will vary depending on the business   we ll need to figure this out.
Retail chain pharmacies may be exempted

- Formula for AT Clinics
- Formula for Distributors  -
- Formula for Wholesalers
- Formula for ??
- Formula for ??  ______ ______

____________________________________________________________
________________________________________________________________________


Upon receipt of notification from the Director of Security that a specific order or customer has
been deemed Peculiar, the Customer Service Manager will forward notification to the
appropriate business director, manager and sales representative.


Security Director  and DEA Compliance
Provides blank Site Survey Checklist forms for New Controlled Substance Customers to be
completed by Field Sales
Reviews results of Site Survey Checklist for New Controlled Substance Customers and provides
authorization to proceed with new customer account set-up
Determines if Peculiar Orders are to be shipped or designated as Suspicious Orders and not
shipped  based upon information received from the Credit Department, Customer Service, Field


  QSP 00.00  Rev 1  TITLE  5  of 5

Sales, and DEA Webpage  Drugs of Concern Listing .  Notifies Customer Service of final
decision on each peculiar and/or suspicious order/customer.

Maintains a file for record retention of Suspicious Order Monitoring documents and reports
per Covidien Record Retention Policy.

Conducts training on the Controlled Substance Suspicious Order Monitoring Procedure for
Credit Department, Field Sales, and Customer Service.

From: HDMA Weekly Digest <digest@hdmanet.org>

{HDMA Weekly Digest: A Newsletter for HDMA Members} 
{A Newsletter for HDMA Members} May 14, 2013 
  

 
   
In This Issue   
  Safeguarding America's Pharmaceuticals Act of 2013 Introduced 
 Legislators Send Letter to FDA on Hydrocodone-Combination Product Rescheduling 
 California Board of Pharmacy Establishes E-Pedigree Committee, Announces June Meeting

 {corner}  
{divider}

Safeguarding America's Pharmaceuticals Act of 2013 Introduced

Reps. Bob Latta (R-Ohio) and Jim Matheson (D-Utah) introduced the Safeguarding America's Pharmaceuticals Act of 2013 (H.R. 1919) on May 9. The bill reflects the legislative discussion draft on pharmaceutical supply chain safety and traceability that was marked up May 7 by the House Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health. During the markup, legislators discussed wholesaler licensure standards, federal preemption of state pedigree laws, returns processing and verification and the migration to unit-level serialization and traceability. Members on both sides of the aisle urged bipartisan cooperation and supported the process moving forward with patience and collaboration.

The House Energy and Commerce Committee scheduled a full committee markup of H.R. 1919 for May 14 at 4:00 p.m. in room 2123 of the Rayburn House Office Building, which will continue into a legislative markup on May 15 at 10:00 a.m. Additional details are available through the committee website.

For more information, contact Liz Gallenagh.
{top of page}

Legislators Send Letter to FDA on Hydrocodone-Combination Product Rescheduling

Senators Mark Kirk (R-Ill.), Joe Manchin (D-W.Va.) and a bipartisan, bicameral group of legislators sent a March 9 letter to FDA Commissioner Margaret Hamburg urging the agency to take action on rescheduling hydrocodone combination products. This letter is a follow up to one sent earlier this year imploring the FDA to act quickly on the FDA Advisory Committee's recommendation.

In addition to Senators Kirk and Manchin, the letter also was signed by Senators Jay Rockefeller (D-W.Va.), Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.), Dianne Feinstein (D-Calif.), Kirsten Gillibrand (D-N.Y.), Bill Nelson (D-Fla), Marco Rubio (R-Fla) and Representative Vern Buchanan (R-Fla).

Additional details, including the text of the letter, are available in the press release.

For more information, contact Jewelyn Cosgrove.
{top of page}

California Board of Pharmacy Establishes E-Pedigree Committee, Announces June Meeting

The California Board of Pharmacy established a separate E-Pedigree Committee, which will focus solely on matters pertaining to the implementation of California's e-pedigree law. The next meeting is set for June 24 in Sacramento. An agenda will be released 10 days prior to the meeting.

For more information, contact Liz Gallenagh.
{top of page}

Florida DWDAC to Hold Conference Call

The Florida Drug Wholesale Advisory Council (DWDAC) is hosting a conference call on May 16 at 9:30 a.m. (EDT). The agenda and meeting materials will be posted prior to the call and may be accessed here. The DWDAC provides input to the Division of Drugs, Devices and Cosmetics.

For more information, contact Dan Bellingham.
{top of page}

Original Formulation of Opana ER Can Stay on Market — FDA

On May 10, FDA responded to a petition filed by Endo Pharmaceuticals Inc., and concluded that the original formulation of Opana ER (oxymorphone hydrochloride) Extended-Release Tablets should not be be withdrawn from the market for reasons of safety or effectiveness. For further information, see the FDA website.

For more information, contact Allison Tuszynski.
{top of page}

DEA Hosting Manufacturer/Importer/Exporter Conference

DEA is hosting a national two-day Manufacturer/Importer/Exporter Conference on Tuesday, June 18 and Wednesday, June 19 in National Harbor, Md. The conference will present federal laws and regulations that affect the pharmaceutical and chemical manufacturing, importing, and exporting industry and tiscuss practices to prevent diversion while minimizing the impact on legitimate commerce. In addition, topics such as quotas, year-end reporting, ARCOS reporting, import/export permits and declarations will be discussed.

Registration is available on a first-come, first-served basis. Further information, including an agenda and a registration form, can be found on the DEA website.

For more information, contact Anita Ducca.

January 20, 2012

Police say nurse took meds from patients
By Julie Manganis and Ethan FormanStaff writersThe Salem NewsFri Jan 20, 2012,
05:00 AM EST
DANVERS — A now-former nurse at a Danvers assisted-living facility is facing
charges that she stole pain medications from at least six residents for months, secretly
replacing their Vicodin and oxycodone with a generic version of Tylenol.
Investigators were led to Amy Martin, 29, of 24 Barnard St., Marblehead, a registered
nurse, after a complaint in September from the niece of an elderly resident at
Brightview Danvers. She said the pills she found in her aunt's medication container did
not look like the ones she had been picking up for her at a pharmacy, according to a
police report.
Martin is due in Salem District Court this morning, where she is expected to be
arraigned on six counts of larceny of prescription drugs and a charge of possessing
Class B controlled substances — other patients' medications that police found after
they questioned her last October.
Martin confessed to police when confronted, according to court papers. When asked
what she thought as she deprived residents of their pain medications, she told
investigators she could not explain, other than to say that she herself was in pain
"every day."
The case came to light in September, when the niece went to officials at the assistedliving facility on Endicott Street.

MNKOI 0004228209

 She said that not only did the supposed Vicodin pills in her aunt's case look different,
but they had jagged edges where they had been split, according to Sgt. William
Carleton's report. The niece said she uses a pill splitter to cut her aunt's medications,
and that usually left smooth edges.
When officials at the facility checked the pills, they discovered that they were actually
acetaminophen.
The facility arranged to leave more Vicodin in the aunt's medications case, and within
a couple of days, those pills had been switched, as well.
The niece told officials that she had noticed something similar last January and had
asked Martin, the nurse working with her aunt, about it. Martin said she would look into
it, the niece said.
Management at Brightview contacted Danvers police at the beginning of October, and
over the next several weeks, an investigation — including hidden cameras placed in
several residents' rooms — revealed that more medication was being taken from
patients.
Martin was caught on camera taking the medication container of one patient to a
dining table, then returning it a few moments later. When investigators checked, the
prescription pills had been replaced with acetaminophen.
Martin, who had worked at the facility for about a year at that point, was questioned by
police on Oct. 25 and admitted to taking pills, Carleton wrote.
Police opted to seek a summons for her to appear in court instead of arresting her
immediately.
"They followed the best protocol to protect their residents," police Sgt. Robert
Bettencourt said of Brightview's role in the investigation. "They did the right thing and
followed the proper procedure to keep their residents safe."
"At Brightview Danvers, our residents' safety and well-being is our top priority," said
Beth Vellante, executive director of the facility, which has 185 residents.
"We applaud the alert action of our staff who immediately reported the former nurse's
inconsistency in standard procedure, and we appreciate the Danvers Police
Department for their guidance, support and direction throughout the investigation, as
well as their discretion and respect for our residents as the matter was investigated."

The use of intravenous acetaminophen for acute pain in the emergency department
 
Billy Sin, Mabel Wai, Tamara Tatunchak, Sergey M Motov
 
Academic Emergency Medicine: Official Journal of the Society for Academic Emergency Medicine 2016 January 29
 
OBJECTIVES: Acetaminophen is a mainstay for pain management worldwide. The intravenous (IV) formulation has been widely used in Europe for more than 20 years in adults and children. In the United States, IV acetaminophen (APAP) obtained full approval from the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in 2010. There is emerging literature to suggest the use of IV APAP for pain reduction in the Emergency Department (ED). This evidence-based review examines the evidence pertaining to the use of IV APAP for acute pain control in the ED.
 
METHODS: The MEDLINE and EMBASE databases were searched. Randomized controlled trials (RCT) that described or evaluated the use of IV APAP for acute pain in the ED were included. Duplicate articles, unpublished reports, abstracts, review articles, and non-English literature were excluded. The primary outcome of interest in this review was the difference in pain score between IV APAP and active comparator or placebo from baseline to a cutoff time specified in the original trials. Secondary outcome measures were the incidence of adverse events and reduction in the amount of adjuvant analgesics consumed by patients who received IV APAP. Methodological quality of the trials was assessed using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation criteria.
 
RESULTS: Fourteen randomized controlled trials (RCT) with various methodological flaws which enrolled a total of 1472 patients met the inclusion criteria. The level of evidence for the individual trials ranged from very low to moderate. In three of the fourteen trials, a significant reduction in pain scores was observed in patients who received IV APAP. The first trial found a significant reduction in mean pain scores when IV APAP was compared to IV morphine at 30 minutes after drug administration (4.7±2.3 vs. 2.9±2.2). In the second trial, patients who received IV APAP reported of lower pain scores (31.7mm+18, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 8.2-25.2) compared to those who received IV morphine (48.3mm+14.1, 95%CI: 8.2-25.2), 15 minutes after drug administration. A third trial found a significant reduction (p=0.005) in the mean pain scores when IV APAP was compared to intramuscular piroxicam at 90 minutes after drug administration. In the remaining 8 trials, pain scores were not statistically different when IV APAP was compared to other pain medications. The incidence of side effects associated with IV APAP was very low.
 
CONCLUSION: Fourteen randomized controlled trials with various methodological flaws provided limited evidence to support the use of IV APAP as the primary analgesic for acute pain control in patients who presents to the ED. This article is protected by copyright. All rights reserved.

Top Stories in the News Disclaimer: Articles and links within articles do not necessarily reflect the views or opinions of the National Rx Drug Abuse & Heroin Summit or Operation UNITE.



 

 

 
Lawsuits against pharmaceuticals effective weapon in war
against prescription opioids
David Whiting, The Orange County Register This nation’s billion-dollar opioid industry is finally starting to crack thanks to a series of successful lawsuits aimed at curtailing the ever-spiraling epidemic of pharmaceutical drug addiction. After Orange and Santa Clara counties led the charge three years ago, a series of counties, states and the Drug Enforcement Administration followed with numerous lawsuits against manufacturers and distributors of opioids alleging lax security, deceptive marketing and failing to check suspicious orders.

{Read More}
-----
Opioid costs push struggling states to dust off tobacco strategy
Jef Feeley and John Laureman, Bloomberg News State and local leaders fighting a worsening opioid-abuse epidemic are studying tactics used in the tobacco lawsuits of the 1990s, as they try to claw back billions from the companies who make and sell the powerful painkillers. More than 20 U.S. states, counties and cities have sued firms in the past year, claiming they fueled a public-health crisis with misleading marketing and aggressive distribution of opioids. It’s a strategy cigarette manufacturers will recognize: Two decades ago, they faced similar allegations as states and local governments sued, saying they’d shouldered huge costs for treating diseases blamed on tobacco.

{Read More}
-----
Michigan’s PDMP to merge into hospital, physician record systems
Jay Greene, Crain’s Detroit Business Michigan state officials have partnered with health systems, physician organizations and pharmacies to merge provider electronic medical record systems into the state's newly improved online prescription drug reporting and tracking system. At Henry Ford Health System corporate headquarters in Detroit on Monday, Lt. Gov. Brian Calley, Henry Ford officials and the state's vendor, Appriss Health, announced that about $2.1 million in state and federal funding will be used to connect the state's Michigan Automated Prescription System with existing patient data systems such as Henry Ford's Epic Systems Corp. electronic medical record.

{Read More}
-----
Ohio coroner warns of fentanyl-laced marijuana, cocaine
WLWT TV-5, Cincinnati Synthetic opiates like fentanyl have been found in marijuana, Hamilton County Coroner Dr. Lakshmi Sammarco said Monday, June 19. Fentanyl, a drug 50 to 100 times more powerful than morphine, has been linked to a surge of fatal overdoses across the county. It has been showing up in other drugs across the area.

Subject: Dr Chwistek: Dosing Administration for Patients With Breakthrough Cancer Pain

Having trouble viewing this e-mail?

 {Logo Header}

  

 


 
 


 

 
 
 Dr Marcin Chwistek provides expert commentary on FENTORA  (fentanyl buccal tablet) [CII] Dosing and Administration


  

 


 
 


 

 
 {Image 270x200}

 

 
 Featured Expert

  
 
 MARCIN CHWISTEK, MD, FAAHPM
Associate Professor
Department of Medical Oncology
Pain and Palliative Care Program
Fox Chase Cancer Center
Philadelphia, Pennsylvania


  
 

 


 
 


 

 This promotional program was developed and sponsored by Teva Pharmaceuticals, based on an interview with Marcin Chwistek, MD, FAAHPM.

Dr Chwistek received a fee for participation in this program.

  


 


 


 

 


 

   

 
 
 "I have found that FENTORA blister packs are highly portable and simple to open and discard. FENTORA makes it possible for patients to have the medication with them and permits buccal administration for either titration or maintenance dosing, and sublingual administration option for maintenance dosing. It is important to explain to patients that, in a pivotal trial, 70% of patients who found a successful dose of FENTORA during titration did so at a dose greater than or equal to 400 mcg."   Marcin Chwistek, MD, FAAHPM


FENTORA is indicated for the management of breakthrough pain in cancer patients 18 years of age and older who are already receiving and who are tolerant to around-the-clock opioid therapy for their underlying persistent cancer pain.

Patients considered opioid tolerant are those who are taking around-the-clock medicine consisting of at least 60 mg of oral morphine daily, at least 25 mcg/hr of transdermal fentanyl, at least 30 mg of oral oxycodone daily, at least 8 mg of oral hydromorphone daily, at least 25 mg oral oxymorphone daily, or an equianalgesic dose of another opioid daily for a week or longer. Patients must remain on around-the-clock opioids while taking FENTORA.

This product must not be used in opioid non-tolerant patients because life-threatening hypoventilation and death could occur at any dose in patients not on a chronic regimen of opioids. For this reason, FENTORA is contraindicated in the management of acute or postoperative pain.

FENTORA is intended to be used only in the care of opioid-tolerant patients and only by healthcare professionals who are knowledgeable of and skilled in the use of Schedule II opioids to treat cancer pain.

Limitations of Use:
FENTORA may be dispensed only to patients enrolled in the TIRF REMS Access program.

Fatal respiratory depression has occurred in patients treated with FENTORA, including following use in opioid non-tolerant patients and improper dosing. The substitution of FENTORA for any other fentanyl product may result in fatal overdose.

Due to the risk of respiratory depression, FENTORA is contraindicated in the management of acute or postoperative pain including headache/migraine and in opioid non-tolerant patients.

  


 


 

 
 
 VIEW THE PROGRAM

 


  


 


 


 

 
 FENTORA Administration

Flexible and discreet administration options
Buccal administration for titration and maintenance dosing1
Sublingual administration for maintenance dosing1

FENTORA blister packets are highly portable and simple to open and discard
Once tablet is removed from blister unit, the tablet should be used immediately1
Patients should not split the tablet1
Instruct patients to leave tablet in place until it dissolves   generally 14 to 25 minutes1
After 30 minutes, if any tablet residue is left in mouth, patient may drink a glass of water to help swallow it1
The FENTORA tablet should not be crushed, chewed, or swallowed whole as this will result in lower plasma concentrations than when taken as directed1


  

 


 
 


 

 
IMPORTANT SAFETY INFORMATION

WARNING: RISK OF RESPIRATORY DEPRESSION, MEDICATION ERRORS,
ABUSE POTENTIAL

RESPIRATORY DEPRESSION
Fatal respiratory depression has occurred in patients treated with FENTORA, including following use in opioid non-tolerant patients and improper dosing. The substitution of FENTORA for any other fentanyl product may result in fatal overdose.

Due to the risk of respiratory depression, FENTORA is contraindicated in the management of acute or postoperative pain including headache/migraine and in opioid non-tolerant patients.

FENTORA must be kept out of reach of children.


The concomitant use of FENTORA with CYP3A4 inhibitors may result in an increase in fentanyl plasma concentrations, and may cause potentially fatal respiratory depression.

MEDICATION ERRORS
Substantial differences exist in the pharmacokinetic profile of FENTORA compared to other fentanyl products that result in clinically important differences in the extent of absorption of fentanyl that could result in fatal overdose.


When prescribing, do not convert patients on a mcg per mcg basis from any other fentanyl products to FENTORA.
When dispensing, do not substitute a FENTORA prescription for other fentanyl products.

ABUSE POTENTIAL
FENTORA contains fentanyl, an opioid agonist and a Schedule II controlled substance, with an abuse liability similar to other opioid analgesics. FENTORA can be abused in a manner similar to other opioid agonists, legal or illicit. This should be considered when prescribing or dispensing FENTORA in situations where the physician or pharmacist is concerned about an increased risk of misuse, abuse or diversion.

Because of the risk for misuse, abuse, addiction, and overdose, FENTORA is available only through a restricted program required by the Food and Drug Administration, called a Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS). Under the Transmucosal Immediate Release Fentanyl (TIRF) REMS Access program, outpatients, healthcare professionals who prescribe to outpatients, pharmacies, and distributors must enroll in the program. Further information is available at www.TIRFREMSAccess.com or by calling 1-866-822-1483.

 


Contraindications:

FENTORA is contraindicated in opioid non-tolerant patients. Life-threatening respiratory depression and death can occur at any dose in opioid non-tolerant patients
FENTORA is contraindicated in the management of acute or postoperative pain including headache/migraine and dental pain
FENTORA is contraindicated in patients with known intolerance or hypersensitivity to any of its components or the drug fentanyl

Warnings and Precautions:

Clinically significant respiratory and CNS depression can occur. Monitor patients accordingly
FENTORA is not bioequivalent to other fentanyl products. Do not convert patients on a mcg per mcg basis from other fentanyl products
FENTORA contains a medicine in an amount which can be fatal to a child
Use with other CNS depressants and cytochrome P450 3A4 inhibitors may increase depressant effects including hypoventilation, hypotension, and profound sedation. Consider dosage adjustments if warranted
FENTORA may impair the ability to drive a car or perform other potentially dangerous tasks. Counsel patients accordingly
Titrate FENTORA cautiously in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or preexisting medical conditions predisposing them to respiratory depression and in patients susceptible to intracranial effects of CO2 retention
Application site reactions occurred in 10% of patients in clinical trials and ranged from paresthesia to ulceration and bleeding
Use FENTORA with caution in patients with bradyarrhythmias

Adverse Reactions:

Most common (frequency ?10%): nausea, dizziness, vomiting, fatigue, anemia, constipation, edema peripheral, asthenia, dehydration, and headache

Drug Interactions:

The concomitant use of FENTORA with CYP3A4 inhibitors may result in an increase in fentanyl plasma concentrations, and may cause potentially fatal respiratory depression
FENTORA is not recommended for use in patients who have received MAO inhibitors within 14 days, because severe and unpredictable potentiation by MAO inhibitors has been reported with opioid analgesics

Use in Specific Populations:

Administer FENTORA with caution to patients with severe hepatic or renal impairment

Attached is supporting documentation of suspicious activity we have discovered surrounding the sale of Crossroads Recovery, Inc. in Dallas, TX with the following details for your consideration:


 


·         Controlled Substance Compliance was notified by our credit department that customer Crossroads Recovery, Dallas TX (DEA Reg# RC0270974) had an outstanding bill that was in dispute between the old owners of the NTP clinic and the new owners of clinic from February 2010. 

·         The clinic was sold by Diane Day and purchased by Joseph Baiamonte and Frances McGrady.  The sales contract is dated February 15, 2010.  Attached is a letter from the new owners with specific pages from the sales contract, it is not inclusive.  Cover letter provided by the purchasers state that they did not close on the sales contract until February 19, 2010 and that they were not responsible for any fees until March 1, 2010. 

·        A letter was sent to Mallinckrodt on march 8, 2010 from Diane Day (attached) updating Joseph Baiamonte and Francis McGrady as being authorized to order and receive methadone, however it does not state that the clinic was sold or transferred ownership.  Thus, we did not change any of our accounts as the current DEA Registration for Crossroads Recovery was in effect until August 31, 2010 and we simply thought they were updating their authorized signors list.

·         Attached are also copies of 2 different 222 forms, one from February and one from March.  The March invoice has been paid, the February invoice has not and was the cause for the sale to be brought to our attention.  Based on the signature of the sales contract it appears that Diane Day did sign the 222 form from February 17, 2010, however it appears that someone else could have potentially signed Diane Day's name on the March 222 form with their initials after her name.  Mallinckrodt continued to ship at this time as we had not been made aware of the change of ownership and 222 used to order was for the same DEA Reg# RC0270974 currently on file.

·         A review of shipping records from March 1, 2010 to date, shows 4 orders have been shipped, all using the DEA Reg# RC0270974 and sequential DEA Form 222 numbers.  The March order was signed with the name Diane Day and the subsequent 3 orders (May, June, August) were signed by Lillian Williams McGrady.

As part of our ongoing Suspicious Order Monitoring program, Mallinckrodt will be incorporating the requirement for any clinic to provide proof of ownership and/or sale immediately upon notification to us of the sale of a NTP clinic.

Press Release
 
 
  MCKESSON AGREES TO PAY RECORD $150 MILLION SETTLEMENT FOR FAILURE TO REPORT SUSPICIOUS ORDERS OF PHARMACEUTICAL DRUGS
 
JAN 17 - (Washington, DC) – McKesson Corporation (McKesson), one of the nation’s largest distributors of pharmaceutical drugs, agreed to pay a record $150 million civil penalty for alleged violations of the Controlled Substances Act (CSA), the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) announced today.
 
The nationwide settlement requires McKesson to suspend sales of controlled substances from distribution centers in Colorado, Ohio, Michigan and Florida for multiple years. The staged suspensions are among the most severe sanctions ever agreed to by a DEA-registered distributor. The settlement also imposes new and enhanced compliance obligations on McKesson’s distribution system.
 
In 2008, McKesson agreed to a $13.25 million civil penalty and administrative agreement for similar violations. In this case, the government alleged again that McKesson failed to design and implement an effective system to detect and report “suspicious orders” for controlled substances distributed to its independent and small chain pharmacy customers– i.e. orders that are unusual in their frequency, size, or other patterns. From 2008 until 2013, McKesson supplied various U.S. pharmacies an increasing amount of oxycodone and hydrocodone pills, frequently misused products that are part of the current opioid epidemic.
 
The government’s investigation developed evidence that even after designing a compliance program after the 2008 settlement, McKesson did not fully implement or adhere to its own program. In Colorado, for example, McKesson processed more than 1.6 million orders for controlled substances from June 2008 through May 2013, but reported just 16 orders as suspicious, all connected to one instance related to a recently terminated customer. 
 
"This groundbreaking resolution is tough and appropriate and underscores our commitment to hold accountable all DEA registrants, including those who distribute controlled substances," said DEA Acting Administrator Chuck Rosenberg.  "DEA is committed to fighting the opioid epidemic with all of the tools at our disposal."
 
In addition to the monetary penalties and suspensions, the government and McKesson agreed to enhanced compliance terms for the next five years. Among other things, McKesson has agreed to specific, rigorous staffing and organizational improvements; periodic auditing; and stipulated financial penalties for failing to adhere to the compliance terms. Critically, the settlement will require McKesson to engage an independent monitor to assess compliance – the first independent monitor of its kind in a CSA civil penalty settlement.
 
This was a multi-district investigation that involved the following DEA Field Divisions:  Boston Field Division, Chicago Field Division, Denver Field Division, Detroit Field Division, Miami Field Division, New Jersey Field Division, San Francisco Field Division, St. Louis Field Division, and Washington Division Office. The following U.S. Attorneys’ Offices participated in the case: Central District of California, Eastern District of California, District of Colorado, Middle District of Florida, Eastern District of Kentucky, Northern District of Illinois, District of Massachusetts, Eastern District of Michigan, District of Nebraska, District of New Jersey, Northern District of West Virginia, and Western District of Wisconsin.
 
U.S. Attorneys’ Offices for the District of Colorado and the Northern District of West Virginia, along with DEA’s Office of Chief Counsel and its Diversion Control Division, led the civil settlement negotiations.  DEA’s Denver, Detroit and Miami Field Divisions and its Washington Division Office led the administrative and civil investigation. The U.S. Department of Justice Criminal Division’s Narcotic and Dangerous Drug Section (NDDS) also coordinated and assisted in negotiating certain portions of the settlement. Assistant United States Attorneys Amanda Rocque (Colorado) and Alan McGonigal (NDWV) represented the United States in the civil penalty investigations and negotiations.  Associate Chief Counsel Lee Reeves and Senior Attorneys Dedra Curteman, Dana Hill and Krista Tongring represented DEA in the investigations and negotiations. Trial Attorneys Harry Matz and Kirtland Marsh were involved for NDDS.

Subject: Published Op-Ed in today's St. Louis Post-Dispatch



Good morning:

 

Today’s St. Louis Post-Dispatch – as noted – features our Opinion Editorial, submitted by Mark on behalf of the company. Attached shows how the article appears in print. We also attach a PDF of the online article, and include the link and text below. This will also be included in our morning daily news clips report.

 

Link: http://www.stltoday.com/news/opinion/mallinckrodt-helps-address-opioid-misuse-diversion/article_0b0e8c93-3349-575a-948f-241e6a53a463.html

 

Text

 

Opinion

Mallinckrodt helps address opioid misuse, diversion

{http://www.stltoday.com/news/opinion/columns/the-platform/editorial-the-mallinckrodt-connection-to-america-s-opioid-epidemic/article_cac8edcf-dd6c-5628-beb3-141d1352a352.html}The Post-Dispatch editorial “The Mallinckrodt connection” (April 10) overlooks Mallinckrodt’s efforts to ensure responsible use of its medications and the complexity of the broader issue. As a Missouri-founded company celebrating 150 years in this state, we believe the editorial board criticized Mallinckrodt without, perhaps, fully understanding this complicated issue and all the facts.

As a publicly traded company, Mallinckrodt routinely discloses information affecting the company, such as the agreement in principle reached with the U.S. Drug Enforcement Agency and U.S. Attorneys’ Offices to settle the previously disclosed investigations of the company’s monitoring programs for controlled substances.

The disclosure of the $35 million settlement was in no way meant to downplay the seriousness of the opioid epidemic. Mallinckrodt recognizes that prescription drug abuse is one of the St. Louis region’s — and the nation’s — greatest health and safety concerns, with devastating societal and emotional effects as well as an economic burden on the healthcare system.

Mallinckrodt’s medications are approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, and Mallinckrodt supplies its controlled substance products to legitimate national and regional distributors that are registered with the DEA. Mallinckrodt has long had processes in place to monitor its distributor customers, as the law requires. Mallinckrodt has limited ability to monitor downstream sales at the pharmacy level, where diversion has historically occurred, but it has also been a leader among manufacturers in helping distributors better monitor their pharmacy customers.

Although the company has reached an agreement in principle with the government, it does not agree with government allegations that it violated the law in connection with its suspicious order monitoring program. In discussions with the government, the company has responded to unfounded claims and successfully refuted factual inaccuracies in the government’s allegations. In fact, Mallinckrodt has been and is a leader in developing and sharing best practices related to its innovative suspicious order monitoring program, which we believe exceeds DEA requirements.

Prescription drugs are designed to heal, not harm. Mallinckrodt is dedicated to providing safe and effective medications for the treatment of patients with chronic and acute pain. In addition to helping those patients, Mallinckrodt is equally committed to working with patient groups, policymakers, law enforcement and industry to address the complex issues of opioid misuse and diversion.

Mallinckrodt has invested millions of dollars in its comprehensive program to address opioid abuse and misuse. For years, Mallinckrodt has been a vocal advocate for a prescription drug monitoring program in Missouri to help doctors identify potential opioid misuse. The company also purchased and donated more than 1.5 million drug deactivation pouches distributed in our communities and across the U.S. so that families can safely dispose of unused medication.

Mallinckrodt regularly works with law enforcement to help prevent diversion, including by providing no-cost placebo tablets of Mallinckrodt opioids to officers and prosecutors for use in law enforcement operations; attacking drug theft through tracking devices in selected Mallinckrodt drug bottles; and contributing testimony on behalf of prosecution in drug diversion cases. We helped to found the Anti-Diversion Industry Working Group, a collective of leading manufacturers and distributors of pharmaceutical controlled substances coming together to collaborate and share best practices with the purpose of exceeding DEA obligations for opioid anti-diversion programs.

The opioid epidemic is a complex and confounding problem, and no one policy initiative or program will solve it. We commend the Post-Dispatch for its focus on this issue and its support of prescription drug monitoring in the state. However, to truly make an impact on opioid abuse, all stakeholders must better understand the various interrelated causes and contributors to the problem, and work together to address all of them in a comprehensive, thoughtful manner. We continue to work to be part of the solution.

Mark Trudeau is chief executive officer and president of Mallinckrodt Pharmaceuticals.

Subject: Media Win: St. Louis Post-Dispatch to publish MNK Op-Ed to recent editorial



 

All,

 

I’m happy to report the St. Louis Post-Dispatch has agreed to publish an Opinion Editorial from Mark/Mallinckrodt this coming Tuesday, April 18. We had an exchange with the editor and revised our initial submission to the one you see attached here, so we believe they will likely publish it as written, or nearly so.

 

The editor also agreed to our proposal that their team sit down with members of ours (Don Lohman, John Gillies, Kevin Webb and me) so we can provide additional context on the settlement matter. That meeting looks likely to take place sometime in early May.

 

Finally, it is our intent, when (strong belief it’s definitely when, not if), the PDMP passes in Missouri to run an ad in the Post-Dispatch applauding that achievement and reinforcing Mallinckrodt’s commitment to fighting opioid abuse. The House bill that we believe is best for the state passed in the Missouri Senate yesterday, through additional steps are required before complete passage. There is hope that can be completed in the coming weeks.

 

Please don’t share this file further with your teams until after it is published. We will share that alert with you when it is complete, and also include it in the following day’s Daily News Report. Special thanks to Rhonda for shepherding this through to success.

 

Good Friday, indeed. Victories, large and small, must be savored. Happy Easter weekend to you all.

FDA approves abuse-deterrent labeling for reformulated OxyContin
Agency will not approve generics to original OxyContin
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today approved updated labeling for Purdue Pharma L.P.'s
reformulated OxyContin (oxycodone hydrochloride controlled-release) tablets. The new labeling indicates
that the product has physical and chemical properties that are expected to make abuse via injection
difficult and to reduce abuse via the intranasal route (snorting).
Additionally, because original OxyContin provides the same therapeutic benefits as reformulated
OxyContin, but poses an increased potential for certain types of abuse, the FDA has determined that the
benefits of original OxyContin no longer outweigh its risks and that original OxyContin was withdrawn
from sale for reasons of safety or effectiveness. Accordingly, the agency will not accept or approve any
abbreviated new drug applications (generics) that rely upon the approval of original OxyContin.
The FDA approved the original formulation of OxyContin in Dec. 1995. The product was abused, often
following manipulation intended to defeat its extended -release properties. Such manipulation causes the
drug to be released more rapidly, which increases the risk of serious adverse events, including overdose
and death. In April 2010, the FDA approved a reformulated version of OxyContin, which was designed to be
more difficult to manipulate for purposes of misuse or abuse. Purdue stopped shipping original OxyContin
to pharmacies in August 2010.
"The development of abuse-deterrent opioid analgesics is a public health priority for the FDA," said
Douglas Throckmorton, M.D., deputy director for regulatory programs in the FDA's Center for Drug
Evaluation and Research. "While both original and reformulated OxyContin are subject to abuse and misuse,
the FDA has determined that reformulated OxyContin can be expected to make abuse by injection difficult
and expected to reduce abuse by snorting compared to original OxyContin."
The FDA has determined that the reformulated product has abuse-deterrent properties. The tablet is more
difficult to crush, break, or dissolve. It also forms a viscous hydrogel and cannot be easily prepared
for injection. The agency has determined that the physical and chemical properties of the reformulated
product are expected to make the product difficult to inject and to reduce abuse via snorting. However,
abuse of OxyContin by these routes, as well as the oral route, is still possible. The reformulated
product also may reduce incidents of therapeutic misuse, such as crushing the product to sprinkle it onto
food or to administer it through a gastric tube. When FDA finds that a new formulation has abuse
deterrent properties, the agency has the authority to require generics to have abuse-deterrent properties
also
The agency review of this issue included an analysis of the following:

MNKOI 0000602185

 Citizen petitions requesting that the agency determine whether original oxyContin was
voluntarily withdrawn from sale for reasons other than safety or effectiveness;
comments submitted to the public dockets associated with these petitions;
Information concerning original and reformulated oxyContin and the withdrawal of original
oxyContin;
clinical data, peer-reviewed literature, and other information concerning postmarketing adverse
events associated with original oxyContin, reformulated oxyContin, and other extended -release oxycodone
products.
Postmarketing assessments of the impact of reformulated oxyContin on abuse are ongoing, and the FDA will
update its evaluation of the effects of reformulated oxyContin on abuse as new data become available.
The FDA, together with other public health agencies, continues to encourage the development of abusedeterrent formulations of opioids and believes that such products will help reduce prescription drug
abuse. At the same time, the FDA remains committed to ensuring that patients with pain have appropriate
access to °plaid analgesics.
For more information:
Federal Register Notice<http://www.ofr.gov/OFRUpload/OFRData/2013-09092_PI.pdf>
FDA Actions on OxyContin Products</Drugs/DrugSafety/InformationbyDrugClass/ucm347857.htm>
The FDA, an agency within the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, protects the public health by
assuring the safety, effectiveness, and security of human and veterinary drugs, vaccines and other
biological products for human use, and medical devices. The agency also is responsible for the safety and
security of our nation's food supply, cosmetics, dietary supplements, products that give off electronic
radiation, and for regulating tobacco products.

SAMHSA and ONDCP Report 12 Percent Drop in U.S. Prescription Drug
Abuse
Yesterday, the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA), along with
White House Office of National Drug Control Policy (ONDCP), announced the results of its 2011
National Survey on Drug Use and Health CNSDUH). This year's NSDUH survey found that a decline in
the number of young adults who used prescription drugs for non-medical purposes in the past month
has led to an overall 12 percent drop in the number of Americans abusing prescription drugs.
This annual survey is the government's primary vehicle for determining how many persons are using
illegal drugs, alcohol and tobacco and misusing pharmaceuticals. Additional information is available
from ONDCP and SAMHSA.

Last week, Senator Dianne Feinstein (D-Calif.) introduced Senate Resolution 564, designating October
2012 as "National Medicine Abuse Awareness Month," which was passed under unanimous consent by
the Senate. The resolution underlines the importance of taking medications as prescribed, notes recent
studies and research identifying the growing problem of prescription drug abuse and highlights the
efforts of the DEA and law enforcement agencies to establish drug disposal programs. The resolution
is non-binding, but is a symbolic effort by the Senate to recognize the importance of the prescription
drug abuse problem.

Congressman Hal Rogers (R-Ky.), Chairman of the House Appropriations Committee, held a
September 20 briefing featuring findings from a new white paper entitled, "Prescription Drug Monitoring
Programs: An Assessment of the Evidence of Best Practices."
The white paper finds that PDMPs are an "underutilized resource" in the overall effort to address
prescription drug abuse. The report provides background information on the establishment of PDMPs,
a framework to measure effectiveness, describes best practices and proposes research into additional
practices to properly determine effectiveness to enhance PDMP use in addressing prescription drug
abuse. The report, authored by Brandeis University's Prescription Drug Monitoring Program Center of
Excellence, and sponsored by the Pew Charitable Trust, makes a number of recommendations,
including:

CMS Releases Supplemental Guidance on Drug Utilization Reviews in
Medicare Part D
On August 31, CMS released additional supplemental guidance to Part D plan sponsors related to
improving drug utilization reviews (DURs) to understand and comply with the opioid overutilization
policy for Medicare Part D in 2013. More specifically, the 2013 Medicare Part D Call Letter requires
plan sponsors to comply with drug utilization management requirements to prevent overuse of opioids,
and in particular, CMS' guidance focuses observations from case management pilots, modifications
from the agency's previous memo and analysis of the morphine equivalent dose in Medicare Part D
Program.
For more information, contact Allison Wilms.

Prescriptions

regarding the definitions related to electronic orders for controlled substances and electronic
prescriptions for controlled substances.
For more information, contact Anita Ducce or Moon Wiley.

FTC Extends Pet Medication Workshop Comment Deadline
On October 2, the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) will host a workshop and has requested

consumer protection issues. Originally, comments on the questions included in the notice were due

From: DocAlert <docalert@epocrates.com>

To: Chelsey Homan <choman@epocrates.com>


Dear Clinician:

Here is the information you requested (sponsored by Mallinckrodt).

 

Once-Daily EXALGO  (hydromorphone HCl) Extended-Release Tablets (CII)

May Help Reduce Pill Burden

How many 20 mg or 40 mg pills are your OxyContin  (oxycodone) patients taking each day? 44% of all OxyContin  prescriptions are for 20 mg and 40 mg tablets strengths.1 For many patients taking OxyContin  20 mg or 40 mg tablets, converting to EXALGO may reduce the pill burden. See the conversion charts below:

 

Please see IMPORTANT RISK INFORMATION, including boxed warning.

Please see Full Prescribing Information for EXALGO.

 

For Your Opioid-Tolerant Chronic Pain Patients

EXALGO Offers Once-Daily Dosing With Potentially Fewer Pills



 



 

Generally, reduce the calculated equianalgesic dose by 25% to 50% to obtain the starting

dose2-4*

 

*In the pivotal trial, a 25% dose reduction of equianalgesic dose was used to determine a starting dose.2,3

 

Please see IMPORTANT RISK INFORMATION, including boxed warning.

Please see Full Prescribing Information for EXALGO.

 

Effectively Transition Patients to EXALGO  (hydromorphone HCl) Extended-Release Tablets (CII)

1. SET expectations

          There is no immediate-release component; plasma levels rise for the first 6 to 8 hours after the initial dose.2

          It takes 3 to 4 days to reach steady state.2,5

          Prescribe supplemental pain medication to help your patients get to steady state, through titration, and as needed thereafter.

 

2. START with an appropriate dose

Consider the reasons for switching when calculating a starting dose.
Generally, reduce the calculated equianalgesic dose by 25% to 50% to obtain the starting dose.2-4 
EXALGO is available in 8, 12, 16, and 32 mg tablets to provide flexibility when determining a starting dose; all tablets should be taken together once daily.2

 

3. TITRATE to an effective dose

Titration should not occur more frequently than every 3 to 4 days.2
If more than 2 doses of supplemental medication are needed for 2 consecutive days, it may be time to titrate upward.2
When titrating, consider a 25% to 50% increase in dose.2
It may take multiple titration steps to achieve effective pain control with tolerable side effects.

 

 In the pivotal trial, a 25% dose reduction of equianalgesic dose was used to determine a starting dose.2,3

 

Please see IMPORTANT RISK INFORMATION, including boxed warning.

Please see Full Prescribing Information for EXALGO.

                                                   

 

IMPORTANT RISK INFORMATION

 

INDICATION

EXALGO  (hydromorphone HCl) Extended-Release Tablets (CII) is indicated for the management of moderate to severe pain in opioid tolerant patients requiring continuous, around-the-clock opioid analgesia for an extended period of time.

 

IMPORTANT RISK INFORMATION

 

WARNING: ABUSE POTENTIAL, LIFE-THREATENING RESPIRATORY DEPRESSION, and ACCIDENTAL EXPOSURE

 

Abuse Potential

 

EXALGO contains hydromorphone, an opioid agonist and a Schedule II controlled substance with an abuse liability similar to other opioid agonists, legal or illicit. Assess each patient s risk for opioid abuse or addiction prior to prescribing EXALGO. The risk for opioid abuse is increased in patients with a personal or family history of substance abuse (including drug or alcohol abuse or addiction) or mental illness (e.g., major depressive disorder). Routinely monitor all patients receiving EXALGO for signs of misuse, abuse, and addiction during treatment.

 

Life-threatening Respiratory Depression

 

Respiratory depression, including fatal cases, may occur with use of EXALGO, even when the drug has been used as recommended and not misused or abused. EXALGO is for use in opioid tolerant patients only. Proper dosing and titration are essential and EXALGO should be prescribed only by healthcare professionals who are knowledgeable in the use of potent opioids for the management of chronic pain. Monitor for respiratory depression, especially during initiation of EXALGO or following a dose increase. Crushing, dissolving, or chewing the tablet can cause rapid release and absorption of a potentially fatal dose of hydromorphone.

 

Accidental Exposure

 

Accidental ingestion of EXALGO, especially in children, can result in a fatal overdose of hydromorphone.


 

          EXALGO is contraindicated in:

-         Opioid non-tolerant patients. Fatal respiratory depression could occur in patients who are not opioid tolerant.

-         Patients with significant respiratory depression

-         Patients with acute or severe bronchial asthma in an unmonitored setting or in the absence of resuscitative equipment

-         Patients with known or suspected paralytic ileus

-         Patients who have had surgical procedures and/or underlying disease resulting in narrowing of the gastrointestinal tract, or have  blind loops  of the gastrointestinal tract or gastrointestinal obstruction

-         Patients with hypersensitivity (e.g., anaphylaxis) to hydromorphone or sulfite-containing medications

 

          EXALGO is indicated for opioid tolerant patients only. Patients considered opioid tolerant are those who are taking at least 60 mg oral morphine per day, 25 mcg transdermal fentanyl/hour, 30 mg oral oxycodone/day, 8 mg oral hydromorphone/day, 25 mg oral oxymorphone/day or an equianalgesic dose of another opioid, for a week or longer.

 

          EXALGO  (hydromorphone HCl) Extended-Release Tablets (CII) is not intended for use as an as-needed analgesic and is not indicated for the management of acute or postoperative pain. It is contraindicated in patients who need management of mild pain or pain not expected to persist.

 

          Avoid concurrent use of alcohol and EXALGO. Concurrent use of EXALGO with CNS depressants, including alcohol, increases risk of respiratory depression, hypotension, and profound sedation, potentially resulting in coma or death. EXALGO may impair the ability to drive a car or operate machinery.

 

          Not intended in patients who have received MAO inhibitors within 14 days of starting EXALGO.

 

          Use with caution and in reduced doses in older or debilitated patients, as well as patients with renal or hepatic insufficiency, Addison s disease, delirium tremens, myxedema or hypothyroidism, prostatic hypertrophy or urethral stricture, toxic psychosis. May aggravate convulsions in patients with convulsive disorders; may induce or aggravate seizures in some clinical settings. Consider use of an alternate analgesic in patients with severe renal impairment.

 

          Respiratory depression, which occurs more frequently in elderly or debilitated patients, is the chief hazard with EXALGO.

 

          Serious adverse events could also include hypotensive effects, GI effects, cardiac arrest from overdose and precipitation of withdrawal. Most common adverse events (>10%) seen in clinical studies (N=2474) were: constipation (31%), nausea (28%), vomiting, somnolence, headache, asthenia and dizziness. Post marketing events include hypersensitivity reactions, angioedema and urticaria.

 

          Use EXALGO with extreme caution in patients susceptible to intracranial effects of CO 2 retention.

 

          Do not abruptly discontinue EXALGO.

 

Please see Full Prescribing Information for EXALGO.

Attached are mine and Gina’s comments on draft 1 of the dossier – there are quite a few, but many of them are regarding consistency of the document as a whole.

 

Regarding the BIM, I do not think that Xcenda made any errors in transcribing the model to Section 4 of the dossier. I think it just comes down to whether or not we are comfortable using Elia 2005 and Marret 2005 to support the 1:1 correlation presented in the BIM.

 

The BIM states:

·         “The default value for ADE reduction is 10%, and thus, the default set-up for the correlation is “a 10% reduction in opioid use would result in a 10% reduction in ADEs,” which was estimated based on two systemic review publications (Source: Elia 2005 and Marret 2005; full citations found on the “References” screen).

 

Information from these references:

·         Elia N, Lysakowski C, Tramèr MR. Does multimodal analgesia with acetaminophen, nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs, or selective cyclooxygenase-2 inhibitors and patient-controlled analgesia morphine offer advantages over morphine alone? Meta-analyses of randomized trials. Anesthesiology. 2005;103(6):1296-304.

o   http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16306743

o   Article attached

o   IV APAP was associated with a 24 h morphine consumption decrease by 8.3 mg but was not associated with a significant decrease in incidence of respiratory depression, combined NV, urinary retention, or sedation

·         Marret E, Kurdi O, Zufferey P, Bonnet F. Effects of nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs on patient-controlled analgesia morphine side effects: meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Anesthesiology. 2005 Jun;102(6):1249-60.

o   http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15915040

o   Article attached

o   Of note, this article examined NSAIDs (not IV apap) so I think it could be a typo – maybe they meant to reference Remy 2005 (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15681586; article attached)

o   NSAIDs were associated with a significant decrease in PONV by 30%, nausea alone by 12%, vomiting alone by 32% and sedation by 29%. A linear relation was documented between the incidence of postoperative nausea (r=0.61; p=0.007) and vomiting (r=0.51; p=0.02) and morphine consumption in the postoperative period. For each milligram of morphine spared by NSAIDs, the incidences of postoperative nausea and vomiting decreased by 0.9% and 0.3%, respectively.

§  Perhaps this bolded part is where the BIM creators got the 1:1 assumption from, though I think it’s a stretch since this study evaluated NSAIDs and the 0.9:1 correlation was only observed in postoperative nausea (not all ADEs)

6.9.1      Chart Review Studies (Proposed)

Chart review studies will be used to evaluate appropriate prescribing of EXALGO and especially the 32 mg tablet. Direct evaluation of patient charts provide the ability to verify appropriate prescribing practices from actual data, including: patient selection (eg, use in opioid-tolerant patients, use in adults only); dosing and administration (eg, appropriate conversion and titration, reduction of starting dose after conversion, use of the 32 mg tablet as a starting dose, use with other sedating medications [eg, benzodiazepines, other long-acting/extended-release opioid analgesics]). Subject: Label Review Committee
From: "Nosco, Dennis L" <dennis.nosco@covidien.com>
Date: Fri, 26 Apr 2013 09:43:13 -0500
To: "Wuestner, Joe  A" <joe.wuestner@covidien.com>,
    "Haynes, Elaine E" <elaine.haynes@covidien.com>,
    "Terifay, Terry W" <terry.terifay@covidien.com>,
    "Bozzini, Alfredo" <alfredo.bozzini@covidien.com>
Cc: "Lassiter, Anthony" <anthony.lassiter@covidien.com>


Colleagues,

I wanted to share with you a new initiative that Anthony Lassiter and I feel is crucial to moving forward as an independent pharmaceutical company.

That initiative is the creation of a Label Review Committee (LRC).  This committee would be responsible for three major areas:


1)     Driving changes to labels (i.e., package inserts) globally (and, in some cases, regionally) based on new information and/or requests from either internal (e.g., from our Signal Action Committee or other internal sources like the CCSI working group (see below)) or external (e.g., FDA or O-US regulatory agencies) sources.

2)     Approving company core safety information (sometimes referred to as CCDS or CCSI) documents.  These documents, common throughout the pharmaceutical industry but lacking for all but a couple (Optimark and Optiray) of our products, contain the core safety concepts that the company feels should appear in all labels, globally, for a product.   These documents are currently being generated by our relatively newly-formed CCSI working group.  The first one will be ready for approval by the second week in May at the latest.

3)     Helping to ensure alignment of labels (globally) to CCSI content.  This includes aiding, if requested, in addressing questions from local regulatory personnel and/or local regulatory agencies as variations are filed to account for changes due to CCSI content.

Anthony and I have talked through this and we believe that the membership of this committee should be:

Regulatory/Global Labeling: Dennis Nosco, chairperson
Pharmacovigilance: Anthony Lassiter
Legal: Joe Wuestner
Commercial: (business head of area, either Imaging or Specialty Pharma)
Scientific Affairs: Alfredo Bozzini

This committee could also include ad hoc members from other areas (e.g., Regulatory Strategy and CMC Regulatory, PK, Clinical Studies) as their special expertise is needed.

By this e-mail I am asking if all of you would either (a) agree to be on this committee or (b) designate someone from your area to be the representative on this committee.

Once I get agreement as to membership I will call our first meeting.  The timing of formation of this committee is crucial as we have our first new CCSI document that is about ready to be submitted to the LRC for review.  In addition, we have a company initiative regarding EXALGO labeling and inclusion of abuse deterrent safety language that will require this committee's input on language and help on getting these changes implemented globally)

As timing is short to get this committee operational please get back to me AND Anthony with any questions you have.  I would like to set up our first meeting for sometime in the next 3 weeks.

Thanks,

Dennis Nosco, PhD, RAC

Dear Lisa,

Please find attached Exalgo PI with FDA changes accepted and additional changes tracked.  Our global labeling group has edited the margins, spacing and footer to reflect the current revision, as well as replacing several instances of the infinity sign with a corrected symbol.  Two instances of EXALGO in all caps are also included as minor edits.

 

For the FDA comment to include increments in mg for dose increases, Mallinckrodt proposes to edit the revised text to replace 4 mg with 8 mg as the lowest available strength of EXALGO, for which multiples of the same strength could be prescribed until the patient was stabilized on a dose.  The rationale comment from the labeling is copied into this email for ease of reading.

 

               Comment as Rationale for Change from 4-mg to 8-mg Incremental Dose Increase:

The 4?mg dose increment is problematic from a prescription/patient instructions-logistics perspective, creating prescribing issues for physicians and safety issues for patients.  The concerns with this prescriptive approach are that it would not only hinder appropriate management of the opioid-tolerant patient s pain but could also result in safety issues due to patient confusion and the potential for medication errors when multiple tablet strengths were required to achieve a prescribed dose.  There is also the additional safety concern for patients attempting to split tablets to save money on the additional strength prescriptions.

 

This prescriptive approach is especially concerning combined with the removal of the proposed 25% dose reduction from previous opioid therapy, which was based on the EXALGO clinical trial (50% reductions were never studied).  Drastic dose reductions in this opioid tolerant population could lead to repeat, i.e., over-dosing due to inadequacy of the first dose and the 4 days that are required to achieve steady state for EXALGO.  Similarly, the minimal 4-mg dose increment could increase the rates of withdrawal symptoms in the opioid-tolerant patients who would be prescribed EXALGO.

 

Mallinckrodt recommends initiation at 8, 12, 16, 24, or 32 mg followed by an 8-mg titrating dose for EXALGO until stabilized. 

 

Thank you for your efforts to finalize this class labeling for EXALGO.

Kind regards,

Linda

DEA Suspends North Spokane Pharmacy's
License
Jeff Humphrey I KXLY4 Reporter
Posted: 6:07 pm PDT April 6, 2011Updated: 6:40 pm PDT April 6, 2011
Text Size
AAA
SPOKANE, Wash. -- The Drug Enforcement Administration has suspended the license of a North Spokane pharmacy,
leaving their customers scrambling to find other pharmacies to fill their prescriptions.
The Bates Pharmacy has been in Spokane since 1942 and competes with larger corporate stores with good customer
service and home deliveries. However, according to company officials, last November the DEA did an audit on Bates and
found problems with the way it handles controlled substances.
For example, the pharmacy was letting its customers return unused portions of their prescriptions and then destroying
them at the waste-to-energy plant.
KXLY.com Video
EmbedSharePurchase

DEA Suspends North Spokane Pharmacy's License
April 6, 2011
The Drug Enforcement Administration has suspended the license of a North Spokane pharmacy, leaving their
customers scrambling to find other pharmacies to fill their prescriptions. KXLY4's Jeff Humphrey reports.
More

KXLY.com Video

Pharmacy managers worked to fix the problem and in a statement issued Wednesday said, "upon their (DEA)
recommendation, we immediately corrected deficiencies and streamlined methods to ensure compliance."

Confidential

MAL-MI 000024102
MNKOI 0003298210

 Bates officials say the DEA also felt the pharmacy needed to better protect its controlled substances from theft,
particularly during deliveries. Bates says it tightened up security but on Friday the DEA showed up again and seized all
of the narcotics in their inventory.
The pharmacy says, "in spite of our efforts and good faith, the DEA has suspended our license to dispense controlled
substances. We are surprised by this action."
Bates customers are surprised too as now hundreds of them need to find a new pharmacy to fill their narcotic
prescriptions and Bates is trying to help saying, "we are working with local pharmacies to ensure the needs of our
patients are met and they have access to critical medications."
DEA officials said Wednesday they couldn't discuss anything about their enforcement action at Bates Pharmacy as their
case remains under investigation.
Bates officials say they are not suspected of black market sales or allowing drugs to fall into the wrong hands. Bates
continues to fill non-narcotic prescriptions and selling other medical supplies.

Bruce is working the ASR for single sided H transactions where the registration number is improperly captured.

Eileen,

 

Yes, this is a known problem in BPCS.  BPCS switched from the U transaction to the H transaction to receive inter-company shipments.  However the single sided H transaction has never worked in ARCOS or DEA Annual. 

 

ASR516327 - BPCS-ST/HB-(ASR MFG00605) Re-supply order receipts not picking up correct DEA registration (Bruce Barker)

 

This ASR was for the DEA system only.  I asked about ARCOS, but they said that would need a separate ASR (it has not been submitted).

 

The fix is to create separate Hobart customer numbers for each inter-company H transaction, then enter vendor information on that customer number.

St. Louis manufacturer à Hobart (new Hobart number with St. Louis manufacturer registration)

St. Louis distributor à Hobart (new Hobart number with vendor registration)

Webster manufacturer à Hobart  (new Hobart number with vendor registration)

Webster researcher à Hobart  (new Hobart number with vendor registration)

Etc.

Then copy the B transaction look-ups into the H transaction code (customer registration will now be associate registration).

You should be okay on your side because it will record a "S" transaction to my registration, but all my "P" transactions are also registering my registration and it appears that I am buying the material from myself.

Subject: Response to Phil's discussion about PARC
From: "nosco, dennis l"
Date: Wed, 17 Mar 2010 23:24:06 +0000
To: "neuman, herbert r"


Herb,

Phil said you wanted me to respond to his detailed description that he sent you last night.  The reason for the volatility of the meeting centered around Marketing's misunderstanding that I had told them that they could  put the study results they considered pertinent on the reprint carriers of the PENNSAID articles and then have the sales force present all these results to customers.  My understanding is that these included all the secondary endpoints and the AE data from the studies, very similar to what was presented in the various training modules that they submitted for our review.  As I remember, each time we reviewed these modules I expressed my concern about this data because it was not in the PI and, at the last review, said I wouldn't find it acceptable from a regulatory point of view to have this type of information in the reprint carriers.  I also remember us eliminating the sales manager section where the reps would be quizzed on points from these studies not in the PI there were covered twice before.  All the time we were being told that this was just for sales rep knowledge in case they were asked by the doctor.  Clearly, when I started this process with Kevin I went over the five pivotals with him and told him that I didn't see anything in any of them that would keep me from approving them as disseminated leave behinds.  I said that some of them would not be able to be detailed and some of them would have to have reprint carriers which limited what the reps said about them.  Specifically, I allowed for the reprint carrier for the Simon article to contain, in the reprint carrier, the methodology for the entire study (summary of all the comparators) but only speak in the results section about the three placebo/vehicle vs PENNSAID arms.  We also had some language in place, I thought, that said if the customer asked about the other two arms, the sales rep would direct them to Medical Affairs or that the customer could choose to read the paper themselves.  I have been unwavering from that position all along and, frankly, don't understand how I could possibly be misunderstood as I said the same thing all along.

Based on our conversations (you and me) and those of PARC, we acknowledged that presenting the study results in the physician's slide deck in a peer-to-peer presentation would make more palatable the presentation of all the study results, including the secondary endpoints.  We still did not want to see it in any sales aid and, obviously, Kevin and Caroline have a different idea about how much of it we should allow the sales reps to present and put in the reprint carriers.  So, Phil is incorrect in his statement regarding the negative endpoint.  In the slide deck Marketing mentioned all the efficacy variables that Pennsaid was positive for but failed to mention one it was not positive for, stiffness.  So I asked for that endpoint to be mentioned for fair balance.  FYI, subsequently PARC agreed not to have summary slides for any of the clinical studies.  He is also incorrect in his statements about the results of the Simon study in the two arms with oral diclofenac.  We want no mention in sales materials, including the reprint carriers.  Personally, I also want no mention of the individual study AE data in the reprint carrier, which I will discuss below.

My main disagreement with Marketing centers around the reprint carriers in terms of what can be in them.  I don't want the AE data or secondary endpoint results.  Marketing thinks I told them that they could put them there.  I have, again, been completely consistent and rock solid on this from day 1 and the AE data was NEVER addressed.

Our main disagreement among all members was on how the individual study AE data should be presented, if at all, in the speaker slide deck.  To me, its presentation is difficult and becomes even more so if it is presented where it might make scientific sense, with efficacy results and AE data from the study together.  My suggestion, that I thought Kevin took, was to present the AE data from the PI and then the AE data from the individual studies.  While that may not the most sense scientifically I have seen enough clinical study presentations to know that this has been done and that most doctors are interested in the efficacy of the drug and its overall safety profile, not the safety profile in one study.  Thus, creating one AE section that talks about the overall AE data (PI) and those from the individual studies, with results but little or no discussion, save maybe a summary slide that is approved by PARC.

We can talk more about the reasons that I hold this position relative to AE data from individual studies if you would like.

Regarding EXALGO and cancer, we HAVE reached agreement on this.  Similar to what we did for the unbranded Tofranil webinar, we allow it but only where it is important to describe the study.  Where it isn't important, we leave it out. 

Finally, the only person who is fighting for the two color PENNSAID logo not being a claim is Caroline.  PARC is unanimous on this and, to me, the point is moot as we are beyond 'reminder' ads with this product, although it does pop up every once in a while as Marketing doesn't like the compromise of a one color logo on pieces that they don't want the boxed warning and IRI on.  Also, Marketing kind of screwed themselves on this issue as the refused my suggestion to just send a reminder ad to DDMAC for comment to see if DDMAC considered the two colored logo a claim.  Now they are trying to revisit it.

Regarding personalities, to me this is a non-issue.  We have personality clashes in every group in this company.  We are working our way through them on PARC as we do every time they creep up.  Will they always be there?  Yeah, maybe.  But they are clearly workable.

Dennis Nosco, PhD, RAC
Director, Regulatory Affairs
Covidien
Pharmaceuticals

Executive Summary
