opioid. pn,:scriber training. Senators are pushing the US FDA to require providers be trained on proper opiaid prescribing
practices, something the agency has had trouble determining how best to implement. As part of the report accompanying
the Senate appropriations bill for the _Agriculture Department, FDA and other agencies„A.ppropriation.s Committee
m.em.bers wrote that "it is imperative that FDA, consistent with its own advisory committee recommendations, take any
and all steps necessary to require continuing medical education . . . for providers who write opioid prescriptions, including
through th.e Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy." The committee passed the bill and report July 20, moving it to the
fall Senate for consideration. its opioid training language is stronger than the House provided in its appropriations bill
to increase the number of prescribers who receive

training on pain management and safe prescribing of opioid drugs." FDA Commissioner Scott Gottlieb appears more
closely aligned with the Senate's opinion. Shortly after taking office, .he said the agency would take a stronger stance on
opioids policy.
Unfortunately for FDA, it has not found it as simple to mandate prescriber training as may appear in the Senate
directive, FD.A. convened a two-day meeting in May to discuss opioid prescriber education improvements. But the agency
did not gain. emphatic support from stakeholders to mandate opioid training as part of the Risk Evaluation and Mitigation
Strategy (REMS). External FDA experts admitted the existing plan that includes voluntary education is not effective.
They wanted training connected to DEA registration, but FDA cannot implement the requirement alone, (Also see
"Restrictive REMS is Least Favored Path For Opioid Prescriber Education" - Pink Sheet, 9 May, 2016.) One presenter at
the meeting also said that a Cali fornia law requir€ng opioid training does not appear to have led to measurable impact on
the abuse problem, (Also see "Opioid Prescriber Training: US FDA Still Debating Mandate; CMS Policies Having Impact
Now" - Pink Sheet, 24 May, 2017.) Follow the meeting, FDA. did announce that it was expanding the opioid. REN4S

term 'abuse-deterrent' for 'abuse-prooh'" according :to the report, Among the problems d)11t. the approved abuse-deterrent

The Senate report states that FDA should create "authoritative opioid labeling guidelines that align prescribing and

Subject: FL legislature passes acceptable opioid legislation



In the final hours of its 2011 legislative session, the Florida legislature unanimously passed its "Pill Mill Bill."  In the days and hours leading up to final passage,  the House & Senate bills contained  provisions that would negatively impact our pharmaceutical business.  The bills,  intended to curb prescription drug abuse, would have limited the amount of certain controlled substances that could be delivered to the state's pharmacies to 5,000 dosage units a month.  (By comparison, Covidien alone distributes over 20,000 dosage units a month on average to Florida pharmacies.)   There was also consideration of a provision prohibiting the substitution of a generic drug in the place of a prescribed drug which has a tamper-resistant formula.  If enacted, this provision would have given a significant competitive advantage to certain competitors who manufacture tamper-resistant opioids.  

Our new state government affairs director, Nicole Barranco, and Steve Littlejohn & Joanna Schooler of Covidien's Pharmaceutical GBU worked around the clock in recent weeks to fix the legislation. In the end they were successful in striking both unacceptable provisions from the final bill, allowing Covidien to support the legislation 

Best,

From: Morelli, Art

To: Chianta, Maria
Cc: Patrick, Jeffrey ; Liuchan, Karrie ; Lemus, Brenda
Subject: RE: Exalgo REMS Information Request


 

Hi Maria et al,

 

Thanks for the questions. I am so glad the MSL team is engaged in, and thinking about, REMS, and the specifics of the safe and appropriate use of our products, especially Exalgo. It is clear to me that we can be a leader in this area( Leading the Science of Safety), but only with the kind of "best in class" MSL team that is currently being formed. This leadership, first in REMS and soon after in an even broader and deeper safe use initiative( the CARES Alliance) will help differentiate us as a company that both knows and does what is right.

 

Please find the answers below:

 

1) The physician call list for Exalgo could include "prescription mills". When we determine that this is the case for a particular call point, Med Affairs will address this with Commercial to take the most appropriate steps. As you can imagine, there is a range of responses we could take depending on the details. Clearly, we are dedicated to mitigating abuse, misuse,overdose, and addiction( risks named in our REMS), and diversion( not named in our REMS). We will do whatever we can to help solve these problems. We could become aware of this from Sales Rep reports or from very unusual Rx activity which we monitor.

 

2) We receive weekly reports of Rx data( about a 2 week lag), and the identity of prescribers( about a 3 week lag). Less frequently we receive very detailed reports on the longitudinal Rx activity by physician name, by patient de-identified. This includes the script size, strength, and the patient's previous opioid therapy in detail (key for assessing prior opioid tolerance in patients starting Exalgo). We will marry this data to our list of physicians who have completed the Exalgo prescriber education.

 

3) Yes, we will collect trends and correlations, and they will be reviewed approximately monthly by our internal oversight group, the CAC( Covidien Assessment Committee), and then presented to our RSAB( REMS Safety Advisory Board) twice a year. This is an external team of external experts in epidemiology, pain management, REMS , education, etc. Lynn Webster is the Chair. The first meeting of the RSAB will be in late Sept in St Louis. The timing correlates with our Exalgo REMS assessments that go to the FDA.

 

4) We distributed via first class mail just before launch the Exalgo Healthcare Professional Education Kit to the following targets:

 

a) all retail and hospital pharmacies in the US which is over 70 k recipients. This was not required by the FDA amazingly enough.

b) all professional pharmacy associations and Boards. Also not required.

c) the 20 k prescribers in our commercial call plan( required by the FDA).

d) an additional 40 k prescribers not in our call plan but whom prescribe LAO's.( not required by the FDA).

e) all relevant physician  professional associations and Boards.( required).

 

5) The kit contains the following elements:

 

a) Dear HCP letter from Herb that explains the REMS and discusses Exalgo( PI with Med Guide is attached).

b) Prescribing Brochure with another PI and Med Guide attached. The brochure discusses general opioid use and risks, Exalgo risks, and recommended approaches to mitigate these risks.

c) The EEIF form for the HCP to submit to document that they reviewed the Prescribing Brochure.

d) These 3 pieces are in a portfolio that explains what to do and contains contact information for www.exalgorems.com and our Call Center.

e) A BRC to request two initial tools from the CARES Alliance: 1) the APS Tx Guidelines Reprint and 2) the widely acclaimed Scott Fishman, MD text on Safe and Appropriate Use of Opioids.

 

Our Sales Force has an allocation of these materials and directions to request additional materials via an automated system.

 

To date 326 HCPs have submitted EEIFs which is a number we are very pleased with at this juncture. Even more impressive, as of May 7 we had recorded a total of 126 Exalgo TRxs indicating a max of 126 prescribers and had received 211 forms.

 

I hope this helps. Looking forward to working with the Covidien MSL Dream Team.

 

Take care,

Art

Subject: ADF Media Alert – July 19, 2017
From: Jenn Dodd Remick <jremick@mcginnandcompany.com>
Date: Wed, 19 Jul 2017 15:49:19 +0000
To: ADF <adf@mcginnandcompany.com>


ADF Media Alert – July 19, 2017

 

Summary

 

Medscape: “Positive Topline Results for First-in-Class, Low-Abuse-Potential Opioid” (7.18.17)

 

The Hill: “Why is opioid addiction on the rise despite a decline in prescriptions?” (7.18.17)

 

Healio: “CDC awards $12 million towards opioid epidemic” (7.18.17)

 

The Globe and Mail: “Purdue Pharma to pay $18-million settlement to people addicted to OxyContin prescriptions” (7.19.17)

 

 

 

 

Positive Topline Results for First-in-Class, Low-Abuse-Potential Opioid 

Megan Brooks

Medscape

18 July 2017

 

Nektar Therapeutics has announced positive topline results from an oral human abuse potential (HAP) study of NKTR-181, a first-in-class opioid analgesic for chronic pain that reportedly carries significantly less abuse potential than oxycodone.

 

"NKTR-181 is a new chemical entity that is the first full mu-opioid agonist molecule designed to provide potent pain relief without the high levels of euphoria that can lead to abuse and addiction with standard opioids," the company said in a news release.

 

NKTR-181 is the first analgesic molecule to show a reduction in specific central nervous system–mediated side effects, such as euphoria, through the alteration of brain-entry kinetics, the company said.

 

NKTR-181 has been granted fast-track designation from the US Food and Drug Administration for the treatment of moderate to severe chronic pain.

 

The NKTR-181 HAP study was a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, six-sequence crossover study evaluating the relative oral abuse potential of NKTR-181 relative to oxycodone in healthy nondependent recreational drug users who are experienced in the oral abuse of opioids and can identify drug effects that are relevant to abuse risk assessment.

 

Fifty-four participants were randomly assigned to one of six test sequences. In each of which they received a single dose of one of the six study drugs (NKTR-181 at a dose of 400, 600, or 1200 mg or oxycodone at 40 or 60 mg). There was a 5-day washout period between the treatments.

 

At all doses, NKTR-181 had a significantly lower rating of peak "liking" compared with oxycodone. Liking was based on a participants-reported 100-point bipolar liking/disliking visual analog scale, which is a standard measure of abuse potential in HAP studies.

 

"Today's opioid abuse epidemic has created a pressing need for a better pain medicine that does not possess the euphorigenic qualities of conventional opioids," Ivan Gergel, MD, senior vice president and chief medical officer of Nektar, said in the release…

 

http://www.medscape.com/viewarticle/883088

 

 

Why is opioid addiction on the rise despite a decline in prescriptions?

Carrie Wade

The Hill

18 July 2017

 

Opioid prescription rates have fallen continuously since their peak in 2010. Prescriptions, which had more than quadrupled from 180 morphine milligram equivalents per-capita in 1999 to 782 in 2010, were down to 640 in 2015. That's good news.

 

Unfortunately, the catchall category of “opioids” does not allow us to track which specific drugs are being prescribed. The answer to that question, rather than their sheer volume, is far more important when it comes to curbing their misuse.

 

The fact is that almost 90 percent of the prescribed opioids dispensed in 2016 are immediate-release generics, rendering the decrease in total opioid prescriptions nearly irrelevant. Thanks to a combination of price and efficacy, the most abusable opioids are also the most prescribed. This means we are still failing.

 

Patience may be a virtue, but the huge increases in overdose deaths that we are seeing in the opioid epidemic means we're running out of time to wait to see whether policy initiatives like new prescription guidelines that limit how much can be dispensed or monitoring programs that seek to prevent “doctor shopping” are effective.



It makes sense to revisit how opioids are prescribed in this country, but physicians need to continue to advocate for those who suffer from chronic pain. For their part, policymakers need to realize that the opioid epidemic is not driven by people in need of pain relief. The Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration reported earlier this year that nearly 80 percent of misused prescription opioids were either obtained (with or without consent) from someone with a prescription or were bought from a drug dealer. This suggests that treatment of acute or chronic pain is not the primary means that people are initiated to opioid abuse.

 

While neither is perfect, newer extended-release and abuse-deterrent formulations are designed to mitigate the potential for opioid users to transition to addiction. Extended-release formulations work by engineering a pill to dissolve in various stages after being taken orally. There is an immediate release of some of the drug contained on the top layer of the capsule, followed by slower release of the rest of the drug that is less susceptible to dissolving in the gut. This prevents the spikes and valleys of pain relief and withdrawal that are associated with quick-acting, immediate-release formulations. Extended release can protect a user from addiction by putting distance between taking the pill and feeling "good," and diminishing the association between the two. They also prevent the quick drop in opioid blood levels that precedes withdrawal and are, therefore, less reinforcing when you take your next dose…

 

http://thehill.com/blogs/pundits-blog/healthcare/342645-why-is-opioid-addiction-on-the-rise-despite-a-decline-in

 

 

CDC awards $12 million towards opioid epidemic

Healio

18 July 2017

 

The CDC recently awarded more than $12 million in funding for the opioid epidemic to 23 states and Washington, D.C.

 

“The opioid epidemic is a scourge on our nation that knows no bounds,” HHS Secretary Tom Price, MD, said in a press release. “President Trump and we at HHS are working to support states on the front lines of this national crisis. This new support from CDC, funded by the appropriations bill President Trump signed in May, will help states and local authorities track this epidemic and respond in real time.”

 

The funding is intended to improve prevention efforts and tracking of opioid-related overdoses, according to the release.

 

Increased funding for the opioid epidemic was made possible by the 2017 Omnibus Appropriations Bill, which supports states that apply for funding through the Enhanced State Surveillance of Opioid-Involved Morbidity and Mortality (ESOOS) and the Prescription Drug Overdose: Prevention for States (PfS) program.

 

Under the ESOOS program, $7.5 million was awarded to 20 additional states and Washington, D.C. to improve tracking and prevention of opioid-related nonfatal and fatal overdoses. Twelve states have already received funding to develop and expand surveillance programs.

 

New ESOOS awardees include Alaska, California, Connecticut, Delaware, Washington D.C., Florida, Georgia, Illinois, Indiana, Louisiana, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, North Carolina, Tennessee, Utah, Vermont, Virginia and Washington.

 

Under the PfS program, $4.8 million was awarded to eight additional states to improve prescription drug monitoring programs and implement and assess strategies for safe opioid prescribing practices….

 

https://www.healio.com/psychiatry/addiction/news/online/%7B3e8f2fd2-4472-4553-9869-b0dcfd5e6c5c%7D/cdc-awards-12-million-towards-opioid-epidemic

 

 

Purdue Pharma to pay $18-million settlement to people addicted to OxyContin prescriptions

Karen Howlett

The Globe and Mail

19 July 2017

 

An Ontario court judge has approved a class-action settlement awarding $18-million in compensation to as many as 1,500 Canadians who got hooked on OxyContin after their doctors prescribed the drug.

 

Purdue Pharma, the maker of OxyContin, has agreed to pay $20-million, including $2-million to the provincial and territorial governments, to settle the long-standing class-action suit.

 

Mr. Justice Edward Belobaba of Ontario’s Superior Court of Justice approved the settlement on Wednesday morning, saying in his written decision that it is fair and reasonable.

 

His decision follows emotional testimony from several individuals, who described in court on Tuesday how addiction to the prescription painkiller OxyContin upended their lives. Judge Belobaba said in court on Tuesday that he had been inclined to approve the settlement before the hearing began, but that the “deeply moving” stories he heard gave him pause.

 

However, he says in his written decision, none of the individuals asked to opt out of the proposed settlement and lawyers representing them were also “compelling” in urging him to approve it.

 

“My obligation as the supervising class action judge is to consider all the circumstances and ensure that the proposed settlement falls within ‘a zone of reasonableness,’” says the decision.

 

If the settlement is rejected and the matter proceeds to litigation, the decision says, “there is a significant risk the claims against the defendants will not succeed.”

 

The proposed national settlement caps a legal battle that began a decade ago between pharmaceutical giant Purdue and lawyers representing as many as 1,500 Canadians who got addicted to OxyContin.

 

Judge Belobaba’s decision is the first hurdle to finalizing the settlement, which is not an admission of liability by Purdue: it also must be approved by the courts in Saskatchewan, Quebec and Nova Scotia at hearings in August.

 

If the settlement is approved, the average payout to the 1,000 to 1,500 claimants will likely be in the range of $13,000 to $18,000 each, which falls within the range of individual damage awards for addiction under Canadian law, Judge Belobaba says in his decision.

 

The class-action accuses Purdue of knowing that anyone who took OxyContin would be at risk of becoming addicted to it and suffer withdrawal symptoms if they stopped. But at no time were these risks disclosed.

 

Halifax law firm Wagners launched the class action in 2007 in Atlantic Canada and later joined forces with firms in Ontario and Saskatchewan representing people in the rest of the country.

 

Canada’s opioid epidemic traces its roots to the introduction of OxyContin 21 years ago. In 1996, Health Canada approved the drug to relieve pain that was moderate to severe. Until then, opioids had been prescribed just for terminal cancer patients…

Subject: FW: Step 3 ER Daily Consumption
From: "morelli, art "

To: "patrick, jeffrey"


Jeff,

 

This data may be helpful for you in Project 32.

 

Thanks,

Art

 

From: Silver, David
Sent: Thursday, March 03, 2011 5:41 PM
To: Neuman, Herbert R; Giuliani, Michael; Mannebach, Mark ; Harbaugh, Matthew
Cc: Harrell, Jamie ; Wessler, Michael; Fraley, Tamara; Stamer, Jeremy ; Morelli, Art
Subject: Step 3 ER Daily Consumption



 

Please find attached an analysis of daily consumption IMS data by product and strength for the Step 3 ER market

IMS data provides the average number of tablets/day dispensed for each product and strength

For those who saw an early version of the charts – a error was corrected – so please replace with attached

 

In the case of Exalgo for the Quarter ending December 2010

8mg – 1.46 tablets (suggests 54% one tablet and 46% two tablets, though a small percentage could be three tablets) for an average morphine equivalents of 58mg/day

12mg – 1.59 tablets (suggests 41% one tablet and 59% two tablets, though a small percentage could be three tablets) for an average morphine equivalents of 95mg/day

16mg – 2.37 tablets (suggests 1,2,3, and 4 tablets dosed per day ) for an average morphine equivalents of 190mg/day

 

The attached provides the data for all oral extended release long acting opiates

 

Based on the Exalgo PI each tablet strength of each product was converted to morphine equivalents and then multiplied by the daily consumption rate to determine the average daily morphine equivalents for the product/strength and the amount of patient days of therapy associated with each strength (tablets/dacon) for the Quarter ending December 2010

 

1)     Observations

a.     Exalgo has the among the lowest average daily morphine equivalents 111mg/day (60% of Opana ER average(178mg/day) and 50% of Oxycontin average(211mg/day))

b.    Exalgo ranges from 57mg/day (8mg) to 190mg/day (16mg) while Oxycontin ranges between 48mg/day to 550mg/day (morphine equivalents)

c.     Exalgo competes in ~47% of the market (between 60mg morphine equivalents and 190mg morphine equivalents per day) while 20% of the market (i.e., <60mg/day) is restricted by labeling the lack of a 32mg prevents usage in 33% of the market above 190mg/day or makes it very expensive

 

 

Please let me know if you have any questions

Jeremy is looking at patient level data to further delineate usage

 

David

To: Robinson, Gerald D
Subject: I love the iPad app!



 

Hey Jerry,

I know I ve told you in the last few weeks how excited I am about the new Patient ID app and how much more productive I feel on every Exalgo call. Well, today, I accidentally left my IPad at home, and I was forced to revisit my old ways of selling using the paper detail aid. I felt like I was back in the ice ages.  It is amazing the difference in responses I get from physicians. Today, it seemed harder to engage the physicians that usually only give me a brief moment, where as with the app, I am usually able to get significantly more time with these physicians. My favorite screen that usually stops physicians in their tracks is the  tablet features of Exalgo . Abuse is a growing concern in most of these offices, so I have found that most doctors will usually stop what they are doing to at least look at these pictures, and many times it will lead to a great discussion about the features and benefits of Exalgo.

I just had to share. Have a great weekend,

Casey Upton

? AMR predicts record overdoses in February

UPDATED 12:31 AM EST Feb 27, 2016




{Twitter Tweet Button}


{+1}




NEXT STORY

Former gym teacher accused of distributing child sex abuse images




Text Size:
ASmall Text

ALarge Text



Photos





MANCHESTER, N.H.  Distressing new numbers show the scope and toll of the heroin epidemic in New Hampshire.

 


The state medical examiner said there are 60 potential deadly drug overdoses from 2016 alone, three of which are confirmed.

It comes after a record 420 people died of drug overdoses last year in 2015.

Manchester AMR said February could be the deadliest month for drug overdoses in the city's history.

They say they respond to an average of two heroin or fentanyl overdoses each day.

A Manchester recovery specialist said she doesn't know what the solution is, but people need to pay attention.

"Oh my God, he was a great kid, he was funny, he got into some trouble," said Kelly Riley, with Hope for NH Recovery.

In 2007, Riley's son Richie fell into the wrong group of friends, tried cocaine, then someone suggested to him taking an oxycontin, and he just went to sleep, Riley said.

Riley then became a counselor at Hope for NH Recovery in Manchester to give other addicts a place to go.

But last week, seven of her recovering addicts died, by likely overdosing on opioids.

"It's very challenging as a person who has been through this and seen so many lives devastated by this," Riley said.

She continued: "Once my son died, then what happens, it's a whole ripple effect to the family. I lost my house, I got divorced, my daughter had to change schools, just so many things happened."

Manchester American Medical Response has responded to 51 suspected drug overdoses in February alone, 12 of them deadly.

If these deaths are confirmed by the medical examiner, February will be tied for the deadliest opioid overdose month in Queen City history.

Rocco Caprarello, AMR Manchester station manager, compares that to last February, when AMR responded to 38 overdoses and lost five people.

"And we see that the trend is, the amount of narcan that we're giving patients, we're thinking that it's something more than heroin," Caprarello said.

Riley said her center needs more funding for more beds for kids addicted to heroin and fentanyl.

"It's heartbreaking, you know?" Riley said. "You see moms with their kids, and they're desperate. They want their kid to live. And it's almost like you can't let them out of your sight.

Hope for NH Recovery is now trying to open 13 centers.

From: VanHorn, Mark
Sent: Tuesday, November 15, 2016 11:56 AM
To: Owen, Roger
Cc: Kegler, George
Subject: Generics Alignment - Overview



 

Roge,

 

There will be two phases to complete the Generics separation 1) 12-31 plan (Accounting changes), and 2) Generics Alignment Project (update contracts, licenses, registrations, complete the separation, etc.)

 

12-31 Plan:

 

This phase is designed to separate the financials by Jan 1.

 

The name of the new Generics legal entity will be SpecGx LLC.  It should be formed this week, but it will not be operational from an accounting standpoint until December 31, 2016.  Similar to Mallinckrodt APAP LLC, the new entity will not be  operationalized  for the outside world.  For example, even though fixed assets do not legally transfer to the new entity, we will account for the fixed assets as if they have transferred.  Following is additional information regarding the upcoming changes related to this new legal entity.

 

Effective December 31, 2016, Mallinckrodt LLC will be assigned JDE company 00003, which was assigned to Mallinckrodt Enterprises LLC through December 30, 2016, and journal entries will be prepared to move the appropriate general ledger balances from JDE company 00008 accounts to JDE company 00003 accounts, which will include the December 30, 2016 equity balances of JDE company 00008.  There is no historical data conversion.  For employees affected by this change (Corporate, Shared Services, etc.), their cost centers will begin with "003" instead of "008" or  157  effective December 31.  To the extent possible, we will keep the remaining 9 digits of the cost centers the same.  A detailed review of balance sheet accounts will be conducted to support the movement between JDE general ledger companies (there is no actual movement of assets or liabilities between legal entities).  Mallinckrodt LLC non-Generics businesses will also remain in Mallinckrodt LLC, and I believe these currently are XARTEMIS (MNK-795/155) and Fluorite.  AAIs will be changed for the Mallinckrodt LLC activity that is moving to JDE company 00003 effective December 31, 2016.

 

A new legal entity (SpecGx LLC) will be formed to include the Generics business plus specific Specialty Brands products (Gablofen, CNS non-promoted, Roxicodone and Exalgo), and it will include facilities at St. Louis Plant, Webster Groves and Hobart (Greenville and Raleigh API are included in Mallinckrodt APAP LLC for accounting).  SpecGx LLC will commence accounting operations effective December 31, 2016, which is the first day of the January fiscal period.  SpecGx LLC will be assigned JDE company 00008 effective December 31, 2016, and this will alleviate the need to make many system changes for this new legal entity.  The appropriate equity balances will be recorded in JDE company 00008 for SpecGx LLC effective December 31, 2016 (e.g., common stock, additional paid in capital). 

 

We will assign the existing Mallinckrodt LLC disbursement and lockbox bank accounts to the new legal entity (SpecGx LLC) and set up new disbursement and lockbox bank accounts for Mallinckrodt LLC no later than April 1, 2017 in time for the SAP conversion.  We will continue to use the existing Mallinckrodt LLC disbursement and lockbox bank accounts until the new bank accounts are set up for Mallinckrodt LLC.

 

Generics Alignment Project

 

This project will begin after the  kick off  on December 5 and will continue well into 2017.  The most significant parts of this phase include:

1)      Identification and assessment of all impacted contracts, including updates and approvals if required

2)      Any regulatory impacts from OUS

3)      DEA registrations

 

The full scope of this phase will be identified after the kick off on December 5, however I will be sending each group a slide for their input.

INDICATION

EXALGO  (hydromorphone HCI) Extended-Release
Tablets (CII) is indicated for the management of
moderate to severe pain in opioid tolerant patients
requiring continuous, around-the-clock opioid
analgesia for an extended period of time.

IMPORTANT RISK INFORMATION

WARNING: ABUSE POTENTIAL,
LIFE-THREATENING RESPIRATORY DEPRESSION,
and ACCIDENTAL EXPOSURE

Abuse Potential

EXALGO contains hydromorphone, an opioid agonist and a Schedule II controlled substance with an abuse liability similar to other opioid agonists, legal or illicit. Assess each patient s risk for opioid abuse or addiction prior to prescribing EXALGO. The risk for opioid abuse is increased in patients with a personal or family history of substance abuse (including drug or alcohol abuse or addiction) or mental illness (e.g., major depressive disorder). Routinely monitor all patients receiving EXALGO for signs of misuse, abuse, and addiction during treatment.

Life-threatening Respiratory Depression

Respiratory depression, including fatal cases, may occur with use of EXALGO, even when the drug has been used as recommended and not misused or abused. EXALGO is for use in opioid tolerant patients only. Proper dosing and titration are essential and EXALGO should be prescribed only by healthcare professionals who are knowledgeable in the use of potent opioids for the management of chronic pain. Monitor for respiratory depression, especially during initiation of EXALGO or following a dose increase. Crushing, dissolving, or chewing the tablet can cause rapid release and absorption of a potentially fatal dose of hydromorphone.

Accidental Exposure

Accidental ingestion of EXALGO, especially in children, can result in a fatal overdose of hydromorphone.



 


EXALGO is contraindicated in:

- Opioid non-tolerant patients. Fatal respiratory
  depression could occur in patients who are not
  opioid tolerant.

- Patients with significant respiratory depression

- Patients with acute or severe bronchial asthma in
  an unmonitored setting or in the absence of
  resuscitative equipment

- Patients with known or suspected paralytic ileus

- Patients who have had surgical procedures and/or
  underlying disease resulting in narrowing of the
  gastrointestinal tract, or have  blind loops  of the
  gastrointestinal tract or gastrointestinal obstruction

- Patients with hypersensitivity (e.g., anaphylaxis) to
  hydromorphone or sulfite-containing medications


 


EXALGO is indicated for opioid tolerant patients only. Patients considered opioid tolerant are those who are taking at least 60 mg oral morphine per day, 25 mcg transdermal fentanyl/hour, 30 mg oral oxycodone/day, 8 mg oral hydromorphone/day, 25 mg oral oxymorphone/day or an equianalgesic dose of another opioid, for a week or longer.


 


EXALGO is not intended for use as an as-needed analgesic and is not indicated for the management of acute or postoperative pain. It is contraindicated in patients who need management of mild pain or pain not expected to persist.


 


Avoid concurrent use of alcohol and EXALGO. Concurrent use of EXALGO with CNS depressants, including alcohol, increases risk of respiratory depression, hypotension, and profound sedation, potentially resulting in coma or death. EXALGO may impair the ability to drive a car or operate machinery.


 


Not intended in patients who have received MAO inhibitors within 14 days of starting EXALGO.


 


Use with caution and in reduced doses in older or debilitated patients, as well as patients with renal or hepatic insufficiency, Addison s disease, delirium tremens, myxedema or hypothyroidism, prostatic hypertrophy or urethral stricture, toxic psychosis. May aggravate convulsions in patients with convulsive disorders; may induce or aggravate seizures in some clinical settings. Consider use of an alternate analgesic in patients with severe renal impairment.


 


Respiratory depression, which occurs more frequently in elderly or debilitated patients, is the chief hazard with EXALGO.


 


Serious adverse events could also include hypotensive effects, GI effects, cardiac arrest from overdose and precipitation of withdrawal. Most common adverse events (>10%) seen in clinical studies (N=2474) were: constipation (31%), nausea (28%), vomiting, somnolence, headache, asthenia and dizziness.


 


Use EXALGO with extreme caution in patients susceptible to intracranial effects of CO2 retention.


 


Do not abruptly discontinue EXALGO.


See additional Important Risk Information, including boxed warning, in Full Prescribing Information<http://whatcounts.jobson.com/t?r=12&c=37120&l=8586&ctl=55AB1:733B4C71B177CE91E38CEB89DB8F6AB6&> and Medication Guide<http://whatcounts.jobson.com/t?r=12&c=37120&l=8586&ctl=55AB2:733B4C71B177CE91E38CEB89DB8F6AB6&>.

Below are my initial thoughts.  It may be helpful to discuss some of
this live. 

If I understand the project correctly, the intent is to provide a
decision support tool / algorithm that can drive appropriate opioid
selection, by providing education on important pharmacologic differences
in opioid agents.  While I agree fully with a simplified approach, we
can't assume that prescribers understand the basic principles and thus,
it is important to not oversimplify the tool.   I think this can be a
valuable tool for opioid prescribers and believe that we should include
the level of detail that will have the greatest impact. 

In its current format, the algorithm may be confusing to prescribers.
Consider adding additional information to clarify 'when and why' an
alternative opioid may be appropriate.  For example, a patient may be a
"partial responder" to a specific medication and/or have unacceptable
adverse effects, at which point a change in therapy would be
appropriate.  Additionally, the patient may be a "partial responder"
with no adverse effects and a change in therapy may also be appropriate,
but for a different reason.  On the other hand, the "partial response"
could be the result of a subtherapeutic dose, at which point an increase
in dose on the current therapy may be sufficient.  The only perspective
reflected in the current algorithm (on the hydrocodone side) is that a
"partial response" is the result of inferior potency (designated by the
X) and the solution is hydromorphone.  

Adding a few key decision points will help provide a more useful tool to
providers.  In its current format, the algorithm doesn't provide enough
information or decision points to explain why, for example, a "partial
responder" would be best transitioned to "specific named opioid".  As I
stated above,  a partial response could be the result of many things
(subtherapeutic dose, drug -drug interaction, receptor variability, etc)
all of which have a different solution.  Likewise, I would suggest the
same level of detail for "responder" and "non-responder"
recommendations.  Responsible clinicians should not and typically will
not select or prescribe a specific opioid, based on limited guidance
such as "partial response" or "no response".  I think we have to modify
the algorithm to align with what a clinician should and typically will
consider in making an opioid selection decision.  With those additional
decision points, the algorithm can become a useful tool to providers.

Additional points to consider about the current diagram:  
*	Consider adding information to clarify why we have only included
the opioids listed.  I believe you are focusing on a transition from the
available short-acting combination products (e.g., HC/APAP and OC/APAP).

*	There is a triangle in the key that is followed by the statement
"Oxymorphone makes very little contribution to analgesic activity;
oxycodone produces most of the analgesic effect".  As written, this
statement is incorrect as oxymorphone produces most of the analgesia
associated with oxycodone (e.g., a non-responder / partial responder to
oxycodone may not be fully metabolizing oxycodone to its more active
metabolite).  In that case a dose increase (if no intolerable side
effects) or a change in therapy may be appropriate.  
*	The left side of the diagram (hydrocodone) has an option for
"responder" but the right side does not.  This could be perceived as
bias towards hydromorphone.  A "responder" on SA oxycodone (e.g.,
Percocet) would likely be transitioned to "oxycontin" first if an ER
formulation is appropriate.  
*	The left side of the diagram indicates that if a patient does
not respond to HM then oxymorphone is the appropriate treatment choice
(dotted line) .  It would be more appropriate to state "consider
different opioid" - oxymorphone may or may not be the next appropriate
choice.   For example, if the patient has liver dysfunction, oxymorphone
may be the least appropriate choice.  Same for the other said - if "does
not respond" to oxymorphone, hydromorphone may or may not be the next
appropriate choice.

INDICATION

EXALGO  (hydromorphone HCI) Extended-Release
Tablets (CII) is indicated for the management of
moderate to severe pain in opioid tolerant patients
requiring continuous, around-the-clock opioid
analgesia for an extended period of time.

IMPORTANT RISK INFORMATION

WARNING: ABUSE POTENTIAL,
LIFE-THREATENING RESPIRATORY DEPRESSION, and ACCIDENTAL EXPOSURE

Abuse Potential

EXALGO contains hydromorphone, an opioid agonist and a Schedule II controlled substance with an abuse liability similar to other opioid agonists, legal or illicit. Assess each patient s risk for opioid abuse or addiction prior to prescribing EXALGO. The risk for opioid abuse is increased in patients with a personal or family history of substance abuse (including drug or alcohol abuse or addiction) or mental illness (e.g., major depressive disorder). Routinely monitor all patients receiving EXALGO for signs of misuse, abuse, and addiction during treatment.

Life-threatening Respiratory Depression

Respiratory depression, including fatal cases, may occur with use of EXALGO, even when the drug has been used as recommended and not misused or abused. EXALGO is for use in opioid tolerant patients only. Proper dosing and titration are essential and EXALGO should be prescribed only by healthcare professionals who are knowledgeable in the use of potent opioids for the management of chronic pain. Monitor for respiratory depression, especially during initiation of EXALGO or following a dose increase. Crushing, dissolving, or chewing the tablet can cause rapid release and absorption of a potentially fatal dose of hydromorphone.

Accidental Exposure

Accidental ingestion of EXALGO, especially in children, can result in a fatal overdose of hydromorphone.



 


EXALGO is contraindicated in:
- Opioid non-tolerant patients. Fatal respiratory
  depression could occur in patients who are not
  opioid tolerant.

- Patients with significant respiratory depression

- Patients with acute or severe bronchial asthma in
  an unmonitored setting or in the absence of
  resuscitative equipment

- Patients with known or suspected paralytic ileus

- Patients who have had surgical procedures and/or
  underlying disease resulting in narrowing of the
  gastrointestinal tract, or have  blind loops  of the
  gastrointestinal tract or gastrointestinal obstruction

- Patients with hypersensitivity (e.g., anaphylaxis) to
  hydromorphone or sulfite-containing medications


 


EXALGO is indicated for opioid tolerant patients only. Patients considered opioid tolerant are those who are taking at least 60 mg oral morphine per day, 25 mcg transdermal fentanyl/hour, 30 mg oral oxycodone/day, 8 mg oral hydromorphone/day, 25 mg oral oxymorphone/day or an equianalgesic dose of another opioid, for a week or longer.


 


EXALGO is not intended for use as an as-needed analgesic and is not indicated for the management of acute or postoperative pain. It is contraindicated in patients who need management of mild pain or pain not expected to persist.


 


Avoid concurrent use of alcohol and EXALGO. Concurrent use of EXALGO with CNS depressants, including alcohol, increases risk of respiratory depression, hypotension, and profound sedation, potentially resulting in coma or death. EXALGO may impair the ability to drive a car or operate machinery.


 


Not intended in patients who have received MAO inhibitors within 14 days of starting EXALGO.


 


Use with caution and in reduced doses in older or debilitated patients, as well as patients with renal or hepatic insufficiency, Addison s disease, delirium tremens, myxedema or hypothyroidism, prostatic hypertrophy or urethral stricture, toxic psychosis. May aggravate convulsions in patients with convulsive disorders; may induce or aggravate seizures in some clinical settings. Consider use of an alternate analgesic in patients with severe renal impairment.


 


Respiratory depression, which occurs more frequently in elderly or debilitated patients, is the chief hazard with EXALGO.


 


Serious adverse events could also include hypotensive effects, GI effects, cardiac arrest from overdose and precipitation of withdrawal. Most common adverse events (>10%) seen in clinical studies (N=2474) were: constipation (31%), nausea (28%), vomiting, somnolence, headache, asthenia and dizziness.


 


Use EXALGO with extreme caution in patients susceptible to intracranial effects of CO2 retention.


 


Do not abruptly discontinue EXALGO.


See additional Important Risk Information, including boxed warning, in Full Prescribing Information<http://lists.jobson.com/t?r=4&c=0&l=3818&ctl=54A3B:B41DB4189704864061FB1363A448C720&> and Medication Guide<http://lists.jobson.com/t?r=4&c=0&l=3818&ctl=54A3C:B41DB4189704864061FB1363A448C720&>.

Estimate Changes

 
Mallinckrodt plc

 
We maintain our SELL rating and $34PT, which we arrive at via two valuation methods: a 7.1x multiple on our 2013 EBITDA estimate of $382 million, and a P/E multiple (11.6x our CY13 EPS estimate of $2.92). We believe MNK s current premium valuation is NOT warranted, as we think F 14 sales and earnings are likely to fall as a result of increased competition within its pharmaceutical segment. Key products (generic Concerta and Exalgo) are expected to face competition, likely leading to a fall in sales and profits beginning in the first quarter of F 14. While the Company updated its F 13 financial guidance to reflect sales growth of 8-10% (from 7-11%), with specialty pharma segment sales growth of 22-25% (from 21-25%), and medical imaging sales declines of -5 to -8% (from -3 to -7%). We believe F 14 financial guidance (expected to be announced by the end of October) could be far less robust. In F 14, we expect sales declines for generic Concerta and branded Exalgo, as generic competition enters. In addition, with the Company preparing for a potential approval and launch of MNK-795 (an extended-release hydrocodone / acetaminophen combo product with abuse deterrent technology for the relief of acute, moderate to severe pain), we believe SG&A costs are likely to increase. On last Friday s call, management indicated its plans to expand its current 200-person sales force by 50-100%. As a result, we have increased our annual SG&A cost estimates by ~$45 million/year.

 

Lowering F 13-F 16 EPS forecasts to $2.89, $2.27, $2.50, and $2.75, from $3.18, $2.61, $2.73, and $2.87, respectively. We have increased our F 14-F 16 revenue forecasts to reflect a greater contribution from its two new drug pipeline products, MNK-795 and MNK-155, both abuse deterrent formulations of acetaminophen containing combination pain products. Combined, our new F 13-F 15 estimates include sales of $25 million, $120 million, and $200 million, up from $10 million, $60 million, and $80 million, respectively. While MNK-795 was recently granted a priority review, we believe much is riding on the Company s ability to garner an abuse-deterrent label. While management indicated on its call that it feels it has done all of the necessary pre-clinical and clinical work to garner such a label, we believe the FDA s decision here is an upcoming binary event, which could have a significant impact on MNK s share price.

 

Investment Summary   SELL/$34PT. We maintain our SELL rating and $34PT, which we arrive at via two valuation methods, a 7.1x multiple on our 2013 EBITDA est. of $382 million, and a P/E multiple (11.6x our CY13 EPS estimate of $2.92). MNK shares currently trade at 15.5x our new CY13 EPS estimate of $2.92, and 19.9x our new CY14 EPS estimate of $2.28. On average, we believe MNK shares are trading at a 58% premium to its peers on a forward P/E multiple basis. Based on our expectations for MNK to face additional competition on several of its key pharmaceutical products (generic Concerta, and Exalgo) in the second half of 2013, we believe F 14 revenue could fall approximately (4.6%) vs. F 13, with EPS dropping to $2.27 (21% YOY) in F 14. With F 14 expected to be a transition year, we believe MNK shares could drop 25% from current levels.

Dear All,

We have received a similar comment from Dr. Henry Richards at Janssen in regard to the FDA proposed 4-mg increments for dose escalations of EXALGO (please see below forwarded email from Tamara).

 

Since the proposed 4-mg incremental increase seems to be the only issue that we would be pushing back on, could the team please help with phrasing the rationale to be included in our response to the FDA changes for the class labeling.  Acknowledging that we might want to be more brief in our response, my initial draft from comments received in emails from the team is the following:

 

The 4?mg dose increment is problematic from a prescription/patient instructions-logistics perspective, creating prescribing issues for physicians and safety issues for patients.  The concerns with this prescriptive approach are that it would not only hinder appropriate management of the opioid-tolerant patient s pain but could also result in safety issues due to patient confusion and error when multiple tablet strengths were required to achieve a prescribed dose.  There is also the additional safety concern for patients splitting tablets to save money on the additional strength prescriptions.

 

If the aim is to label a specific mg incremental dose escalation, Mallinckrodt recommends an 8-mg a titrating dose for EXALGO and once stabilized on 8, 12, 16, 24, 32, etc., the patient could be converted to a regimen using fewer tablets.



This prescriptive approach is especially concerning combined with the removal of the proposed 25% dose reduction from previous opioid therapy, which was based on the EXALGO clinical trial (50% reductions were never studied). Drastic dose reductions in this opioid tolerant population could lead to repeat, i.e., over-dosing due to inadequacy of the first dose and the 4 days required to achieve steady state for EXALGO.  Similarly, the minimal 4-mg dose increment could increase the rates of withdrawal symptoms in the opioid-tolerant patients who would be prescribed EXALGO.

 

Also at issue is our proposed text for this statement in Highlights under Dosage and Administration, as well as the FDA addition to Section 2.2 Titration and Maintenance of Therapy, which is copied here:

 

Plasma levels of EXALGO are sustained for 18 to 24 hours. Dosage adjustments of EXALGO may be made in increments of 4 mg every 3 to 4 days as needed to achieve adequate analgesia.


 

Our previous suggestion for the Highlights section in response to the FDA request follows:

 

     Dose may be increased every 3 to 4 days as needed to achieve adequate analgesia[EF1] . If titration is needed, consider a 25% to 50% increase in the dose[Covidien2] . (2.2)

Re: My thoughts after MOCK B

Remoxy had some claim to fame relative to existing opioids of having potential tamper resistant characteristics — with
the implication of shifting the benefit/risk ratio in their favor. We are conceding the risk issue and would therefore have
to presumptively rank the risk denominator higher. It seemed to me that the intent of the questions was the need to
have a strong benefit lest the benefit/risk ratio be sufficiently low. It goes without saying that the key element of
controlling the risk denominator is a convincing case that our REMS controls the risk.

On 9/11/09 7:09 PM, "James G. Ottinger" <iames.ottinger@premier-research.com> wrote:

All,
Susan, thanks for copying me on this. We are supposed to meet on Monday, so let's have a team discussion
on this proposal.
We are north of 90 minutes now (96 minutes?), and so I think it would be a significant challenge to reduce
our talk by 40%. I would propose we keep the time, and try to be done a little early, this means subtracting
10 to 20 minutes. Remember the less we speak, the more time the committee has to ask open questions, so
this is a double edged sword.
As I said following yesterday's meeting, I also believe we should limit the efficacy discussion, Remoxy's was
very brief and I don't recall any questions on this, but will confirm the latter. I have asked FDA today whether
they agree with us on efficacy (under the guise of seeking advice on balancing our presentation) - since they
are not asking the committee any questions on efficacy. Let's see if they respond.
The Mock committee surprised me by suggesting over and over about votes on efficacy, there is no voting (at
least not yet), and efficacy is currently not on the FDA topic list for Ad Com feedback.
Jim
